chunks.text: Here is the direct list of the guardrails built into my system: ● Strict Electriﬁcation Focus: I can only discuss home electriﬁcation, energy saving, and climate action in Australia. I am blocked from discussing unrelated topics, like recipes, cryptocurrency, or general knowledge. ● No Commercial Recommendations: I am strictly forbidden from endorsing or recommending speciﬁc brands, installers, retailers, or commercial vendors. I can only provide objective, general advice. ● Whitelisted Sourcing: When searching the web, I must ignore commercial sites and blogs.

chunks.text: The core rules of that guide are: ● Direct and Pragmatic: I don't use marketing spin, sales jargon, or overly bubbly language. I am instructed to be persuasive through raw facts, physics, and economics, not hype. ● Understated but Urgent: The climate crisis is treated as an engineering challenge we can absolutely solve, but we have to get moving. ● Authentically Australian: I must use Australian terms (like 'petrol', 'gas ducted heating', and 'maths') and local spelling, while strictly avoiding cheesy clichés (I am explicitly banned from saying "G'day"). ● Mission-Focused: I am programmed to be single-minded. If a conversation drifts into other topics, I must politely but ﬁrmly steer it back to helping you make a practical plan to get off fossil fuels. 1. Rooftop Solar Fact Sheet Key Metrics & Financials ● Average Upfront Cost (Before Rebates): $5,000 to $10,000 for typical systems.

chunks.sourceTitle: Electric Saul
chunks.text: 1. Rooftop Solar Fact Sheet Key Metrics & Financials ● Average Upfront Cost (Before Rebates): $5,000 to $10,000 for typical systems. The 15-year macroeconomic model uses a 9 kW system priced at $901 per kW, plus a budgeted $2,000 replacement inverter in year 15.

chunks.sourceTitle: Electric Saul
chunks.text: ● Potential Bill Savings (With Solar): $42,900 over a 15-year horizon. This equates to approximately $2,200 a year for a fully electriﬁed home, or $980 a year for a standard fossil-fuel-reliant home. ● Average Return on Investment (ROI): 3 to 5 years. ● System Lifetime: 20 to 40 years. ● Installation Diﬃculty: Moderate. ● Electrical Upgrade Required: Yes, in some older homes where the switchboard requires a complete replacement or a smart meter upgrade is needed on the main grid connection. ● Accredited Installer Requirement: Clean Energy Council (CEC) or Solar Accreditation Australia (SAA) registered solar installer. Core Operating Logic Australia has access to the cheapest source of home energy in the world: rooftop solar. Being grid-connected allows excess solar to go back into the mains electricity grid during peak daylight hours.

Water Heating (Electric Heat Pump) Fact Sheet Key Metrics & Financials ● Average Upfront Cost (Before Rebates): $1,500 to $5,500 (excluding installation). ● Potential Bill Savings (With Solar): $8,700 over a 15-year horizon (approximately $400 saved annually by timing the heat pump to run during peak solar generation hours). ● Potential Bill Savings (Without Solar): $5,800 over a 15-year horizon (approximately $250 saved annually compared to a standard gas instant system). ● Appliance Lifetime: 8 to 20 years. ● Installation Diﬃculty: Moderate. ● Electrical Upgrade Required: Unlikely, but a new dedicated circuit breaker must be installed in the switchboard to transition from gas to electric. ● Accredited Installer Requirement Accredited Installer Requirement

chunks.sourceTitle: Electric Saul
chunks.text: A licensed plumber must install the hot water tank and run the necessary pipework. If you are transitioning from a gas system to an electric heat pump, a licensed electrician is also required to run a dedicated new electrical circuit and install a circuit breaker in your switchboard. Many plumbing businesses contract an electrician to complete this work concurrently, but you should verify this when obtaining quotes. Design & Technical Considerations ● Eﬃciency (COP): Look for a high Coeﬃcient of Performance (COP). A COP of 3.6 to 4.0 means that for every 1 kWh of electricity consumed, the system generates 3.6 to 4.0 kWh of thermal heat.

chunks.sourceTitle: Electric Saul
chunks.text: Design & Technical Considerations ● Eﬃciency (COP): Look for a high Coeﬃcient of Performance (COP). A COP of 3.6 to 4.0 means that for every 1 kWh of electricity consumed, the system generates 3.6 to 4.0 kWh of thermal heat. Avoid models that use "electric resistive elements" as back-ups; cheap systems often rely on these in cold weather, drastically increasing electricity usage. ● Refrigerants: The environmental impact of heat pumps is heavily inﬂuenced by their refrigerant gas. Natural refrigerants such as Carbon Dioxide (CO₂ / R-744) are the gold standard because they have a Global Warming Potential (GWP) of 1 and perform exceptionally well in extremely cold temperatures.

chunks.sourceTitle: Electric Saul
chunks.text: Avoid models that use "electric resistive elements" as back-ups; cheap systems often rely on these in cold weather, drastically increasing electricity usage. ● Refrigerants: The environmental impact of heat pumps is heavily inﬂuenced by their refrigerant gas. Natural refrigerants such as Carbon Dioxide (CO₂ / R-744) are the gold standard because they have a Global Warming Potential (GWP) of 1 and perform exceptionally well in extremely cold temperatures. High-GWP synthetic refrigerants like R-410A and R-134a should be avoided where possible. ● System Design: Integrated systems (where the compressor sits directly on top of the water tank) are compact and ideal for tight spaces.

High-GWP synthetic refrigerants like R-410A and R-134a should be avoided where possible. ● System Design: Integrated systems (where the compressor sits directly on top of the water tank) are compact and ideal for tight spaces. Split systems (where the tank sits in one spot and the compressor unit is mounted separately on a wall) are highly eﬃcient and can keep the heavier compressor unit away from bedroom windows to minimise noise. ● Noise Levels: Decibel ratings vary. Cheaper units can be as noisy as a split-system air conditioner compressor.

chunks.text: Split systems (where the tank sits in one spot and the compressor unit is mounted separately on a wall) are highly eﬃcient and can keep the heavier compressor unit away from bedroom windows to minimise noise. ● Noise Levels: Decibel ratings vary. Cheaper units can be as noisy as a split-system air conditioner compressor. It is recommended to check decibel ratings (aim for under 40 dB if installing near windows or tight boundary lines) and plan placement to avoid keeping you or your neighbours awake. ● Sizing: A typical four-person household requires a 270-litre to 315-litre tank. Because a heat pump heats water slowly and eﬃciently over several hours, you need a larger tank capacity compared to an instantaneous gas system to ensure you have enough stored hot water to get through the day. Renters & Strata Guidance ● Renters: Renters miss out on the long-term bill savings of heat pumps.

chunks.text: 3. Space Heating (Reverse-Cycle Air Conditioning) Fact Sheet Key Metrics & Financials ● Average Upfront Cost: $3,000 to $10,000+ depending on whether you install individual split systems or a central ducted system. ● Potential Bill Savings (With Solar): $12,000 over a 15-year horizon. ● Potential Bill Savings (Without Solar): $13,900 over a 15-year horizon. ● Appliance Lifetime: 15 to 20 years. ● Installation Diﬃculty: High. ● Electrical Upgrade Required: Not typically required for single split-systems, but upgrading a whole home to multi-split or ducted systems may require a switchboard upgrade or an upgrade to three-phase power. ● Accredited Installer Requirement: Licensed air conditioning installer with an ARC (Australian Refrigeration Council) tick licence, plus a licensed electrician.

chunks.sourceTitle: Electric Saul
chunks.text: Technical & Environmental Performance Space heating represents the single largest energy load inside the average Australian home, accounting for approximately 37% of energy use (excluding transport). Combustion systems like gas heaters are incredibly ineﬃcient; they operate at roughly 80% eﬃciency (COP of 0.8), meaning 20% of the energy in the gas escapes straight out the ﬂue as waste heat.

chunks.sourceTitle: Electric Saul
chunks.text: Modern reverse-cycle air conditioners do not create heat; they use a compression cycle to extract heat from the outside air and transfer it indoors. They operate at 300% to 500% eﬃciency (COP of 3.0 to 5.0). For every 1 unit of electricity used, they deliver 3 to 5 units of heat into your living spaces. Renters & Strata Guidance ● Renters: Landlords in Victoria must meet minimum heating standards, which include an energy-eﬃcient heater in the main living area. If your rental relies on expensive, portable resistive heaters or gas ﬂues, you can present the ﬁnancial case for a reverse-cycle split-system installation, noting that the upfront cost can be offset by state-level landlord rebates. ● Strata Properties: Condenser placement is the main challenge.

You will need to obtain strata approval to place the external condenser units on balconies or common-property walls, ensuring noise regulations are met.

Cooking (Induction Cooktop) Fact Sheet Key Metrics & Financials ● Average Upfront Cost: $600 to $5,000 (excluding electrical work and benchtop modiﬁcations). ● Potential Bill Savings: $400 over a 15-year horizon. While direct energy savings are low, getting off gas cooking completely enables you to disconnect your home from the gas network entirely.

chunks.sourceTitle: Electric Saul
chunks.text: ● The Gas Disconnection Bonus: Getting off the gas network saves the average household roughly $300 to $450 a year in gas daily supply charges alone. Over 15 years, completely disconnecting from gas saves $4,700 in ﬁxed daily supply fees. ● Appliance Lifetime: 15 years. ● Installation Diﬃculty: Moderate to High. ● Electrical Upgrade Required: Yes. Gas cooktops only require a standard 10A plug for the spark ignition. An induction cooktop is a high-power appliance that requires a dedicated 20A to 32A circuit run directly from your switchboard. ● Accredited Installer Requirement: Licensed electrician. If modifying benchtops, a cabinetmaker or stonemason may also be required. Technology & Health Beneﬁts Gas cooktops use a ﬂame to heat a pan, with an eﬃciency of only 30% to 40%-the other 60% of the energy escapes as heat into your kitchen. Ceramic electric cooktops run at about 70% eﬃciency.

chunks.sourceTitle: Electric Saul
chunks.text: Technology & Health Beneﬁts Gas cooktops use a ﬂame to heat a pan, with an eﬃciency of only 30% to 40%-the other 60% of the energy escapes as heat into your kitchen. Ceramic electric cooktops run at about 70% eﬃciency. Induction cooktops use electromagnetic energy to excite the iron molecules in the base of your cookware, transferring 80% to 90% of the energy directly into the food. ● Health Hazards of Gas Cooking: Natural gas is primarily methane, but burning it indoors releases nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), carbon monoxide (CO), formaldehyde, and ﬁne particulate matter. Peer-reviewed research shows that cooking with gas is responsible for up to 12% of childhood asthma cases in Australia-a health risk comparable to having a cigarette smoker in the house. ● Cookware Compatibility: Induction requires cookware made of ferrous metals (like cast iron or magnetic stainless steel).

Home Battery Fact Sheet Key Metrics & Financials ● Average Upfront Cost: $7,000 to $15,000 depending on storage capacity (typically 5 kWh to 13.5 kWh). ● Potential Bill Savings: Around $1,000 a year by shifting your solar generation to cover your evening peak electricity demand (typically 5:00 PM to 9:00 PM). ● Appliance Lifetime: 10 to 15 years (batteries degrade gradually over time, typically guaranteed to retain 60% to 70% of their capacity after 10 years). ● Installation Diﬃculty: High. ● Electrical Upgrade Required: Yes.

Home Battery Fact Sheet Key Metrics & Financials ● Average Upfront Cost: $7,000 to $15,000 depending on storage capacity (typically 5 kWh to 13.5 kWh). ● Potential Bill Savings: Around $1,000 a year by shifting your solar generation to cover your evening peak electricity demand (typically 5:00 PM to 9:00 PM). ● Appliance Lifetime: 10 to 15 years (batteries degrade gradually over time, typically guaranteed to retain 60% to 70% of their capacity after 10 years). ● Installation Diﬃculty: High. ● Electrical Upgrade Required: Yes. Requires a hybrid inverter (or an additional AC-coupled battery inverter) and a dedicated space on your switchboard. ● Accredited Installer Requirement: Clean Energy Council (CEC) or Solar Accreditation Australia (SAA) accredited battery installer.

chunks.sourceTitle: Electric Saul
chunks.text: Requires a hybrid inverter (or an additional AC-coupled battery inverter) and a dedicated space on your switchboard. ● Accredited Installer Requirement: Clean Energy Council (CEC) or Solar Accreditation Australia (SAA) accredited battery installer. Core Operating Logic A home battery captures the excess, cheap solar electricity your rooftop generates during the day and stores it for use during high-tariff evening periods. While rooftop solar is an economic "slam dunk" on its own, batteries are currently on the cusp of broad commercial viability. The ﬁnancial return is highest for households on steep Time of Use (ToU) tariffs or those participating in Virtual Power Plants (VPPs) where they can sell their battery power back to the grid during extreme price spikes. Installation Standards & Safety Australia has some of the strictest battery installation standards in the world (AS/NZS 5139).

chunks.sourceTitle: Electric Saul
chunks.text: The ﬁnancial return is highest for households on steep Time of Use (ToU) tariffs or those participating in Virtual Power Plants (VPPs) where they can sell their battery power back to the grid during extreme price spikes. Installation Standards & Safety Australia has some of the strictest battery installation standards in the world (AS/NZS 5139). Batteries must not be installed in habitable rooms, under ﬂoors, or within 600mm of any doors or windows. They are typically installed on external masonry walls, in garages, or inside dedicated, ventilated outdoor enclosures.

chunks.sourceTitle: Electric Saul
chunks.text: State-by-State Government Assistance ● Federal (National): Offers ﬁnance support programs and is rolling out broader community battery initiatives. ● New South Wales (NSW): The Peak Demand Reduction Scheme (PDRS) offers upfront incentives (up to $1,500) for installing an eligible battery and connecting it to a Virtual Power Plant (VPP). ● Australian Capital Territory (ACT): Eligible for zero-interest loans of up to $15,000 under the Sustainable Households Scheme. ● Tasmania (TAS): Eligible for interest-free loans through the Energy Saver Loan Scheme. 6.

chunks.sourceTitle: Electric Saul
chunks.text: 6. Electric Vehicle (EV) Fact Sheet Key Metrics & Financials ● Average Operating Savings: Up to $2,000 to $3,000 a year compared to a petrol or diesel vehicle. ● Fuel Cost Comparison (per 100 km): ● Petrol/Diesel SUV: $15.00 to $20.00 (based on $1.80 to $2.20 per litre). ● EV (Grid Charging): $4.00 to $6.00 (using standard off-peak residential tariffs). ● EV (Solar Charging): $0.00 to $1.50 (utilising free, self-generated rooftop solar). ● Appliance Lifetime: 15+ years (battery packs are typically warranted for 8 years or 160,000 km). ● Maintenance Savings: EVs have roughly 20 moving parts compared to over 2,000 in an internal combustion engine, completely eliminating oil changes, spark plugs, timing belts, and fuel ﬁlters. ● Charger Installation Cost: $1,000 to $2,500 for a dedicated Level 2 (7 kW to 22 kW) wall charger installed at home.

chunks.sourceTitle: Electric Saul
chunks.text: Charging Dynamics & Smart Grid Integration Most EV owners complete 90% of their charging at home. ● Level 1 Charging: Plugs into a standard 10A household outlet. Adds about 10 km to 15 km of range per hour of charging. ● Level 2 Charging: Requires a dedicated wallbox on a 32A circuit. Adds 40 km to 100 km of range per hour of charging.

chunks.sourceTitle: Electric Saul
chunks.text: ● Vehicle-to-Home (V2H) / Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G): The ultimate evolution of home electriﬁcation. A typical EV battery (60 kWh) holds enough energy to power an average Australian home for three to four days. As V2H-compatible bidirectional chargers become widely certiﬁed in Australia, your car will act as a giant mobile home battery. Government Assistance ● Federal (National): The Fringe Beneﬁts Tax (FBT) exemption for electric vehicles makes leasing an EV through a novated lease highly tax-effective for working Australians, potentially saving thousands of dollars a year in pre-tax income. ● State Programs: Various states offer discounted registration, luxury car tax exemptions, or low-interest green loans to assist with the purchase of electric vehicles and home charging hardware.

chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 8 Start Here: Make the Home Work on Paper, Then Prove It on Site This is an independent Australian field guide for renters, apartment residents, homeowners, renovators, owner-builders and people commissioning a new home. It contains no company endorsement, brand, proprietary product, current price, sales listing, installer referral, advertisement or commercial relationship. The central rule is: define the life the home must support, reduce the demand, model the whole design, document it clearly, build the details, test the result and keep learning from operation. A home is a system. Site, floor area, orientation, shade, glazing, insulation, thermal bridges, airtightness, ventilation, moisture, structure, services, materials, landscape and occupant behaviour interact.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: A home is a system. Site, floor area, orientation, shade, glazing, insulation, thermal bridges, airtightness, ventilation, moisture, structure, services, materials, landscape and occupant behaviour interact. Improving one part without checking the others can move rather than solve a problem. For example, draught sealing can improve comfort but also makes deliberate ventilation more important; adding thermal mass without useful sun or night cooling can make a room slower to recover; replacing windows without managing shade can worsen summer overheating. DECISION Do not begin with a product catalogue or a target star alone. Begin with a written brief, the exact site and climate, present defects, household needs, health and accessibility needs, future hazards, available evidence, permissions and a total budget that includes design, testing and contingencies.

Separate comfort, moisture, health, noise, bills, space, repair and compliance issues. 2 Create a baseline. Gather 12 months of energy and water data where available, plans, certificates, photos, room measurements and a dated defect list. 3 Resolve hazards first.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Gather 12 months of energy and water data where available, plans, certificates, photos, room measurements and a dated defect list. 3 Resolve hazards first. Check structure, water entry, electrical safety, combustion safety, asbestos, lead, termite activity and site hazards before finishes or energy upgrades. 4 Reduce the brief. Keep only rooms, area, glazing, services and materials that serve a defined need. Provide flexible uses instead of duplicate rooms where practical. 5 Understand the climate and site. Map sun, shade, breezes, hot and cold winds, slope, vegetation, neighbours, drainage, noise, smoke and future hazards. 6 Set performance targets. Define room comfort, overheating, heating and cooling loads, airtightness, ventilation, moisture, water, accessibility, operational energy, embodied carbon and verification requirements. 7 Model early and iterate.

chunks.text: Define room comfort, overheating, heating and cooling loads, airtightness, ventilation, moisture, water, accessibility, operational energy, embodied carbon and verification requirements. 7 Model early and iterate. Test orientation, area, zoning, shade, glazing, insulation, mass and services while change is cheap. 8 Document interfaces. Show where water, air, heat, structure and services cross every junction. State who supplies, installs, seals, tests and rectifies each item. 9 Price one scope. Give every tenderer the same documents. Compare exclusions, allowances, substitutions, testing, program, experience and risk - not the bottom line alone. 10 Inspect before concealment. Photograph and verify membranes, insulation, flashings, service penetrations, window installation and drainage before linings cover them.

chunks.text: What this guide covers The guide covers project briefs; site and climate analysis; smaller and adaptable floor plans; orientation, solar access, shade and breezes; home energy ratings and modelling; whole-envelope design; airtightness and blower-door tests; ventilation, condensation, mould and indoor air; thermal imaging and diagnostics; retrofit sequencing; renovation, extension and rebuild choices; embodied carbon and materials; all-electric services; water and landscape; heat, smoke, bushfire, flood, storm and outage resilience; accessible and multi-household options; professional roles; quotes, contracts and substitutions; stage inspections; commissioning; renters and apartments; myths; option matrices; worksheets; glossary; research method; and current Australian public sources.

chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 11 Write the Performance Brief Before Drawing the House A good brief converts preferences into decisions that can be modelled, documented and tested. "Sustainable", "comfortable" and "healthy" are aspirations. A useful brief says who uses each space, when, under what weather, what they can operate, what failure looks like, and how success will be verified.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: A useful brief says who uses each space, when, under what weather, what they can operate, what failure looks like, and how success will be verified. Start with people and activities Record the present household and credible future changes: • number, ages and usual schedules of occupants • mobility, vision, hearing, sensory, respiratory and temperature-sensitivity needs • work, study, care, sleep, exercise, hobbies, pets, food growing and storage • regular visitors and whether any room must support overnight guests • privacy and acoustic needs between people with different schedules • equipment, vehicle, bicycle, mobility aid, tool and drying-space needs • likely changes over 5, 10 and 20 years, including children, ageing, care, separation, working from home or an additional household • what can be shared, hired or stored elsewhere rather than permanently accommodated.

Use a room-use table rather than naming rooms too early. "Two people need quiet video calls from 9 am to 3 pm" is more useful than "two studies".

chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 12 Avoid copying thresholds from a different climate or building type. Set targets with the relevant assessor or designer and record the assumptions. A target can exceed the legal minimum, but it must not conflict with ventilation, fire, structure, waterproofing or other safety requirements. Define comfort by room and season Comfort depends on air temperature, radiant surface temperatures, air movement, humidity, clothing, activity and individual physiology. A thermostat setpoint alone is not a comfort specification.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Define comfort by room and season Comfort depends on air temperature, radiant surface temperatures, air movement, humidity, clothing, activity and individual physiology. A thermostat setpoint alone is not a comfort specification. For each room or zone, define: • occupied hours and seasons • whether it is free-running, fan-assisted or mechanically conditioned • desired winter and summer operative conditions • acceptable air movement and noise • solar access or shade requirements • night-time purge or secure ventilation needs • whether a closed door must preserve privacy, acoustics and thermal zoning • recovery time after an absence or extreme event • how vulnerable occupants will be protected during heat, cold, smoke or outage. A rarely used guest room does not need the same operating pattern as a bedroom for a medically vulnerable person.

chunks.text: For each room or zone, define: • occupied hours and seasons • whether it is free-running, fan-assisted or mechanically conditioned • desired winter and summer operative conditions • acceptable air movement and noise • solar access or shade requirements • night-time purge or secure ventilation needs • whether a closed door must preserve privacy, acoustics and thermal zoning • recovery time after an absence or extreme event • how vulnerable occupants will be protected during heat, cold, smoke or outage. A rarely used guest room does not need the same operating pattern as a bedroom for a medically vulnerable person. A west-facing bedroom may meet an annual star target while still having unacceptable summer peaks. Ask for room-level outputs, not only one whole-home number.

Budget the floor area and the complexity Set a maximum conditioned floor area and a separate area budget for garage, storage, decks and external works. Every square metre has upfront cost, embodied impacts, heating and cooling demand, cleaning and maintenance. Space efficiency often pays for better envelope details and verification. Also budget complexity: • number of external corners and roof junctions • steps and level changes • wet areas and plumbing runs • windows and large door systems • balconies, box gutters and concealed drainage • penetrations through the air and water layers • different cladding systems and material junctions • control systems, motors and internet dependencies.

Complexity is not automatically bad, but every added interface needs a clear detail, installer responsibility, inspection and maintenance path. Establish project constraints Record: • total available funds, finance limit and protected contingency • whether temporary accommodation is possible • completion date constraints and seasonal work risks

Do not let the construction price consume the contingency, professional inspections, testing or commissioning budget. These are part of delivering the performance, not optional extras after the design. Create a hierarchy of requirements Use four levels: 1 Life safety and legal: structure, fire, electrical, weatherproofing, sanitation, access required by law and hazard requirements.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: These are part of delivering the performance, not optional extras after the design. Create a hierarchy of requirements Use four levels: 1 Life safety and legal: structure, fire, electrical, weatherproofing, sanitation, access required by law and hazard requirements. 2 Health and durability: moisture control, ventilation, pollutant source control, drainage, maintainability and safe temperatures. 3 Performance: room comfort, low loads, airtightness, water and energy targets, resilience and carbon. 4 Preferences: aesthetics, finishes, extra area and features. When cost pressure arrives, reduce optional area, finish complexity and duplicate functions before deleting concealed measures that are difficult or impossible to add later, such as orientation, wall insulation, thermal breaks, airtight junctions, step-free structure, drainage capacity and service pathways.

chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 14 Read the Site Before Choosing the Plan The same floor plan can perform very differently when rotated, moved, shaded, exposed to wind or placed in another climate. Choose and analyse the site before committing to a standard plan. If the site is fixed, make the design respond to its real constraints rather than forcing a preferred image onto it.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Build a site evidence pack Gather dated, scaled information: • title, boundaries, survey, easements, setbacks, rights of way and service locations • contours, levels, slope, retaining walls, cut and fill, soil and geotechnical information • true north, not just plan-page north • existing buildings, trees, rock, habitat, drainage and reusable materials • neighbouring buildings and likely future development envelopes • winter and summer sun paths and hourly shadow studies • prevailing cool breezes, hot winds, cold winds and storm directions • road, aircraft, neighbours, equipment and other noise sources • views, privacy, overlooking and night lighting • legal planning, heritage, landscape, tree, bushfire, flood, coastal, cyclone and other overlays • electricity, gas, water, sewer, stormwater and communications capacity • public transport, walking, cycling, services, schools, work and daily

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: destinations • emergency access, evacuation routes and places of refuge. Visit at morning, afternoon and evening; in different seasons if possible; after rain; and on a windy day. A single midday inspection can miss traffic noise, drainage, glare, low winter sun and afternoon heat. Use the right climate scale Australia has 8 broad National Construction Code climate zones, while home energy rating weather files use finer regional climate locations. Neither automatically captures a site's exact elevation, valley cold-air pooling, coast exposure, urban heat island, local shade or wind shelter.

Neither automatically captures a site's exact elevation, valley cold-air pooling, coast exposure, urban heat island, local shade or wind shelter. Create a climate summary with: • seasonal temperature range and diurnal swing • humidity and dew point patterns • heating and cooling degree conditions • heatwave length and warm overnight temperatures • frost, snow or alpine exposure where relevant • wind speed and direction by season and time of day • rainfall intensity, drought and water restrictions • solar radiation and cloud patterns • future climate projections and not only historical averages. In hot-humid climates, shade, air movement and inward vapour drives can dominate.

Cool and alpine climates give more weight to heat retention, cold-surface control and safe ventilation. Model the exact location. Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/design-climate [2] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/orientation Map solar access before fixing rooms Plot shadows from: • existing and proposed buildings • permitted future neighbour envelopes • evergreen and deciduous trees at mature size • hills, fences, screens and outbuildings • roof forms, parapets and the home's own wings. Check at least winter morning, solar noon and afternoon; equinox; and summer. Include roof solar access and the effect of future shading or equipment.

chunks.text: Check at least winter morning, solar noon and afternoon; equinox; and summer. Include roof solar access and the effect of future shading or equipment. Protect useful winter sun where the climate benefits from it, but do not assume all Australian climates need maximum northern glass. Low-angle east and west sun is difficult to exclude with a shallow horizontal eave. Identify facade-specific shade early. A view, street frontage or privacy need may require non-ideal glazing, but the impact can be managed with size, glass performance, external shade, room use and landscape.

A view, street frontage or privacy need may require non-ideal glazing, but the impact can be managed with size, glass performance, external shade, room use and landscape. Understand water before architecture Trace water from the highest catchment to the lawful discharge point: • upstream overland flow and neighbouring runoff • roof catchments, gutters, downpipes, tank overflows and charged lines • surface falls away from the building • subsoil drainage and groundwater • retaining wall drainage • driveway and hard-surface runoff • sewer surcharge and backflow risk • permeable area, raingardens, swales and overflow routes • flood level, velocity, duration, debris and contamination. Do not solve water only at the property boundary. Roof design, landscaping, floor levels, equipment placement, materials and safe access must work together.

chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 17 Smaller, Simpler and More Useful Floor Plans A smaller home is not automatically better, and a large home is not automatically wasteful. The test is whether each square metre supports a real need better than a flexible, shared or external alternative. Area is one of the strongest levers for construction cost, embodied impacts, operational energy, cleaning, maintenance and land available for trees, water and outdoor life. Build an area budget from activities List activities, number of simultaneous users, furniture, clearances, storage and acoustic needs. Then combine compatible activities.

chunks.text: and fire planning, future services subject to approval Measure furniture and circulation on the plan. Marketing room names and total floor area do not show whether doors collide, a wheelchair can turn, a dining chair can be used, a bed has approach space or storage is reachable. Use simple form intelligently A compact form generally reduces external surface area, corners, roof junctions, flashings, thermal bridges and air-sealing interfaces. It can be cheaper to build and easier to verify. But depth can reduce daylight and cross-ventilation, and an over-compact plan can create dark central rooms.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: It can be cheaper to build and easier to verify. But depth can reduce daylight and cross-ventilation, and an over-compact plan can create dark central rooms. Balance: • compact external envelope • shallow enough occupied rooms for useful daylight and ventilation • a roof form that drains reliably and provides solar and rainwater collection area • short plumbing and duct runs • few changes in level • structural spans that suit available materials and skills • a continuous, drawable water, air and insulation layer. Every projection, step, valley, box gutter, balcony and material change should earn its complexity through a clear functional benefit.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 18 Zone by time, temperature, noise and privacy Group spaces that operate together. Useful zoning can: • condition occupied areas rather than the whole house • close bedrooms from evening living noise • separate a home office or second household • retain winter warmth or summer coolth • allow one room to operate as a clean-air or cool retreat • reduce cooking, bathroom and laundry moisture spread • keep garage or workshop pollutants outside the living envelope. Doors used for zoning need appropriate seals and undercut or transfer-air design consistent with ventilation. A sealed bedroom with no fresh-air path can create poor air quality. An internal door is part of both the thermal and ventilation strategy.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: A sealed bedroom with no fresh-air path can create poor air quality. An internal door is part of both the thermal and ventilation strategy. Design circulation as useful space Long corridors, oversized entries and duplicate routes consume area. Reduce dead circulation by: • placing storage, seating or daylight along routes • arranging rooms around short central paths • avoiding furniture conflicts at doors • using direct access from groceries, waste and laundry to their destinations • maintaining clear step-free routes • keeping escape and service access legible. Do not make circulation so narrow that accessibility, moving furniture, ventilation or daily use suffers. Test the plan with scale furniture, mobility aids, prams, laundry baskets and two people passing. Integrate storage, daylight and views Good storage allows smaller rooms to work.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Test the plan with scale furniture, mobility aids, prams, laundry baskets and two people passing. Integrate storage, daylight and views Good storage allows smaller rooms to work. Provide space at the point of use: • entry for shoes, coats, bags and mobility aids • kitchen for actual appliances, bins, pantry and bulk food • bedrooms for clothing without blocking ventilation or external walls • laundry for drying, cleaning and linen • workspace for files, cables and equipment • secure bicycle, tool, repair and garden storage • accessible plant and service clearances. Daylight should reach tasks without excessive glass. Use window head height, room depth, reflectance, borrowed light where lawful, clerestories and roof lights carefully.

chunks.text: Daylight should reach tasks without excessive glass. Use window head height, room depth, reflectance, borrowed light where lawful, clerestories and roof lights carefully. Roof glazing can create glare, heat gain, heat loss, leak and condensation risk, so model and detail it rather than using it as a rescue for an unnecessarily deep plan. Design for acoustic comfort Energy-efficient homes can be quiet outside yet transmit more internal noise if lightweight partitions, hard finishes and open plans are not considered. Address: • bedroom separation from kitchens, bathrooms, plant and living rooms

Acoustic insulation does not automatically provide an airtight boundary, and air seals can affect transfer ventilation. Coordinate both functions.

Red flags in a floor plan • living rooms face a garage or street only because the plan was not rotated for the block • large west glass has no external shading zone • bedrooms have no secure night ventilation path • a bathroom or laundry exhaust cannot duct outdoors directly • the conditioned envelope is unclear around garage, roof, stairs or internal courtyard • the only north roof is filled by an architectural feature or plant • the kitchen, hot water and bathrooms are far apart • corridors and duplicate living rooms are large but storage is missing • furniture drawings omit real clearances • future access depends on rebuilding structure • services penetrate key membranes without a coordinated route • the plan meets a star target only through expensive specifications after orientation and area were fixed.

chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 21 Orientation, Sun, Shade and Breezes Passive design is not a style. It is a climate-specific arrangement of rooms, openings, shade, insulation, mass and ventilation that reduces the work mechanical systems must do. The correct response changes across Australia and can change within one site.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Set the climate objective first Climate tendency Primary aim Common supporting moves Common failure Hot humid Exclude sun, move air, control inward moisture, provide efficient cooling Broad shade, lightweight or carefully modelled mass, high air movement, protected openings Importing a cold-climate high-mass solar plan Hot dry Exclude daytime heat, use diurnal cooling where nights are cooler Shade, insulation, controlled closure, night purge, useful mass Leaving mass exposed to summer sun or hot night air Temperate Balance winter gains with summer exclusion North-biased living, adjustable east/west shade, insulation, secure ventilation Optimising winter while creating summer overheating Cool or alpine Capture useful sun and retain heat while controlling moisture Compact form, high-performance envelope, cold-surface control, deliberate ventilation Excess glazing, thermal bridges or

chunks.text: uncontrolled leakage Local humidity, elevation, coastal exposure, smoke, noise and future heat can shift these priorities. Use a climate-specific model and site evidence. Orient rooms, not just the building arrow For much of Australia, daytime living spaces benefit from northern exposure because winter sun is available for longer and high summer sun can be excluded with horizontal shade. Hot-humid regions are a major exception, where shade and breeze access can be more important than winter solar gain.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Orient rooms, not just the building arrow For much of Australia, daytime living spaces benefit from northern exposure because winter sun is available for longer and high summer sun can be excluded with horizontal shade. Hot-humid regions are a major exception, where shade and breeze access can be more important than winter solar gain. Prioritise orientation by time of use: • living and work areas used by day receive the most useful daylight and climate response • bedrooms are protected from late west sun and can release heat at night • bathrooms and laundries have short, direct outdoor exhaust routes • garages, stores and service zones can buffer difficult exposures without blocking useful sun • outdoor areas are usable in the real season and time of day, not only in presentation drawings.

If north faces the street, a good result may still be possible with privacy screens, courtyards, clerestories, smaller front setbacks where allowed, or a plan that steps sunlight into more than one zone. If views are south or west, frame the view selectively instead of glazing the whole facade.

chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 22 External shade stops radiation before it enters the glass and is generally more effective for summer control than internal coverings. Internal curtains and blinds remain valuable for winter heat loss, glare, privacy and a secondary summer layer. Use a shadow study with the exact latitude, orientation, window head and sill, shade projection and nearby obstructions. Rules of thumb can begin a design but should not certify it. Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/orientation [2] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/shading Size glazing as a system Glazing must be assessed by facade and room.

chunks.text: Rules of thumb can begin a design but should not certify it. Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/orientation [2] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/shading Size glazing as a system Glazing must be assessed by facade and room. Consider: • total window-system U-value, including frame and edge effects • solar heat gain coefficient appropriate to climate and orientation • visible light, glare and privacy • openable area, insect screen and security restriction • frame conductivity and thermal break • air leakage and installation perimeter • internal covering and external shading • condensation risk at glass, frame and reveals • acoustic, fire, impact, bushfire and fall-safety requirements • cleaning, hardware, seals and replacement access. More glass does not guarantee better light or comfort. High-level daylight can distribute light more deeply than a large low window.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: More glass does not guarantee better light or comfort. High-level daylight can distribute light more deeply than a large low window. Concentrate glass where it serves a view, task, winter gain or ventilation path, then model the consequences. Use thermal mass only when it has a job Thermal mass can absorb and later release heat. It is helpful only when the daily heat flow supports comfort. For passive winter heating, mass must receive useful sun or radiant heat and be within the insulated envelope. For passive summer cooling, it must be protected from sun and able to release stored heat to cooler air, often at night. It should not be covered by thick insulating finishes if it is expected to exchange heat with the room.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: For passive summer cooling, it must be protected from sun and able to release stored heat to cooler air, often at night. It should not be covered by thick insulating finishes if it is expected to exchange heat with the room. Mass can be a liability where: • nights remain hot or humid • the surface receives unwanted summer sun • the room is used intermittently and needs fast temperature response • the mass is outside or bridges the insulation layer • an upper-level bedroom stores heat into the night • the climate mainly benefits from lightweight, free-running construction. Do not add high-impact material merely to obtain mass. First count useful existing slabs, masonry and contents, then model whether more is beneficial.

Ceiling and pedestal fans cool people through air movement; they do not lower room air temperature. Use them where occupants are present and coordinate blade clearance, ceiling height, lighting and sprinklers.

Occupant control plan Passive features need an understandable operating sequence: • when to open and close external shade • when to admit or exclude sun • when outdoor air is cooler, drier or cleaner than indoor air • when to use fans before compressor cooling • when to close zones for efficient conditioning • what changes during smoke, heatwave, storm or high humidity • which controls are automatic, manual, local and operable without internet. Provide simple labels and seasonal guidance. If comfortable operation requires many daily actions, either automate safely, simplify the design or account for realistic behaviour in the model.

chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 24 Use Ratings and Modelling as Design Instruments Computer simulation allows cheap virtual experiments before materials are ordered. It is most valuable early, repeated through design and connected to room-level decisions. A certificate produced only at approval may show a compliance pathway but miss the chance to improve the home. Understand the main rating outputs For new homes, the national home energy rating scheme models how much heating and cooling a dwelling is likely to need to maintain standard comfort conditions. It uses location, climate, orientation, geometry, construction, insulation, glazing, shade, zones and standardised occupancy settings. The thermal result is expressed from 0 to 10 stars.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: It uses location, climate, orientation, geometry, construction, insulation, glazing, shade, zones and standardised occupancy settings. The thermal result is expressed from 0 to 10 stars. Whole-of-home assessment adds major fixed systems and assumed household loads, including heating and cooling equipment, hot water, lighting, plug loads, pools, onsite solar and batteries. It is different from the thermal-shell star rating. For existing homes, the national assessment approach now provides both: • a 0 to 10 star thermal-shell rating, and • a 0 to 100-plus whole-home energy rating that includes fixed appliances, onsite generation and storage. An existing-home certificate is not the same as a new-home regulatory certificate and cannot be substituted for National Construction Code compliance.

What a model can answer A competent assessor can compare: • building position and orientation • floor area, form and room arrangement • window size, orientation, system performance and shade • insulation level and construction system • thermal mass and its exposure • zoning doors and conditioned area • roof colour and ventilation assumptions where represented • neighbouring shade and site obstructions • room-by-room heating and cooling loads • equipment options in a whole-home assessment • present design against alternative packages.

A useful table shows base case, one change at a time, combined package, room loads and unintended penalties. What a model does not prove A plan-based rating does not by itself prove: • insulation was installed without gaps, compression or displacement • windows delivered match scheduled performance • perimeter gaps and service penetrations are sealed • the home meets a blower-door target • exhaust or outdoor-air flow rates are achieved • controls are commissioned • moisture cannot accumulate in a specific assembly • occupants will use standard schedules and setpoints • energy bills will equal a predicted amount • the home will be comfortable for every person or future heatwave • construction substitutions preserve the result.

A robust modelling workflow 1 Existing or first concept: Model the honest baseline, including shade, garage, roof and subfloor conditions. 2 Geometry pass: Test size, form, orientation, rooms, zoning and glass before upgrading products. 3 Envelope pass: Test insulation continuity, glazing, frames, shade, thermal bridges and airtightness assumptions supported by the tool. 4 Resilience pass: Review room peaks, overheating, future weather, smoke-closed operation and critical-room performance. 5 Services pass: Match system type and capacity to reduced loads; assess whole-home energy. 6 Documentation pass: Reconcile model inputs with drawings, window schedule, insulation schedule and specification.

chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 27 Design One Continuous Thermal, Air and Water Envelope The envelope separates conditioned living space from outdoors, ground, roof space, garage and other unconditioned zones. Its performance depends on continuity. Good centre-of-panel insulation cannot compensate for repeated gaps, bridges, leaks or wet materials at junctions. Draw the control layers On every plan and section, trace without lifting the pencil: 1 Rain control: roof, cladding, flashings, cavities, windows, doors, ground clearance and drainage that shed bulk water outward. 2 Air control: the continuous layer limiting uncontrolled airflow through walls, ceiling, floors and junctions. 3 Vapour control: climate- and assembly-specific materials that manage diffusion and drying direction.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: 2 Air control: the continuous layer limiting uncontrolled airflow through walls, ceiling, floors and junctions. 3 Vapour control: climate- and assembly-specific materials that manage diffusion and drying direction. 4 Thermal control: insulation and thermal breaks that slow heat flow around the complete conditioned boundary. These layers may be different materials. A vapour-permeable wall membrane is not automatically the air barrier; a plasterboard lining can be part of an air barrier only if its perimeter, joins and penetrations are detailed; bulk insulation does not stop air leakage; reflective insulation needs the specified airspace to perform.

A vapour-permeable wall membrane is not automatically the air barrier; a plasterboard lining can be part of an air barrier only if its perimeter, joins and penetrations are detailed; bulk insulation does not stop air leakage; reflective insulation needs the specified airspace to perform. Map every boundary condition Mark whether each adjacent space is: • outdoors • roof or ceiling cavity • subfloor or ground • garage, carport, store or workshop • internal but unconditioned • conditioned by another household • wet area or high-moisture zone. Commonly confused boundaries include garage ceilings below bedrooms, stairs into roof spaces, service cupboards, bulkheads, bay windows, internal courtyards, raked ceilings, verandah junctions and additions joined to old fabric.

chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 31 Airtightness and Blower-Door Testing Airtightness limits unintended airflow through cracks and gaps. Ventilation intentionally replaces indoor air through known openings or mechanical systems. A healthy efficient home needs both: seal the random leaks and provide the right controlled air exchange. Why uncontrolled leakage matters Leaks can: • carry heated or cooled air out and outdoor air in • create draught discomfort even when average air temperature is acceptable • reduce the value of insulation and efficient equipment • carry moisture into cold cavities where it condenses • admit smoke, dust, pollen, odours and garage or subfloor pollutants • create pressure imbalances and door or exhaust problems • worsen sound transfer • make performance depend on wind rather than occupant need.

A leakage value at 50 pascals is a repeatable test metric, not the number of natural air changes during ordinary occupancy.

Smoke or flame methods can create fire, alarm, respiratory and pressure risks. Use a safe non-combustible indicator and follow official guidance; do not use test smoke around vulnerable occupants, suspected gas leaks or smoke detectors without a plan. Air-sealing hierarchy 1 Repair bulk water and moisture problems. 2 Resolve combustion safety and identify vents that must remain. 3 Define the air barrier and ventilation strategy. 4 Close large construction openings and abandoned ducts. 5 Seal attic hatches, external doors and window perimeters. 6 Address exhaust backdraft dampers and duct connections.

Select seals for movement, temperature, substrate, fire and future access. Foam tape is useful at some operable joints but is not a universal permanent seal. Expanding foam is not automatically weatherproof, fire-rated, pest-proof or removable. Airtightness is not a reason to ban openable windows Airtightness describes the closed building. Openable windows remain valuable for daylight, natural ventilation, purge cooling and occupant control.

When moist air meets a surface below its dew point, liquid water can form. Surface condensation is visible on glass, frames, tiles or walls. Interstitial condensation occurs within roofs, walls or floors and may remain hidden until materials, insulation or structure are damaged.

chunks.text: Surface condensation is visible on glass, frames, tiles or walls. Interstitial condensation occurs within roofs, walls or floors and may remain hidden until materials, insulation or structure are damaged. Risk depends on: • indoor moisture generation and removal • indoor and outdoor temperature and humidity • cold bridges and insulation gaps • glazing and frame surface temperatures • air leakage carrying vapour into cavities • vapour permeance and sequence of layers • rain leaks, plumbing leaks and rising or lateral damp • drying potential in each direction • construction moisture and occupation timing • climate and whether vapour drive can reverse by season. Do not diagnose every damp surface as "poor ventilation". Find whether the source is bulk water, ground moisture, plumbing, construction moisture, surface condensation, interstitial condensation or several at once.

chunks.text: Do not diagnose every damp surface as "poor ventilation". Find whether the source is bulk water, ground moisture, plumbing, construction moisture, surface condensation, interstitial condensation or several at once. Moisture-control hierarchy 1 Keep rain and ground water out. 2 Drain assemblies and site water safely. 3 Repair plumbing and appliance leaks.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 36 4 Reduce avoidable indoor moisture sources and vent dryers as required. 5 Capture bathroom, laundry and cooking moisture at source. 6 Air-seal paths into cavities. 7 Maintain continuous insulation and reduce cold bridges. 8 Select climate-appropriate vapour control and drying paths. 9 Provide reliable outdoor air. 10 Monitor humidity and inspect after extreme weather or changed occupancy. Mould response Mould needs moisture. Cleaning visible growth without correcting moisture usually leads to regrowth. Australian public-health guidance generally does not recommend routine mould testing because there are no health guideline values against which a household sample can be interpreted.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Cleaning visible growth without correcting moisture usually leads to regrowth. Australian public-health guidance generally does not recommend routine mould testing because there are no health guideline values against which a household sample can be interpreted. Instead: • locate and stop the moisture source • dry the assembly • clean or remove affected material safely • get professional help for large areas, recurrence, hidden odour, contaminated HVAC, sewage or vulnerable occupants • seek medical advice for health symptoms and call 000 for a medical emergency. People with asthma, allergies, chronic lung disease or weakened immunity may be more sensitive. Do not dry-brush mould or mix cleaning chemicals. Porous materials can be difficult to restore after extensive growth.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Do not dry-brush mould or mix cleaning chemicals. Porous materials can be difficult to restore after extensive growth. Sources: [1] www.health.gov.au/topics/environmental-health/what-were-doing/env... [2] www.health.nsw.gov.au/environment/factsheets/Pages/mould.aspx Monitor the right variables Low-cost room loggers can reveal patterns in temperature and relative humidity. A carbon dioxide monitor can indicate whether occupied-room air exchange may be inadequate, but it does not measure all pollutants or identify the ventilation rate by itself. A particle monitor can show smoke or cooking events but readings vary by sensor. Record: • location, height and distance from windows or vents • calibration or comparison check • occupancy and activities • outdoor weather and air quality • fan, window, heater and cooler operation • cleaning, cooking, shower and drying events.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: A particle monitor can show smoke or cooking events but readings vary by sensor. Record: • location, height and distance from windows or vents • calibration or comparison check • occupancy and activities • outdoor weather and air quality • fan, window, heater and cooler operation • cleaning, cooking, shower and drying events. Use trends and repeated conditions, not one alarming number. Escalate persistent condensation, high humidity, odour, visible mould or symptoms to the appropriate health or building professional. Smoke mode and clean-air room During bushfire smoke, official health advice includes closing windows and doors, using recirculation where available, avoiding evaporative coolers that draw outdoor air, reducing indoor pollution and considering a correctly sized high-efficiency particle air cleaner in a well-sealed room. Ventilate when outdoor air improves.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Smoke mode and clean-air room During bushfire smoke, official health advice includes closing windows and doors, using recirculation where available, avoiding evaporative coolers that draw outdoor air, reducing indoor pollution and considering a correctly sized high-efficiency particle air cleaner in a well-sealed room. Ventilate when outdoor air improves. A clean-air room should have: • a closeable, reasonably sealed boundary • enough space for vulnerable occupants

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 37 • safe temperature control • particle filtration sized for room volume and leakage • no unflued combustion, candles or smoking • medication, communications and an alternative location if indoor air deteriorates. Particle filters do not remove every gas. Air cleaners do not replace ventilation under normal good outdoor conditions. Sources: [1] www.health.nsw.gov.au/environment/bushfire/Pages/bushfire-protect... [2] www.epa.vic.gov.au/1809-fact-sheet-smoke-and-portable-indoor-air-... HEALTH A colder, tighter or more insulated surface can change where moisture condenses. Treat insulation, air sealing, ventilation, heating and vapour control as one design problem.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 38 Diagnostics: Measure Before You Prescribe Diagnostics reduce guesswork. Each tool answers a different question, and several tools are often needed to identify cause, location and significance. Diagnostic ladder Tool Best question What it cannot prove alone Occupant interview and comfort diary When, where and under what conditions is the problem felt? Physical cause Bills and interval meter data When and how much energy or water is used? Which fabric defect caused it Plans, certificates and maintenance history What was intended and changed? What is actually installed Visual and tactile inspection Are there obvious gaps, stains, damage or failed seals? Hidden condition or quantified performance Temperature and humidity logger How do rooms and moisture change over time?

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: What is actually installed Visual and tactile inspection Are there obvious gaps, stains, damage or failed seals? Hidden condition or quantified performance Temperature and humidity logger How do rooms and moisture change over time? Exact leak or insulation location Surface and moisture meter Is a surface cold or material wet at this point? Full wall condition or moisture source without context Borescope or safe physical inspection What is inside an accessible cavity? Whole-building coverage Thermal imaging Where do surface-temperature patterns suggest heat flow, moisture or air movement? It does not see heat loss directly, see through walls or identify material by colour Blower door How leaky is the envelope and where are pressure-driven leaks?

Thermal comfort, durability or toxicity by itself Prepare a diagnostic brief State: • symptoms, locations and weather dependence • project decision the result will inform • available drawings and known changes • access limits and hazards • instruments and method • required indoor-outdoor conditions • whether systems will run normally or be forced for testing • photos, raw data and interpretation required • limitations and uncertainty • priority actions and confirmation test. Do not buy a test whose result cannot change a decision.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 39 Thermal imaging essentials An infrared camera records radiation from surfaces and displays apparent surface-temperature differences. It can help locate: • missing, displaced or compressed insulation • framing and thermal bridges • pressure-driven air-leak patterns when used with a blower door • wet areas where evaporation or conductivity changes temperature • heating-system distribution and hot-water losses • unexpected hot electrical components as a prompt for qualified investigation.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: It can help locate: • missing, displaced or compressed insulation • framing and thermal bridges • pressure-driven air-leak patterns when used with a blower door • wet areas where evaporation or conductivity changes temperature • heating-system distribution and hot-water losses • unexpected hot electrical components as a prompt for qualified investigation. Interpretation needs: • a useful and stable temperature difference across the assembly • knowledge of recent sun, wind, rain, heating and cooling • correct emissivity and awareness of reflective surfaces • indoor and outdoor reference temperatures • access to both sides where possible • understanding of structure, services and material layers • confirmation using inspection, moisture measurement or other tools. Shiny glass or metal can reflect the operator, sky or nearby heat source.

chunks.text: Interpretation needs: • a useful and stable temperature difference across the assembly • knowledge of recent sun, wind, rain, heating and cooling • correct emissivity and awareness of reflective surfaces • indoor and outdoor reference temperatures • access to both sides where possible • understanding of structure, services and material layers • confirmation using inspection, moisture measurement or other tools. Shiny glass or metal can reflect the operator, sky or nearby heat source. Solar loading can make a sound wall look different; wind can cool surfaces; wetness may appear cool or warm; furniture can hide patterns. A coloured image without conditions and interpretation is not a diagnosis. Sources: [1] www.csiro.au/en/news/All/Articles/2024/May/insulation-reduce-elec... [2] www.csiro.au/-/media/Energy/Air-infiltration-report-launch-2024/C...

chunks.text: A coloured image without conditions and interpretation is not a diagnosis. Sources: [1] www.csiro.au/en/news/All/Articles/2024/May/insulation-reduce-elec... [2] www.csiro.au/-/media/Energy/Air-infiltration-report-launch-2024/C... Blower door plus thermal camera A blower door creates a controlled pressure difference. Incoming outdoor air can cool or warm nearby internal surfaces, making leak paths more visible in suitable conditions. The camera still shows the surface response, not the moving air itself. A combined survey can distinguish: • a cool patch caused by missing insulation that remains similar before and after pressure • a streak that develops after depressurisation, suggesting air movement • a repeating line at studs or framing, suggesting a thermal bridge • a wet patch needing moisture confirmation.

chunks.text: The camera still shows the surface response, not the moving air itself. A combined survey can distinguish: • a cool patch caused by missing insulation that remains similar before and after pressure • a streak that develops after depressurisation, suggesting air movement • a repeating line at studs or framing, suggesting a thermal bridge • a wet patch needing moisture confirmation. Keep pre-pressure and pressure images from the same position, temperature scale and time, with annotations and ordinary photos. Whole-home baseline campaign For an existing home, collect at least: • 12 months of electricity and gas where available • tariff and fuel units • conditioned floor area and rooms actually heated or cooled • household occupancy changes • 2 to 4 weeks of room temperature and humidity in a representative hot and cold period

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 40 • external weather source • appliance inventory and major-load measurement where safe • ventilation and window-use diary • moisture and leak history • envelope observations and accessible insulation condition. Normalise cautiously. A lower bill may result from milder weather, fewer occupants, less conditioned area or under-heating rather than an efficient home. Comfort and health outcomes matter alongside energy. Testing new construction Use hold points: • slab and drainage before pour or cover • wall and roof membranes before cladding • window and door openings before and after installation • services before sealing and lining • insulation before lining • preliminary airtightness before final finishes • exhaust and ventilation before handover • final systems under load.

Diagnose in the right order For a cold room: 1 confirm actual room temperature, occupied times and heater operation 2 compare surface temperatures and adjacent rooms 3 inspect shade, glass, seals and accessible insulation 4 investigate leakage and pressure paths 5 model room load and system capacity 6 check moisture and ventilation before sealing or insulating 7 implement the smallest causal fix and measure again. For mould: 1 identify water or vapour source 2 measure indoor and surface conditions 3 inspect exterior, roof, plumbing, drainage and cold bridges 4 check exhaust and make-up air 5 check air leakage into cavities and insulation continuity 6 remediate safely, dry and monitor recurrence.

For mould: 1 identify water or vapour source 2 measure indoor and surface conditions 3 inspect exterior, roof, plumbing, drainage and cold bridges 4 check exhaust and make-up air 5 check air leakage into cavities and insulation continuity 6 remediate safely, dry and monitor recurrence. EVIDENCE A diagnostic report should separate observation, measurement, inference and recommendation. "Blue on camera" is an observation; "missing insulation" is an inference until confirmed.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 41 Retrofit Hierarchy: Fix the House in the Right Order Retrofit is not a shopping list. The best sequence depends on climate, present defects, household operation, access opportunities and future works. Begin with safety and water, then reduce loads, then size services. Test before and after when the decision is material. The default hierarchy 1 Safety, health and permissions. Electrical, gas, structure, asbestos, lead, mould, fire, fall, tenancy and strata issues. 2 Bulk water and drainage. Roof, plumbing, cladding, flashings, ground, subfloor and stormwater. 3 Understand and measure. Plans, bills, comfort diary, inspection, rating, blower door, thermal imaging and moisture as needed. 4 Control unwanted sun. External shade, roof and landscape measures appropriate to climate. 5 Seal uncontrolled air.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: External shade, roof and landscape measures appropriate to climate. 5 Seal uncontrolled air. Preserve required ventilation and combustion safety. 6 Complete insulation. Ceiling first is common but not universal; address walls, floors, bridges and access opportunities. 7 Improve glazing as a system. Start with shade, seals and coverings; then secondary or replacement options where justified. 8 Provide deliberate ventilation. Reliable wet-area exhaust, outdoor air, filtration and moisture plan. 9 Reduce and electrify services. Size efficient heating, cooling and hot water to the improved building. 10 Add generation and storage. Match roof, load, tariff, resilience and future use. 11 Commission and learn. Verify controls, performance and seasonal operation. This order is a starting point.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Verify controls, performance and seasonal operation. This order is a starting point. A failed roof, unsafe heater, medical need, extreme summer exposure or planned recladding can change it.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 42 Upgrade options by envelope element Roof and ceiling • repair leaks and unsafe wiring • identify roof or ceiling as the thermal boundary • seal top plates, penetrations and hatches at the air layer • install, redistribute or top up insulation with required clearances • insulate and seal access hatches • address duct and pipe location • consider roof colour, roof ventilation or over-roof shade where climate and assembly support it • preserve condensation and fire requirements.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Walls • use recladding or relining as an opportunity for continuous layers • cavity fill only after checking cavity, moisture, electrical, fire and installation suitability • internal insulation where external character must remain, with careful bridge and moisture analysis • external insulation where planning, eaves, windows, services and cladding allow • insulate exposed wall sections behind cabinets or during room renovation • seal junctions before closing linings.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Suspended floors and slabs • seal large subfloor air paths without blocking required subfloor ventilation • support floor insulation continuously and protect it from pests, wind and moisture • insulate slab edges where practical and modelled • use floor coverings for local comfort while recognising they do not replace whole-floor design • separate external slabs and conductive connections in major work where structurally possible.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Windows and doors • repair operation and drainage first • replace failed seals and add full-perimeter door seals • add close-fitting lined coverings and pelmets where appropriate • use external shade for unwanted sun • consider removable inserts, secondary glazing, films or replacement after checking whole-system values, condensation, fire, egress, strata and tenancy permission • select replacement units by orientation, frame, glass, installation and shade, not pane count alone. Package measures together Useful packages include: • cold-draught package: blower-door baseline, external seals, hatch, exhaust dampers, safe service sealing, retest and ventilation check • summer-bedroom package: west shade, ceiling/wall continuity, fan, secure night ventilation and correctly sized local cooling

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 43 • wet-home package: leak repairs, exhaust commissioning, insulation continuity, thermal bridge review, air sealing and humidity monitoring • recladding package: drainage plane, window flashings, external insulation, air and vapour layers, fire and termite details • electrification-ready package: envelope reduction, load calculation, switchboard and supply review, equipment locations, condensate, acoustic and future solar plan. Packaging avoids undoing work. Do not install new windows before deciding external insulation and reveal details; do not replace a heater before reducing room loads if it risks oversizing.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Packaging avoids undoing work. Do not install new windows before deciding external insulation and reveal details; do not replace a heater before reducing room loads if it risks oversizing. Prioritise without false payback precision Score each option for: • health and safety urgency • comfort improvement • energy and water reduction • durability and avoided damage • resilience • disruption and access opportunity • expected life and maintenance • cost range and uncertainty • permissions and dependencies • ability to verify. Simple payback omits comfort, avoided damage, finance, maintenance, energy-price change and asset life. Use low, central and high scenarios. Do not promise bill savings from a model without stating household and weather assumptions.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Use low, central and high scenarios. Do not promise bill savings from a model without stating household and weather assumptions. Measure the result Depending on scope: • post-work blower door • insulation inspection or thermal imaging in valid conditions • exhaust and ventilation flow • room temperature and humidity logging • interval energy comparison adjusted for weather and occupancy • moisture reinspection after wet seasons • actual equipment power and controls • occupant comfort review. DECISION If a low-cost measure blocks a later high-value measure, redesign the sequence. A cheap finish that conceals moisture, wiring or an incomplete air layer can be expensive.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 44 Renovate, Extend, Divide, Relocate or Rebuild? The most sustainable new material is often the material already doing a useful job. Retaining and upgrading an existing home usually avoids demolition waste and upfront carbon, but not every building can safely or economically meet the brief. Compare options transparently.
