chunks.text: Get comparable concept-level information before selecting a path. A detailed quote for one option compared with a rough allowance for another is not a fair comparison. Audit the existing building Before design, investigate: • survey and title constraints • structure, movement, footings and retaining walls • roof, cladding, flashings, damp proofing and drainage • termite, rot and corrosion • asbestos, lead and other hazardous materials • electrical, plumbing, gas, sewer and stormwater condition • room sizes, level changes and accessibility • orientation, shade, glazing and ventilation • insulation, air leakage and moisture • heritage or character value • capacity for reuse, salvage and deconstruction. Open-up inspections may be justified before final documentation. Budget for discoveries in concealed old work.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Open-up inspections may be justified before final documentation. Budget for discoveries in concealed old work. Do not assume a standard building inspection includes asbestos assessment, energy assessment or invasive moisture investigation. Make an addition earn its area An addition should solve more than one problem where possible: • bring winter light to existing rooms • shade a difficult facade • create a clear step-free entry • reorganise circulation and storage • enable thermal zoning • provide a direct wet-area exhaust route • improve garden connection and surveillance • create future household separation • repair roof or drainage geometry. Avoid leaving existing central rooms dark, unventilated and stranded. Model the whole resulting home, not only the new work.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Avoid leaving existing central rooms dark, unventilated and stranded. Model the whole resulting home, not only the new work. Retain and repurpose Options include: • repair structure and durable finishes • retain foundations, slabs, masonry, framing and roof where sound

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 46 • reuse doors, timber, bricks, fixtures and cabinetry where safe and practical • deconstruct rather than mechanically demolish selected assemblies • resize or reconfigure a large home into two zones • convert a little-used room to work, care or bedroom use • use reclaimed material only where its structural, fire, moisture and contamination performance is known. Salvage requires space, protection, inventory, labour and a planned destination. Stockpiling without a design use can create damage and cost.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Salvage requires space, protection, inventory, labour and a planned destination. Stockpiling without a design use can create damage and cost. Old-to-new performance boundary An addition may have better insulation and windows than the existing home but still perform poorly if: • no door allows thermal zoning • the old roof and floor dominate losses • new glazing shades useful old windows • the air layer stops at the junction • existing damp is concealed • the new heater serves the whole uninsulated house • exhaust or pressure paths draw from the old roof or subfloor. Draw and test the combined envelope. Stage improvements so the household benefits before or with the addition.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Draw and test the combined envelope. Stage improvements so the household benefits before or with the addition. Multigenerational and two-household conversion Define: • private and shared rooms • independent entry and address needs • fire and acoustic separation • kitchen, bathroom and laundry access • energy, water and internet metering • heating, cooling and ventilation zones • parking, waste, mail, storage and outdoor areas • accessibility and care routes • legal ownership, finance, rates, insurance and decision rights • what happens when one household leaves, dies or wants to sell. Obtain planning, building, legal and financial advice. A family agreement should not rely only on goodwill when people contribute different money, land, labour or care.

chunks.text: Obtain planning, building, legal and financial advice. A family agreement should not rely only on goodwill when people contribute different money, land, labour or care. Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/renovations-and-additions [2] www.yourhome.gov.au/live-adapt/liveable-adaptable-home [3] www.asbestossafety.gov.au/about-asbestos/finding-asbestos/home DECISION Before demolition, require a written option comparison and a materials audit. "Renovation is too hard" and "old is always greener" are both claims that need site-specific evidence.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 47 Materials, Embodied Carbon and Circular Construction Operational energy is the energy used while a home is occupied. Embodied impacts arise from material extraction, manufacture, transport, construction, maintenance, replacement, demolition and disposal. A good project considers both, without using one to hide the other. Use the reduction hierarchy 1 Avoid: Do not build unnecessary area, finishes, structure or duplication. 2 Retain: Keep sound buildings, foundations, frames, masonry, roofs, landscape and infrastructure. 3 Repair and adapt: Extend useful life before replacement. 4 Reuse: Design existing components into the project; use verified salvaged components where suitable. 5 Reduce: Simplify spans, junctions, layers and quantities while meeting performance.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: 4 Reuse: Design existing components into the project; use verified salvaged components where suitable. 5 Reduce: Simplify spans, junctions, layers and quantities while meeting performance. 6 Select lower-impact alternatives: Compare functionally equivalent assemblies using consistent data. 7 Design for durability: Protect materials from water, ultraviolet exposure, pests and incompatible contact. 8 Design for disassembly: Prefer accessible mechanical fixings and separable layers where appropriate. 9 Recover: Plan source separation, take-back and lawful recycling. 10 Dispose safely: Identify hazardous and contaminated materials before work. The greatest carbon saving can come from not constructing an extra room, retaining a slab or using a simple lightweight assembly - not from choosing a highly marketed finish.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: 10 Dispose safely: Identify hazardous and contaminated materials before work. The greatest carbon saving can come from not constructing an extra room, retaining a slab or using a simple lightweight assembly - not from choosing a highly marketed finish. Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/materials/embodied-energy [2] www.dcceew.gov.au/environment/protection/circular-economy/framework Define the assessment boundary Carbon claims are meaningless without scope.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Ask: • Is the result for one product, one square metre of assembly or the whole building? • Does it include product manufacture only, or transport and construction? • Does it include replacement, maintenance, operational effects and end of life? • What service life and replacement cycles are assumed? • Are biogenic carbon storage and later release both treated consistently? • Is electricity based on current, past or future grid emissions? • Are onsite solar exports credited, and if so, are operational and embodied results being mixed? • Are all materials counted from a bill of quantities or only selected products? • Are environmental product declarations current, verified and comparable? • What is excluded, and how sensitive is the answer to those exclusions?

chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 48 Stage Typical scope End of life Deconstruction, transport, waste processing and disposal Beyond boundary Potential reuse, recovery or recycling benefits reported separately Do not subtract a future recycling benefit from today's emissions without showing it separately and stating the assumptions. Compare assemblies, not ingredients A wall must provide structure, rain control, air control, vapour behaviour, insulation, fire, acoustics, durability, finish and fixing support. Compare complete walls delivering equivalent performance, not a kilogram of one material against a kilogram of another.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Compare assemblies, not ingredients A wall must provide structure, rain control, air control, vapour behaviour, insulation, fire, acoustics, durability, finish and fixing support. Compare complete walls delivering equivalent performance, not a kilogram of one material against a kilogram of another. For each option, record: • quantity and thickness • structural and thermal performance • service life and replacements • manufacturing evidence and transport • installation waste • fire and smoke behaviour • moisture and pest durability • toxicity and indoor emissions • maintenance coating or treatment • repairability and availability of skills • disassembly and realistic local recovery route. A low-carbon material that fails early, traps moisture, needs frequent replacement or forces more structure may have a worse whole-building outcome.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 49 Environmental product declarations and databases An environmental product declaration can provide third-party-verified life-cycle data for a defined product and standard. It does not mean the product is automatically low impact, healthy, durable or suitable. Compare declarations with: • the same functional unit • compatible standards and assessment versions • the same life-cycle modules • similar geography and electricity assumptions • actual quantity required to deliver the same function • declaration validity date and verifier. Where product data is absent, use a transparent national or research database and label the uncertainty. Current Australian public tools now include a national material emission-factor database and an embodied-carbon rating framework for eligible building types.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Where product data is absent, use a transparent national or research database and label the uncertainty. Construction waste plan Before work: • audit existing materials and hazardous substances • nominate items to retain in place • create a salvage inventory with storage and destination • use accurate ordering and standard dimensions • require source-separated bins where local recovery exists • protect new materials from rain and damage • return pallets, packaging and unused materials where possible • weigh or document waste streams • prohibit unlawful disposal and uncontrolled burning • record reused, recycled and disposed quantities.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 50 Australia generated 29.2 million tonnes of construction and demolition waste in 2022-23. Household projects contribute to a much larger system; deconstruction, accurate ordering and retention are practical levers. Sources: [1] www.dcceew.gov.au/environment/protection/waste/publications/natio... Carbon decision record Decision Baseline quantity and impact Alternative Operational effect Durability effect Selected reason Floor area Existing structure retained Foundation and slab External walls Roof Windows and shade Internal finishes Services DECISION Reduce area and material first. Then compare complete, durable, code-compliant assemblies using the same boundary. Do not let one material claim decide the whole building.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 51 All-Electric Services, Controls and Future Loads Efficient services work best after the building load is reduced. An oversized system can cycle, create noise, cost more, demand a larger electrical supply and perform poorly at part load. Use room and whole-home calculations rather than replacing old equipment like for like. Follow the services sequence 1 Reduce heating, cooling, hot-water and lighting demand. 2 Define occupied zones and operating schedules. 3 Calculate design loads for the local climate and improved envelope. 4 Check electrical supply, switchboard, circuits and maximum demand. 5 Select system type and capacity for the actual duty. 6 Plan locations, airflow, condensate, noise, service and replacement access. 7 Coordinate solar, tariffs, batteries and electric-vehicle charging.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: 6 Plan locations, airflow, condensate, noise, service and replacement access. 7 Coordinate solar, tariffs, batteries and electric-vehicle charging. 8 Commission under realistic modes and teach the household.

chunks.text: Electric resistance heater Low purchase complexity and local backup One unit of heat per unit of electricity; expensive for sustained heating Evaporative cooler Efficient sensible cooling in dry climates Requires open relief air, uses water, poor in humidity and unsuitable during smoke Ground- or water-source heat pump Stable source conditions for suitable projects Ground works, design skill, pumps, capital and maintenance Wood or combustion heater Local heat and outage potential in some locations Air pollution, fuel, fire, flue, leakage, health, regulation and neighbour impact For most Australian households, reverse-cycle air conditioners are the most efficient combined electric heating and cooling option. They move heat and can deliver several units of heating or cooling per unit of electricity under appropriate conditions.

Compare climate-zone labels, capacity at relevant outdoor temperatures, sound, standby and part-load performance. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/heating-and-cooling [2] www.energyrating.gov.au/consumer-information/products/heating-and... Distribution matters For air systems: • locate supplies and returns for occupied-zone mixing

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 52 • avoid short-circuiting supply air directly to a return • size ducts for low pressure and noise • place ducts inside the conditioned envelope where practical • seal and test duct joints • insulate ducts and plenums in unconditioned spaces • provide transfer paths when doors close • commission flow to each room. For hydronic systems: • set flow temperature appropriate to the emitter and heat-pump efficiency • balance circuits • insulate pipework • provide safe expansion, pressure and air removal • control slab systems with their slow response in mind • manage condensation for cooling surfaces.

chunks.text: Hot-water options Type Benefits Watchpoints Heat-pump storage High efficiency and flexible timing Cold-climate performance, noise, airflow, condensate, tank losses, backup element and controls Solar thermal with electric boost Direct solar collection Roof orientation, piping losses, stagnation, frost, booster use, maintenance and future service Electric resistance storage Simple, can shift operation to selected times Higher electricity use, standing loss and switchboard load Electric instantaneous No storage loss, local use potential Very high power demand, flow limits and possible three-phase requirement Shared central system Can serve apartments efficiently at scale Distribution and circulation losses, metering, ownership, maintenance and single-point failure Water heating is a major household load. Size storage for real occupancy and recovery, not an excessive contingency.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Size storage for real occupancy and recovery, not an excessive contingency. Insulate accessible hot pipes, minimise dead legs, use efficient fixtures and place plant close to repeated demand. Heat-pump water heaters are roughly three times as efficient as conventional electric storage in the general government description, but actual performance depends on climate, placement, draw pattern and controls. Unlike many appliances, hot-water systems may not carry a consumer energy label; require test and performance data. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/hot-water-systems [2] www.energyrating.gov.au/consumer-information/products/water-heating Cooking and indoor air Electric resistance and induction are the main electric cooktop families. Induction heats compatible cookware directly and can reduce kitchen heat. Check electrical capacity, cookware, accessible controls and user needs.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Induction heats compatible cookware directly and can reduce kitchen heat. Check electrical capacity, cookware, accessible controls and user needs. Every cooking method produces particles, moisture and odours from food. Provide an effective externally ducted range exhaust, short smooth duct, suitable make-up air and commissioning. Removing combustion also removes one source of nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide and water vapour from the kitchen, but does not remove the need for extraction. Electrical readiness A licensed electrician should assess:

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 53 • service size and phase • switchboard condition and space • main switch, protective devices and earthing • maximum demand and diversity • existing large loads • solar, battery and generator interactions • electric hot water, cooking, heating/cooling and vehicle charging • load control and demand limits • meter and network requirements • outage and isolation behaviour • equipment clearances and flood/fire exposure. Do not assume whole-home electrification requires three-phase supply, or that single-phase is always sufficient. A load schedule and management strategy decide it.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Do not assume whole-home electrification requires three-phase supply, or that single-phase is always sufficient. A load schedule and management strategy decide it. Solar and battery integration Reduce demand first, then assess: • usable unshaded roof by season • current and future daytime load • inverter and export constraints • hot-water and vehicle load shifting • battery energy capacity in kWh and power in kW • essential circuits and islanding capability • outage duration objective • tariff and demand charges • degradation, warranty, fire, flood, access and replacement • monitoring data ownership and offline control. A grid-connected solar system usually shuts down in an outage unless specifically designed and approved to operate safely while isolated. A battery's stored energy does not prove it can start or run every appliance; power output and surge also matter.

chunks.text: A grid-connected solar system usually shuts down in an outage unless specifically designed and approved to operate safely while isolated. A battery's stored energy does not prove it can start or run every appliance; power output and surge also matter. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/electrification [2] www.energy.gov.au/solar/get-know-solar-technology/batteries Controls should fail safely and remain understandable Require: • local manual control • documented default and schedule • sensible operation if internet or app service fails • clear override for heat, smoke, illness or visitors • no hidden subscription required for essential comfort • temperature sensors in representative locations • accessible controls and readable labels

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 54 • privacy and data-reset procedure on sale or tenancy change. Commissioning evidence • electrical certificates and settings • heating and cooling capacity and measured room flows where applicable • refrigerant and condensate checks • hot-water temperature, timer and backup operation • range and wet-area exhaust flows • noise and vibration review • solar/battery modes and shutdown demonstration • maximum-demand or load-control test • filters, maintenance and isolation shown to occupants • one-page seasonal operation guide. DECISION A high-efficiency appliance cannot rescue a leaky, unshaded or moisture-damaged home. Reduce the load, size the service, then verify the installed system.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 55 Water, Landscape, Trees and Urban Cooling Water and landscape are building systems. They affect comfort, drainage, biodiversity, fire risk, maintenance, water bills and resilience. Design roof, tank, overflow, soil, planting and shade together. Begin with a water balance Estimate monthly rather than annual totals: • roof catchment area by material and connection • rainfall by month and first-flush losses • tank size and starting level • indoor demands suitable for rainwater • irrigation demand by season • drought and restriction period • pump energy, pressure and maintenance • overflow path and storm intensity. A large annual rainfall total can still leave an empty tank through a long dry season. A tank must have both a useful demand and lawful safe overflow.

chunks.text: Rainwater options Configuration Benefits Critical checks Garden-only Simple use and low treatment burden Demand may be low in wet periods; mosquito and overflow control Toilets and laundry Regular year-round demand and mains reduction Plumbing separation, backflow, pump, labelling and maintenance Whole-house in non-mains areas Essential independent supply Catchment safety, treatment, monitoring, storage and drought plan Slimline or modular tank Fits constrained sites Structural base, access, cost per litre, cleaning and stability Underground tank Preserves surface space and temperature Excavation, groundwater, traffic loads, pump, access and contamination Bladder or underfloor Uses otherwise vacant space Structural support, ventilation, leaks, access and replacement Mains and rainwater connections require compliant separation or backflow prevention. State and local requirements differ.

chunks.text: State and local requirements differ. Public health agencies generally recommend mains water for drinking and cooking where a safe reticulated supply is available; obtain current local advice. Do not collect from unsealed asbestos roofs. Check lead paint, lead flashing, industrial fallout, animal access and other contaminants. Maintain roof, gutters, screens, first flush, tank, pump and treatment. Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/water/rainwater [2] www.health.gov.au/topics/environmental-health/what-were-doing/wat... Stormwater as a site resource Slow, spread, infiltrate, store and safely overflow water where site, soil and law allow. Options include: • retained deep-rooted vegetation • permeable paths and drive strips

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 56 • raingardens and bioretention beds • swales and level spreaders • infiltration trenches and soakwells • dished lawns and planted detention areas • rainwater tanks • detention tanks or controlled outlets where required • erosion-resistant overflow routes. Do not infiltrate water against footings, retaining walls, contaminated soil, unstable slopes or where groundwater and reactive soils make it unsafe. An engineer, hydraulic designer or local authority may be needed. Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/water/stormwater Greywater and wastewater Options include direct diversion to subsurface garden use, treated reuse for irrigation or approved indoor uses, and onsite treatment where sewer is unavailable. Rules vary.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/water/stormwater Greywater and wastewater Options include direct diversion to subsurface garden use, treated reuse for irrigation or approved indoor uses, and onsite treatment where sewer is unavailable. Rules vary. Key principles: • do not store untreated greywater for extended periods • use subsurface distribution to reduce contact and aerosols • avoid runoff to neighbours and waterways • do not apply to saturated soil • match water, salts and nutrients to plant and soil capacity • select compatible detergents • keep blackwater and higher-risk sources within approved treatment systems • provide bypass to sewer or lawful disposal • maintain filters and treatment equipment.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/water/wastewater-reuse Landscape for thermal performance Use planting and structures to: • shade west and east walls and windows • provide climate-appropriate seasonal north shade • reduce hot hard surfaces • shade outdoor units without blocking airflow • channel or protect from winds • create a cooler outdoor source for ventilation • protect soil moisture and reduce reflected heat • preserve winter solar access and roof generation. Trees take years to replace. Survey, assess health and protect root zones during design and construction. Do not compact, excavate or store materials under retained canopies without an approved protection plan. Select plants for local climate, soil, water, biodiversity and hazard conditions. Indigenous species can support habitat; deciduous species may provide seasonal solar control; drought-tolerant plants reduce irrigation.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Select plants for local climate, soil, water, biodiversity and hazard conditions. Indigenous species can support habitat; deciduous species may provide seasonal solar control; drought-tolerant plants reduce irrigation. In bushfire-prone areas, planting location, continuity and fuel properties must follow site-specific fire advice.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 57 Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/live-adapt/landscaping-garden-design Reduce outdoor water demand • group plants by water need • improve soil organic matter where appropriate • mulch without creating termite or fire problems • use drip irrigation and soil-moisture control • water deeply and at lower-evaporation times • minimise thirsty lawn and unnecessary pool evaporation • cover pools • design shade and windbreaks to reduce evaporation • use rainwater or approved greywater where suitable • choose plants that will survive projected future conditions.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Food, habitat and shared resources Consider: • productive gardens near daily paths and water • composting with pest and odour control • habitat layers and safe water for wildlife • avoidance of invasive species • shared tools, sheds and garden facilities in multi-household settings • clothes drying, bicycle repair and outdoor work spaces • lighting that limits glare and unnecessary ecological impact. Construction-phase protection Require: • erosion and sediment controls before excavation • stockpile and washout locations • tree protection fencing before machinery arrives • no waste, paint or concrete wash into stormwater • topsoil salvage and reuse • protected tank and pipe entries • permanent surface falls and overflow verified before handover • landscape establishment and maintenance responsibility.

chunks.text: Construction-phase protection Require: • erosion and sediment controls before excavation • stockpile and washout locations • tree protection fencing before machinery arrives • no waste, paint or concrete wash into stormwater • topsoil salvage and reuse • protected tank and pipe entries • permanent surface falls and overflow verified before handover • landscape establishment and maintenance responsibility. Water commissioning • confirm every downpipe and overflow destination • test charged lines and visible leaks • verify tank isolation, backflow and labels • operate pump, mains backup and low-level mode

chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 58 • clean screens and first-flush devices • test irrigation zones and rain/soil controls • confirm site falls in rain or with controlled testing • provide maintenance intervals and lawful discharge plans. DECISION Do not size a tank from roof area alone. Match catchment, monthly rainfall, demand, drought objective, available space, pump energy, maintenance and overflow.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 59 Climate Resilience: Heat, Smoke, Fire, Flood, Storm and Outage Resilience means reducing harm, remaining safely habitable where possible and recovering faster. It begins with site selection and passive protection, not emergency equipment alone. Hazard design must use current mapping, qualified advice and local emergency guidance.

chunks.text: protection • reduce internal heat gains • place bedrooms in protected zones • create secure openings for useful night air where climate permits • provide fans and efficient conditioning • create a small well-insulated cool retreat that can be conditioned efficiently • select a light or high-reflectance roof where appropriate • protect equipment and occupants during grid outage • use future weather and heatwave sequences in modelling where available. Night purge is ineffective when outdoor air remains hotter, very humid, smoky or unsafe. Controls should compare indoor and outdoor conditions rather than assuming windows should always open at night. chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 60 Bushfire There is no single material or gadget that guarantees survival. Risk reduction combines: • correct site assessment and bushfire attack level • separation from hazards and managed fuel • access and evacuation • water and utilities • building siting and form • ember-resistant roofs, gutters, vents, gaps and subfloors • protected openings and glazing appropriate to exposure • compliant materials and construction • landscape and maintenance • household emergency plan. Current Australian guidance states that construction to the relevant bushfire standard reduces risk but cannot guarantee survival. Leaving early is the safest option when emergency authorities advise it. Airtightness and ember resistance can align, but normal ventilation and fire-mode closure must both be designed.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Leaving early is the safest option when emergency authorities advise it. Airtightness and ember resistance can align, but normal ventilation and fire-mode closure must both be designed. Do not add unapproved mesh or seals that compromise required ventilation, drainage, egress or equipment operation. Where risk remains, assess: • design flood level plus appropriate allowance • water velocity, debris and structural loads • safe access and evacuation • floor and service levels

Do not raise one property or build a wall without checking impacts on neighbours and lawful flow paths. After flooding, electricity, structure, sewage, mould and asbestos may make entry unsafe. Check: • continuous load path from roof to foundation • tie-downs and connections • roof edges, flashings and penetrations • garage doors and large openings • impact protection where required • debris and outdoor equipment restraint • gutter, overflow and intense-rain capacity • trees and falling limbs • solar and equipment attachment • safe room or refuge advice. Retrofit options vary by building type and region. The national resilience library provides evidence-based actions for storm, cyclone, flood and bushfire.

chunks.text: Retrofit options vary by building type and region. The national resilience library provides evidence-based actions for storm, cyclone, flood and bushfire. Sources: [1] www.nema.gov.au/our-work/resilience/hazards-insurance-partnership Outage-ready design First reduce critical demand. Then define: • essential medical, refrigeration, communications, lighting and water loads • desired hours or days of operation • summer and winter critical room • battery energy capacity and power output • solar recharge conditions • approved islanding and changeover • generator fuel, ventilation, noise and carbon monoxide safety where used • manual overrides and offline operation • safe connection - never backfeed a home through an improvised lead. Test the outage mode before it is needed. Label essential circuits, isolation and restart procedure. Keep a non-electronic copy.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 62 Annual resilience maintenance • clear gutters and ember traps safely • maintain vegetation and separation • test shutters, seals and accessible vents • inspect roof, flashings, drainage and tank overflow • service cooling, ventilation and filters • review clean-air room and medication plan • test battery or approved backup operation • update emergency contacts and evacuation plan • check insurance sum insured, exclusions and hazard changes • photograph property condition and key assets. SAFETY Building resilience supports emergency planning; it does not replace it. Follow emergency services and health authorities during an event.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 63 Accessibility, Adaptability and Different Ways to Live A home that can change use lasts longer, serves more people and avoids disruptive future building work. Accessibility is not a niche feature: injury, pregnancy, ageing, deliveries, children, visitors and care can all change how space is used.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Accessibility is not a niche feature: injury, pregnancy, ageing, deliveries, children, visitors and care can all change how space is used. Low-cost features to decide early • a continuous step-free path from boundary, parking or garage to an entrance • a weather-protected entry with manoeuvring space • door and corridor widths that support mobility aids and moving furniture • slip-resistant, even surfaces and controlled thresholds • lever handles and reachable switches, controls and outlets • at least one usable toilet and shower on the entry level • wall reinforcement for future rails • shower and floor falls that preserve access and waterproofing • ground-floor room able to become a bedroom • good lighting without glare and visible contrast at hazards • accessible storage and work surfaces • space for a future lift or stair aid where a multilevel design is justified.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Low-cost features to decide early • a continuous step-free path from boundary, parking or garage to an entrance • a weather-protected entry with manoeuvring space • door and corridor widths that support mobility aids and moving furniture • slip-resistant, even surfaces and controlled thresholds • lever handles and reachable switches, controls and outlets • at least one usable toilet and shower on the entry level • wall reinforcement for future rails • shower and floor falls that preserve access and waterproofing • ground-floor room able to become a bedroom • good lighting without glare and visible contrast at hazards • accessible storage and work surfaces • space for a future lift or stair aid where a multilevel design is justified. Current National Construction Code livable-housing provisions cover relevant new dwellings, but adoption and variations differ across jurisdictions.

chunks.text: Current National Construction Code livable-housing provisions cover relevant new dwellings, but adoption and variations differ across jurisdictions. Designing only to the legal minimum may not meet a particular person's needs. An occupational therapist, access consultant or other competent adviser can translate individual needs into dimensions and details. Sources: [1] ncc.abcb.gov.au/editions/ncc-2022/adopted/volume-two/h-class-1-an... [2] www.yourhome.gov.au/live-adapt/liveable-adaptable-home Flexible room design A flexible room needs more than a generic label.

[2] www.yourhome.gov.au/live-adapt/liveable-adaptable-home Flexible room design A flexible room needs more than a generic label. Check: • size and shape for bed, desk, care or living use • privacy and acoustic separation • daylight, shade and openable ventilation • thermal control as a separately occupied zone • access to bathroom without stairs • storage that supports changing use • power, data and lighting locations • whether future plumbing would create major structural or waterproofing work • compliant egress and smoke-alarm implications. Movable furniture and storage are often more adaptable than fixed joinery.

Movable furniture and storage are often more adaptable than fixed joinery. Structural walls and wet services should be placed so future changes do not require dismantling the whole home.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 64 Multigenerational and interdependent living Options range from shared rooms within one household to two self-contained dwellings. Consider: • shared versus private kitchen, living, laundry and outdoor space • line of sight for care versus privacy • acoustic separation and different sleep schedules • step-free routes between households • independent temperature and ventilation control • shared energy, water, internet, waste, vehicles and tools • private address, mail and emergency access • secure separation if household relationships change • fair allocation of bills, maintenance and capital works • legal rights to occupy, sell, inherit or withdraw. A large existing home may be reconfigured into two smaller homes without adding area, subject to approvals.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Consider: • shared versus private kitchen, living, laundry and outdoor space • line of sight for care versus privacy • acoustic separation and different sleep schedules • step-free routes between households • independent temperature and ventilation control • shared energy, water, internet, waste, vehicles and tools • private address, mail and emergency access • secure separation if household relationships change • fair allocation of bills, maintenance and capital works • legal rights to occupy, sell, inherit or withdraw. A large existing home may be reconfigured into two smaller homes without adding area, subject to approvals. This can improve space utilisation, support care and reduce per-person resource use. Fire separation, planning, services and legal structure are critical.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: This can improve space utilisation, support care and reduce per-person resource use. Fire separation, planning, services and legal structure are critical. Secondary dwellings, dual occupancy and subdivision Possible models include: • attached secondary suite • detached small dwelling • two dwellings on one title • dual occupancy with separate titles where allowed • conversion of one home into two lawful dwellings • cooperative or co-ownership model. Check local planning, minimum lot and open-space rules, parking, trees, private open space, solar access, overlooking, fire access, waste, service capacity, metering, title and finance before design. A physically separate room with a kitchenette is not automatically a lawful dwelling.

Collaborative housing and shared facilities Collaborative housing can preserve private homes while sharing selected assets: • guest rooms • large dining or gathering room • laundry or workshop • garden, tools and storage • vehicles and charging • care and play spaces • renewable generation and batteries. Shared space can reduce private dwelling area, but needs governance: • ownership and voting • booking and access

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide

The social model must be designed as carefully as the architecture.

Define responsibility for module joints and site services. Small homes and tiny dwellings Small homes reduce material and operational demand, but can be vulnerable to: • rapid overheating or cooling • high moisture per unit volume • inadequate storage and accessibility • loft sleeping with heat and evacuation risks • unapproved or non-compliant siting • limited ventilation when closed • condensation around compact wet areas • dependence on external shared space. Model and ventilate the actual volume. Provide safe egress, sanitation, structure, fire and weather protection. "On wheels" does not automatically remove planning or building obligations.

chunks.text: Model and ventilate the actual volume. Provide safe egress, sanitation, structure, fire and weather protection. "On wheels" does not automatically remove planning or building obligations. Design for separation and recombination Useful provisions include: • two logical entries without creating unsafe dead space • service zones that can be separately metered later • doors at a natural acoustic and fire separation line • two thermal-control zones

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 66 • a bathroom accessible from each future side • kitchens that can be added without long new drains • shared plant located for lawful access • outdoor and waste routes that do not cross private rooms. Do not build duplicate services unless the likely benefit exceeds upfront cost and material. Conduit, space and layout can preserve an option without installing everything. DECISION Adaptability means a credible low-disruption conversion path. A room described as flexible but lacking access, privacy, services, comfort or approval potential is not genuinely adaptable.

chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 67 Build the Right Project Team Residential performance crosses disciplines. One person may hold several competencies, but responsibilities must remain explicit. Registration and licensing differ by jurisdiction; check the current regulator.

chunks.text: That is not the same as comprehensive quality assurance, contract administration or verification of every performance detail. Builder due diligence • verify licence and entity name • check current insurance required by jurisdiction and project value • check regulator complaints or disciplinary history where available • check the contracting entity matches the quote, licence and bank details • speak to recent clients, including one with a defect or variation • inspect workmanship in membranes, windows, insulation and services, not only finishes • review financial and insolvency risk using lawful public records and professional advice • confirm site supervisor and expected workload • ask which trades will deliver the critical envelope and service details • confirm testing and correction are included.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Communication controls • one current drawing and specification register • written requests for information • numbered variations with cost, time and performance effect • site meeting minutes and action owners • photo register by location and date • defect register with closure evidence • no verbal substitution or concealed work approval • direct access for independent tester and inspector • secure owner copy of all final files. DECISION Choose the team that can show how a good design becomes a verified building. Design skill, construction skill and test skill are related but not interchangeable. Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/design-house [2] www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/build-house

chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 70 Documentation, Quotes, Contracts and Substitutions You cannot compare prices or enforce performance if the scope is ambiguous. Good documents convert design intent into exact assemblies, values, locations, responsibilities and tests.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Good documents convert design intent into exact assemblies, values, locations, responsibilities and tests. Minimum coordinated document set Depending on scope: • survey, site and demolition plan • floor, roof and reflected ceiling plans • elevations and sections • structural and civil drawings • water, sewer and stormwater design • electrical, lighting and load schedule • heating, cooling and ventilation design • window and door schedule • insulation and air-barrier plan • critical junction details • finishes and fixtures schedule • landscape and tree-protection plan • energy model and certificate • hazard reports • accessibility requirements • specification • testing and commissioning plan • document register with revision and date. If a detail is performance-critical, do not leave it to a generic note.

chunks.text: Contract essentials to have reviewed Obtain independent legal advice appropriate to the jurisdiction and contract. Topics include: • exact parties, licence and property • complete contract documents and precedence • scope, price and tax • deposit and progress claims tied to completed work • start, completion, extensions and delay • variations only in writing before work • prime cost and provisional-sum adjustment • latent conditions and hazardous materials • owner-supplied items • access for inspections and testing • hold points and notice before concealment • substitution approval • defects, rectification, retest and retention • practical completion criteria • warranties, insurance and statutory rights • suspension, termination and dispute process • intellectual property and owner access to drawings, models and data.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Consumer guarantees generally require services to be delivered with due care and skill, fit for a stated purpose in applicable circumstances, and within a reasonable time if none is agreed. The fit-for-purpose guarantee has an exception for qualified architect or engineer professional services. State building laws add contract, warranty, insurance and dispute rules. Do not rely on a warranty document as the full statement of rights. Sources: [1] www.accc.gov.au/consumers/buying-products-and-services/consumer-r... [2] www.accc.gov.au/consumers/buying-products-and-services/contracts [3] www.accc.gov.au/consumers/buying-products-and-services/warranties Control substitutions Require a written proposal before order or installation with: • reason for substitution • exact proposed assembly or item • cost and program change • evidence against every specified performance criterion

"Equivalent" must mean equivalent across the project requirements, not one headline value. A window with the same U-value but different solar gain can change overheating; insulation with the same nominal R-value but different thickness can affect cavities; a membrane with different vapour properties can change condensation risk.

Hold points Contractual notice should be required before: • excavation and footing placement • slab membranes, insulation and services are covered • wall and roof membranes are concealed • windows and flashings are trimmed or clad • service penetrations are sealed and lined • insulation is covered • waterproofing is tiled • preliminary airtightness repair access closes • final completion and payment. State who attends, notice period, acceptance evidence and consequence of covering without inspection.

Payment and evidence Before approving a progress claim, check: • claimed stage is complete under the contract definition • materials are installed or securely owned as the contract requires • required inspection and test evidence is received • defects affecting the stage are recorded • variations are approved and priced • current drawings were used • statutory certificates are available when due. Do not use payment as improvised technical leverage; use the contract process and professional advice. Record management Keep: • signed contract and all schedules • complete tender and clarification • approved drawings and every revision • meeting minutes and correspondence

Prestart Confirm: • approved current documents on site • project brief and performance schedule • roles and contact paths • survey, boundaries and set-out control • hazard reports and site safety • retained trees and materials protected • erosion and sediment controls • sample and shop-drawing approval • air, water, vapour and insulation layers understood by relevant trades • testing dates, access and failure process • photo and defect registers established.

chunks.text: Hold a performance meeting with builder, supervisor, key carpentry, window, insulation, electrical, plumbing, mechanical and membrane trades. Walk through junctions and penetrations before work. Groundworks, footing and slab Check before cover or pour: • excavation and founding conditions against engineering • unexpected water, fill or contamination • termite management and inspection zones • under-slab membrane continuity and penetrations • slab insulation and thermal breaks where specified • reinforcement, setdowns and service positions • accessible entry levels and future falls • drainage and overland flow • photographic survey with dimensions. After pour, record levels, damage, penetrations and changes before framing. Frame and structure • dimensions, orientation and openings • bracing, tie-down and connections • straightness and moisture condition

Water and weather layers Inspect: • roof underlay, flashings, penetrations and valleys • wall membrane laps, direction, tears and taped joints where specified • cavities, weeps and drainage exits • window sill, jamb and head flashing • cladding clearances to roofs, decks, paving and ground • balcony and deck interfaces • gutters, downpipes and overflow • compatibility of sealants, tapes, membranes and substrates. Do not use internal sealant as the primary repair for an external water path.

chunks.text: Water and weather layers Inspect: • roof underlay, flashings, penetrations and valleys • wall membrane laps, direction, tears and taped joints where specified • cavities, weeps and drainage exits • window sill, jamb and head flashing • cladding clearances to roofs, decks, paving and ground • balcony and deck interfaces • gutters, downpipes and overflow • compatibility of sealants, tapes, membranes and substrates. Do not use internal sealant as the primary repair for an external water path. Water control should shed and drain outward. Conduct a preliminary blower-door test while repair access remains. Protect finished membranes from following trades. chunks.text: Insulation hold point Inspect every room before lining: • correct type, thickness and location • complete coverage at corners, noggings, lintels and services • no gaps, compression, folding or wind exposure • close fit around wiring and plumbing without unsafe contact • required clearances around heat and electrical equipment • wall, roof, floor and internal zoning insulation as scheduled • continuous rigid layers and taped/sealed joints where required • support under suspended floors • moisture-damaged material replaced • delivery labels and installed photos retained. Ceiling spaces can contain live electrical hazards and unsafe access. Use competent installers and inspections. The government recommends a licensed electrician check wiring before insulation work.

chunks.text: Evidence quality A useful site record includes: • date, weather and stage • exact location • drawing and specification reference • photograph with scale and context • observed condition • acceptance criterion • responsible party and due date • correction photograph or test • closure by the appropriate reviewer. Do not rely on hundreds of unlabelled photos. Organise by room, elevation, stage and issue. If a test fails 1 Preserve raw test data and preparation record. 2 Confirm geometry, equipment and method. 3 Locate causes without damaging completed work unnecessarily. 4 Assign corrective work against the contract. 5 Assess whether correction affects moisture, fire, structure or services. 6 Repair using approved details and materials.

chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 80 Commissioning, Handover and the First Year Practical completion should mean the home and its systems have been demonstrated against the contract, not merely switched on. No single certificate proves all work is correct. Reconcile addresses, plan revisions, installed specifications and serialised equipment.

Common myths "A high star rating proves a high-quality build" No. A design rating models documented plans under standard assumptions.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Common myths "A high star rating proves a high-quality build" No. A design rating models documented plans under standard assumptions. Verify installation, airtightness, ventilation, systems and final specifications. "Airtight homes cannot breathe" Homes do not need random cracks. People need reliable ventilation. Seal unintended leaks and provide controlled outdoor air and exhaust. "Below one magic leakage number every home needs the same ventilation system" No. Airtightness is one input. Occupancy, volume, climate, moisture, outdoor air and natural-ventilation reliability also matter. Design ventilation for the actual building. "More insulation is always better" Continuity, climate, moisture, thermal bridges, clearances and installation matter. Insulation can be misplaced or create risk in a poorly designed assembly. "Double glazing is automatically the best first retrofit" Not always.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: Design ventilation for the actual building. "More insulation is always better" Continuity, climate, moisture, thermal bridges, clearances and installation matter. Insulation can be misplaced or create risk in a poorly designed assembly. "Double glazing is automatically the best first retrofit" Not always. Shade, seals, coverings, air leakage and insulation may deliver more value first. When replacing, assess the whole window, orientation and installation. "Thermal mass makes every home comfortable" Only when it receives and releases heat at useful times. In the wrong climate or location, it can prolong discomfort. "A thermal camera can see inside walls" It records surface radiation. Patterns require suitable conditions and confirmation. "Mould testing tells me whether my home is safe" Routine household testing generally lacks health guideline values for interpretation.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: In the wrong climate or location, it can prolong discomfort. "A thermal camera can see inside walls" It records surface radiation. Patterns require suitable conditions and confirmation. "Mould testing tells me whether my home is safe" Routine household testing generally lacks health guideline values for interpretation. Find and correct dampness and mould sources; obtain professional help where needed. "Natural material means low carbon and healthy" No. Check complete assembly, quantities, processing, binders, emissions, fire, moisture, durability and end of life.

chunks.sourceTitle: Home by Evidence: Australian Home Design and Retrofit Guide
chunks.text: HOME BY EVIDENCE AUSTRALIAN HOME PERFORMANCE FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 92 "A large solar system makes a large new home sustainable" Generation can reduce operational grid energy. It does not erase material use, land, maintenance or upfront emissions. Reduce demand and area first. "Demolition and rebuild is always more efficient" New fabric may perform better operationally, but demolition and replacement create upfront impacts. Compare deep retrofit, partial retention and rebuild using one brief and boundary. "Renovation is always greener" Not if the building cannot safely, durably or reasonably meet the brief, or if repeated work consumes more resources. Investigate and compare. "Compliance is best practice" Compliance is a legal minimum in a jurisdiction and approval context.

chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 8 Start Here: Change the Trip Before Changing the Car This is an independent, Australia-wide field guide for households, renters, apartment residents, drivers, riders, workplaces and community decision-makers. It contains no company endorsement, brand, vehicle model, product listing, current price, sales lead, charging-network promotion, installer referral, advertisement or commercial relationship. The central rule is: solve mobility first, then size the vehicle and charging system to the journeys that remain. Replacing a large combustion vehicle with a large electric vehicle can reduce operational emissions, but it does not remove congestion, road trauma, parking demand, tyre wear, resource use or the cost of owning a car.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: The central rule is: solve mobility first, then size the vehicle and charging system to the journeys that remain. Replacing a large combustion vehicle with a large electric vehicle can reduce operational emissions, but it does not remove congestion, road trauma, parking demand, tyre wear, resource use or the cost of owning a car. A smaller vehicle, fewer trips, shared travel, public transport, walking, cycling or an electrically assisted cycle may sometimes deliver more benefit for less money and material. DECISION Do not begin with a vehicle catalogue. Begin with 8 to 12 weeks of actual trips, parking access, passenger and load needs, home electricity constraints, public-charging alternatives and the household budget. The avoid, shift, improve hierarchy Level Question Practical options Avoid Can the trip or vehicle-kilometres be removed?

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Begin with 8 to 12 weeks of actual trips, parking access, passenger and load needs, home electricity constraints, public-charging alternatives and the household budget. The avoid, shift, improve hierarchy Level Question Practical options Avoid Can the trip or vehicle-kilometres be removed? Combine errands, remote access, local services, delivery consolidation, school or workplace planning Shift Can the trip use a lower-impact mode? Walk, mobility aid, bicycle, electrically assisted cycle, public transport, shared ride, car share or rail for long trips Improve What is the least vehicle needed for trips that remain? Smaller and more efficient vehicle, better occupancy, efficient driving, battery-electric power, renewable charging Integrate Can transport support the home and electricity system?

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Walk, mobility aid, bicycle, electrically assisted cycle, public transport, shared ride, car share or rail for long trips Improve What is the least vehicle needed for trips that remain? Smaller and more efficient vehicle, better occupancy, efficient driving, battery-electric power, renewable charging Integrate Can transport support the home and electricity system? Solar-timed charging, managed demand, workplace charging, and compatible vehicle-to-load or bidirectional systems Electrification is not an all-or-nothing identity. A household may use a small electric vehicle for most travel, retain occasional access to a different vehicle for towing, use an electrically assisted cycle for local trips, or postpone purchase while improving parking and charging access. The correct transition is the one that safely performs the required journeys with the lowest whole-of-life burden.

chunks.text: SAFETY Never use a power board or ordinary extension lead for routine vehicle charging. Do not charge equipment that is damaged, wet, recalled, incompatible or connected through a loose or heat-damaged outlet. Fixed charging work belongs to a licensed electrician. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/owning-electric-vehicle/elect... [2] www.fire.nsw.gov.au/fire-safety/home-fire-safety/battery-and-char... [3] www.productsafety.gov.au/consumers/be-safe-around-the-home/safely... A practical transition sequence 1 Record travel. Log every trip, purpose, distance, passengers, load, parking, departure flexibility and exceptional need. 2 Remove avoidable kilometres. Combine trips and test alternatives before buying. 3 Define the hard cases. Identify the longest frequent day, repeated highway travel, towing, remote travel, accessibility needs and emergency obligations.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: 3 Define the hard cases. Identify the longest frequent day, repeated highway travel, towing, remote travel, accessibility needs and emergency obligations. 4 Audit charging. Check the actual parking bay, electrical supply, renter or strata permissions, public backup and travel corridor. 5 Set performance gates. Required usable range, efficiency, charge rate, connector, payload, towing, safety, accessibility, warranty and service support. 6 Compare whole-of-life outcomes. Purchase or lease cost, interest, depreciation, insurance, registration, energy, tyres, servicing, repairs, charging equipment and resale risk. 7 Test the workflow. Trial the intended mode or vehicle type and practise a representative charging or travel day where possible. 8 Buy only what passes. Reject options that depend on optimistic range, unavailable charging, uncertain permissions or unsupported tax claims.

chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 10 Five questions that prevent most mistakes • Where will it charge on an ordinary week, and who legally controls that place and electricity supply? • How many kilowatt-hours must be added between arriving and the next departure, rather than how fast could charging theoretically be? • What is the longest frequent day in poor conditions, not the single longest trip ever imagined? • Which rare jobs can be hired, shared, delivered or handled differently instead of enlarging the everyday vehicle? • What happens if the home charger, preferred public site, mobile service, payment method or vehicle is unavailable?

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: What this guide covers The guide covers battery-electric, plug-in hybrid, non-plug-in hybrid and hydrogen-fuel-cell terminology; trip and parking audits; new and used vehicle decisions; range and efficiency; batteries; AC and DC charging; home electrical readiness; solar and tariffs; renters and strata; public charging; road trips; towing and remote travel; maintenance; emergencies; vehicle-to-load, vehicle-to-home and vehicle-to-grid; tax, finance, insurance and incentives; fleets and workplaces; electrically assisted cycles and scooters; lifecycle impacts; consumer rights; decision matrices; worksheets; calculations; myths; and current public sources. It does not tell the reader which company, model, charging operator, finance provider, insurer, installer or app to select.

chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 11 Vehicle Types and the Language That Matters Labels are useful only when they predict energy source, charging behaviour, emissions and household fit. Ask what powers the wheels, whether the vehicle plugs in, how far it travels on electricity, what happens when the battery is low and which energy inputs must be paid for. Passenger vehicle types Type Energy path Must plug in?

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Best fit Main caution Battery-electric vehicle Grid or local electricity charges a traction battery that powers electric motors Yes Regular access to suitable charging and trips within the charging plan Parking and charging access are part of the purchase Plug-in hybrid electric vehicle A rechargeable traction battery and combustion fuel can power travel Yes, to gain the intended electric benefit Daily trips fit within useful electric range but unusual trips need another energy source Without frequent charging it can carry two powertrains while using substantial fuel Non-plug-in hybrid Combustion fuel supplies all net journey energy; braking and engine operation charge a smaller battery No Reduced fuel use where plugging in is unavailable It is not an externally charged electric vehicle and still depends on fuel Fuel-cell electric vehicle Stored hydrogen feeds a fuel cell, which supplies

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: electricity to an electric drivetrain Refuels rather than plugs in Specialised routes or fleets with dependable hydrogen supply Sparse infrastructure and fuel pathway make it a niche household choice Internal-combustion vehicle Petrol, diesel or another fuel is burned in an engine No Legacy or exceptional cases during transition Tailpipe emissions, fuel cost, noise and more mechanical service items Do not confuse these terms • Battery capacity, kWh: how much energy the traction battery can store. Distinguish gross capacity from usable capacity. • Power, kW: the rate at which energy is delivered or used. Charger power is not battery capacity. • Energy consumption, Wh/km or kWh/100 km: efficiency.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Distinguish gross capacity from usable capacity. • Power, kW: the rate at which energy is delivered or used. Charger power is not battery capacity. • Energy consumption, Wh/km or kWh/100 km: efficiency. Lower consumption generally means more distance from the same stored energy. • State of charge, percent: current stored energy relative to the usable range defined by the control system. • State of health, percent: an estimate of remaining battery capability compared with a reference state. The calculation method matters. • AC charging: alternating current reaches the vehicle and its onboard charger converts it for the battery. • DC charging: charging equipment supplies direct current to the battery under vehicle control, usually at higher power. • EVSE: the equipment that safely controls and supplies electricity to a plug-in vehicle.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: The calculation method matters. • AC charging: alternating current reaches the vehicle and its onboard charger converts it for the battery. • DC charging: charging equipment supplies direct current to the battery under vehicle control, usually at higher power. • EVSE: the equipment that safely controls and supplies electricity to a plug-in vehicle. It is often casually called a charger. • Onboard charger: the vehicle component that limits AC charging power. • Charging curve: DC power changes as battery temperature and state of charge change; a peak number is not a session average. • Regenerative braking: the motor recovers some kinetic energy while slowing. It cannot recover all energy and does not replace efficient driving.

chunks.text: typically 7 to 22 kW, and Level 3 as DC charging from about 25 to 350 kW. Labels vary between documents, so compare the actual kW, voltage, phase, connector and vehicle limit rather than relying on the word fast. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/electric-vehicle-basics/defin... [2] www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/owning-electric-vehicle/elect... Range labels need context An official test result gives a controlled basis for comparison. It is not a promise for every trip.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Range labels need context An official test result gives a controlled basis for comparison. It is not a promise for every trip. Real range depends on: • starting state of charge and the vehicle's usable capacity; • speed, acceleration, wind and road surface; • temperature and battery conditioning; • cabin heating, cooling and demisting; • hills, payload, roof loads, trailers and tyre pressure; • traffic, stops and opportunity for regenerative braking; • battery age and condition; • reserve held for an unavailable charger or detour. Compare vehicles on energy consumption as well as range. A very large battery can produce a long nominal range while increasing mass, cost and material use. A more efficient vehicle may add more kilometres per hour from the same home circuit and recover useful range faster at a constrained site.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: A very large battery can produce a long nominal range while increasing mass, cost and material use. A more efficient vehicle may add more kilometres per hour from the same home circuit and recover useful range faster at a constrained site. Charging speed has four ceilings Actual charging power is no higher than the lowest current limit created by: 1 the electrical supply and circuit; 2 the charging equipment and cable; 3 the vehicle's AC onboard charger or DC charging capability; 4 the battery management system at the current state of charge and temperature. A nominal 22 kW AC unit does not make a vehicle with a 7 kW AC limit charge at 22 kW. A nominal 350 kW DC unit does not make a vehicle whose battery accepts less charge at 350 kW. Shared public sites may divide power between vehicles.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: A nominal 350 kW DC unit does not make a vehicle whose battery accepts less charge at 350 kW. Shared public sites may divide power between vehicles. Charging commonly slows at high state of charge, so the time from 80 to 100 percent can be disproportionately long.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 13 Energy losses are normal The energy measured at the wall is higher than the increase stored in the battery because charging electronics, battery conditioning and other systems use energy. Low-power charging can spend a greater share on fixed overheads in some conditions. For household cost planning, use measured wall energy when available; otherwise apply a transparent loss allowance and later replace it with actual data. CALCULA TION Estimated wall energy = battery energy added divided by assumed charging efficiency. Example: adding 36 kWh to the battery at an assumed 90 percent efficiency requires about 40 kWh from the supply. The assumption is illustrative, not a specification. Driver-assistance language Electric power does not make a vehicle autonomous.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: The assumption is illustrative, not a specification. Driver-assistance language Electric power does not make a vehicle autonomous. Treat lane support, adaptive speed control, parking aids, monitoring and remote features according to their documented operational design domain. The licensed driver remains responsible unless Australian law explicitly establishes otherwise. Keep software current, but review release notes and do not assume an update makes a feature safe outside its defined conditions.

A neutral specification line Record each candidate without its name: Body size and mass; seats; accessibility; payload; rated towing and towball limits; usable battery; official range and test cycle; Wh/km; AC acceptance; DC charging curve or representative time window; inlet; supplied cables; tyre size; safety result and date; warranty terms; service requirements; parts and repair support; data and connectivity requirements; bidirectional functions; total delivered cost. chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 14 Audit the Journeys, Parking and Electricity A useful vehicle brief comes from observed life, not averages. Record enough weeks to include work, school, caring, shopping, recreation and a busy weekend. Add seasonal and exceptional trips separately rather than letting a once-a-year journey dictate the everyday vehicle.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Record enough weeks to include work, school, caring, shopping, recreation and a busy weekend. Add seasonal and exceptional trips separately rather than letting a once-a-year journey dictate the everyday vehicle. Travel log For each trip record: • date, origin, destination and purpose; • distance and total distance that day; • departure and return time; • passengers, child seats, mobility equipment, tools, pets or luggage; • payload and whether roof load or trailer was actually used; • parking location and duration at home, work and destination; • whether walking, cycling, public transport, sharing or combining could replace it; • weather, road type and speed where they materially affect energy; • how inconvenient a delay or charging stop would be.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: After 8 to 12 weeks calculate: Measure Why it matters Median daily kilometres Shows the ordinary day without being distorted by rare trips 90th or 95th percentile daily kilometres Useful range design point for frequent long days Longest repeated day Tests range and overnight recharge requirement Longest single trip A travel-planning problem, not automatically a battery-sizing target Kilometres replaceable by another mode Often the cheapest transition action Hours parked at home, work and destinations Reveals charging opportunities Days with towing, high payload or remote travel Determines whether a separate solution is justified Separate needs from preferences Statement Test We need a very long-range vehicle How many days per year exceed a smaller vehicle's practical range, and what alternatives exist?

chunks.text: We need the fastest home charger How much energy must be restored before the next departure? We need a large vehicle What actual passengers, payload, dimensions or tow ratings require it? We cannot charge at home Is there a lawful outlet, dedicated circuit, shared building plan, workplace option or destination routine? Public charging will cover everything Are the required connectors, hours, redundancy, accessibility and payment methods verified? A plug-in hybrid removes charging risk Will it actually be plugged in most days, and how much fuel will it use after electric range is depleted? Parking audit Record each candidate parking place:

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 15 • exclusive title, leased space, common property, visitor space, street or workplace; • distance from switchboard and likely cable route; • walls, columns, doors, fire egress, accessible paths and vehicle orientation; • indoor, outdoor, flood-prone, coastal, exposed or vandalism risk; • mobile or network coverage if equipment depends on connectivity; • whether another vehicle blocks access; • future second vehicle or shared-use requirements; • physical protection from impact without obstructing access; • a place to hang the cable so it cannot be driven over or create a trip hazard. Photograph the parking bay, path to the electrical board, board labels, meter arrangement and any existing outlet. Do not remove covers or enter electrical enclosures.

chunks.text: Photograph the parking bay, path to the electrical board, board labels, meter arrangement and any existing outlet. Do not remove covers or enter electrical enclosures. Electricity audit Gather 12 months of electricity bills and, where accessible, interval data. Record: • supply phase and main-switch rating, subject to electrician verification; • switchboard age, space and safety-switch protection; • major simultaneous loads such as cooking, water heating, space conditioning, pool equipment and household battery charging; • rooftop generation capacity and typical surplus by season; • tariff structure, demand charge, controlled load and export terms; • existing automation and whether it fails safely if internet access is lost; • likely charging window and minimum energy needed in that window.
