SAFETY A label, photograph or bill does not establish that a circuit is safe for sustained charging. The electrician must verify the installation, maximum demand, protection, earthing, cable route and equipment requirements.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: SAFETY A label, photograph or bill does not establish that a circuit is safe for sustained charging. The electrician must verify the installation, maximum demand, protection, earthing, cable route and equipment requirements. Convert travel to charging demand Use a conservative consumption value for the actual route and season. If only a test value is known, add an explicit allowance for highway speed, cold or hot weather, hills, load and charging losses. Example only: • daily travel: 52 km; • assumed road consumption: 190 Wh/km; • battery energy used: 52 x 190 / 1000 = 9.88 kWh; • assumed wall-to-battery efficiency: 90 percent; • wall energy: 9.88 / 0.90 = about 11.0 kWh; • charging window: 10 hours; • average power needed: 11.0 / 10 = about 1.1 kW. This does not prove a standard outlet is suitable.

chunks.text: Example only: • daily travel: 52 km; • assumed road consumption: 190 Wh/km; • battery energy used: 52 x 190 / 1000 = 9.88 kWh; • assumed wall-to-battery efficiency: 90 percent; • wall energy: 9.88 / 0.90 = about 11.0 kWh; • charging window: 10 hours; • average power needed: 11.0 / 10 = about 1.1 kW. This does not prove a standard outlet is suitable. It shows why daily energy and available time, rather than maximum charger power, should drive the electrical design.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 16 Resilience audit Ask what happens during: • a local power outage; • a charger fault or cable failure; • a blocked or occupied public bay; • mobile data or payment failure; • extreme heat, flood, bushfire smoke or road closure; • evacuation with a partially charged vehicle; • household medical, disability or caring needs; • remote travel where recovery is slow. A resilience plan may include keeping a practical minimum state of charge, having two independently powered public alternatives, carrying the correct AC cable, retaining a physical payment fallback where possible, downloading route information, and agreeing on a non-electric transport fallback. It should not involve unsafe improvised wiring or charging a damaged vehicle.

A vehicle that fails access, payload, charging, safety or support is not rescued by a lower advertised payment or a larger display.

Do not assume a roof box or trailer has no range consequence.

chunks.text: CALCULA TION Total ownership cost = acquisition and finance + energy + insurance and registration + equipment + maintenance and repairs + other operating costs - realistic resale value - verified incentives. Use low, central and high cases. An advertised weekly lease deduction is not the whole cost. Request the underlying vehicle price, finance rate or method, fees, term, residual, inclusions, exclusions, early-termination outcome, end-of-lease options, insurance assumptions and effect on payroll or benefits. Tax outcomes depend on the vehicle, price, date, employment arrangement and personal circumstances.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: New purchase checklist • Obtain a written drive-away figure and itemised contract before paying. • Record build or compliance date, odometer, promised equipment and delivery condition. • Confirm which charging cables and portable equipment are included. • Read the full vehicle, traction-battery and accessory warranties. • Identify warranty exclusions for storage, charging, towing, water damage, modification and commercial use. • Confirm service intervals, time limits and required inspections. • Check safety recalls and rectification before handover. • Verify charging inlet, AC rate and DC performance against the intended network and home design. • Reject pressure to treat an expiring incentive or delivery estimate as guaranteed. • Keep advertisements, representations, order, invoice, finance documents, inspection report and handover record.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Lease or subscription decision Ask: • Who owns the vehicle, charging equipment and accessories at each stage? • Who carries damage, excess-kilometre, tyre and residual-value risk?

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 19 • Can the vehicle be retained after changing job or address? • What happens during extended repair or battery-warranty assessment? • Are energy, public charging, servicing or insurance inclusions capped? • Does a bundled arrangement limit repair, insurer, energy-plan or charging choice? • What personal information is shared between employer, financier, administrator and service providers? Consumer-law baseline Automatic consumer guarantees apply to new and second-hand vehicles bought from a licensed dealer. A voluntary manufacturer or extended warranty is additional; it cannot remove those rights. The remedy depends on the failure and circumstances. Dealer, auction and private-sale protections differ, as do state statutory warranties and cooling-off rules.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: The remedy depends on the failure and circumstances. Dealer, auction and private-sale protections differ, as do state statutory warranties and cooling-off rules. If a material representation influenced the purchase, record it in writing before signing. If a problem appears, document symptoms, dates, warnings, diagnostic reports, downtime and communications; notify the selling dealer clearly; and request a remedy under the applicable rights rather than relying only on the warranty label. Sources: [1] www.accc.gov.au/consumers/specific-products-and-activities/new-an... [2] www.accc.gov.au/consumers/buying-products-and-services/consumer-r... [3] moneysmart.gov.au/loans/car-loans

chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 20 Used Electric Vehicle and Battery Check A used electric vehicle needs the ordinary inspection of any used car plus a traction-battery, charging, software and support assessment. Battery condition matters, but it is not the only expensive risk. Collision repair, tyres, suspension, water ingress, charge-port damage, an unsupported import or missing equipment can matter just as much.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 21 Ask the seller or inspector to document: • the source of the state-of-health value and software or instrument used; • battery temperature and state of charge during the test; • whether usable energy was measured or estimated; • cell or module imbalance and diagnostic warnings, where accessible; • charging power and whether the vehicle completes AC and DC sessions normally; • full-charge and low-charge behaviour without deliberately running the vehicle unsafe; • any battery repair or module replacement; • capacity-warranty threshold, test method and claim process. A controlled energy test can be more informative than a displayed range. Record wall energy, charging loss assumptions, start and end state of charge, route, weather and consumption. Do not infer usable capacity from one short drive.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Record wall energy, charging loss assumptions, start and end state of charge, route, weather and consumption. Do not infer usable capacity from one short drive. Charging compatibility Verify the actual inlet and cables physically. Older and imported vehicles may use connections that are less common on future routes. Check: • AC inlet type and phase support; • DC inlet type and corridor coverage; • maximum AC acceptance and representative DC performance; • whether adapters are approved for the exact vehicle and direction of energy flow; • whether a portable EVSE is Australian-compliant, undamaged and suitable for the outlet; • whether a socketed public AC cable is included; • whether navigation and charging-location data work locally without a paid service. Never assume a plug that physically fits provides a safe or supported conversion.

The lower purchase price must be compared with longer downtime, parts freight, unsupported software and lower resale demand.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 23 Range, Efficiency and Real-World Energy Range is an outcome of usable energy divided by consumption. The most useful number is not the largest range claim; it is the vehicle's likely consumption on the household's difficult repeated route, with a deliberate reserve.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: The most useful number is not the largest range claim; it is the vehicle's likely consumption on the household's difficult repeated route, with a deliberate reserve. Core calculations Calculation Formula Use Trip energy at battery kilometres x Wh/km / 1000 Energy used for the drive Theoretical distance usable battery kWh x 1000 / Wh/km Starting point before reserve and conditions Wall energy battery energy added / charging efficiency Electricity cost and circuit planning Kilometres added per hour charger kW x charging efficiency x 1000 / Wh/km Approximate AC replenishment rate Cost per 100 km wall kWh/100 km x tariff per kWh Comparable home-energy cost Example only: a vehicle using 185 Wh/km needs 18.5 kWh at the battery for 100 km. At 90 percent charging efficiency, it uses about 20.6 kWh at the wall.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Core calculations Calculation Formula Use Trip energy at battery kilometres x Wh/km / 1000 Energy used for the drive Theoretical distance usable battery kWh x 1000 / Wh/km Starting point before reserve and conditions Wall energy battery energy added / charging efficiency Electricity cost and circuit planning Kilometres added per hour charger kW x charging efficiency x 1000 / Wh/km Approximate AC replenishment rate Cost per 100 km wall kWh/100 km x tariff per kWh Comparable home-energy cost Example only: a vehicle using 185 Wh/km needs 18.5 kWh at the battery for 100 km. At 90 percent charging efficiency, it uses about 20.6 kWh at the wall. At a hypothetical tariff of 30 cents per kWh, the energy component is about $6.18 per 100 km. Replace every assumption with the bill, wall measurement and route data; do not treat the example as a price forecast.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: At a hypothetical tariff of 30 cents per kWh, the energy component is about $6.18 per 100 km. Replace every assumption with the bill, wall measurement and route data; do not treat the example as a price forecast. Why actual consumption changes Speed and air Aerodynamic demand rises quickly with speed. Highway travel, headwinds, roof racks, open windows and bulky loads can use materially more energy than lower-speed urban travel. Remove unused roof equipment and compare route time with energy consequences rather than assuming the fastest road is always best. Temperature Cold batteries may accept and deliver energy differently, and cabin heating consumes energy. Hot conditions can require cabin and battery cooling. Precondition while plugged in where the vehicle supports it, especially before a long journey or fast charge, but remember that preconditioning still uses energy.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Hot conditions can require cabin and battery cooling. Precondition while plugged in where the vehicle supports it, especially before a long journey or fast charge, but remember that preconditioning still uses energy. Hills and regenerative braking Climbing converts battery energy into gravitational potential energy. Descending can recover some energy, but conversion and traction limits prevent full recovery. A round trip over a hill still consumes net energy. Begin steep or remote climbs with reserve and identify charging alternatives before the descent creates a misleading range estimate. Payload, towing and tyres Passengers, cargo, trailer mass and aerodynamic drag increase consumption. Tyre pressure below specification increases resistance and can impair safety; excessive pressure can reduce grip and comfort. Use the vehicle placard and adjust for load as instructed.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Tyre pressure below specification increases resistance and can impair safety; excessive pressure can reduce grip and comfort. Use the vehicle placard and adjust for load as instructed. Replacement tyres must meet size, load and speed requirements. Rain, road and traffic Water displacement, standing water, rough surfaces and strong winds increase demand. Stop-start traffic can be efficient when regenerative braking is used smoothly, but congestion still consumes time and auxiliary energy. Build a route-specific range model 1 Start with the official consumption value on a known test cycle. 2 Obtain independent data for similar speed, climate and load without relying on one extreme report. 3 Add explicit allowances for highway speed, adverse temperature, wind, rain, hills, payload or trailer. 4 Reserve enough energy for charger failure, detour, queue, closed road or emergency.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 24 5 Recalculate using expected battery condition at the end of the ownership period. 6 Validate after purchase with repeated trips and wall-energy records. DECISION A range plan passes when the destination or next charger can still be reached after a realistic adverse-condition allowance and the planned reserve. It does not pass merely because the nominal test range exceeds the map distance. Practical reserve policy Choose a simple policy appropriate to consequence: • ordinary local driving: a modest minimum that still reaches a known alternative; • regional corridor: enough for the next independent charger or safe town; • remote, extreme weather or evacuation: a larger reserve based on road closure and recovery risk; • towing: reserve derived from a measured towing consumption, not solo-driving data.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: It does not pass merely because the nominal test range exceeds the map distance. Practical reserve policy Choose a simple policy appropriate to consequence: • ordinary local driving: a modest minimum that still reaches a known alternative; • regional corridor: enough for the next independent charger or safe town; • remote, extreme weather or evacuation: a larger reserve based on road closure and recovery risk; • towing: reserve derived from a measured towing consumption, not solo-driving data. The reserve is not always a fixed percentage. Twenty percent of a small battery and twenty percent of a large battery represent different kilometres. Convert the reserve to route-specific distance at the adverse consumption assumption. Understand the dashboard estimate The displayed distance remaining is an estimate based on recent or assumed consumption.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Convert the reserve to route-specific distance at the adverse consumption assumption. Understand the dashboard estimate The displayed distance remaining is an estimate based on recent or assumed consumption. A change in route, speed, weather or load can make it change rapidly. Use state of charge, distance to the next verified charger and recent consumption together. Do not chase the estimate by driving unpredictably or unsafely.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Use state of charge, distance to the next verified charger and recent consumption together. Do not chase the estimate by driving unpredictably or unsafely. Efficient driving without obstruction • Accelerate smoothly and anticipate traffic. • Use regenerative settings that remain predictable and comfortable. • Maintain a safe, steady speed appropriate to conditions. • Avoid unnecessary cabin extremes; use seat or local comfort features if suitable. • Precondition while connected when helpful. • Remove unnecessary load and external racks. • Maintain tyres and wheel alignment. • Plan stops where the battery reaches a useful fast-charging window rather than routinely waiting for 100 percent. Safety and arrival time constraints come first. Do not drive below a safe speed, coast illegally, follow closely or disable demisting to save energy.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Safety and arrival time constraints come first. Do not drive below a safe speed, coast illegally, follow closely or disable demisting to save energy. PHEV energy accounting For a plug-in hybrid, record electricity and liquid fuel together. A low fuel figure can hide electricity use, while a low electricity figure can mean the vehicle was rarely plugged in. Calculate: • electric kilometres and fuel-powered kilometres; • wall kWh and litres purchased; • total cost per 100 km; • tailpipe and fuel-lifecycle implications; • how often trips exceeded useful electric range; • whether the engine ran for heating, power or system maintenance.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 25 If regular charging is not available, compare the actual uncharged fuel use and carrying cost of two powertrains against simpler alternatives. Make a personal consumption envelope After three months, record best, typical and adverse Wh/km for: • local mixed travel; • motorway travel; • winter and summer; • full passenger or cargo load; • towing, if applicable. Use the adverse but repeatable value for critical planning and the typical value for annual cost. Keep the best result as a driving-efficiency reference, not a promise. Sources: [1] greenvehicleguide.gov.au/pages/LowAndZeroEmissionVehicles/Electri... [2] www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/owning-electric-vehicle/plann...

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 26 Traction Batteries: Health, Warranty and End of Life A traction battery is a managed system of cells, modules or structural pack components, sensors, cooling or heating equipment, isolation devices and control software. Its usable capacity is normally smaller than its gross chemical capacity because buffers protect operation. The household should manage it through the vehicle's approved controls, not by opening or modifying the pack.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Its usable capacity is normally smaller than its gross chemical capacity because buffers protect operation. The household should manage it through the vehicle's approved controls, not by opening or modifying the pack. What changes battery condition • calendar age, even when the vehicle is not driven; • energy throughput and charge-discharge cycles; • long periods at very high or very low state of charge; • cell temperature and time exposed to heat; • repeated high-power charging or discharging under conditions the control system cannot manage well; • deep discharge, long storage and failure to follow storage instructions; • collision, underbody impact, flood or water ingress; • manufacturing variation and control-software calibration. Battery degradation is not perfectly linear. An early change, long stable period and later decline can occur.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Battery degradation is not perfectly linear. An early change, long stable period and later decline can occur. A software update may change displayed usable energy or the estimate without representing sudden physical damage. Chemistry is not a verdict Different lithium-ion chemistries trade energy density, cost, thermal behaviour, power, cycle life and material composition. Pack design, thermal management, control limits, cell quality, repair approach and vehicle efficiency can matter as much as chemistry. Do not assume one chemistry is always safer, longer-lived or environmentally superior in every pack. Use the exact vehicle instructions for routine charge limits. Broad advice to remain around 20 to 80 percent may suit many vehicles, but some designs or balancing procedures require different periodic charging.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Use the exact vehicle instructions for routine charge limits. Broad advice to remain around 20 to 80 percent may suit many vehicles, but some designs or balancing procedures require different periodic charging. A long-trip charge to 100 percent can be reasonable when departure follows soon; prolonged hot storage at full charge may be less desirable.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: A long-trip charge to 100 percent can be reasonable when departure follows soon; prolonged hot storage at full charge may be less desirable. Practical care • Use charging equipment and adapters approved for the exact vehicle and connection. • Set a routine charge target consistent with the manual and daily need. • Schedule completion near departure when charging high for a trip. • Use battery preconditioning when documented and useful for conditions. • Avoid leaving the vehicle near empty for long periods. • Follow long-storage instructions and maintain the 12 V system. • Keep thermal-system service current. • Investigate repeated charging interruptions, unusual noises, odours, heat or warnings promptly. • Do not charge after collision, underbody strike, flood immersion or suspected battery damage until cleared.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 27 Read the battery warranty Record: Term Question Time and distance Which limit ends coverage first? Capacity threshold What measured capacity or state of health triggers a remedy? Test method Who performs the test, under what conditions and with which diagnostic method? Remedy Repair, module replacement, refurbished pack, replacement pack or another outcome? Result standard Must the remedy restore full capacity or only exceed the threshold? Exclusions Storage, modification, water, collision, charging, towing, commercial use or missed service? Transfer Does coverage transfer automatically to a later owner? Territory Does it apply to imports and interstate use? Costs Diagnosis, removal, transport, labour, hire vehicle and consequential loss?

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Territory Does it apply to imports and interstate use? Costs Diagnosis, removal, transport, labour, hire vehicle and consequential loss? Keep baseline evidence: delivery state, capacity report if supplied, charging records, service history and warning screenshots. A warranty promise does not replace consumer guarantees, but a clear history makes either pathway easier to use. Battery health monitoring Do not obsess over small short-term fluctuations. Track comparable observations: • measured wall energy for a known state-of-charge increase; • route consumption at similar temperature, speed and load; • full or controlled charge range under comparable conditions; • diagnostic state of health from a documented method; • charging curve or session time at comparable battery temperature; • cell imbalance or fault codes assessed by a qualified technician.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Battery health monitoring Do not obsess over small short-term fluctuations. Track comparable observations: • measured wall energy for a known state-of-charge increase; • route consumption at similar temperature, speed and load; • full or controlled charge range under comparable conditions; • diagnostic state of health from a documented method; • charging curve or session time at comparable battery temperature; • cell imbalance or fault codes assessed by a qualified technician. If range declines, first check tyres, alignment, weather, route, accessories, software, cabin conditioning and measurement method. Escalate persistent, unexplained or warning-associated changes. Repairability questions Before purchase ask whether the pack is serviced only as a complete unit or whether approved module, sealing, cooling, contactor or control repairs exist.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Escalate persistent, unexplained or warning-associated changes. Repairability questions Before purchase ask whether the pack is serviced only as a complete unit or whether approved module, sealing, cooling, contactor or control repairs exist. Also ask: • which workshops may isolate and diagnose it; • parts lead times and transport constraints; • whether structural damage requires pack replacement; • insurer policy for underbody impact and water exposure; • whether repaired packs receive a warranty; • how battery data and faults are supplied to the owner. End-of-life hierarchy 1 Keep the vehicle and battery in safe use while they remain fit for purpose. 2 Repair or remanufacture through an approved high-voltage pathway where safe and economic. 3 Reuse or repurpose only through a properly engineered, traceable system.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 28 4 Recover valuable materials through an authorised large-battery recycling pathway. 5 Never place a traction battery or loose lithium cells in household rubbish, kerbside recycling or ordinary scrap. Second-life use is not automatic. A battery unsuitable for vehicle power may still contain dangerous energy and needs electrical, structural, thermal and fire-safe engineering. Do not build a home battery from vehicle modules as a household project.

chunks.text: A battery unsuitable for vehicle power may still contain dangerous energy and needs electrical, structural, thermal and fire-safe engineering. Do not build a home battery from vehicle modules as a household project. Environmental claim check Ask whether a claim includes: • vehicle and battery manufacturing; • electricity generation by place and time; • fuel extraction, processing and transport for the comparison vehicle; • vehicle lifetime and kilometres; • vehicle size and efficiency; • repair, reuse, recycling and disposal; • non-exhaust particles from tyres, brakes and roads. The Australian Government advises that electric vehicles have higher manufacturing emissions than comparable combustion vehicles in typical cases, but lower total lifecycle emissions, with the electricity source affecting the result.

chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 29 Charging Fundamentals: Match Energy, Time and Place Charging is an energy-delivery task governed by the vehicle, equipment, circuit, battery and available time. The best charger is not automatically the highest-power unit. It is the lowest-complexity safe system that restores the required energy inside the parking window while protecting the building and leaving a workable backup.

chunks.text: Charging modes in practice Arrangement Typical power Suitable use Main checks Standard outlet plus compatible portable EVSE Up to about 2.4 kW Low daily kilometres, long parking window, travel backup where approved Outlet and circuit condition, dedicated use, weather, sustained load, cable management Dedicated single-phase AC EVSE Commonly about 7 kW Most detached-home overnight charging Maximum demand, circuit, protection, load management, cable route Dedicated three-phase AC EVSE Up to 22 kW where vehicle accepts it Larger daily energy need, fleets or special dwell times Three-phase supply, vehicle AC limit, demand and cost justification Public or destination AC Commonly up to 22 kW Long parking at work, accommodation or destinations Bring-your-own cable, access, time limit and billing DC fast or ultra-fast About 25 to 350 kW equipment rating Journey charging and high-utilisation

chunks.text: operations Vehicle curve, connector, battery temperature, site sharing, queue and price These ranges are categories, not guarantees. Actual delivery can be lower. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/owning-electric-vehicle/elect... AC charging chain For AC charging, power passes through the site supply, protective devices, circuit, EVSE, cable, vehicle inlet and onboard charger. The vehicle requests current only after safety communication. The lowest supported limit sets the rate. Rough single-phase values at 230 to 240 V: • 10 A is about 2.3 to 2.4 kW; • 15 A is about 3.5 to 3.6 kW; • 32 A is about 7.4 to 7.7 kW. These arithmetic values do not authorise an outlet, circuit or setting. Voltage varies, continuous-load requirements apply and electrical design belongs to a licensed electrician.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: These arithmetic values do not authorise an outlet, circuit or setting. Voltage varies, continuous-load requirements apply and electrical design belongs to a licensed electrician. DC charging and the curve DC equipment bypasses the vehicle's onboard AC charger, but the vehicle still controls safe battery charging. Power is usually strongest through a middle state-of-charge window and tapers toward full. Battery temperature, previous driving, preconditioning, shared site power and faults affect the session. Compare candidates using a useful metric such as time to add the energy required between planned stops, or minutes from a stated starting to ending state of charge under stated conditions. A peak kW number alone can be misleading. Plan with energy, not percentages Battery percentage does not equal the same energy across vehicles. To estimate energy added:

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 30 Energy added to battery = usable battery capacity x change in state of charge. Example only: a 60 kWh usable battery moved from 30 to 75 percent gains 60 x 0.45 = 27 kWh. At 90 percent charging efficiency, wall energy is about 30 kWh. If the effective average power is 6.8 kW, the session is about 4.4 hours. For public DC charging, use the session's average power, not its peak. Average power = energy delivered divided by elapsed charging time.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: For public DC charging, use the session's average power, not its peak. Average power = energy delivered divided by elapsed charging time. Cables and handling • Confirm the correct AC cable is carried when a socketed station requires one. • Check connector rating, vehicle inlet and equipment instructions. • Inspect plugs, pins, latch, cable sheath and strain relief before use. • Keep connectors off the ground and dry within their rating. • Fully uncoil portable leads and EVSE as instructed so heat can dissipate. • Route cables inside the bay, not across pedestrian paths. • Do not place a cable where it will be crushed by a wheel or door. • Replace damaged equipment through a qualified pathway; do not tape or splice it. • Keep covers closed and ports clean when disconnected. Portable charging boundaries A portable EVSE is a controlled charging device, not an invitation to use any socket.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Cables and handling • Confirm the correct AC cable is carried when a socketed station requires one. • Check connector rating, vehicle inlet and equipment instructions. • Inspect plugs, pins, latch, cable sheath and strain relief before use. • Keep connectors off the ground and dry within their rating. • Fully uncoil portable leads and EVSE as instructed so heat can dissipate. • Route cables inside the bay, not across pedestrian paths. • Do not place a cable where it will be crushed by a wheel or door. • Replace damaged equipment through a qualified pathway; do not tape or splice it. • Keep covers closed and ports clean when disconnected. Portable charging boundaries A portable EVSE is a controlled charging device, not an invitation to use any socket. Before regular charging, have the intended outlet and circuit assessed.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Portable charging boundaries A portable EVSE is a controlled charging device, not an invitation to use any socket. Before regular charging, have the intended outlet and circuit assessed. Avoid: • power boards, double adapters and ordinary extension leads; • loose, cracked, scorched, weather-exposed or untested outlets; • sharing the circuit with unpredictable loads; • travel adapters or plug conversions not approved for the equipment; • reducing current merely to conceal a defective installation; • suspending the control box by its plug or cable. If an outlet or plug becomes unusually hot, discoloured, smells hot, crackles or trips protection, stop charging and have it inspected.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: If an outlet or plug becomes unusually hot, discoloured, smells hot, crackles or trips protection, stop charging and have it inspected. Charging etiquette • Use a charging bay only while charging and comply with parking signs. • Choose the lowest-power facility that meets the dwell time, leaving journey chargers for vehicles that need them. • Move the vehicle promptly when the useful session is complete. • Do not unplug another vehicle unless the equipment and local practice clearly permit it. • Keep cables tidy and accessible routes clear. • Report faults accurately without claiming a bay is broken merely because the vehicle limited power. • At busy DC sites, leave before the slow final portion if enough energy has been added safely. • Do not use an accessible bay without entitlement, even if its charger is free.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 31 Backup design A charging plan should not depend on one point of failure. Identify: • another home or destination method that is electrically approved; • at least two public locations on critical routes where possible; • the correct cable and connector for each; • access hours, parking restrictions and likely dwell time; • an alternate payment or contact method; • a non-driving fallback for time-critical travel. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/owning-electric-vehicle/how-c... [2] www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/owning-electric-vehicle/plann...

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 32 Home Electrical Readiness and Charger Design Treat home charging as part of the whole electrical installation. The design must account for sustained load, other appliances, protection, cable route, outdoor exposure, future electrification, metering and the vehicle's actual energy requirement.

chunks.text: The design must account for sustained load, other appliances, protection, cable route, outdoor exposure, future electrification, metering and the vehicle's actual energy requirement. Information for the electrician Provide: • the vehicle's AC charging limit and inlet; • average and high daily kilometres; • wall energy to restore on an ordinary and difficult day; • arrival, departure and solar-availability windows; • desired location and parking orientation; • whether a second vehicle is likely; • bills and interval data where accessible; • rooftop solar, household battery, electric water heating, cooking, space conditioning, pool and workshop loads; • renter, strata or heritage permissions; • flood, weather, impact and cable-management risks; • any intended vehicle-to-home or vehicle-to-grid future use, clearly labelled as future and unverified.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Electrical assessment scope The licensed electrician should determine: • supply type, service capacity and network constraints; • switchboard condition, main switch, protective devices, earthing and available space; • maximum demand under applicable rules; • whether dynamic load management is required or advantageous; • dedicated circuit, conductor sizing, voltage drop and route; • residual-current and DC-fault protection required by the equipment and standards; • isolation, labelling and emergency switching arrangements; • equipment rating for indoor, outdoor, heat, sun, water and mechanical exposure; • mounting height, accessibility and impact protection; • testing, certification and documentation; • whether solar, storage or tariff controls interoperate without compromising safety. Do not prescribe a protective-device type from generic internet advice.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Do not prescribe a protective-device type from generic internet advice. The exact equipment architecture and applicable wiring rules determine the design.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 33 Size from the daily energy task Daily wall energy to restore Parking window Average power needed before allowance 8 kWh 10 h 0.8 kW 15 kWh 10 h 1.5 kW 25 kWh 10 h 2.5 kW 40 kWh 10 h 4.0 kW 50 kWh 6 h 8.3 kW This table is arithmetic, not an installation recommendation. Real systems need charging losses, current limits and margin. It demonstrates that many households can meet daily travel without the maximum available AC power. DECISION Prefer managed charging over an unnecessary supply upgrade when it safely meets the energy window and household priorities. Prefer a supply upgrade when measured need, future loads and engineering show management cannot meet the requirement.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DECISION Prefer managed charging over an unnecessary supply upgrade when it safely meets the energy window and household priorities. Prefer a supply upgrade when measured need, future loads and engineering show management cannot meet the requirement. Single phase and three phase Three-phase supply can support higher total power and distribute loads, but it does not automatically justify 22 kW vehicle charging. Consider: • whether the vehicle accepts three-phase AC; • whether daily energy requires it; • supply and switchboard upgrade cost; • other future three-phase loads; • network approval and phase balance; • whether dynamic control on the existing supply is simpler. A household may choose three-phase readiness during major renovation even if current charging is lower. Document the reason and leave a safe, labelled pathway rather than oversizing every component without a plan.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: A household may choose three-phase readiness during major renovation even if current charging is lower. Document the reason and leave a safe, labelled pathway rather than oversizing every component without a plan. Load management Static load control sets a fixed charging limit. Scheduled control shifts charging to a chosen time. Dynamic load management measures or receives site load and reduces vehicle charging to keep total demand within a limit. More advanced systems coordinate solar, battery, water heating and tariffs.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Dynamic load management measures or receives site load and reduces vehicle charging to keep total demand within a limit. More advanced systems coordinate solar, battery, water heating and tariffs. Ask: • What sensor or meter determines available capacity? • Does charging fail safely if communications or internet fail? • Is control local, cloud-dependent or both? • Can the household override it for a necessary departure? • What is the fallback current? • Are all controlled chargers coordinated, or can each assume the same spare capacity? • Who maintains software, accounts and cybersecurity? • Can data be exported and the system operate if a subscription ends?

chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 34 Location and cable design Place the connection so the normal vehicle position does not require cable stretching, tight bends or pedestrian crossings. Consider vehicles with charge ports in different positions. Provide storage that supports the cable and keeps the connector clean. Outdoor equipment needs the correct environmental rating and installation. A rating is not permission to install in a flood path, direct vehicle impact zone or place where water pools. Do not mount equipment where it narrows an accessible route or obstructs fire egress.

Periodic inspection Regularly inspect the visible cable, plug, connector, housing, mounting and impact protection.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 35 Solar, Tariffs and Smart Charging An electric vehicle can become one of the largest flexible household loads. Flexibility is valuable: charging can often move within a long parking window without reducing comfort. The goal is to add the required energy at a safe time and power while balancing solar self-use, tariffs, household demand and network conditions. Start with interval data Use at least several representative weeks in different seasons. Plot or tabulate: • household import and export by interval; • rooftop generation, if separately available; • major appliance timing; • vehicle arrival, departure and required energy; • tariff periods and any demand-charge window; • household battery charge and discharge; • days when solar surplus is not enough.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Start with interval data Use at least several representative weeks in different seasons. Plot or tabulate: • household import and export by interval; • rooftop generation, if separately available; • major appliance timing; • vehicle arrival, departure and required energy; • tariff periods and any demand-charge window; • household battery charge and discharge; • days when solar surplus is not enough. A monthly bill can show total energy but not whether charging coincides with solar or creates a new peak.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: A monthly bill can show total energy but not whether charging coincides with solar or creates a new peak. Three common strategies Strategy Works when Watch for Solar-surplus charging Vehicle is parked during daylight and controller can follow surplus Clouds, minimum charge power, other loads and winter production Off-peak scheduled charging Vehicle is home overnight and tariff has a genuine low-rate window Demand charges, changed tariffs and simultaneous water heating Dynamic whole-home control Several large loads compete for limited supply Sensor accuracy, interoperability, cloud dependence and fallback These strategies can be combined. For example, add solar during the day, then schedule only the remaining energy overnight. Solar-matching calculation Estimate available surplus in each interval: Solar surplus = generation - non-vehicle household load - chosen battery charging.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: For example, add solar during the day, then schedule only the remaining energy overnight. Solar-matching calculation Estimate available surplus in each interval: Solar surplus = generation - non-vehicle household load - chosen battery charging. Vehicle energy from surplus is the sum of the lower of available surplus and permitted EV charging power across connected intervals, after charging loss. A controller that simply charges at 7 kW whenever solar produces anything may still import most of the session. Example only: if four midday hours average 3 kW genuine surplus, about 12 kWh is available at the meter before charging losses. If the vehicle needs 20 kWh at the wall, the remaining 8 kWh must come from another solar interval or grid import.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Example only: if four midday hours average 3 kW genuine surplus, about 12 kWh is available at the meter before charging losses. If the vehicle needs 20 kWh at the wall, the remaining 8 kWh must come from another solar interval or grid import. Tariff comparison Calculate annual cost using actual charging intervals: Annual charging cost = sum of interval wall kWh x interval import price, plus any incremental demand charge or fixed fee.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 36 Subtract export revenue forgone when solar is diverted to the vehicle: Economic cost of solar charging = lost export value, not zero, unless export has no value. Compare at least: • flat tariff; • time-of-use tariff; • demand tariff; • controlled or special charging window if lawfully available; • current plan with better scheduling before changing plan. A tariff with a very low overnight price can be worse overall if daytime household electricity or a demand charge increases more. Use a government comparison service where available and verify meter, eligibility and contract terms.

chunks.text: A tariff with a very low overnight price can be worse overall if daytime household electricity or a demand charge increases more. Decide priorities explicitly: 1 essential household reserve; 2 required departure energy; 3 solar self-use or tariff outcome; 4 optional export or grid service. Check round-trip losses and battery wear.

chunks.text: Decide priorities explicitly: 1 essential household reserve; 2 required departure energy; 3 solar self-use or tariff outcome; 4 optional export or grid service. Check round-trip losses and battery wear. Moving energy through a stationary battery into a vehicle is not automatically cheaper or lower-emission than charging the vehicle directly when solar is available.

Smart charging requirements Ask for: • local schedule and current limit that still operate without internet; • dynamic load limit based on total site demand; • solar-surplus threshold and minimum charging power; • manual boost with a defined end time; • exportable session energy and timestamp data; • household ownership of account and credentials; • software-update and security policy; • ability to change electricity retailer or controller; • behaviour after power failure, vehicle reconnect and daylight-saving change; • no automatic increase above the electrician's commissioned limit. SAFETY Software is not a substitute for circuit protection or electrical design.

SAFETY Software is not a substitute for circuit protection or electrical design. A smart setting must never exceed the certified installation limit.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 37 Network-friendly charging Avoid creating a new household or local peak when the vehicle can wait. Stagger EV charging, water heating, cooking and battery charging. Solar-timed daytime charging can absorb local generation; overnight charging can use lower-demand periods in some areas. The best time depends on local network signals and tariff, not a national slogan.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Solar-timed daytime charging can absorb local generation; overnight charging can use lower-demand periods in some areas. The best time depends on local network signals and tariff, not a national slogan. When the car is not home during solar hours Options include: • charge at a workplace or destination with appropriate arrangements; • use solar on days the vehicle is home and grid charging on others; • shift other flexible loads to solar, leaving the best tariff window for the vehicle; • avoid buying a household battery solely to time-shift EV energy until measured economics support it; • reduce vehicle energy through fewer kilometres and efficient driving.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 38 Renters, Apartments, Strata and Kerbside Parking Charging access is a property and governance problem before it is an equipment problem. A safe cable from a lawful supply to an allocated bay may require owner consent, common-property approval, electrical capacity, billing, fire-safety review and a long-term building plan. Renter pathway 1 Record ordinary daily kilometres, energy required and parking hours. 2 Identify the legal status of the bay and the electricity account. 3 Ask a licensed electrician for a preliminary, non-invasive feasibility opinion if permitted. 4 Prepare a written proposal describing location, cable route, load limit, metering, removal and making-good. 5 Ask for written owner and, where relevant, strata approval before fixed work.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: 4 Prepare a written proposal describing location, cable route, load limit, metering, removal and making-good. 5 Ask for written owner and, where relevant, strata approval before fixed work. 6 Use a licensed electrician selected under the approved process. 7 Keep permission, certificate, settings, photos and responsibility agreement. The proposal should state who pays for design, installation, electricity, communications, maintenance, insurance impact, damage, removal and future upgrades. It should not promise that the tenant will waive legal rights or accept unbounded liability.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: The proposal should state who pays for design, installation, electricity, communications, maintenance, insurance impact, damage, removal and future upgrades. It should not promise that the tenant will waive legal rights or accept unbounded liability. Reversible renter options • Charge at a workplace or long-dwell destination where lawful and reliable. • Use an existing outlet only if permission, vehicle instructions and an electrician's assessment support regular sustained use. • Choose a vehicle and travel pattern that requires less daily energy. • Use public charging as a planned routine only after testing cost, access and backup. • Use an electrically assisted cycle for suitable local trips, with safe battery storage and charging. • Build evidence for a future fixed installation rather than improvising across doors, windows or paths.

chunks.text: It should not promise that the tenant will waive legal rights or accept unbounded liability. Reversible renter options • Charge at a workplace or long-dwell destination where lawful and reliable. • Use an existing outlet only if permission, vehicle instructions and an electrician's assessment support regular sustained use. • Choose a vehicle and travel pattern that requires less daily energy. • Use public charging as a planned routine only after testing cost, access and backup. • Use an electrically assisted cycle for suitable local trips, with safe battery storage and charging. • Build evidence for a future fixed installation rather than improvising across doors, windows or paths. Do not trail a lead through a window, across common property or over a public footpath. A cable cover does not automatically make an unapproved crossing lawful or accessible.

Buildings should first assess likely future demand, then choose a scalable backbone.

Layer Building-wide decision Governance Approval authority, alteration agreement, allocation, records and dispute process Electrical Maximum demand, supply, distribution boards, cabling backbone, protection and load management Metering Revenue or cost allocation, meter ownership, data access and billing method Parking Allocated bays, visitor use, accessible bays, cable reach and changes of ownership Fire and safety Egress, detection, emergency information, equipment location, isolation, impact and damaged-vehicle procedure Communications Local or network control, coverage, cybersecurity and provider-change path

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 39 Layer Building-wide decision Operations Fault contact, inspections, cleaning, damage, upgrades and end-of-life removal Equity Costs for early and later users, non-drivers, tenants and people with disability Building feasibility study brief Request a study that includes: • carpark and title or lease plan; • existing electrical single-line diagram and switchboards; • measured building demand, not only connected load; • spare capacity and constraints at relevant times; • staged uptake scenarios, such as 10, 25, 50 and 100 percent of bays; • options for central backbone, local boards, busway or other compliant distribution; • dynamic charging control responsive to total building demand; • individual sub-metering and billing options; • cable distances, voltage drop and physical routes; • communications

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: coverage and offline behaviour; • fire-safety and emergency-services considerations; • accessibility, egress, impact, water and flood risks; • capital stages, operating cost, maintenance and replacement; • rules for individual equipment compatibility; • drawings and a path that avoids stranded early work. New-building readiness The National Construction Code includes provisions intended to assist future EV charging in carparks associated with specified building classes. For apartment buildings, the provisions address dedicated electrical distribution boards, charging control responsive to building demand, capacity for future circuits and space for individual sub-circuit metering. They are readiness requirements, not a statement that a charger is installed at every bay. State or territory adoption and the exact building classification and approval date matter.

chunks.text: They are readiness requirements, not a statement that a charger is installed at every bay. State or territory adoption and the exact building classification and approval date matter. Motion or proposal outline Purpose: approve a staged, building-wide EV charging feasibility study and governance framework. Scope: demand measurement, scalable electrical backbone, load management, sub-metering, billing, fire and emergency review, accessibility, data ownership, cost allocation, maintenance and an interim process for individual requests. Decision required: approve the study budget and nominate an authorised contact. No charger purchase is authorised by this motion unless separately resolved.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 40 • exact bay and equipment location; • approved cable route and penetrations; • electrician and certification requirements; • commissioned current limit and building control interface; • meter, tariff and billing responsibility; • maintenance, inspection and fault response; • insurance notification and damage responsibility; • data access and privacy; • what happens when the resident moves or bay allocation changes; • removal and making-good; • right to integrate with a future building-wide system. Kerbside reality Street parking does not create a right to run private electrical equipment across public land. Contact the local road or land authority about lawful kerbside programs, accessibility, trenching or overhead proposals, insurance and removal.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Kerbside reality Street parking does not create a right to run private electrical equipment across public land. Contact the local road or land authority about lawful kerbside programs, accessibility, trenching or overhead proposals, insurance and removal. Do not place a cable, ramp, mat or charger on a footpath without approval. Public-path access must remain safe for wheelchairs, prams, vision-impaired pedestrians and emergency use. Building load fairness Fairness is not achieved by making every car charge at maximum power. A shared system can allocate energy over dwell time, prioritise urgent departures through a declared rule and bill measured use. Governance should prevent one early user from monopolising capacity while also avoiding an unfair building-wide subsidy. The calculation and appeal process should be transparent.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 41 Public Charging: Access, Reliability and Etiquette Public charging is not one uniform service. Sites differ in connector, power, access hours, parking law, price structure, payment, mobile coverage, reliability, lighting, toilets, shelter, trailer access and personal safety. Treat every critical stop as a small logistics task.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Treat every critical stop as a small logistics task. Pre-trip site check For the preferred and backup site record: • exact address and direction of access; • opening hours and gates; • connector and number of compatible plugs; • equipment power and likely vehicle-limited power; • recent operational status from more than one source where possible; • whether power is shared; • parking time limit and idle fee; • payment method, account or pre-authorisation requirement; • mobile coverage and support number; • lighting, shelter, toilets and food or water; • wheelchair-accessible route, kerb, bollard and cable reach; • trailer approach, turning and whether uncoupling is lawful and safe; • an independent alternative reachable with reserve. Download or write down critical information before entering a low-coverage area. Do not rely on one live map, one phone or one payment token.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Download or write down critical information before entering a low-coverage area. Do not rely on one live map, one phone or one payment token. Choose the right power Destination AC charging suits vehicles parked for hours. DC charging suits journeys and high-use operations. Occupying a high-power journey charger for a long final charge can delay others while adding energy slowly. Conversely, choosing a low-power point for a short stop may not add enough energy. Estimate required departure energy first: Required battery energy = distance to next secure stop x adverse Wh/km / 1000 + reserve kWh. Then charge to the resulting state of charge, allowing for usable battery and route changes. Start a public session 1 Park wholly within the correct bay without blocking another connector or access aisle. 2 Check the equipment, cable and connector for damage or contamination.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Start a public session 1 Park wholly within the correct bay without blocking another connector or access aisle. 2 Check the equipment, cable and connector for damage or contamination. 3 Confirm the vehicle inlet and intended connector. 4 Follow the displayed sequence for identification, connection and payment.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 42 5 Check that energy is actually flowing and the vehicle shows no fault. 6 Estimate finish time from required energy and observed power. 7 Remain contactable and return before the time limit or useful session ends. 8 Stop the session through the documented process, disconnect safely and return the cable. 9 Move the vehicle promptly and retain the receipt or session record. Diagnose a slow session Check, without opening equipment: • battery state of charge: high charge often tapers; • battery temperature and whether preconditioning occurred; • vehicle charging limit or scheduled setting; • site power sharing with another outlet; • station screen and vehicle warning; • whether the unit rating is shared or per plug; • whether the cable and connector are fully latched.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: 9 Move the vehicle promptly and retain the receipt or session record. Diagnose a slow session Check, without opening equipment: • battery state of charge: high charge often tapers; • battery temperature and whether preconditioning occurred; • vehicle charging limit or scheduled setting; • site power sharing with another outlet; • station screen and vehicle warning; • whether the unit rating is shared or per plug; • whether the cable and connector are fully latched. If safe, stop and restart once according to instructions. Then contact the operator and move to the backup rather than repeatedly cycling a damaged connection.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: If safe, stop and restart once according to instructions. Then contact the operator and move to the backup rather than repeatedly cycling a damaged connection. Etiquette that improves capacity • Do not park in a charging bay while not charging. • Leave when enough energy is added, particularly at a busy DC site. • Respect signed limits, accessible-bay rules and queue order. • Keep the charging area clean and cables returned safely. • Do not reserve a bay with a person, cone or unconnected vehicle. • Do not unplug another vehicle without an explicit, lawful permission mechanism. • If towing, avoid blocking several bays; uncouple only where safe and permitted. • Report faults with unit identifier, time, connector, error and observed behaviour. • Offer practical courtesy in emergencies without surrendering safety or legal requirements.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Accessibility Before depending on a site, assess: • width beside the charging side of the vehicle; • kerbs, gradients and bollards; • reach and weight of tethered cable; • screen height, glare and input method; • payment and support access for hearing or vision needs; • safe path to amenities; • whether an accessible charging bay is legally reserved. A technically working charger can still be unusable. Record access failures and report them through the relevant facility and public authority pathways.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 43 Price and payment Possible components include energy per kWh, time, session fee, parking, idle fee, membership or roaming surcharge. Check whether a pre-authorisation hold is placed on a card and when it is released. Save receipts and compare delivered energy with the vehicle's state-of-charge change, allowing for battery and thermal overheads. Do not assume a high public-charging price proves electric travel is always expensive. Separate home, work, destination and journey energy by kWh. Public DC equipment has greater grid, equipment, land and service costs than a household circuit, but the household decision must use the prices actually available.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Separate home, work, destination and journey energy by kWh. Public DC equipment has greater grid, equipment, land and service costs than a household circuit, but the household decision must use the prices actually available. If the site fails • Keep sufficient reserve to leave the site safely. • Try another compatible unit only if it appears undamaged. • Contact support with clear fault evidence. • Recalculate the backup route using current consumption and conditions. • Reduce optional load or speed only within safe and lawful limits. • If no safe destination is reachable, stop in a safe place and arrange assistance before depleting the battery. Never improvise from an unauthorised building outlet, generator or damaged cable. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/owning-electric-vehicle/how-c... [2] www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/owning-electric-vehicle/plann...

chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 44 Road Trips, Towing, Camping and Remote Travel Long electric journeys are an energy-and-time plan. Good planning uses actual route consumption, the vehicle's charging curve, reliable alternatives and human rest. It does not require arriving near zero or charging to 100 percent at every stop. Road-trip plan 1 Check vehicle condition, tyres, cable, software warnings and charging limits. 2 Map the route, elevation, speed, weather, closures and mobile-coverage gaps. 3 Select preferred and backup chargers with compatible connectors. 4 Estimate energy for each leg using adverse route consumption. 5 Add a consequence-based reserve. 6 Choose stops that combine charging with safe driver breaks. 7 Confirm access, payment and operational reports close to departure.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: 6 Choose stops that combine charging with safe driver breaks. 7 Confirm access, payment and operational reports close to departure. 8 Begin with enough energy for the first backup, not merely the first site. 9 Recalculate after each leg from actual consumption. 10 Stop before uncertainty becomes an emergency. The Australian Government recommends planning breaks around at least every two hours of driving. Fatigue management outranks a theoretical minimum travel time. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/owning-electric-vehicle/plann...

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Fatigue management outranks a theoretical minimum travel time. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/owning-electric-vehicle/plann... Leg worksheet Field Preferred stop Backup stop Distance and elevation Adverse consumption Wh/km Drive energy kWh Reserve kWh Required departure state of charge Connector and site power Expected arrival and departure Access, payment and support Amenities and personal safety Cables for travel Carry only equipment that is compatible, compliant and within the vehicle instructions. Common needs may include the vehicle's portable EVSE for an approved outlet and a Type 2 cable for socketed AC stations. DC stations normally have a tethered cable. Confirm before travel; older or unusual inlets require route-specific checking. Do not carry a collection of unverified adapters as a substitute for compatible infrastructure.

chunks.text: Confirm before travel; older or unusual inlets require route-specific checking. Do not carry a collection of unverified adapters as a substitute for compatible infrastructure. A physical connection does not prove safe communication, protection, earthing or current rating.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 45 Accommodation charging Obtain permission before plugging in. Tell the host the vehicle, equipment, current and expected duration. Ask whether the nominated outlet and circuit have been assessed for sustained EV charging. Avoid windows, door gaps, shared walkways, coiled leads and general extension cords. Confirm any cost or access condition in advance. Towing energy Trailer aerodynamic shape, frontal area, speed, mass, tyres, wind and hills can materially reduce range. Rated towing capacity alone does not predict energy use.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Towing energy Trailer aerodynamic shape, frontal area, speed, mass, tyres, wind and hills can materially reduce range. Rated towing capacity alone does not predict energy use. Before a long tow: • verify braked towing, gross combination, axle, payload and towball limits; • subtract passengers, cargo, accessories and towball download from available payload correctly; • perform a controlled representative test on a safe route; • record Wh/km in both directions and relevant wind; • locate pull-through sites or safe uncoupling areas; • plan shorter legs and larger reserve; • verify trailer electrical and braking operation; • check recovery provider capability for vehicle and trailer. CALCULA TION Towing leg energy = towing distance x measured adverse towing Wh/km / 1000. Add reserve in kWh. Do not scale solo range by guesswork.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Add reserve in kWh. Do not scale solo range by guesswork. Charging with a trailer Many bays are arranged for nose-in or reverse-in cars. Before arrival determine whether the combination can enter, turn and connect without blocking roads, accessible routes or other bays. If uncoupling is necessary: • use a lawful, level and safe area; • secure the trailer against movement; • maintain visibility and do not obstruct circulation; • reconnect and recheck coupling, chains, plug and brakes before departure. Remote and regional planning Remote travel increases consequence.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: If uncoupling is necessary: • use a lawful, level and safe area; • secure the trailer against movement; • maintain visibility and do not obstruct circulation; • reconnect and recheck coupling, chains, plug and brakes before departure. Remote and regional planning Remote travel increases consequence. Add: • larger energy and water reserve; • at least one independent charging or transport fallback; • opening-hour confirmation by direct, current public information; • offline maps and written contact details; • weather, fire, flood and road-condition checks; • recovery membership or provider capability for high-voltage vehicles; • warm clothing, shade, water, medication and communications appropriate to the route; • a person who knows the route and check-in plan. Do not count an ordinary rural outlet as available merely because a building exists.

Do not count an ordinary rural outlet as available merely because a building exists. Permission, circuit capacity, access and charging equipment all matter.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 46 Camping and vehicle-to-load Vehicle-to-load can power compatible appliances within the vehicle's documented voltage, current, energy, earthing and environmental limits. It does not authorise connection to a building switchboard or inlet. Keep equipment dry and ventilated, observe total power, use suitable leads and protect cables from vehicles and people. Retain enough driving reserve to leave. Do not use a vehicle in an enclosed sleeping area if it creates ventilation, heat or egress risk. Never connect a vehicle outlet to a house socket to energise wiring.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Do not use a vehicle in an enclosed sleeping area if it creates ventilation, heat or egress risk. Never connect a vehicle outlet to a house socket to energise wiring. Breakdown or depleted battery • Move to a safe position if possible and activate hazard warnings. • Tell roadside or emergency responders that the vehicle is electric. • Follow the manual for towing, neutral selection, wheel lift and transport. • Do not flat tow unless expressly permitted; some drivetrains can be damaged or generate voltage. • Use a recovery vehicle and lifting points appropriate to the vehicle. • Do not attempt a high-voltage repair roadside. Extreme weather Before heat, cold, flood or bushfire conditions, maintain more reserve and avoid leaving charging until the last moment.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Breakdown or depleted battery • Move to a safe position if possible and activate hazard warnings. • Tell roadside or emergency responders that the vehicle is electric. • Follow the manual for towing, neutral selection, wheel lift and transport. • Do not flat tow unless expressly permitted; some drivetrains can be damaged or generate voltage. • Use a recovery vehicle and lifting points appropriate to the vehicle. • Do not attempt a high-voltage repair roadside. Extreme weather Before heat, cold, flood or bushfire conditions, maintain more reserve and avoid leaving charging until the last moment. In a flood, do not drive through water because an electric vehicle is not a boat; road, traction and hidden-depth risks apply to all vehicles. Any immersed or suspected water-damaged electric vehicle should not be used or charged until cleared by a qualified technician.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 47 Maintenance, Tyres, Repair and Software Electric vehicles remove engine oil, spark plugs, exhaust and some other combustion-service items, but they are not maintenance-free. Safety still depends on tyres, brakes, steering, suspension, lights, glass, cooling systems, low-voltage power, software and charging equipment. Maintenance schedule Follow both time and distance intervals. Low kilometres do not prevent brake-fluid ageing, corrosion, tyre ageing, cabin-filter loading or 12 V battery failure.

chunks.text: System Household observation Qualified service Tyres Pressure, tread, cuts, bulges, embedded objects and uneven wear Rotation, alignment, balance, replacement and wheel repair Friction brakes Noise, pull, vibration and corrosion visible without dismantling Pads, discs, calipers, fluid and parking-brake function Steering and suspension Wandering, knocks, vibration and ride change Joints, bushes, dampers, bearings and alignment Thermal system Cooling or heating warning, leak, weak cabin conditioning Coolant, pumps, valves, refrigerant and battery thermal management 12 V system Slow wake-up, warning messages and age Battery test, charging-system diagnosis and safe replacement High-voltage system Dashboard warnings, charge faults, range change Isolation, diagnostics, battery, inverter, motor and onboard charger Charging equipment Cable, connector, housing, mounting, cleanliness and abnormal
