Tyres are an efficiency and safety system Vehicle mass, torque and regenerative braking can create different wear patterns, but driving style, alignment, compound, size and pressure matter. Use tyres that meet the vehicle's load, speed, size and construction requirements.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Tyres are an efficiency and safety system Vehicle mass, torque and regenerative braking can create different wear patterns, but driving style, alignment, compound, size and pressure matter. Use tyres that meet the vehicle's load, speed, size and construction requirements. Compare: • wet grip and braking; • load and speed rating; • energy efficiency or rolling resistance evidence; • noise; • tread life and warranty conditions; • repairability and local availability; • price per expected kilometre, not purchase price alone. Check pressure when cold using the placard and instructions. Recheck after large temperature change, heavy load or towing. Uneven wear calls for diagnosis, not merely another set of tyres. Brakes and regeneration Regenerative braking can reduce friction-pad wear, but little use can allow discs and calipers to corrode or bind.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Uneven wear calls for diagnosis, not merely another set of tyres. Brakes and regeneration Regenerative braking can reduce friction-pad wear, but little use can allow discs and calipers to corrode or bind. The vehicle still needs reliable friction braking for emergency stops, low speed, a full or cold battery and system faults. Use any documented brake-maintenance mode and service intervals. Do not deliberately perform unsafe hard braking to clean discs.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 48 12 V battery Most electric vehicles use a low-voltage battery to power computers, locks and the contactors that connect the traction battery. A weak 12 V battery can make a charged vehicle appear dead. Learn the approved access and jump-start procedure, because connecting to the wrong point can damage systems or create risk. Do not assume the traction battery will always maintain the 12 V system while parked. Thermal management Battery longevity, fast charging and cabin comfort depend on thermal systems. Investigate coolant loss, pump noise, weak heating or cooling, reduced charging power and temperature warnings. Only use specified fluids and qualified procedures; some circuits have electrical isolation requirements.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Investigate coolant loss, pump noise, weak heating or cooling, reduced charging power and temperature warnings. Only use specified fluids and qualified procedures; some circuits have electrical isolation requirements. Software and connected services Before an update: • read the release notice and charging or state-of-charge requirement; • park safely with reliable power or connectivity as instructed; • record critical settings such as charge limit and schedule; • avoid beginning immediately before essential travel; • verify operation and warnings after completion. Connected features create data and continuity questions. Determine what location, driving, camera, voice, contact and charging data is collected; who receives it; how long it is retained; how consent is managed; and whether core functions remain if a communications service ends.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Connected features create data and continuity questions. Determine what location, driving, camera, voice, contact and charging data is collected; who receives it; how long it is retained; how consent is managed; and whether core functions remain if a communications service ends. Remove accounts and personal data before sale, disposal or rental return. Repairs after collision Use a repair pathway with appropriate high-voltage training, isolation, lifting information and battery damage assessment.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Remove accounts and personal data before sale, disposal or rental return. Repairs after collision Use a repair pathway with appropriate high-voltage training, isolation, lifting information and battery damage assessment. Ask: • Is the repairer authorised and equipped for this vehicle architecture? • Will the traction battery be isolated and inspected as required? • Are structural measurement and battery-clearance tolerances documented? • Will scans, calibrations and charging tests be completed? • Who stores the damaged vehicle, and what fire separation is required? • Are parts new, remanufactured or used, and what warranty applies? • Will a post-repair report and wheel alignment be supplied? Right-to-repair and support questions Before purchase, ask whether independent qualified repairers can access service information, diagnostic tools, parts and software functions.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Ask: • Is the repairer authorised and equipped for this vehicle architecture? • Will the traction battery be isolated and inspected as required? • Are structural measurement and battery-clearance tolerances documented? • Will scans, calibrations and charging tests be completed? • Who stores the damaged vehicle, and what fire separation is required? • Are parts new, remanufactured or used, and what warranty applies? • Will a post-repair report and wheel alignment be supplied? Right-to-repair and support questions Before purchase, ask whether independent qualified repairers can access service information, diagnostic tools, parts and software functions. A lower scheduled-service cost can be overwhelmed by long parts delays, restricted body repair or replacement of a whole assembly that could otherwise be repaired.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Right-to-repair and support questions Before purchase, ask whether independent qualified repairers can access service information, diagnostic tools, parts and software functions. A lower scheduled-service cost can be overwhelmed by long parts delays, restricted body repair or replacement of a whole assembly that could otherwise be repaired. Maintenance record Keep a single digital and paper record containing: • service invoices and inspection results; • tyre model, size, date, mileage and alignment; • battery health reports and warning history;

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 49 • charging-equipment inspection and electrical certificate; • recalls and software updates; • collision, underbody impact, flood and repair details; • energy and consumption trends; • warranty and consumer-law correspondence. This record improves safety, diagnosis, warranty claims and resale transparency.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 50 Emergency, Fire, Flood, Collision and Breakdown The safest household action around a suspected traction-battery incident is distance, warning others and early contact with emergency services. Do not approach to diagnose the battery, touch exposed components or attempt to disconnect high-voltage cabling. Warning signs Treat these seriously after stopping in a safe location where possible: • smoke, vapour, popping, hissing or unusual chemical odour; • rapid or localised heat; • flames, sparks or melted material; • coolant or unknown fluid after an underbody strike; • high-voltage, isolation, battery-temperature or charge-system warning; • charging connector that is scorched, stuck or unusually hot; • damage after collision, road debris, flood or immersion.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Do not approach to diagnose the battery, touch exposed components or attempt to disconnect high-voltage cabling. Warning signs Treat these seriously after stopping in a safe location where possible: • smoke, vapour, popping, hissing or unusual chemical odour; • rapid or localised heat; • flames, sparks or melted material; • coolant or unknown fluid after an underbody strike; • high-voltage, isolation, battery-temperature or charge-system warning; • charging connector that is scorched, stuck or unusually hot; • damage after collision, road debris, flood or immersion. If an incident occurs 1 Engage the parking brake and switch the vehicle off if this can be done safely. 2 Evacuate everyone and move well away from traffic and the vehicle. 3 Warn others to keep clear.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: 2 Evacuate everyone and move well away from traffic and the vehicle. 3 Warn others to keep clear. 4 Call Triple Zero (000) for smoke, fire, fumes, injury or immediate danger and state that an electric or hybrid vehicle is involved. 5 Give the exact location, vehicle description and known collision, flood or charging circumstances. 6 Keep remote keys far enough away to prevent unintended activation. 7 Follow emergency-services directions and do not return for possessions. Fire and Rescue NSW advises keeping at least 30 metres away from an EV incident even if smoke or flame is not visible. Local emergency responders control the scene; their direction overrides a generic guide. Sources: [1] www.fire.nsw.gov.au/fire-safety/home-fire-safety/battery-and-char... Damaged-vehicle quarantine A vehicle involved in collision, fire or immersion may have delayed ignition risk.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Sources: [1] www.fire.nsw.gov.au/fire-safety/home-fire-safety/battery-and-char... Damaged-vehicle quarantine A vehicle involved in collision, fire or immersion may have delayed ignition risk. Do not drive or charge it until inspected and cleared by a qualified technician. Tell the tow operator, storage facility, insurer and repairer about the event. Fire and Rescue NSW advises damaged EVs be kept in an open area at least 15 metres from vehicles, buildings and other exposures. Site owners and emergency services must determine the safe location; do not move a dangerous vehicle yourself to meet a distance rule.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Fire and Rescue NSW advises damaged EVs be kept in an open area at least 15 metres from vehicles, buildings and other exposures. Site owners and emergency services must determine the safe location; do not move a dangerous vehicle yourself to meet a distance rule. Floods and water • Do not enter floodwater in any vehicle. • If water may have reached the traction battery, charge port or electrical equipment, do not plug in. • Isolate household charging equipment through the safe, documented method only if this can be done without entering water or approaching damaged equipment.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 51 • Treat salt-water exposure as particularly serious and disclose it to responders and technicians. • Have the vehicle, charger and affected building circuits separately inspected. • Record water depth and duration only from a safe place for insurance and repair evidence. An EV's sealed components do not make floodwater safe. Hidden depth, current, road collapse and delayed battery damage remain.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: An EV's sealed components do not make floodwater safe. Hidden depth, current, road collapse and delayed battery damage remain. Charging fire or equipment fault If smoke, flame, arcing or strong heat occurs while charging: • do not touch the plug, cable, vehicle or switchboard; • evacuate, warn others and call 000; • use a remote emergency isolation only if it is identified, accessible and emergency services direct or the plan clearly permits safe operation; • do not re-energise after the event; • preserve evidence after the scene is made safe. Do not rely on a household fire blanket or small extinguisher to control a traction-battery fire. Escape and emergency response come first. Collision and first responders Australian electric and hybrid vehicles may carry an identifying label on number plates under state or territory rules to alert responders to high voltage.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Escape and emergency response come first. Collision and first responders Australian electric and hybrid vehicles may carry an identifying label on number plates under state or territory rules to alert responders to high voltage. Keep required labels in place. Emergency-response guides can identify cut zones, isolation points and battery location, but untrained occupants should not use them to perform high-voltage work. National vehicle standards include electric-powertrain safety requirements for new vehicles. They reduce risks but do not make a damaged battery harmless. Sources: [1] www.infrastructure.gov.au/department/media/news/new-standards-acc... [2] www.infrastructure.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/Australia...

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide

[2] www.infrastructure.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/Australia... Breakdown without visible damage • Move out of traffic if the vehicle can be moved safely. • Use hazard lights, warning devices and roadside procedures. • Tell the assistance provider the powertrain and exact warning. • Follow the manual for transport mode, neutral release and towing. • Do not crawl under the vehicle on a road or touch orange cables. • Do not tow with driven wheels on the ground unless the manual expressly permits it. • Request a suitable recovery vehicle when uncertain. Depleted traction battery Do not deliberately run to zero to test range.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Depleted traction battery Do not deliberately run to zero to test range. If energy becomes critically low: • select the nearest safe reachable charging or stopping place; • reduce optional climate load only if visibility, health and safety remain protected; • drive smoothly and lawfully; • contact assistance before the vehicle stops in a dangerous place; • use only an approved charging or recovery method.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 52 Emergency plan for the home or building Document: • address and charging location; • main and charging isolation identified by the electrician; • equipment emergency contact; • vehicle emergency information; • fire detection and evacuation arrangements; • process for collision-damaged or flooded vehicles; • who can authorise tow and quarantine location; • resident communication, including disability assistance; • post-incident electrical inspection and evidence preservation. Do not write a plan that requires an untrained resident to approach a smoking vehicle or open an electrical enclosure.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 53 Vehicle-to-Load, Vehicle-to-Home and Vehicle-to-Grid Bidirectional claims must be split into distinct functions. A vehicle that can power an appliance is not necessarily able or approved to power a building or export to the grid.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: The functions Function Energy destination Typical boundary Main gate Vehicle-to-load, V2L Plug-in appliance or external load Vehicle-provided outlet or approved adapter Vehicle power and energy limit, appliance compatibility and safe lead use Vehicle-to-home, V2H Selected or whole building circuits Approved bidirectional equipment and changeover or isolation architecture Exact vehicle and equipment compatibility, electrical design and lawful islanding Vehicle-to-grid, V2G Electricity network Approved bidirectional equipment, metering, control and network connection Network approval, market arrangement, standards and export settings Vehicle-to-vehicle Another vehicle under a supported method Purpose-designed connection or energy transfer Both vehicles and equipment must expressly support it Vehicle-to-load safety • Read the exact continuous and surge power limits. • Add appliance watts

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: and consider motor-starting current. • Keep all connections dry and protected from damage. • Use suitable leads within instructions; do not daisy-chain power boards. • Maintain ventilation and clear egress. • Set a traction-battery reserve for driving. • Do not power fixed wiring through a wall socket or improvised backfeed lead. • Do not assume an appliance requiring protective earthing or a special neutral arrangement is compatible. SAFETY Never connect a vehicle outlet to a home's socket, switchboard or generator inlet unless a licensed electrician has installed an approved system specifically designed for that vehicle, equipment and building. Improvised backfeeding can energise wiring unexpectedly and endanger occupants and line workers. V2H and islanding A home backup system must disconnect from the grid when required so exported energy cannot reach a de-energised network.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Improvised backfeeding can energise wiring unexpectedly and endanger occupants and line workers. V2H and islanding A home backup system must disconnect from the grid when required so exported energy cannot reach a de-energised network. It must manage earthing, neutral, protection, changeover, inverter limits, essential circuits and reconnection. The design must specify: • compatible vehicle models and software versions by technical certification, not sales promise; • compatible bidirectional EVSE and communication protocol; • network-service-provider approval; • maximum import and export power; • essential-load board or whole-home limitation; • automatic or manual changeover;

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 54 • black-start capability and behaviour when the vehicle is absent; • minimum vehicle reserve and departure override; • solar and household-battery behaviour during outage; • testing, maintenance and emergency isolation. V2G value test Grid export can provide tariff arbitrage or grid services, but value depends on: • hours the vehicle is connected; • minimum driving reserve; • export price and program availability; • import cost, losses and taxes; • cycling energy and any effect on battery life; • equipment, electrical work, metering and communications cost; • availability payments and performance penalties; • vehicle, equipment and network warranty; • ability to change energy retailer or aggregator; • data and remote-control permissions.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: V2G value test Grid export can provide tariff arbitrage or grid services, but value depends on: • hours the vehicle is connected; • minimum driving reserve; • export price and program availability; • import cost, losses and taxes; • cycling energy and any effect on battery life; • equipment, electrical work, metering and communications cost; • availability payments and performance penalties; • vehicle, equipment and network warranty; • ability to change energy retailer or aggregator; • data and remote-control permissions. CALCULA TION Net annual value = export and service revenue + avoided high-price imports - energy bought - conversion losses - incremental fees - equipment annualised cost - expected wear or warranty cost. Use scenarios; do not count gross export revenue as savings.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Use scenarios; do not count gross export revenue as savings. Compatibility matrix Do not purchase until every required cell is confirmed in writing: Layer Evidence Vehicle Function enabled in Australia, exact variant, software and warranty Connector and protocol Supported direction, communication standard and power EVSE Certification, vehicle interoperability and local support Building Switchboard, essential loads, isolation, earthing and protection design Network Connection approval, export limit and commissioning Meter and tariff Import/export measurement and settlement Control Reserve, schedule, outage mode, local fallback and cybersecurity Contract Ownership, data, remote dispatch, fees, exit and liability The Australian Government notes that only a limited range of compatible vehicles and equipment may be verified for bidirectional use at a given time.

chunks.text: Compatibility matrix Do not purchase until every required cell is confirmed in writing: Layer Evidence Vehicle Function enabled in Australia, exact variant, software and warranty Connector and protocol Supported direction, communication standard and power EVSE Certification, vehicle interoperability and local support Building Switchboard, essential loads, isolation, earthing and protection design Network Connection approval, export limit and commissioning Meter and tariff Import/export measurement and settlement Control Reserve, schedule, outage mode, local fallback and cybersecurity Contract Ownership, data, remote dispatch, fees, exit and liability The Australian Government notes that only a limited range of compatible vehicles and equipment may be verified for bidirectional use at a given time. Availability changes, so check the current official pathway immediately before contracting.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Availability changes, so check the current official pathway immediately before contracting. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/owning-electric-vehicle/vehic... Backup sizing List only essential loads and their energy: • refrigeration; • medical or communications equipment;

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 55 • selected lighting; • water or sanitation equipment; • limited heating or cooling for health; • internet and device charging. For each, record watts, hours, surge and whether it can cycle. Daily essential energy is the sum of kW x hours. Keep driving reserve separate. Example only: 3 kWh of essential household energy plus a 12 kWh driving reserve requires at least 15 kWh usable above the system's low-charge limit. Real systems have conversion loss and power limits. This calculation does not establish that the vehicle can legally or technically power the home.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Real systems have conversion loss and power limits. This calculation does not establish that the vehicle can legally or technically power the home. Contract exit questions • Can the household keep charging if the service closes? • Can bidirectional control be disabled locally? • Who can discharge the vehicle and to what reserve? • Is export guaranteed or discretionary? • Who owns interval and mobility data? • What happens when the vehicle, charger, retailer or resident changes? • Is equipment removable and interoperable? • Who pays if an update breaks compatibility? Design normal charging to remain safe and useful even if bidirectional services never arrive.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 56 Tax, Finance, Insurance, Incentives and Current Rules Financial support is highly date- and circumstance-dependent. Use this chapter as a verification workflow, not a promise of savings. Never sign a vehicle or charging contract solely because a salesperson calculates a tax result. Current-source hierarchy 1 Legislation and the administering government authority. 2 Current official ruling, guideline or program page with effective date. 3 Written employer, payroll, financier, insurer or network terms. 4 Advice from a qualified professional who has the complete facts. 5 Calculator with visible assumptions. 6 Marketing estimate only as a question to test. Electric-car FBT checkpoint Australian fringe-benefits-tax law can exempt eligible electric car benefits when all statutory conditions are met.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: 6 Marketing estimate only as a question to test. Electric-car FBT checkpoint Australian fringe-benefits-tax law can exempt eligible electric car benefits when all statutory conditions are met. The conditions concern matters including vehicle type, first held and used date, price threshold and the employment arrangement. Associated benefits such as charging may have specific treatment and records. For plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, the general exemption ended for benefits provided from 1 April 2025, subject to limited transitional treatment where the earlier exempt use and financially binding commitment requirements are satisfied. A new or changed commitment can alter the result. Do not apply an old lease example to a new arrangement.

It is not a universal electricity rebate or automatic household deduction.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Home-charging tax records The tax authority publishes a compliance guideline for an EV home-charging rate in defined income-tax and fringe-benefits-tax circumstances. It is not a universal electricity rebate or automatic household deduction. Eligibility, vehicle type, kilometres, home-charging proportion, records and choice of method matter. Mixed home and commercial charging, a vehicle that reports charging location, and plug-in hybrid fuel use require careful treatment. Keep: • opening and closing odometer records; • logbook where required; • home-charging percentage evidence;

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 57 • electricity bills and separately measured charging where used; • public-charging receipts; • work-use basis and employer declarations; • the chosen method for the whole relevant year. Use the current guideline for the exact tax year and obtain advice before claiming. Incentives and concessions Vehicle rebates, registration concessions, stamp duty, charging grants and loans vary by state, territory, applicant, date, vehicle, price and whether the commitment occurred before closure. Some historical purchase rebates are closed even though old pages remain searchable.

chunks.text: Incentives and concessions Vehicle rebates, registration concessions, stamp duty, charging grants and loans vary by state, territory, applicant, date, vehicle, price and whether the commitment occurred before closure. Some historical purchase rebates are closed even though old pages remain searchable. Before counting a benefit: • confirm the program is open on the decision date; • check eligible applicant, postcode, vehicle type and purchase date; • check price, registration, ownership and retention conditions; • check whether funding is capped or competitive; • identify tax interaction and repayment or clawback; • obtain written approval before treating it as certain; • calculate the decision both with and without it. Use the Australian Government rebate directory and the linked administering authority.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 58 Compare effective total cost, flexibility and risk, not only a periodic deduction. A longer term can lower the payment while increasing interest and exposure to negative equity. Insurance Obtain quotes for the exact vehicle before signing.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: A longer term can lower the payment while increasing interest and exposure to negative equity. Insurance Obtain quotes for the exact vehicle before signing. Ask about: • agreed or market value and treatment of rapid price changes; • battery, charge port, cable and portable equipment cover; • home charging equipment under motor or home policy; • flood, underbody impact, towing and off-road exclusions; • choice of repairer and high-voltage repair capability; • replacement vehicle and charging-cost cover during long repair; • salvage and battery assessment; • modifications, accessories and bidirectional equipment; • young, learner and multiple drivers; • business, rideshare, delivery or fleet use; • roadside recovery for depleted battery and trailer. Notify both motor and property insurers about fixed charging or bidirectional equipment where the policy requires it.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Ask about: • agreed or market value and treatment of rapid price changes; • battery, charge port, cable and portable equipment cover; • home charging equipment under motor or home policy; • flood, underbody impact, towing and off-road exclusions; • choice of repairer and high-voltage repair capability; • replacement vehicle and charging-cost cover during long repair; • salvage and battery assessment; • modifications, accessories and bidirectional equipment; • young, learner and multiple drivers; • business, rideshare, delivery or fleet use; • roadside recovery for depleted battery and trailer. Notify both motor and property insurers about fixed charging or bidirectional equipment where the policy requires it. Keep electrical certificates and installation photographs.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Notify both motor and property insurers about fixed charging or bidirectional equipment where the policy requires it. Keep electrical certificates and installation photographs. Financial stress test Calculate whether the household can carry: • a higher insurance renewal; • electricity and public charging at adverse prices; • tyre replacement earlier than hoped; • home electrical work beyond the first quote; • several months of repair delay; • lower resale value; • job change that ends a salary arrangement; • no rebate or tax benefit. If the decision fails without optimistic resale or tax assumptions, reduce vehicle cost or delay the purchase.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 59 Workplaces, Fleets, Vans, Utes, Buses and Heavy Transport Fleet transition is an operational-design task. Vehicle choice follows duty cycle, payload, route, dwell time, depot power, driver needs and service continuity. Start with data from existing vehicles rather than replacing every asset like for like. Fleet baseline For each vehicle or route collect: • kilometres by day and shift; • start and finish location and dwell time; • route elevation, speed, temperature and congestion; • payload by trip, not only average; • towing, auxiliary power, refrigeration, lifting or tool loads; • driver breaks and changeovers; • fuel, service, tyre, repair and downtime history; • parking, depot and workplace electrical access; • exceptional emergency or remote tasks; • replacement date and residual value.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Start with data from existing vehicles rather than replacing every asset like for like. Fleet baseline For each vehicle or route collect: • kilometres by day and shift; • start and finish location and dwell time; • route elevation, speed, temperature and congestion; • payload by trip, not only average; • towing, auxiliary power, refrigeration, lifting or tool loads; • driver breaks and changeovers; • fuel, service, tyre, repair and downtime history; • parking, depot and workplace electrical access; • exceptional emergency or remote tasks; • replacement date and residual value. Cluster duty cycles. A short fixed urban route, regional service vehicle, home-garaged employee vehicle and long-haul truck need different solutions.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Cluster duty cycles. A short fixed urban route, regional service vehicle, home-garaged employee vehicle and long-haul truck need different solutions. Avoid like-for-like oversizing • Consolidate low-utilisation vehicles into a booking pool. • Redesign routes to reduce empty kilometres. • Move suitable travel to public transport, video or electrically assisted cycles. • Use smaller vehicles where payload and safety allow. • Separate rare towing or remote tasks from daily vehicles. • Improve loading and occupancy. • Schedule work around charging and rest rather than adding a larger battery automatically. Pilot design Choose a representative but recoverable duty cycle.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Pilot design Choose a representative but recoverable duty cycle. Define pass criteria before the pilot: Measure Pass criterion example Operational completion Completes all normal shifts with declared reserve Energy Wall kWh by route and season within planning envelope Charging Required energy added within dwell time without depot overload Payload Legal axle and mass compliance for real loads Driver Training complete; access and comfort issues resolved Reliability Charging and vehicle faults tracked with recovery process

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 60 Measure Pass criterion example Cost Full operating and capital costs recorded, not fuel alone Safety Risk assessment, emergency and isolation processes implemented Do not pilot only the easiest summer week and extrapolate nationally. Include adverse but normal conditions.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Include adverse but normal conditions. Depot charging design Depot design should model: • simultaneous arrival and next departure; • energy required per vehicle; • diversity and managed charging; • distribution-board and transformer capacity; • redundancy for charger or communications failure; • cable reach, traffic movement and impact protection; • metering by vehicle, route or cost centre; • solar and battery interaction; • future fleet stages; • maintenance access and spare equipment; • fire, emergency, flood and evacuation arrangements; • network lead time and connection approval. The sum of charger nameplate ratings is usually a poor estimate of necessary site capacity. Optimise energy across dwell time, then model contingencies.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: The sum of charger nameplate ratings is usually a poor estimate of necessary site capacity. Optimise energy across dwell time, then model contingencies. Home-garaged fleet vehicles When an employee charges a fleet vehicle at home, define: • who approves and owns fixed equipment; • electrician assessment and landlord or strata permission; • electricity reimbursement evidence and tax treatment; • personal and business energy separation; • maintenance, insurance and removal at job or address change; • vehicle availability, charge target and privacy; • what happens when home charging is impossible. Do not pressure a renter or apartment resident to accept unsafe wiring or property obligations as a condition of using a fleet vehicle. Workplace visitor and employee charging Decide whether charging is for fleet operations, employee commuting, visitors or the public.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Do not pressure a renter or apartment resident to accept unsafe wiring or property obligations as a condition of using a fleet vehicle. Workplace visitor and employee charging Decide whether charging is for fleet operations, employee commuting, visitors or the public. Each needs different access, dwell time and billing. Publish rules for: • eligibility and priority; • booking or queue; • time limits and bay turnover;

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 61 • energy fee and any taxable benefit; • accessible bays; • fault support and misuse; • data collection and retention; • charging outside work hours; • future expansion. Commercial-vehicle payload trap Battery mass can reduce available payload in some vehicle configurations. Confirm: • tare and actual as-delivered mass; • gross vehicle mass and axle limits; • body, shelving, tools, driver, passengers and accessories; • trailer and towball contribution; • gross combination mass; • licence, fatigue and road-access implications. Use weighbridge evidence for representative loaded vehicles. A nominal cargo volume does not establish legal payload. Auxiliary loads Refrigeration, pumps, lifts, lighting, power take-off equivalents, tools and cabin conditioning can be material.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: A nominal cargo volume does not establish legal payload. Auxiliary loads Refrigeration, pumps, lifts, lighting, power take-off equivalents, tools and cabin conditioning can be material. Measure duty-cycle energy and decide whether it draws from the traction battery or a separate system. Include idle time, standby, preconditioning and extreme weather. Buses and heavy vehicles Heavy transport may use depot charging, opportunity charging, battery swapping in specialised settings, electric road systems or hydrogen where infrastructure and duty cycle justify it. Household-style assumptions do not apply.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Buses and heavy vehicles Heavy transport may use depot charging, opportunity charging, battery swapping in specialised settings, electric road systems or hydrogen where infrastructure and duty cycle justify it. Household-style assumptions do not apply. Analyse: • route energy and timetable recovery; • passenger or freight mass; • depot land and grid connection; • charger redundancy and pantograph or cable interfaces; • driver fatigue and mandated breaks; • maintenance skills and high-voltage isolation; • emergency recovery of a heavy disabled vehicle; • electricity demand and resilience; • lifecycle cost per passenger-kilometre or tonne-kilometre. Fleet total cost Include vehicle, finance, depot work, network connection, demand charges, energy, charging maintenance, telematics, training, tyres, service, downtime, relief vehicles, residual value and tax.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Analyse: • route energy and timetable recovery; • passenger or freight mass; • depot land and grid connection; • charger redundancy and pantograph or cable interfaces; • driver fatigue and mandated breaks; • maintenance skills and high-voltage isolation; • emergency recovery of a heavy disabled vehicle; • electricity demand and resilience; • lifecycle cost per passenger-kilometre or tonne-kilometre. Fleet total cost Include vehicle, finance, depot work, network connection, demand charges, energy, charging maintenance, telematics, training, tyres, service, downtime, relief vehicles, residual value and tax. Report cost per vehicle-kilometre, passenger-kilometre, delivery or tonne-kilometre as appropriate.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 62 Governance dashboard Track monthly: • vehicle and charger availability; • route completion and reserve breaches; • wall kWh, Wh/km and energy cost; • charging by location and time; • peak site demand; • maintenance and tyre cost; • faults, near misses and emergency events; • driver feedback; • avoided kilometres and mode shift; • operational emissions using a declared electricity factor. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/buying-electric-vehicle/elect... [2] www.infrastructure.gov.au/infrastructure-transport-vehicles/trans...

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 63 Electrically Assisted Cycles, Scooters, Active and Shared Transport For short trips, an electrically assisted cycle or other lawful small mobility device can use far less energy, space and material than a car. It can also extend access for people who find hills, distance or cargo difficult. The tradeoffs are exposure to traffic and weather, theft, battery quality, storage, road rules and fire safety. Mode-fit ladder Ask for each trip: 1 Can it be walked or completed with a mobility aid? 2 Can a conventional bicycle or cargo cycle handle it? 3 Would electrical assistance make the route practical? 4 Is public transport available for most of the distance? 5 Can a shared vehicle cover the rare car-dependent trip? 6 Only then, what private motor vehicle is necessary?

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: 5 Can a shared vehicle cover the rare car-dependent trip? 6 Only then, what private motor vehicle is necessary? Electrically assisted cycle check • State or territory definition, permitted power-assistance behaviour and speed. • Pedals, brakes, lights, reflectors, bell and helmet requirements. • Frame and rack load limits for rider, children and cargo. • Battery and charger traceability, compatibility and instructions. • Battery mounting, lock, water exposure and impact protection. • Replacement battery and charger availability. • Safe home, work and destination storage. • Route separation, intersection risk and end-of-trip facilities. • Insurance, theft and public-transport carriage rules. • Service access for brakes, tyres, wheels, drivetrain and electrical system. Rules for cycles, scooters and paths vary by jurisdiction and can change.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Electrically assisted cycle check • State or territory definition, permitted power-assistance behaviour and speed. • Pedals, brakes, lights, reflectors, bell and helmet requirements. • Frame and rack load limits for rider, children and cargo. • Battery and charger traceability, compatibility and instructions. • Battery mounting, lock, water exposure and impact protection. • Replacement battery and charger availability. • Safe home, work and destination storage. • Route separation, intersection risk and end-of-trip facilities. • Insurance, theft and public-transport carriage rules. • Service access for brakes, tyres, wheels, drivetrain and electrical system. Rules for cycles, scooters and paths vary by jurisdiction and can change. Check the current road authority before use or purchase. A high-powered device sold online may not be lawful on public roads or paths.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Check the current road authority before use or purchase. A high-powered device sold online may not be lawful on public roads or paths. Sources: [1] www.productsafety.gov.au/business/e-bikes-e-scooters-and-other-e-... Small lithium-battery safety Small removable batteries can be brought inside homes and escape routes, so their charging discipline is especially important. • Use the charger specified for that battery and device. • Never mix batteries, chargers or connectors because they appear to fit. • Inspect for swelling, dents, crushing, cracks, leaks, overheating, odour or venting. • Allow a battery to cool after use before charging. • Charge while awake and able to respond, on a non-flammable surface. • Keep away from beds, sofas, carpet, curtains and combustible storage.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 64 • Do not charge in an exit path. • Keep cool, dry and out of direct sun or a hot parked vehicle. • Disconnect when charging is complete according to instructions. • Check recalls and stop using recalled equipment. • Use an authorised battery-disposal pathway; never household rubbish, recycling or hard waste. SAFETY If a battery becomes hot, swells, hisses, vents, smokes or catches fire, move people away, close the area only if this does not trap anyone, call 000 and do not re-enter. Do not carry a failing battery through the home. Sources: [1] www.productsafety.gov.au/consumers/be-safe-around-the-home/safely...

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Do not carry a failing battery through the home. Sources: [1] www.productsafety.gov.au/consumers/be-safe-around-the-home/safely... Storage and charging proposal for a rental or apartment Record: • device and battery type; • lawful route and use; • charging location outside exits and sleeping areas where possible; • non-flammable surface and working smoke alarms; • original compatible charger; • no overnight or unattended charging; • cool, dry storage away from impact; • process for damaged battery and recycling; • permission for any fixed anchor, cabinet or outlet work. Shared buildings should not create blanket rules without assessing fire safety, accessibility, theft and resident mobility. Equally, a mobility benefit does not justify unsafe charging in a corridor.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Shared buildings should not create blanket rules without assessing fire safety, accessibility, theft and resident mobility. Equally, a mobility benefit does not justify unsafe charging in a corridor. Cargo and children Check total load, seat and restraint compatibility, wheel guards, stability when parked, braking distance and low-speed handling. Practise away from traffic before carrying a passenger. Heavier loads change hill starts, stopping and battery use. Never exceed frame, rack or accessory limits. Scooter decision Small-wheeled scooters can be portable but may be sensitive to potholes, wet surfaces and abrupt obstacles. Verify local legality, wheel and brake capability, rider visibility, lighting, battery quality and secure storage. A claimed maximum speed above the lawful assisted limit is a warning, not a benefit.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Verify local legality, wheel and brake capability, rider visibility, lighting, battery quality and secure storage. A claimed maximum speed above the lawful assisted limit is a warning, not a benefit. Active-travel readiness at home • Secure, step-free or ramped storage where practicable. • Anchor designed for the structure, with permission. • Dry area with ventilation and no obstruction to egress. • Nearby lawful charging outlet assessed for the intended equipment. • Helmet, wet-weather gear, lights and pannier or cargo storage. • Pump and basic mechanical tools kept separate from battery repair. • Route maps prioritising protected infrastructure.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 65 Shared vehicles and car share Compare membership, hourly or daily fee, kilometre charge, booking reliability, child-seat or accessibility needs, damage excess, cleaning, charging responsibility and coverage. A shared solution works when vehicles are available at the times and places of need. Retain a fallback for emergency caring or accessibility obligations. Public transport integration Plan the whole door-to-door chain: safe walk or ride, secure parking, service frequency, transfer time, late-night return, weather and accessibility. A folding cycle or mobility device may be permitted only under specific operator rules. Test a representative trip before disposing of a household vehicle.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: A folding cycle or mobility device may be permitted only under specific operator rules. Test a representative trip before disposing of a household vehicle. Measure the result Track car kilometres avoided, mode-share, cost, travel time, exercise, incidents and trips abandoned. The best transport transition improves access, not merely vehicle technology.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 66 Emissions, Resources and the Whole Energy Transition Electric mobility connects household energy to transport, but the cleanest kilometre is often the one avoided or shifted to a lighter mode. Assess tailpipe pollution, electricity, manufacturing, vehicle size, total kilometres, occupancy and end of life together.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Assess tailpipe pollution, electricity, manufacturing, vehicle size, total kilometres, occupancy and end of life together. Emissions boundaries Boundary Includes Does not include unless added Tailpipe Gases emitted from the vehicle while driving Electricity, fuel supply, manufacturing, tyres and roads Fuel lifecycle Extraction or generation, processing, transport and combustion of energy Vehicle and battery manufacture and disposal Vehicle lifecycle Manufacture, use energy and end of life Road construction, congestion and broader land use unless modelled Mobility system Vehicle lifecycle plus occupancy, mode, infrastructure and avoided trips Social outcomes unless explicitly assessed Battery-electric vehicles have no tailpipe exhaust, but electricity generation and manufacturing create emissions. The electricity result varies by state, time and renewable share. Tyre and road wear remain.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: The electricity result varies by state, time and renewable share. Tyre and road wear remain. Regenerative braking can reduce friction-brake particles but cannot remove non-exhaust pollution. Sources: [1] greenvehicleguide.gov.au/pages/UnderstandingEmissions/LifecycleEm... [2] www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/electric-vehicle-basics/elect... Use the public calculator correctly The Australian Government fuel-lifecycle calculator estimates emissions from fuel production, electricity generation and combustion using consumption, grid and kilometres. Record: • source and date; • vehicle Wh/km or fuel consumption and test basis; • state or electricity grid selected; • annual kilometres; • whether home renewable charging is separately modelled; • what manufacturing and disposal effects are excluded. Do not report a fuel-lifecycle result as a complete vehicle lifecycle result.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Record: • source and date; • vehicle Wh/km or fuel consumption and test basis; • state or electricity grid selected; • annual kilometres; • whether home renewable charging is separately modelled; • what manufacturing and disposal effects are excluded. Do not report a fuel-lifecycle result as a complete vehicle lifecycle result. Sources: [1] greenvehicleguide.gov.au/Calculators/FuelLifecycleEmissionsCalcul... Size and utilisation matter A larger battery and body generally require more material and manufacturing energy. They may also increase tyre wear and road space. Compare: • passenger-kilometres, not only vehicle-kilometres; • tonne-kilometres for freight; • annual kilometres and expected life; • battery capacity actually required; • ability to share or use a smaller vehicle; • repair life and parts support; • renewable charging availability.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 67 Keeping a safe, efficient existing vehicle for low annual kilometres can sometimes be preferable to manufacturing a new one immediately. Conversely, replacing a high-use, inefficient vehicle can deliver faster operational benefit. State the assumptions rather than using a universal payback year. Air quality and noise Removing exhaust improves local air around streets, homes and workplaces. Electric drivetrains are quieter at low speed, although tyre and aerodynamic noise remain at higher speeds. Very quiet vehicles can be harder for pedestrians to detect. New Australian requirements phase in acoustic alert systems for relevant new electric, hybrid and hydrogen vehicle models; existing owners should use extra care around pedestrians, children and vision-impaired people.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Very quiet vehicles can be harder for pedestrians to detect. New Australian requirements phase in acoustic alert systems for relevant new electric, hybrid and hydrogen vehicle models; existing owners should use extra care around pedestrians, children and vision-impaired people. Sources: [1] minister.infrastructure.gov.au/c-king/media-release/new-ev-and-hy... Materials and circularity Battery and motor supply chains use lithium, graphite, nickel, iron, phosphate, copper, aluminium and other materials depending on design.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Sources: [1] minister.infrastructure.gov.au/c-king/media-release/new-ev-and-hy... Materials and circularity Battery and motor supply chains use lithium, graphite, nickel, iron, phosphate, copper, aluminium and other materials depending on design. Responsible transition requires: • durable vehicles and batteries; • repair rather than premature replacement; • transparent sourcing and due diligence; • design for disassembly; • reuse only where safety and traceability are maintained; • high-quality recycling and recovered-material markets; • safe transport and storage of damaged batteries; • producer and importer responsibility. A claim that a battery is recyclable does not prove it will be collected, economically recovered or used again in Australia. Ask for the actual end-of-life pathway and who pays. Electricity transition connection EVs add electricity demand but also flexible load.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Ask for the actual end-of-life pathway and who pays. Electricity transition connection EVs add electricity demand but also flexible load. Household and system benefits improve when charging: • occurs in lower-demand or renewable-rich periods; • is coordinated with water heating, space conditioning and household batteries; • avoids unnecessary new peaks; • remains available for essential departures; • uses transparent network and tariff signals; • preserves consumer control and privacy. Bidirectional export may add flexibility but is not necessary for EV value. Simple scheduled charging is often the first practical step. A household carbon priority order 1 Reduce unnecessary travel and flights where practical. 2 Shift trips to walking, cycling, public or shared transport. 3 Improve occupancy and combine trips. 4 Choose the smallest efficient vehicle that passes actual needs.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: 3 Improve occupancy and combine trips. 4 Choose the smallest efficient vehicle that passes actual needs. 5 Charge at lower-emission times or from additional renewable energy where practical.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 68 6 Maintain tyres, alignment and vehicle efficiency. 7 Keep the vehicle and battery in useful service. 8 Repair, resell and recycle through traceable pathways. What completes the home-and-mobility transition This electric-mobility guide rounds out the major energy-upgrade chain when combined with building fabric, efficient electric appliances, hot water, solar, storage and tariffs.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: 8 Repair, resell and recycle through traceable pathways. What completes the home-and-mobility transition This electric-mobility guide rounds out the major energy-upgrade chain when combined with building fabric, efficient electric appliances, hot water, solar, storage and tariffs. Four adjacent subjects still deserve explicit treatment: • Water efficiency and water resilience: leaks, hot-water demand, fixtures, gardens, rainwater, drought and supply interruptions. • Climate resilience: heatwaves, bushfire smoke, flood, storms, outage planning, passive survivability and medically essential loads. • Embodied carbon and materials: renovation quantity, reuse, low-toxicity materials, repair and construction waste. • Access-first transport planning: safe walking, cycling, disability access, public transport, land use and shared mobility.

Claim filter Reject or qualify any claim that: • reports zero emissions without stating the boundary; • compares unlike vehicle sizes or lifetimes; • uses an electricity factor from another place or year; • ignores fuel production for the comparison vehicle; • assumes every kilometre is unavoidable; • treats recycling potential as proven recovery; • counts export revenue without charging losses or equipment cost; • presents one laboratory range as every driver's outcome.

Apartment resident playbook 1 Confirm title, lease and common-property boundaries. 2 Ask whether an EV plan, electrical study or approved equipment standard already exists. 3 Seek a building-wide feasibility study if uptake will extend beyond one bay. 4 Require measured demand, staged scenarios, load management and sub-metering. 5 Resolve fire, egress, accessibility, insurer and emergency issues. 6 Adopt transparent cost allocation and individual agreement. 7 Protect the future backbone from incompatible isolated installations. 8 Keep drawings, approvals, certificates and settings with building records. Used-vehicle playbook 1 Check identity, title, security interest, written-off status and recalls. 2 Verify local supply or import pathway and support.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Used-vehicle playbook 1 Check identity, title, security interest, written-off status and recalls. 2 Verify local supply or import pathway and support. 3 Read battery and vehicle warranties before inspection. 4 Commission an independent mechanical and high-voltage inspection. 5 Test AC charging and, where feasible, compatible DC charging. 6 Document battery-health method rather than accepting a dashboard number. 7 Verify cables, keys, accounts, software and personal-data reset. 8 Price tyres, insurance, charger work and likely repair risk. 9 Keep the advertisement and all written representations. Road-trip playbook 1 Estimate each leg using adverse Wh/km and reserve. 2 Select a preferred and independent backup charger. 3 Confirm connector, access, payment, recent status and amenities.

Towing playbook 1 Confirm legal towing, payload, axle, towball and combination limits. 2 Weigh the actual loaded combination. 3 Measure consumption with the real trailer in both directions. 4 Model wind, hills and reserve. 5 Verify charger approach and turning with the trailer. 6 Plan safe uncoupling where necessary. 7 Confirm recovery covers vehicle and trailer. 8 Recheck tyres, coupling, brakes and lights after every charging stop. Common myths and the useful answer Myth: Every household needs the fastest home charger Reality: Required power equals energy to restore divided by available time, with losses and margin.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Common myths and the useful answer Myth: Every household needs the fastest home charger Reality: Required power equals energy to restore divided by available time, with losses and margin. Many vehicles are parked far longer than they drive. Electrical condition and load management matter more than the largest nameplate. Myth: A standard outlet is always enough Reality: It may supply sufficient energy for low daily travel, but the outlet, circuit, protection, environment and sustained-load suitability must be assessed. An old or shared outlet is not safe because the vehicle accepts a low current. Myth: A large battery eliminates range risk Reality: Speed, weather, towing, charging reliability and route consequence remain. Larger batteries add cost and mass. Redundant planning can be more valuable than unused capacity.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Larger batteries add cost and mass. Redundant planning can be more valuable than unused capacity. Myth: The advertised DC peak tells me charging time Reality: Battery temperature and state of charge shape a curve. Compare energy added or a stated percentage window under stated conditions. Myth: Charging to 100 percent always damages the battery Reality: Vehicle instructions differ. High charge may be appropriate before a trip or for a documented balancing process. Routine target and long storage should follow the exact manual. Myth: Electric vehicles are maintenance-free Reality: Tyres, brakes, suspension, thermal systems, 12 V batteries, software, filters, wipers and charging equipment still need attention. Myth: Regenerative braking means friction brakes do not matter Reality: Friction brakes remain essential and can corrode when lightly used.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Myth: Electric vehicles are maintenance-free Reality: Tyres, brakes, suspension, thermal systems, 12 V batteries, software, filters, wipers and charging equipment still need attention. Myth: Regenerative braking means friction brakes do not matter Reality: Friction brakes remain essential and can corrode when lightly used. They require inspection and safe operation. Myth: Any adapter solves connector differences Reality: Physical fit is only one requirement. Communication, protection, current, approval and vehicle support must match. Myth: A vehicle-to-load outlet can run the house Reality: It can power compatible plug-in loads within limits. Building supply requires approved changeover, isolation, protection and exact system compatibility.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: DRIVE THE TRANSITION AUSTRALIAN ELECTRIC MOBILITY FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 74 Myth: Vehicle-to-grid is guaranteed future income Reality: Vehicle, EVSE, network, tariff, contract and connection time must align. Revenue, losses, cycling and equipment cost are uncertain. Myth: Electric vehicles have zero environmental impact Reality: They have no tailpipe exhaust, but manufacturing, electricity, tyres, roads and end of life matter. Fewer kilometres and smaller modes still help. Myth: Battery fires make all EV parking uniquely unsafe Reality: Battery incidents require specific planning, but risk should be assessed from evidence, vehicle and building design. Safe electrical installation, damage response, detection, egress and emergency procedures matter more than slogans. Myth: Floodwater is safe because the battery is sealed Reality: Floodwater is dangerous to every vehicle.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Safe electrical installation, damage response, detection, egress and emergency procedures matter more than slogans. Myth: Floodwater is safe because the battery is sealed Reality: Floodwater is dangerous to every vehicle. Immersion can damage high-voltage systems and create delayed risk. Do not drive through water or recharge a flooded vehicle. Myth: A plug-in hybrid never needs charging Reality: It can drive without external charging, but failing to charge defeats much of its intended electric operation and can increase fuel use while carrying two powertrains. Myth: An incentive makes the purchase affordable Reality: Programs can close, be capped or have eligibility and tax conditions. The purchase must pass without an unapproved benefit.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Myth: An incentive makes the purchase affordable Reality: Programs can close, be capped or have eligibility and tax conditions. The purchase must pass without an unapproved benefit. Myth: A voluntary warranty defines all rights Reality: Consumer guarantees may apply in addition to warranties for vehicles bought from a licensed dealer. Private sales and auctions differ. Myth: Electrifying every car completes the transport transition Reality: Congestion, road trauma, parking, tyre wear and access remain. Walking, cycling, public transport, sharing, smaller vehicles and fewer trips are part of the solution.

chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: Stop-work and stop-purchase triggers Stop and obtain qualified advice if: • fixed electrical work is proposed without a licence or certificate; • an extension lead, power board or backfeed cable is proposed; • a cable crosses public or common access without written authority; • the vehicle or battery has collision, flood, heat or warning evidence; • payload or towing compliance cannot be demonstrated; • a used import has no credible charging, recall or repair pathway; • a building proposal ignores maximum demand, metering or future users; • a bidirectional system lacks written vehicle, equipment and network compatibility; • a tax or rebate outcome is described as guaranteed without current authority; • contract totals, residual, exclusions or data obligations are hidden; • a small lithium battery is swollen, damaged, hot, leaking or recalled.

It contained 12,332 unique public URLs across 17 child sitemaps, including 9,730 dated articles, 16 pages, 159 vehicle-information entries, 29 categories, 1,791 tags, 209 make-or-model taxonomy entries and 398 author entries. All 12,332 sitemap URLs were captured with zero sitemap failures. Every article URL was classified by practical topic. chunks.sourceTitle: Drive the Transition: Australian Electric Mobility Guide
chunks.text: This is a coverage map, not a quality score. Deep extraction focused on evergreen explainers and recurring reader questions across each topic. Dated reporting, opinion, prices, model launches, sponsored material, company claims and product listings were not carried into the recommendations. Technical, safety, legal, tax and consumer claims were checked against current Australian public authorities. Where current national guidance does not establish a universal answer, the guide directs the reader to the relevant state, territory, network, building, tax or professional decision point. This method is comprehensive in topic coverage, not a claim that every sentence of every historical news article remains current or was reproduced. No commercial source link or proprietary name appears in the reader guidance.

chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 7 Start Here: Fix the Building Before Buying More Heating or Cooling This is an independent, Australia-wide field guide for renters, homeowners, apartment residents, renovators and people planning a new home. It explains insulation and glazing options by function. It contains no company endorsement, brand, product listing, current price, sales lead, installer referral, paid recommendation or commercial relationship. The central rule is simple: diagnose heat, air, moisture and sound pathways before choosing a material or window. Insulation does not stop draughts. Draught sealing does not replace deliberate ventilation. Double glazing does not correct unshaded west-facing glass. A high R-value does not rescue insulation with gaps, compression or unsafe clearances. DECISION Define the outcome first.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: A high R-value does not rescue insulation with gaps, compression or unsafe clearances. DECISION Define the outcome first. Winter warmth, summer heat control, lower bills, reduced condensation, quieter rooms, heritage retention and bushfire resilience are different jobs. One upgrade may help several, but no single product solves them all. The six-part comfort ladder 1 Make hazards safe. Resolve suspect asbestos, unsafe wiring, wet cavities, active roof leaks, rotten frames, broken glass, vermin, unflued gas appliances and unsafe access before disturbing the building. 2 Measure the problem. Record room temperatures, humidity, draughts, sun exposure, heating or cooling runtime, visible insulation coverage, condensation locations and noise character. 3 Control unwanted air and sun. Seal avoidable leakage without blocking required ventilation.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: 3 Control unwanted air and sun. Seal avoidable leakage without blocking required ventilation. Shade unwanted direct sun before trying to insulate against it. 4 Complete the thermal layer. Insulate ceilings, roofs, walls and floors with climate-appropriate, continuous assemblies that manage moisture and thermal bridges. 5 Improve glazing as a system. Consider glass, cavities, coatings, spacers, frames, opening style, seals, orientation, shading and window furnishings together. 6 Verify the result. Retest comfort, temperatures, humidity, draughts, noise and energy use. Obtain photographs, specifications and compliance records for hidden work.

Evidence hierarchy Use evidence in this order: 1 Safety law, building requirements, licensing and property permissions. 2 Site-specific construction, climate, orientation, moisture and access. 3 Measured temperatures, humidity, air leakage, noise and energy use. 4 Whole-assembly performance: total R-value, whole-window U-value, SHGC, air leakage and acoustic rating. 5 Written installation details, drawings, tested data, product suitability and warranty conditions. 6 A transparent model with declared assumptions.

Quick triage One room is much hotter in summer • Identify which glass receives direct sun and at what time. • Shade the glass externally where practical; west and east sun usually need different geometry from north sun. • Check ceiling insulation coverage above the room and whether downlights or access paths create large gaps. • Check roof colour, sarking, roof ventilation design and whether the room is a later addition. • Compare window seals and frame type with adjacent rooms.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: The house is cold despite heating • Check unintended air leakage around doors, windows, floorboards, exhaust fans, chimneys and service penetrations. • Check whether curtains reach the floor, return to the wall and have a pelmet or close top gap. • Inspect ceiling insulation continuity from a safe position or arrange an inspection. • Check suspended floors and wall cavities, especially in older additions. • Check whether the heating system is conditioning unused rooms or losing heat through ducts. Windows are wet in winter • Determine whether moisture is on the room surface, outside surface or between sealed panes. • Measure indoor relative humidity and note cooking, showering, clothes drying and occupancy.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: R-values R-value is resistance to heat flow. Higher is more resistant. Distinguish: • Material or product R-value: the tested resistance of one product at a stated thickness and condition. • Added R-value: the contribution of the added layer. • Total system R-value: the combined roof, ceiling, wall or floor assembly, including air films, linings, cavities, structure and thermal bridges. • Up and down values: reflective systems can perform differently by heat-flow direction because air-space behaviour changes. Do not assume that doubling thickness always doubles installed performance. Compression, air movement, moisture, ageing, settling, structural framing and gaps can change the result. Ask for the installed assembly and its calculation basis.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Compression, air movement, moisture, ageing, settling, structural framing and gaps can change the result. Ask for the installed assembly and its calculation basis. Continuity usually matters more than a small rating increase Heat bypasses insulation at: • Missing batts and irregular cut pieces. • Steel or timber framing, slab edges and balcony connections. • Downlights, exhaust fans, ducts, access hatches and service penetrations. • Wall-to-floor, wall-to-roof and window-to-wall junctions. • Compressed, wind-washed, wet, slumped or fallen material. A moderate, continuous layer can outperform a nominally high-rated layer with repeated gaps. Window U-value Whole-window U-value measures the rate of heat transfer through the complete glazed assembly, including glass, spacer and frame. Lower is better for resisting conductive heat flow in both directions.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Window U-value Whole-window U-value measures the rate of heat transfer through the complete glazed assembly, including glass, spacer and frame. Lower is better for resisting conductive heat flow in both directions. Approximate conductive heat flow can be compared using: DECISION Heat flow in watts = whole-window U-value multiplied by window area in square metres multiplied by the indoor-outdoor temperature difference in degrees Celsius. This is a comparison tool, not a complete energy model. It excludes sun, air leakage, curtains, shading, thermal mass, equipment and occupant behaviour. Ask whether a quoted U-value is:

Solar heat gain coefficient SHGC is the fraction of incident solar heat transmitted through a window, including directly transmitted solar energy and heat absorbed and released inward. It is between 0 and 1. • Lower SHGC rejects more solar heat and can help cooling-dominated rooms or exposed east and west glass. • Higher SHGC admits more winter sun and may help correctly oriented, well-shaded glazing in heating-dominated climates. • The correct value depends on climate, orientation, glass area, external shade and thermal mass.

chunks.text: Solar heat gain coefficient SHGC is the fraction of incident solar heat transmitted through a window, including directly transmitted solar energy and heat absorbed and released inward. It is between 0 and 1. • Lower SHGC rejects more solar heat and can help cooling-dominated rooms or exposed east and west glass. • Higher SHGC admits more winter sun and may help correctly oriented, well-shaded glazing in heating-dominated climates. • The correct value depends on climate, orientation, glass area, external shade and thermal mass. Low U-value is generally useful in all climates. SHGC is a design choice, not a universal race to the lowest number. Visible light and glare Visible light transmittance describes how much visible light passes through. A low-SHGC glass can still have useful daylight, but some tints, films and coatings reduce light or change colour.

Request samples and whole-system values if daylight, views, colour rendering or glare matters. Airtightness and ventilation Airtightness controls unintended leakage. Ventilation intentionally replaces indoor air. A healthy home needs both: • Seal uncontrolled gaps that bypass the intended envelope. • Keep required combustion air and permanent ventilation until a qualified assessment says otherwise. • Exhaust bathroom, kitchen and laundry moisture outdoors where required and practical. • Provide make-up air and a plan for fresh air after major sealing work. • Use opening windows only when outdoor temperature, humidity, smoke, noise and security conditions permit.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Ventilation intentionally replaces indoor air. A healthy home needs both: • Seal uncontrolled gaps that bypass the intended envelope. • Keep required combustion air and permanent ventilation until a qualified assessment says otherwise. • Exhaust bathroom, kitchen and laundry moisture outdoors where required and practical. • Provide make-up air and a plan for fresh air after major sealing work. • Use opening windows only when outdoor temperature, humidity, smoke, noise and security conditions permit. An airtight home with poor ventilation can trap humidity and pollutants. A leaky home is not a reliable ventilation system because airflow varies with wind and temperature.

It can occur: • On the room side of glass, frames, corners or walls. • On the outdoor face of high-performance glazing under some weather conditions. • Between panes when an insulated glass unit seal has failed. • Inside roofs, walls or floors where it is hidden and can damage materials. Control requires a combination of: 1 Reducing indoor moisture generation and exhausting wet-area air.

Control requires a combination of: 1 Reducing indoor moisture generation and exhausting wet-area air. 2 Keeping internal surfaces warmer through insulation, thermal breaks and better glazing. 3 Preventing humid air from leaking into cold assemblies. 4 Selecting vapour-permeable or vapour-resistant layers for the actual climate and assembly. 5 Providing drainage and drying paths.
