Sound fundamentals Sound control depends on frequency and path. • Airborne sound: voices, music, engines and aircraft enter through glass, walls and gaps. • Impact sound: footsteps, doors and machinery excite the structure. • Low-frequency sound: heavy traffic and bass are difficult because long wavelengths pass through light assemblies. • Flanking sound: bypasses the treated element through roofs, floors, ducts, gaps or adjacent walls.

chunks.text: Reflective insulation, foil and membranes Reflective insulation reduces radiant heat transfer only when its reflective surface faces a suitable air space. Direct contact with another solid removes much of the intended radiant effect. Possible roles include: • Roof and wall sarking for secondary weather protection. • Reflective insulation facing a roof or wall cavity. • Vapour-permeable or vapour-resistant control layer selected for climate.

chunks.text: Composite and advanced options • Structural insulated panels combine structure, insulation and facings; junction and service design is critical. • Insulated plasterboard can improve internal walls where external access is impossible, but reduces room area and changes moisture behaviour. • External insulation systems can create a continuous layer over framing, reducing thermal bridges; weatherproofing, fire, termite and cladding design are specialist work. • Vacuum insulation panels provide high resistance in little thickness but lose performance if punctured and require careful edge detailing. • Aerogel blankets or renders can help thin heritage details, reveals and thermal bridges, but need verified whole-assembly performance. • Phase-change materials store heat rather than simply resist its flow. They are not a substitute for insulation and require climate-specific modelling.

chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 20 Roofs and Ceilings: Stop the Largest Continuous Path Choose the thermal boundary Insulation at the ceiling plane Common for vented pitched roofs with an unconditioned roof space. Advantages include smaller conditioned volume and relatively accessible retrofit work. The ceiling layer must remain continuous around external walls, hatches, ducts, exhausts, flues and lighting. Insulation at the roofline Used for cathedral ceilings, conditioned roof spaces, some skillion roofs and selected high-performance renovations. It needs a coordinated roof, insulation, air, vapour, ventilation and condensation design. Moving the thermal boundary can place ducts and services inside the conditioned space, but poor detailing can conceal roof moisture.

chunks.text: It needs a coordinated roof, insulation, air, vapour, ventilation and condensation design. Moving the thermal boundary can place ducts and services inside the conditioned space, but poor detailing can conceal roof moisture. Ceiling plus roof layers Two layers may control different heat paths, but should not create a trapped-moisture assembly or an unintentionally conditioned roof space. Define what each layer does and where the air and vapour control layers are.

chunks.text: Ceiling plus roof layers Two layers may control different heat paths, but should not create a trapped-moisture assembly or an unintentionally conditioned roof space. Define what each layer does and where the air and vapour control layers are. Pitched roof and accessible ceiling options • Batts between ceiling joists. • A second cross-laid batt layer over joists where clearances and access allow. • Loose-fill material distributed to a verified depth with settlement allowance. • Rigid or semi-rigid boards for selected ceiling or roofline details. • Roof blanket under metal roofing, generally installed during roofing work. • Reflective sarking or membrane beneath the roof covering with required air spaces. • Insulated access-hatch cover and durable perimeter seal. Top-up or replace?

chunks.text: Pitched roof and accessible ceiling options • Batts between ceiling joists. • A second cross-laid batt layer over joists where clearances and access allow. • Loose-fill material distributed to a verified depth with settlement allowance. • Rigid or semi-rigid boards for selected ceiling or roofline details. • Roof blanket under metal roofing, generally installed during roofing work. • Reflective sarking or membrane beneath the roof covering with required air spaces. • Insulated access-hatch cover and durable perimeter seal. Top-up or replace? Retain and add to existing insulation only when it is dry, uncontaminated, compatible, correctly supported and reasonably continuous. Remove or remediate when it is wet, mould-affected, pest-contaminated, unsafe, severely displaced, incompatible with the new assembly or blocking essential inspection and services.

Do not bury evidence of leaks, unsafe wiring, overheated fittings or vermin. Cathedral, raked, skillion and flat roofs These assemblies have little spare depth and are sensitive to thermal bridges and condensation. Options include: • High-performance batts between rafters with a ventilation or drainage path where designed. • Continuous rigid insulation above rafters during re-roofing. • Insulated roof panels in new work. • Internal insulated lining below rafters where room height and junctions permit. • Combined reflective and bulk layers with the specified air space.

It is not automatically a substitute for bulk insulation. Confirm: • Whether it is vapour-permeable or vapour-resistant. • Which side faces the cavity and whether an air gap is required. • Overlap, tape, penetration, gutter, ridge and eave details. • Compatibility with roof type, climate, bushfire and high-wind requirements. • How condensation can drain and the assembly can dry. Installation sequence 1 Inspect roof covering, flashings, leaks and structure. 2 Identify asbestos risk, loose fill, pests and contaminated dust. 3 Have wiring, fittings and heat sources checked. 4 Define the thermal, air, vapour and drainage layers.

Required clearances and covers are technical safety requirements, not optional energy details.

chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 23 Walls: New Build, Renovation and Retrofit Options Wall work depends on whether the cavity is open, closed, drained, ventilated, fire-rated or exposed to moisture. Open wall cavities When linings or cladding are removed, options include: • Friction-fit batts between timber or steel studs. • Rigid board between framing with carefully sealed edges. • Spray-applied insulation where the complete system is suitable. • A continuous external insulation layer beneath a compliant cladding system. • An internal service cavity to reduce penetrations through the air and vapour layer. • Acoustic batts plus additional or isolated linings for noise control. This is the best opportunity to inspect framing, plumbing, wiring, fire-stopping, flashing, membranes and termite barriers.

chunks.text: Open wall cavities When linings or cladding are removed, options include: • Friction-fit batts between timber or steel studs. • Rigid board between framing with carefully sealed edges. • Spray-applied insulation where the complete system is suitable. • A continuous external insulation layer beneath a compliant cladding system. • An internal service cavity to reduce penetrations through the air and vapour layer. • Acoustic batts plus additional or isolated linings for noise control. This is the best opportunity to inspect framing, plumbing, wiring, fire-stopping, flashing, membranes and termite barriers. Do not close the wall before documenting the complete installation.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: This is the best opportunity to inspect framing, plumbing, wiring, fire-stopping, flashing, membranes and termite barriers. Do not close the wall before documenting the complete installation. Closed cavity retrofit Possible approaches include: • Blown or dense-packed fibre through small access holes. • Injection foam systems designed for the cavity and climate. • Removing selected cladding or internal lining to install batts or boards. • Adding insulated lining internally. • Adding continuous insulation externally during recladding.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Do not close the wall before documenting the complete installation. Closed cavity retrofit Possible approaches include: • Blown or dense-packed fibre through small access holes. • Injection foam systems designed for the cavity and climate. • Removing selected cladding or internal lining to install batts or boards. • Adding insulated lining internally. • Adding continuous insulation externally during recladding. Before filling, determine: • Cavity width, obstructions and whether it is continuous. • Construction type and drainage path. • Existing sarking, membrane, foil or damp-proofing. • Active moisture, rising damp, roof or plumbing leaks. • Weep holes, vents and required cavity drainage. • Wiring, pipes, fire separation and inaccessible voids. • How fill density and complete coverage will be verified. SAFETY Never inject or blow material into an unidentified cavity.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Before filling, determine: • Cavity width, obstructions and whether it is continuous. • Construction type and drainage path. • Existing sarking, membrane, foil or damp-proofing. • Active moisture, rising damp, roof or plumbing leaks. • Weep holes, vents and required cavity drainage. • Wiring, pipes, fire separation and inaccessible voids. • How fill density and complete coverage will be verified. SAFETY Never inject or blow material into an unidentified cavity. It can block drainage, bridge damp, conceal unsafe wiring, enter occupied rooms, cover fire or ventilation openings, or leave large unfilled sections.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: SAFETY Never inject or blow material into an unidentified cavity. It can block drainage, bridge damp, conceal unsafe wiring, enter occupied rooms, cover fire or ventilation openings, or leave large unfilled sections. Construction-specific considerations Timber-framed weatherboard • External access during recladding provides strong inspection and membrane opportunities. • Internal access may protect heritage cladding but disrupts rooms. • Blown-in retrofit can reduce demolition but needs moisture-safe cavity assessment and verified fill.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 24 • Preserve drainage, ventilation and termite inspection details. Brick veneer • The framed inner wall is the main thermal layer. • Keep the outer masonry drainage cavity and weep holes functional. • Do not let injected material create a water bridge from brick to timber or lining. • Steel framing needs thermal-bridge treatment beyond between-stud batts. Double brick or cavity masonry • The cavity often manages water and should not be filled without specialist confirmation. • Internal insulated lining can improve performance but may shift moisture and reduce thermal-mass interaction. • External insulation may be effective during facade work but changes appearance, openings and boundary details. • Blow-in cavity options require construction-specific evidence, not a generic wall claim.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Double brick or cavity masonry • The cavity often manages water and should not be filled without specialist confirmation. • Internal insulated lining can improve performance but may shift moisture and reduce thermal-mass interaction. • External insulation may be effective during facade work but changes appearance, openings and boundary details. • Blow-in cavity options require construction-specific evidence, not a generic wall claim. Solid masonry, concrete or stone • Internal insulation is possible but makes the existing wall colder and may increase interstitial condensation risk. • External insulation usually preserves internal thermal mass and continuity but requires a complete weatherproof facade design. • Window reveals, floors, roofs and party-wall junctions need thermal-bridge details. Steel framing Steel conducts heat around between-stud insulation.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Solid masonry, concrete or stone • Internal insulation is possible but makes the existing wall colder and may increase interstitial condensation risk. • External insulation usually preserves internal thermal mass and continuity but requires a complete weatherproof facade design. • Window reveals, floors, roofs and party-wall junctions need thermal-bridge details. Steel framing Steel conducts heat around between-stud insulation. Continuous insulation or verified thermal breaks are important. Ask for the total wall R-value including the steel frame, not only the batt rating. Party, garage and fire-rated walls Thermal, acoustic, fire and smoke requirements overlap. Do not drill, fill or alter a fire-rated wall without confirming the tested system and approvals.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Party, garage and fire-rated walls Thermal, acoustic, fire and smoke requirements overlap. Do not drill, fill or alter a fire-rated wall without confirming the tested system and approvals. Internal insulated lining Benefits: • Works where exterior appearance or access cannot change. • Can address solid walls and selected rooms. • Allows a service cavity and interior air sealing. Tradeoffs: • Reduces room dimensions and affects skirtings, cornices, outlets and cabinetry. • Requires careful vapour and condensation design. • Creates junction challenges at internal walls, floors, ceilings and windows. • Can hide existing damp if the source is not fixed. External continuous insulation Benefits: • Covers framing and reduces thermal bridges. • Can improve weather protection during recladding. • Keeps existing structure warmer in cool climates.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 25 Tradeoffs: • Changes eaves, flashings, windows, doors, services and boundary dimensions. • Requires tested fire, weatherproofing, impact, termite and fixing details. • May change heritage or planning appearance. • Must integrate with roof, foundation and opening drainage. Wall retrofit quality checks • Written cavity assessment and moisture findings. • Method for wiring, plumbing, noggings and fire blocks. • Installed density, volume and expected settlement where relevant. • Coverage verification using borescope, process records, thermal imaging under suitable conditions or opened sample points. • All access holes sealed, weatherproofed and finished. • Weep holes, vents and drainage paths clear. • Indoor dust contained and cleaned. • Photos before, during and after work.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Wall retrofit quality checks • Written cavity assessment and moisture findings. • Method for wiring, plumbing, noggings and fire blocks. • Installed density, volume and expected settlement where relevant. • Coverage verification using borescope, process records, thermal imaging under suitable conditions or opened sample points. • All access holes sealed, weatherproofed and finished. • Weep holes, vents and drainage paths clear. • Indoor dust contained and cleaned. • Photos before, during and after work. chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 26 Floors, Subfloors and Slabs Suspended timber floors Suspended floors can lose heat through boards and joists and admit air through gaps. Underfloor insulation works best when it creates a continuous layer while preserving moisture control, ventilation, termite inspection and service access. Between-joist bulk insulation Batts or rolls can be fitted between joists and supported as specified.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Underfloor insulation works best when it creates a continuous layer while preserving moisture control, ventilation, termite inspection and service access. Between-joist bulk insulation Batts or rolls can be fitted between joists and supported as specified. Check: • Product is approved for underfloor use and the direction of heat flow. • Width suits actual joist spacing, including irregular older sections. • Fit is snug at edges without compression or large gaps. • Support does not sag, rust, tear or release over time. • Pipes, wiring, ducts and structural members remain accessible and safe. • Insulation does not block subfloor ventilation, damp-proofing or termite inspection zones. Rigid board below or between joists Rigid boards can provide a more continuous layer and reduce joist bridging. Their edges, fixings and joints need a complete design.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Rigid board below or between joists Rigid boards can provide a more continuous layer and reduce joist bridging. Their edges, fixings and joints need a complete design. Consider fire behaviour, moisture exposure, pests, future access and whether the board conceals framing inspection. Reflective or closed-cell systems Some systems combine insulation, air control and moisture resistance. They need the specified air space and orientation. An impermeable layer can trap moisture against timber if the subfloor or indoor vapour conditions are not understood. Sealing floorboard gaps Options include flexible gap filler, removable rope or strip products, underfloor air barriers, rugs and sealed skirtings. Account for seasonal timber movement. Do not glue boards together or use a rigid filler where movement will cause cracking or damage.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Account for seasonal timber movement. Do not glue boards together or use a rigid filler where movement will cause cracking or damage. Subfloor preconditions Do not insulate over an unresolved subfloor problem. Check for: • Standing water, poor site drainage or plumbing leaks. • Persistently damp soil and missing ground moisture control. • Blocked vents or inadequate crossflow. • Rot, fungal decay, corrosion or structural movement. • Termites, rodents or other pests. • Damaged wiring, exposed connections and unsafe equipment. • Sewer, gas or exhaust discharge. • Asbestos-containing fragments, pipe insulation or debris. SAFETY Low-clearance subfloors can be confined, contaminated and electrically hazardous. Household access is not appropriate when entry, escape, ventilation, structure or services are uncertain.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 27 Concrete slabs Under-slab insulation Usually practical only before a new slab is poured. It can be valuable in cold climates, elevated slabs or hydronically heated slabs. Load capacity, moisture, termite and edge details are part of the structural and building design. Slab-edge insulation Exposed slab edges can be significant thermal bridges. Retrofit options may exist externally or as part of recladding, but must preserve termite inspection, damp-proofing, drainage, durability and fire compliance. Insulation above an existing slab An insulated floating floor or raised floor can reduce heat transfer and improve surface comfort. It changes finished floor height, doors, stairs, wet-area transitions, skirtings and accessibility. Moisture beneath impermeable finishes must be assessed first.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: It changes finished floor height, doors, stairs, wet-area transitions, skirtings and accessibility. Moisture beneath impermeable finishes must be assessed first. Floor coverings Carpet and underlay add some resistance and improve contact comfort. Rugs are reversible and renter-friendly. Hard floors may assist thermal-mass strategies where sun access is intentional, but exposed mass can also feel cold. A floor finish is not a replacement for a properly designed slab or subfloor assembly. Upper floors and floors over garages • Insulate the boundary between conditioned rooms and an unconditioned garage or open space. • Preserve required fire and smoke separation. • Treat cantilevered floors and balcony junctions as thermal bridges. • For impact noise, combine resilient layers, mass and isolated ceilings rather than relying on thermal batts alone.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: A floor finish is not a replacement for a properly designed slab or subfloor assembly. Upper floors and floors over garages • Insulate the boundary between conditioned rooms and an unconditioned garage or open space. • Preserve required fire and smoke separation. • Treat cantilevered floors and balcony junctions as thermal bridges. • For impact noise, combine resilient layers, mass and isolated ceilings rather than relying on thermal batts alone. Verification checklist • [ ] Moisture, drainage, pest and structural defects resolved. • [ ] Exact area and floor type recorded. • [ ] Product suitable for underfloor direction and exposure. • [ ] Continuous fit at joists, blocking and perimeter. • [ ] Durable support method installed. • [ ] Services, vents and termite inspection paths preserved. • [ ] Fire-rated boundaries remain compliant. • [ ] Before-and-after photographs supplied.

Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/insulation [2] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 28 Acoustic Insulation and Window Noise Control Diagnose the sound before treating it Record: • Source: road, rail, aircraft, voices, music, plant, plumbing, footsteps or impact. • Time and duration. • Dominant character: low rumble, mid-frequency voice, high-frequency hiss or impulsive impact. • Direction and whether the sound changes when a window, door or vent is sealed temporarily. • Rooms and surfaces where vibration is strongest. • Existing glazing, wall, roof, door and vent construction. Sound level alone is not enough. Two noises with similar measured loudness may require different assemblies. The five acoustic tools 1 Seal air paths. Sound passes through the same gaps that pass air. Treat window and door perimeters, meeting rails, service penetrations and vents while preserving required ventilation.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Sound passes through the same gaps that pass air. Treat window and door perimeters, meeting rails, service penetrations and vents while preserving required ventilation. 2 Add mass. Dense layers reduce transmission, particularly when properly supported and sealed. 3 Separate layers. Independent leaves with a suitable cavity reduce vibration transfer. 4 Absorb cavity energy. Porous insulation reduces resonances in wall, ceiling and floor cavities. 5 Control flanking. Treat the roof, eaves, doors, walls, floors and ducts that bypass the upgraded element. Window options for noise Option Likely use Important questions Repair and perimeter sealing Rattling or visibly leaky windows Can seals remain continuous while the sash operates? Thick single pane Some airborne sound improvement Is safety glass required and is the frame strong enough?

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Window options for noise Option Likely use Important questions Repair and perimeter sealing Rattling or visibly leaky windows Can seals remain continuous while the sash operates? Thick single pane Some airborne sound improvement Is safety glass required and is the frame strong enough? Laminated glass Traffic and lower-frequency improvement; safety and UV benefits What laminate, thickness and tested whole-window rating apply? Standard insulated glass unit Thermal improvement and some mid-to-high-frequency sound reduction Are panes the same thickness, and what is the cavity? Asymmetric insulated glass unit Broader acoustic response than equal panes What exact pane makeup and test result apply?

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Standard insulated glass unit Thermal improvement and some mid-to-high-frequency sound reduction Are panes the same thickness, and what is the cavity? Asymmetric insulated glass unit Broader acoustic response than equal panes What exact pane makeup and test result apply? Acoustic laminated insulated unit High-performance combined thermal and acoustic work Weight, frame, seals, safety, installation and cost need coordination Secondary glazing Large separation can be useful acoustically and preserves the outer window Perimeter sealing, ventilation, cleaning access and condensation between layers Full window replacement Frame, operation and seals are beyond repair Compare whole-window acoustic, thermal, water and air performance Double glazing is not automatically soundproof.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Asymmetric insulated glass unit Broader acoustic response than equal panes What exact pane makeup and test result apply? Acoustic laminated insulated unit High-performance combined thermal and acoustic work Weight, frame, seals, safety, installation and cost need coordination Secondary glazing Large separation can be useful acoustically and preserves the outer window Perimeter sealing, ventilation, cleaning access and condensation between layers Full window replacement Frame, operation and seals are beyond repair Compare whole-window acoustic, thermal, water and air performance Double glazing is not automatically soundproof. A thermally efficient narrow cavity with equal panes may be less effective against low-frequency traffic than a deliberately asymmetric or laminated acoustic design. Ask for tested whole-assembly data. Walls, ceilings and floors Framed walls

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 29 • Seal perimeter and penetrations. • Add cavity absorption without rigidly bridging isolated layers. • Add dense linings, sometimes in multiple layers with staggered joints. • Use resilient channels, clips or independent frames where structure-borne transmission justifies them. • Treat outlets, doors and return-air paths. Masonry walls Mass can be useful, but windows, doors, roofs and cracks often dominate. An independent internal lining can improve performance if junctions and ventilation are designed. Ceilings and roofs Aircraft and rain noise can enter through lightweight roofing, roof windows, vents and eaves. Options include denser linings, cavity absorption, resilient suspension and roof-system upgrades. Ensure fire, moisture and ceiling-load requirements are met.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Options include denser linings, cavity absorption, resilient suspension and roof-system upgrades. Ensure fire, moisture and ceiling-load requirements are met. Floors • Impact noise: soft coverings, acoustic underlay, resilient layers, isolated ceilings and floating systems. • Airborne noise: mass, sealed penetrations and cavity absorption. • Shared structures: flanking through joists and walls may limit a floor-only treatment. Doors and ventilation A lightweight hollow door or open vent can dominate the room. Options include a heavier door leaf, full perimeter compression seals, an automatic or fitted threshold seal and acoustically designed ventilation. Do not block required combustion or fresh-air paths.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Options include a heavier door leaf, full perimeter compression seals, an automatic or fitted threshold seal and acoustically designed ventilation. Do not block required combustion or fresh-air paths. Quote evidence • Existing and proposed assembly. • Exact glass makeup, cavity and frame. • Rw, Rw+Ctr or STC for the whole assembly and relevant test report. • Treatment of gaps, vents and flanking paths. • Expected result at the problem frequencies. • Weight, structural and operational checks. • Commissioning inspection and defect process. Sources: [1] ncc.abcb.gov.au/news/2023/updated-sound-transmission-and-insulati... [2] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/glazing

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 30 Glazing Options: Treat the Whole Window Glazing includes glass, sealed cavities, spacers, frames, sashes, gaskets, hardware, perimeter installation, shading and furnishings. Compare whole-window performance, not a glass name alone. Upgrade ladder 1. Operate and furnish existing windows • Use external shade to stop unwanted summer sun before it reaches the glass. • Use close-fitting lined curtains, pelmets or cellular blinds to trap still air. • Open coverings for useful winter sun and close them before the room loses heat. • Repair latches and hinges so seals compress consistently. • Keep drainage channels and weep paths clear. 2. Draught-seal and repair Suitable for sound frames with air leakage. Use compatible compression, brush, pile or flexible seals that do not prevent operation or drainage.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Draught-seal and repair Suitable for sound frames with air leakage. Use compatible compression, brush, pile or flexible seals that do not prevent operation or drainage. Repair decayed timber and failed perimeter sealant before adding high-performance glass. 3. Applied film Films can reduce solar heat gain, glare and UV exposure on compatible existing glass. Tradeoffs include lower visible light, changed appearance, edge lift and thermal-stress risk. Confirm compatibility with the glass type, shading pattern and warranty. Film adds little cavity insulation and may not solve winter surface temperatures. 4. Removable interior film or temporary panel Low-cost options can create a still-air layer for renters or seasonal use. They depend on a continuous seal and careful installation.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Removable interior film or temporary panel Low-cost options can create a still-air layer for renters or seasonal use. They depend on a continuous seal and careful installation. They are less durable than permanent glazing and can complicate cleaning, operation and condensation management. 5. Secondary glazing A second sheet of glass or acrylic is installed inside the existing window with a separate frame or removable system. Benefits: • Retains the original external window. • Can provide useful thermal and strong acoustic improvement, especially with a larger sealed separation. • May be reversible for heritage or rental settings. Questions: • How is the perimeter sealed? • Can both layers be cleaned? • How is moisture between layers managed? • Can the original window still open for ventilation and egress? • Does the secondary material meet fire, safety and durability needs? 6.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Questions: • How is the perimeter sealed? • Can both layers be cleaned? • How is moisture between layers managed? • Can the original window still open for ventilation and egress? • Does the secondary material meet fire, safety and durability needs? 6. Retrofit insulated glass into an existing frame The original sash or joinery is modified to accept an insulated glass unit. This can preserve appearance and reduce demolition. Check:

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 31 • Timber or frame condition and structural capacity. • Rebate depth, glass weight and sash balance. • Drainage, glazing blocks, sealants and edge-clearance design. • Whether decorative bars, leadlights or hardware can be retained. • Safety-glass, wind, bushfire and heritage requirements. • Exact whole-window rating after modification. 7. Replace the sash but retain the outer frame A new high-performance sash can address glass, seals and hardware while limiting wall disturbance. The retained frame and perimeter may still be thermal bridges or leakage paths. 8. Full window replacement Appropriate where frames are rotten, distorted, badly leaking, structurally inadequate or incompatible with the required performance.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: 8. Full window replacement Appropriate where frames are rotten, distorted, badly leaking, structurally inadequate or incompatible with the required performance. Replacement creates opportunities to improve opening style, frame, drainage, flashing, safety, shading and ventilation. It also has higher disruption and embodied impact.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: neighbours and daylight Low-emissivity insulated unit Coated pane within a sealed unit Coating position, high- or low-solar-gain selection and edge protection Insulated glass unit details • Pane thickness and whether panes are equal or asymmetric. • Cavity width; wider is not always better because convection can increase. • Air, argon or another gas and the declared performance basis. • Spacer conductivity and edge-of-glass condensation risk. • Desiccant and seal durability. • Drainage and setting blocks that keep the glass edge out of standing water. • Coating surface and cleaning restrictions.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 32 Frame options Timber Low conductivity and repairable, with heritage benefits. Needs durable coating, drainage, joinery maintenance and decay repair. Aluminium without a thermal break Strong and slim but highly conductive. It can reduce the benefit of improved glass and create cold internal surfaces and condensation. Thermally broken aluminium Separates inner and outer metal with a low-conductivity section. Verify the whole-frame and whole-window rating, corner construction and drainage. Rigid polymer frames Low conductivity and good sealing potential. Check reinforcement, UV resistance, colour, expansion, repairability, bushfire suitability and end-of-life. Composite and fibreglass frames Can combine low conductivity, stiffness and weather resistance.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Check reinforcement, UV resistance, colour, expansion, repairability, bushfire suitability and end-of-life. Composite and fibreglass frames Can combine low conductivity, stiffness and weather resistance. Availability, repair, fire performance and tested configurations vary. Steel Strong and suitable for slender or fire-rated work, but conductive unless thermally broken. Heritage steel retrofit needs specialist detailing. Opening style • Casement and awning windows can compress against seals effectively. • Sliding and double-hung windows need durable brush or pile seals and careful meeting-rail details. • Louvre windows provide high ventilation area but have many joints and can be difficult to seal. • Tilt-and-turn windows provide different ventilation modes and strong compression seals. • Fixed panes can be airtight but do not provide ventilation or egress.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Heritage steel retrofit needs specialist detailing. Opening style • Casement and awning windows can compress against seals effectively. • Sliding and double-hung windows need durable brush or pile seals and careful meeting-rail details. • Louvre windows provide high ventilation area but have many joints and can be difficult to seal. • Tilt-and-turn windows provide different ventilation modes and strong compression seals. • Fixed panes can be airtight but do not provide ventilation or egress. chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 33 Orientation, Shading and Window Coverings The same glass can help one room and overheat another. Match U-value, SHGC, area, shade and operation to orientation and climate.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Orientation guide Orientation Typical risk Useful strategies North in much of Australia Winter benefit and summer overheating if poorly shaded Correctly sized horizontal overhang, adjustable shade and climate-appropriate SHGC East Low-angle morning summer sun Vertical or adjustable external shade, vegetation and solar-control glazing where needed West Intense low-angle afternoon heat Strong external shade, reduced glass area where feasible, low-SHGC glazing and insulated coverings South Limited direct winter sun and heat loss in cooler regions Low U-value, controlled area, airtight frames and insulated curtains Roof glazing High solar exposure and winter heat loss Small climate-appropriate area, external or integrated shade, low U-value and suitable SHGC Site obstructions, latitude, slope, neighbouring buildings and trees can reverse simple rules. Record actual sun access by season.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Record actual sun access by season. External shading options • Fixed eaves and horizontal overhangs. • Adjustable external blinds, awnings or shutters. • Vertical fins or side screens for low-angle sun. • Pergolas and seasonal vines. • Shade trees selected for climate, roots, fire and maintenance. • Balcony, verandah or facade screens. • Exterior solar-control film or glass selected for the orientation. External shade is usually more effective for summer heat because it intercepts radiation before the glass absorbs it. Check wind rating, drainage, operation, maintenance, strata appearance and bushfire requirements.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: External shade is usually more effective for summer heat because it intercepts radiation before the glass absorbs it. Check wind rating, drainage, operation, maintenance, strata appearance and bushfire requirements. Internal window coverings Curtains and pelmets Use a close fit to trap still air: • Full floor length where safe and practical. • Returns to the wall at both sides. • A pelmet or close top treatment. • Lined, tightly woven fabric or multiple layers. • Clearance from heaters, damp glass and operable hardware.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 34 Cellular or honeycomb blinds Air pockets can add insulation when the blind fits closely. Side gaps, wet glass, mould, cleaning and cord safety need attention. Roller, Roman and conventional blinds Useful for glare and privacy; thermal performance improves with reflective backing, close fit and side channels. A free-hanging blind with large perimeter gaps provides limited insulation. Interior shutters Can add a sealed air layer and provide privacy and light control. Check perimeter fit, condensation, egress and cleaning access. Temporary options Removable panels, tension-fit curtains, magnetic coverings and reversible films can help renters. Obtain permission before adhesive, screws or altered hardware. SAFETY Blind and curtain cords can strangle children.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Obtain permission before adhesive, screws or altered hardware. SAFETY Blind and curtain cords can strangle children. Choose cordless or inaccessible-cord systems where possible and comply with the mandatory supply and installation standards. Sources: [1] www.productsafety.gov.au/business/search-mandatory-standards/blin... [2] www.energy.gov.au/households/windows Glare, daylight and fading • External shade and adjustable blinds can control glare without permanently darkening the room. • Low-emissivity coatings and laminated interlayers may reduce ultraviolet transmission, but no glazing prevents all fading. • Reflective glass or film can create exterior glare for neighbours or roads. • Dark film or partial shading can raise glass temperature and increase thermal-stress risk. • Maintain useful daylight so electric lighting and wellbeing are not compromised.

Seasonal operating plan Heating season • Admit useful sun when it warms the room. • Close insulated coverings before sunset or when the window becomes a net heat loss. • Dry condensation and manage humidity; do not trap wet air behind closed coverings indefinitely.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Seasonal operating plan Heating season • Admit useful sun when it warms the room. • Close insulated coverings before sunset or when the window becomes a net heat loss. • Dry condensation and manage humidity; do not trap wet air behind closed coverings indefinitely. Cooling season • Deploy external shade before direct sun reaches the glass. • Close internal coverings as a secondary control. • Open windows for night purge only when outdoor air is cooler, drier and safe. • Close and seal the home when outdoor air is hotter than indoor air and mechanical cooling operates. chunks.text: warning label Do not rely on expanding foam as a universal answer. It can obstruct drainage, deform frames, conceal pests or wiring and be difficult to remove. Open-flued and unflued gas warning Some gas appliances depend on room air or permanent ventilation. Sealing the room can increase carbon-monoxide risk or impair combustion. SAFETY Do not seal wall vents, chimneys or other combustion-air paths when an open-flued or unflued gas appliance may be present. Arrange a licensed gas safety assessment and ventilation plan first. Deliberate ventilation options • Openable windows and doors used when outdoor conditions are suitable. • Externally ducted bathroom, kitchen and laundry exhaust.

chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 36 • Passive vents designed for a known airflow path. • Demand-controlled exhaust using humidity or occupancy controls. • Balanced mechanical ventilation. • Heat-recovery or energy-recovery ventilation in suitable climates and airtight homes. • Filtered supply where smoke, pollen, pollution or noise limits window opening. Ventilation must consider make-up air, noise, filters, maintenance, bushfire smoke, security and energy. Mechanical systems do not perform when filters are blocked, ducts leak or occupants do not understand the controls. Airtightness testing A blower-door test can measure leakage and support targeted sealing.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 37 Condensation, Moisture and Mould: Diagnose the Water Path Condensation is not simply a window problem. It occurs when moist air reaches a surface or layer cold enough for water vapour to condense. A window may reveal the problem because it is the coldest visible surface, while the same process may be occurring unseen inside a roof or wall. The durable response is to control moisture at its source, exhaust it outdoors, provide suitable background ventilation, warm cold surfaces and construct assemblies that can drain or dry. Replacing glass alone may move condensation elsewhere.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Identify where the water appears Observation Likely mechanism First checks Water on the room side of glass High indoor humidity plus cold internal glass Humidity, extraction, ventilation, heating pattern, curtains and glass temperature Water on the outdoor face of efficient glass Outer pane cooled below outdoor dew point Usually a weather condition rather than a failed unit; confirm location Mist or droplets between sealed panes Loss of the insulated glazing unit seal Unit age, edge seal, drainage and written replacement scope Mould at reveals, corners or behind curtains Cold bridge, restricted air movement or leakage Surface temperature, curtain position, frame junction and wall insulation Wet frame or sill after rain Water entry or blocked drainage Flashings, seals, weep paths, external joints and sill fall Staining below a ceiling or roof junction Roof, gutter, plumbing or wind-driven

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: rain leak Inspect after rain before assuming condensation Damp insulation or cavity timber Leak, ground moisture, air leakage or interstitial condensation Source, extent, drying capacity and structural condition Musty subfloor Ground evaporation, drainage, plumbing leak or poor cross-flow Soil moisture, ponding, vents, clearances and timber condition DECISION First establish whether the moisture comes from indoor air, rain, plumbing, ground moisture or a failed sealed-glass unit. The repair path is different for each. Use humidity and temperature evidence Relative humidity changes with temperature. Air can reach a high relative humidity as it cools even when no additional water is added.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Use humidity and temperature evidence Relative humidity changes with temperature. Air can reach a high relative humidity as it cools even when no additional water is added. A useful investigation records: • Indoor temperature and relative humidity in the affected room and a comparison room. • Outdoor conditions. • When cooking, showering, drying clothes, using a heater or closing curtains occurs. • Surface temperatures at the pane centre, glass edge, frame, reveal and wall corner. • Whether moisture appears overnight, during rain, after occupancy or only in particular wind directions. • Whether exhaust fans operate, discharge outdoors and continue long enough to clear moisture. A short humidity reading is not a diagnosis. Log conditions over several representative days, including cold mornings and moisture-generating activities.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: A short humidity reading is not a diagnosis. Log conditions over several representative days, including cold mornings and moisture-generating activities. Control moisture at the source • Use lids on pots and operate kitchen extraction that discharges outdoors.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 38 • Run bathroom extraction during bathing and until the room clears; keep the bathroom door positioned so moisture does not spread through the home. • Exhaust clothes dryers outdoors where the appliance and building design require it. • Avoid drying large amounts of washing indoors unless ventilation and dehumidification can manage the load. • Investigate persistent ground, roof, wall and plumbing moisture. • Repair gutters, flashings, sealant joints and drainage rather than coating over stains. • Where safe and suitable, heat occupied rooms consistently enough to reduce extreme surface cooling. Portable unflued gas heaters add combustion moisture to indoor air and also require particular ventilation and safety controls. They are a poor match for a condensation-prone, tightly closed room.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Portable unflued gas heaters add combustion moisture to indoor air and also require particular ventilation and safety controls. They are a poor match for a condensation-prone, tightly closed room. Improve extraction and deliberate ventilation Check that wet-area fans actually move air outdoors, not into a roof space. Confirm the duct route, external termination, backdraft control, make-up air and maintenance access. A noisy or ineffective fan is often left unused. An airtightness upgrade can reduce heat loss and uncontrolled moisture movement, but it must be paired with a ventilation strategy. Options range from occupant-operated windows and effective local exhaust to designed passive supply, demand control or balanced mechanical ventilation. The right choice depends on climate, occupancy, outdoor air quality, noise, smoke, security and the existing building.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: The right choice depends on climate, occupancy, outdoor air quality, noise, smoke, security and the existing building. Warm the surface and remove thermal bridges Potential measures include: • Repairing missing, displaced or compressed insulation. • Adding continuous insulation across framing where the assembly allows it. • Improving whole-window U-value, including the frame and edge, not just the pane centre. • Adding well-sealed secondary glazing while managing the original window's drainage and ventilation. • Insulating reveals and lintels where renovation access allows. • Using insulated window coverings without trapping persistent moisture against cold glass or timber. • Correcting conductive steel, concrete or masonry junctions as part of a designed retrofit.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Warm the surface and remove thermal bridges Potential measures include: • Repairing missing, displaced or compressed insulation. • Adding continuous insulation across framing where the assembly allows it. • Improving whole-window U-value, including the frame and edge, not just the pane centre. • Adding well-sealed secondary glazing while managing the original window's drainage and ventilation. • Insulating reveals and lintels where renovation access allows. • Using insulated window coverings without trapping persistent moisture against cold glass or timber. • Correcting conductive steel, concrete or masonry junctions as part of a designed retrofit. Interstitial condensation Water can condense inside a roof or wall when warm moist air leaks into a cold layer or vapour diffuses through materials.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Interstitial condensation Water can condense inside a roof or wall when warm moist air leaks into a cold layer or vapour diffuses through materials. The risk depends on climate, indoor humidity, layer order, vapour permeance, temperature, ventilation, absorptive materials and drying directions. Do not copy a vapour barrier detail from another climate. A layer that helps one assembly can trap water in another. Cathedral roofs, flat roofs, metal roofs, cool climates, air-conditioned humid climates and buildings with impermeable external finishes deserve assembly-specific analysis.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: A layer that helps one assembly can trap water in another. Cathedral roofs, flat roofs, metal roofs, cool climates, air-conditioned humid climates and buildings with impermeable external finishes deserve assembly-specific analysis. For renovation work, ask the designer to identify: • The continuous air-control layer. • The water-control and drainage plane. • The thermal layer and all major bridges. • Which layers control vapour and in which direction the assembly can dry. • How penetrations, eaves, parapets, balconies, windows and service cavities connect. • Whether a hygrothermal assessment is warranted for a high-risk assembly.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 39 Mould response Do not treat mould only as a cleaning problem. Find and control the moisture source, determine the affected extent, dry the assembly and replace materials that cannot be safely restored. Large, recurring or hidden contamination, sewage, vulnerable occupants or damaged building materials warrants specialist health and building advice. Avoid disturbing suspect asbestos-containing surfaces during investigation or cleaning. Do not paint over active dampness or close a wet cavity.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Avoid disturbing suspect asbestos-containing surfaces during investigation or cleaning. Do not paint over active dampness or close a wet cavity. Post-work verification • Photograph dry cavities and insulation before lining. • Confirm roof and window drainage paths remain open. • Re-log temperature and humidity through comparable weather. • Check glass edges, reveals, corners and behind furnishings at cold times. • Confirm wet-area exhaust airflow and outdoor discharge. • Investigate any new staining, odour, timber swelling or between-pane fog promptly. Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation [2] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/ventilation-airtightness [3] ncc.abcb.gov.au/editions/ncc-2022/adopted/volume-one/f-health-and... [4] ncc.abcb.gov.au/sites/default/files/resources/2023/Condensation-i...

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 40 Older Homes, Heritage Windows, Doors and Skylights An older window is not automatically beyond improvement. Many timber sashes and casements can be repaired, aligned, sealed and combined with a second glazing layer. The appropriate path depends on frame condition, heritage significance, operation, drainage, sightlines, approvals, desired thermal and acoustic performance and whole-life cost.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: The appropriate path depends on frame condition, heritage significance, operation, drainage, sightlines, approvals, desired thermal and acoustic performance and whole-life cost. Start with a condition survey For every opening, record: • Window or door type, dimensions, orientation and exposure. • Frame and sash material, movement, distortion, decay and previous repairs. • Glass type and thickness if known; identify leadlight, patterned or historic glass. • Gaps at sash, meeting rail, parting bead, casement stop and frame-to-wall junction. • Sill fall, flashing, putty, external joints, drainage and water staining. • Hardware condition, lockability, egress, fall risk and accessibility. • Existing shade, curtains, shutters and insect screens. • Heritage, planning, owners-corporation and rental permission constraints.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Start with a condition survey For every opening, record: • Window or door type, dimensions, orientation and exposure. • Frame and sash material, movement, distortion, decay and previous repairs. • Glass type and thickness if known; identify leadlight, patterned or historic glass. • Gaps at sash, meeting rail, parting bead, casement stop and frame-to-wall junction. • Sill fall, flashing, putty, external joints, drainage and water staining. • Hardware condition, lockability, egress, fall risk and accessibility. • Existing shade, curtains, shutters and insect screens. • Heritage, planning, owners-corporation and rental permission constraints. Suspect glazing putty, backing boards, wall sheets, eaves and linings may contain asbestos. Do not sand, drill or cut unknown material. Repair-first sequence 1 Stop water entry and repair decay after identifying the source.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Do not sand, drill or cut unknown material. Repair-first sequence 1 Stop water entry and repair decay after identifying the source. 2 Restore operation so the sash closes squarely against its stops. 3 Repair locks, catches, hinges, cords, weights and balances. 4 Seal the frame-to-wall junction where appropriate. 5 Fit seals suited to the movement: compression for closing faces, brush or pile for sliding faces. 6 Add seasonal shading and close-fitting internal coverings. 7 Reassess whether secondary glazing, replacement glass, an insulated unit or full replacement is needed. This sequence preserves options. A badly aligned window cannot be made airtight by adding a thicker seal, and a new pane cannot correct failed flashings.

chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 41 Retrofit choices for significant windows Option Preserves original fabric Main benefit Critical checks Repair and draught sealing High Air leakage, operation, rain control Seal durability, drainage and ventilation Heavy curtain, pelmet or internal blind High Night heat loss, comfort, glare Edge gaps, moisture behind covering, cords Removable internal panel High Seasonal thermal and noise improvement Safe fixing, egress, cleaning and condensation Purpose-built secondary glazing High Air gap, noise and thermal improvement Perimeter seal, cavity moisture, access, sightline Replace glass in existing sash Medium to high Safety, acoustic, solar or low-emissivity function Rebate depth, sash strength, weight and putty compatibility Retrofit insulated glazing unit Medium to high Lower U-value while retaining much of

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: the frame Rebate, drainage, unit edge, sash weight and workmanship Rebuild sash or insert a new sash Medium Improved glass system and seals Profiles, balances, approvals and frame condition Full frame replacement Low Whole-window redesign Flashing, reveals, heritage impact, embodied resources and installation damage Secondary glazing can be especially useful for noise because a large, well-sealed air space and different pane thicknesses can reduce sound transmission. Its actual performance is governed by the complete system and flanking paths. Leadlight and decorative glazing Possible approaches include careful repair, a protective external layer, an internal secondary layer or encapsulation within a designed glazing system. The design must address trapped moisture, heat stress, ventilation of the cavity, support, cleaning access, visual distortion and conservation significance.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Leadlight and decorative glazing Possible approaches include careful repair, a protective external layer, an internal secondary layer or encapsulation within a designed glazing system. The design must address trapped moisture, heat stress, ventilation of the cavity, support, cleaning access, visual distortion and conservation significance. Obtain specialist advice before sealing a valuable panel into a new assembly. Sash weight and structural capacity Thicker laminated glass and insulated units weigh more than thin single glass. In double-hung windows, balances or counterweights may need redesign. Hinged sashes place added load on joints and hardware. Confirm the sash, frame, fixings and operating mechanism can carry the proposed glass safely.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Hinged sashes place added load on joints and hardware. Confirm the sash, frame, fixings and operating mechanism can carry the proposed glass safely. Doors Treat the door leaf, frame, threshold and glazing as one system. • Adjust hinges and latches before adding seals. • Use continuous perimeter seals compatible with the movement and exposure. • Select a threshold or automatic bottom seal that maintains drainage and accessibility. • Insulate or replace thin, unsealed leaves only after checking fire, security and heritage requirements. • Treat large glazed doors as windows: examine U-value, SHGC, frame, seals, safety glass, drainage and shade. • Do not alter a fire door, smoke door or common-property door without approval and compliant documentation. Skylights, roof windows and roof glazing Roof glazing receives intense sun and loses heat to the sky.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Doors Treat the door leaf, frame, threshold and glazing as one system. • Adjust hinges and latches before adding seals. • Use continuous perimeter seals compatible with the movement and exposure. • Select a threshold or automatic bottom seal that maintains drainage and accessibility. • Insulate or replace thin, unsealed leaves only after checking fire, security and heritage requirements. • Treat large glazed doors as windows: examine U-value, SHGC, frame, seals, safety glass, drainage and shade. • Do not alter a fire door, smoke door or common-property door without approval and compliant documentation. Skylights, roof windows and roof glazing Roof glazing receives intense sun and loses heat to the sky. A small poorly selected skylight can dominate a room's summer load or create winter discomfort. Assess:

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 42 • Glazed area relative to room and roof area. • Slope, orientation, climate and seasonal sun. • Whole-unit U-value and SHGC. • External shade or integral blind suitability. • Shaft length, colour, insulation, air sealing and thermal bridges. • Flashing, condensation drainage and roof compatibility. • Ventilation function, insect control, security and rain sensors if openable. • Safe access for cleaning, servicing and replacement. Tubular daylight devices can reduce roof opening area when daylight rather than view or ventilation is the objective, but the tube, ceiling diffuser, roof penetration, condensation control and fire or acoustic requirements still need attention.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Tubular daylight devices can reduce roof opening area when daylight rather than view or ventilation is the objective, but the tube, ceiling diffuser, roof penetration, condensation control and fire or acoustic requirements still need attention. Approvals and documentation Before fixed work, check heritage overlays, planning controls, building approval, rental consent, strata or owners-corporation rules and whether the opening is common property. Keep drawings of profiles and sightlines, photographs before work, glass and hardware specifications, approvals, installer records and post-work photographs. chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 43 Safety, Building Requirements, Bushfire and Installation Quality Energy work intersects with electrical safety, fire spread, glazing impact, falls, structure, moisture, ventilation and access. A performance claim is not evidence that an installation is lawful or safe. Building requirements vary with building class, location, construction, scope and the edition adopted by the state or territory. Confirm the applicable law, approvals and practitioner requirements before work. The national construction documents are a technical starting point, not a substitute for local approval advice.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Confirm the applicable law, approvals and practitioner requirements before work. The national construction documents are a technical starting point, not a substitute for local approval advice. Stop-work hazards Stop and obtain competent advice if you find: • Suspect loose-fill, sprayed, sheet, backing, putty or debris that may contain asbestos. • Exposed, damaged or buried wiring, overheated fittings or unsafe switchboards. • Water near electrical equipment. • Charred timber, heat damage, leaking flues or missing fire separation. • Roof or floor structure that is sagging, decayed or unstable. • Vermin contamination, sharp debris or inaccessible work areas. • Broken overhead glass or an unprotected fall opening. • Active leaks, widespread mould or wet insulation. Do not use a household vacuum, broom or power tool on suspect asbestos.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Stop-work hazards Stop and obtain competent advice if you find: • Suspect loose-fill, sprayed, sheet, backing, putty or debris that may contain asbestos. • Exposed, damaged or buried wiring, overheated fittings or unsafe switchboards. • Water near electrical equipment. • Charred timber, heat damage, leaking flues or missing fire separation. • Roof or floor structure that is sagging, decayed or unstable. • Vermin contamination, sharp debris or inaccessible work areas. • Broken overhead glass or an unprotected fall opening. • Active leaks, widespread mould or wet insulation. Do not use a household vacuum, broom or power tool on suspect asbestos. Do not enter a hot, cramped or unsafe roof space to collect evidence.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Do not use a household vacuum, broom or power tool on suspect asbestos. Do not enter a hot, cramped or unsafe roof space to collect evidence. Electrical and ceiling-space controls Before adding or replacing ceiling insulation: • Arrange assessment of existing wiring and fittings by a licensed electrician. • Identify downlights, transformers, fans, exhaust ducts, flues and other heat-producing equipment. • Establish the clearances, covers and support details required for each item. • Repair unsafe wiring and remove abandoned hazards. • Plan access paths so future electrical, roof and mechanical work does not destroy insulation coverage. • Photograph the completed clearances and equipment labels before the roof space becomes difficult to inspect. Insulation must not be packed around equipment contrary to its installation and clearance requirements.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Electrical and ceiling-space controls Before adding or replacing ceiling insulation: • Arrange assessment of existing wiring and fittings by a licensed electrician. • Identify downlights, transformers, fans, exhaust ducts, flues and other heat-producing equipment. • Establish the clearances, covers and support details required for each item. • Repair unsafe wiring and remove abandoned hazards. • Plan access paths so future electrical, roof and mechanical work does not destroy insulation coverage. • Photograph the completed clearances and equipment labels before the roof space becomes difficult to inspect. Insulation must not be packed around equipment contrary to its installation and clearance requirements. Foil and other conductive materials introduce additional electrical risk.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Insulation must not be packed around equipment contrary to its installation and clearance requirements. Foil and other conductive materials introduce additional electrical risk. Sources: [1] www.worksafe.vic.gov.au/preventing-electric-shocks-when-working-c... [2] www.energy.gov.au/households/insulation-and-draught-proofing Glazing safety and falls Glass selection is affected by location, pane size, support, wind, human impact and fall risk. Doors, side panels, bathrooms, low-level glass, areas where people can fall against a pane and barriers require particular attention. Ask the designer or installer to document: • Which panes require safety glazing and why. • Glass type, thickness, marking and applicable test evidence. • Edge support, setting blocks, frame bite and compatible sealants.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 44 • Wind and structural design assumptions. • Any barrier load or openable-window fall-protection function. • How restricted openings can still support ventilation, egress, cleaning and emergency needs. A toughened pane and a laminated pane fail differently. Selection should be based on the hazard and required post-breakage behaviour, not a generic claim that one is always safer. Bushfire-prone sites In bushfire-prone areas, insulation, sarking, vents, gaps, glazing, screens, shutters, decks and landscaping are part of one risk strategy. Do not assume an energy upgrade is suitable because its material is described as fire resistant.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Bushfire-prone sites In bushfire-prone areas, insulation, sarking, vents, gaps, glazing, screens, shutters, decks and landscaping are part of one risk strategy. Do not assume an energy upgrade is suitable because its material is described as fire resistant. Confirm: • The site's formal bushfire assessment and applicable construction level. • Requirements for glass, frames, screens, shutters and openable elements. • Ember entry control at roofs, eaves, vents, subfloors and service penetrations. • Whether added insulation or membranes change drainage, ventilation or fire performance. • How occupants will close, maintain and operate shutters, vents or screens. • Access, water, vegetation and broader site measures outside the building fabric. Bushfire design is site-specific. Use the applicable state or territory planning and building process and qualified advice.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Bushfire design is site-specific. Use the applicable state or territory planning and building process and qualified advice. Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/live-adapt/bushfire-protection Fire and acoustic separation Apartment walls, floors, ceilings, service risers and doors may form required fire, smoke or acoustic separations. Cutting, drilling, filling, replacing doors or installing services can reduce their performance. • Identify the tested or assessed system before altering it. • Use compatible fire-stopping and acoustic details at penetrations. • Do not fill a cavity in a way that bridges a required gap or blocks drainage. • Do not alter a common fire or smoke door as a draught project. • Photograph each concealed penetration and retain the specified system evidence.

chunks.text: Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/live-adapt/bushfire-protection Fire and acoustic separation Apartment walls, floors, ceilings, service risers and doors may form required fire, smoke or acoustic separations. Cutting, drilling, filling, replacing doors or installing services can reduce their performance. • Identify the tested or assessed system before altering it. • Use compatible fire-stopping and acoustic details at penetrations. • Do not fill a cavity in a way that bridges a required gap or blocks drainage. • Do not alter a common fire or smoke door as a draught project. • Photograph each concealed penetration and retain the specified system evidence. Installation quality for insulation The stated R-value is achieved only when the installed layer matches its conditions of use.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Installation quality for insulation The stated R-value is achieved only when the installed layer matches its conditions of use. Inspect for: • Full coverage at edges, corners, junctions and narrow strips. • Correct thickness without crushing, folding or large voids. • Neat fitting around framing and services. • Required clearances around heat-producing equipment and flues. • Wind-wash, bulk water and pest protection. • Secure underfloor support without excessive compression. • Continuity of membranes, tapes and air seals where specified. • Labels, batch records, declared R-values and photographs before concealment.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 45 Installation quality for windows and doors Inspect the opening before the old unit is removed. The finished work should address structure, water, air, heat and operation.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: The finished work should address structure, water, air, heat and operation. Check: • Opening dimensions, sill condition and structural support. • Flashing and drainage integrated with the wall's water-control layer. • Plumb, level and square frame without distortion. • Packings and fixings placed to the documented detail. • Perimeter air seal separated from external drainage and weather seals as required. • Insulation to the reveal without blocking drainage. • Correct glass and performance labels for each orientation and opening. • Smooth operation, locks, restrictors, insect screens and accessible thresholds. • Weep holes and tracks clean and open. • No damaged coatings, edge chips, sealant incompatibility or trapped debris.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Handover evidence Collect approvals, drawings, window schedules, insulation locations and R-values, glazing U-value and SHGC evidence, safety-glass records, photographs, electrical or other certificates, operating instructions, cleaning requirements, warranty documents and the final paid invoice. Store them with the property record, not only in an email account. Sources: [1] ncc.abcb.gov.au/editions/ncc-2022 [2] ncc.abcb.gov.au/sites/default/files/resources/2023/NCC-2022-Housi... chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT BY DESIGN INSULATION + GLAZING FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 46 Renters, Apartments, Strata and Shared Buildings Renters and apartment residents can improve comfort, but their permission boundary is different. Portable and reversible measures are usually the safest starting point. Fixed seals, glazing, wall penetrations, external shades, changes to common property and anything affecting fire safety normally need written approval. Tenancy and strata rules differ by state or territory and can change. Check the current official rules before relying on a minimum standard, notice period or alteration right.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Renter action ladder Usually portable or readily reversible • Measure room temperature and humidity and keep a symptom diary. • Use existing curtains correctly; close them before the room becomes very cold or hot. • Add a freestanding curtain support or removable tension system only where it is stable and will not damage the property. • Use removable draught snakes at door bottoms where they do not obstruct egress. • Use removable gap seals only after checking paint, operation, drainage and lease conditions. • Add a freestanding screen or temporary internal shade that is safe, ventilated and clear of heaters. • Move large furniture away from cold, mould-prone external corners to improve air circulation. • Use existing exhaust fans and report fans that do not work or do not clear moisture. • Request repairs for broken glass, water entry, unsafe wiring, failed locks, rotten frames and

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: non-operating windows. Even a reversible measure can create damage or a safety problem. Avoid adhesive film or tape on unknown coated glass, unstable panels, corded blinds that create a child hazard, blocked exits, covered vents and materials near heaters. Ask for written permission • Drilled or screwed curtain tracks and pelmets. • Fixed blinds, shutters or awnings. • Permanent perimeter seals or threshold work. • Removable secondary panels that require fixings. • Window film, replacement glass or sealed glazing units. • Ceiling, wall or underfloor insulation. • Exhaust, ventilation or air-sealing changes. • Any external appearance, waterproofing, electrical, gas, fire-safety or common-property change. Build an evidence-backed request Provide the owner or manager with: 1 A short description of the symptom, room and season. 2 Dated temperature, humidity, condensation or draught records.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort by Design: Australian Insulation and Glazing Guide
chunks.text: Build an evidence-backed request Provide the owner or manager with: 1 A short description of the symptom, room and season. 2 Dated temperature, humidity, condensation or draught records. 3 Photographs of defects and the wider location. 4 The suspected cause without presenting it as confirmed.
