chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 46 Virtual Power Plants, Automation and Grid Services A virtual power plant coordinates many household batteries or other flexible devices. The operator may charge, discharge or reserve capacity in response to energy prices, grid needs or program rules. Benefits can include upfront incentives, ongoing credits or better tariff access. Costs can include lost control, battery wear, reserve changes, lock-in and complex billing. VPP contract checklist 1 Eligible equipment and communications requirements. 1 Who can control charging, discharge and backup reserve. 1 Maximum event frequency, power, duration and energy. 1 Minimum state of charge promised to the household. 1 Whether the operator may grid-charge the battery. 1 Payment, bill credit, upfront benefit or tariff terms.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Whether the operator may grid-charge the battery. 1 Payment, bill credit, upfront benefit or tariff terms. 1 How payment changes with participation or missed events. 1 Energy import and export prices during events. 1 Battery degradation and warranty treatment. 1 Internet outage and communications-failure behaviour. 1 Privacy, interval data, device telemetry and data sharing. 1 Contract term, exit fee and hardware lock-in. 1 What happens when the property is sold, rented or the retailer changes. 1 Whether current government support requires technical capability but not active participation. Ask for a worked example using the household's interval data and battery size. Compare it with self-managed operation under the best available tariff. DECISION "VPP-capable" and "enrolled in a VPP" are different.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Compare it with self-managed operation under the best available tariff. DECISION "VPP-capable" and "enrolled in a VPP" are different. Confirm whether capability is an eligibility condition and whether participation is optional, automatic or tied to a contract. Dynamic tariffs and automated trading Some plans expose households to prices that vary more frequently than traditional tariffs. Automation may charge during low-price periods and discharge during high-price periods. Risks include price spikes, forecasting errors, control failure, demand charges, battery cycling and behaviour that conflicts with backup needs. Before choosing one: 1 Simulate the previous year if historical prices and household data are available. 1 Understand caps, floors, fees and pass-through charges. 1 Define a maximum import price and reserve policy.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Understand caps, floors, fees and pass-through charges. 1 Define a maximum import price and reserve policy. 1 Check whether the algorithm optimises the bill, the operator's portfolio or both. 1 Confirm manual override and fail-safe behaviour. 1 Review results monthly against a simple alternative plan.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 47 Peer-to-peer and community energy Energy sharing arrangements may allocate value among households, buildings or program participants. Treat them as contracts layered over physical electricity flows. Check: 1 Who owns generation and storage. 1 Metering accuracy and settlement method. 1 Network, retailer and platform charges. 1 Price-setting method. 1 Consumer protections and dispute pathway. 1 Data access and privacy. 1 Exit, property sale and participant-default rules. 1 Whether claimed local energy use is physical, financial or certificate-based.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 48 Off-Grid Energy: Design for the Worst Useful Week Going off-grid transfers reliability responsibility from the network to the household. It can be appropriate for a remote site where connection is unavailable or very costly. In a grid-served urban home, a grid-connected hybrid system often provides resilience with less equipment, fuel and maintenance. Off-grid system components 1 Solar array sized for seasonal energy needs. 1 Charge controller or compatible solar inverter. 1 Battery bank with adequate usable capacity and power. 1 Off-grid inverter-charger. 1 Switchboard, earthing, protection and compliant wiring. 1 Backup generator or other firm supply where required. 1 Fuel storage and safe exhaust arrangement. 1 Monitoring, alarms and remote support. 1 Load-shedding controls.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Monitoring, alarms and remote support. 1 Load-shedding controls. 1 Spare parts, service plan and emergency procedures. Off-grid sizing sequence 1. Measure loads List each appliance's energy, power, starting demand, operating hours, season and criticality. Measure where possible. Include pumps, refrigeration, communications, workshop loads, water treatment, septic systems and heating or cooling. 2. Remove avoidable loads Efficiency is cheaper than supplying unnecessary energy. Replace resistance heating where suitable, improve the building shell, use efficient pumps and refrigeration, and separate occasional heavy loads. 3. Establish seasonal solar resource Design around the lowest useful solar period, not annual average. Include orientation, shade, cloud, temperature, soiling and extreme-weather access. 4.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Include orientation, shade, cloud, temperature, soiling and extreme-weather access. 4. Choose autonomy Days of autonomy are the number of low-solar days the battery can support without generation or load reduction. More autonomy increases cost, space and embodied resources. A reliable generator may reduce battery size but adds fuel and maintenance dependence. 5. Check power and starting loads The inverter and battery must start pumps, compressors and motors while other loads are operating. Soft starters, variable-speed drives, staged operation or different equipment may reduce peak demand where properly designed. 6. Define load shedding Separate critical, managed and discretionary circuits. Establish automatic or manual thresholds so a non-essential load cannot exhaust the system.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 49 7. Model failures Consider inverter failure, battery module failure, generator failure, communications loss, extended cloud, fire, flood, road closure and occupant error. Decide which spare parts and expertise are locally available. Daily energy worksheet Appliance or circuit Quantity W Hours/day Wh/day Season Critical? Refrigeration Water pumping Wastewater Lighting Communications Heating or cooling Cooking Workshop or farm Add conversion and standby losses. Validate the worksheet against measured whole-site energy. Off-grid battery sizing concept Required usable battery kWh = critical daily kWh multiplied by autonomy days, adjusted for conversion losses and permitted depth of discharge. This is only an energy calculation.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Off-grid battery sizing concept Required usable battery kWh = critical daily kWh multiplied by autonomy days, adjusted for conversion losses and permitted depth of discharge. This is only an energy calculation. The battery and inverter must also meet continuous and starting power, charge-rate, temperature and warranty requirements. A qualified off-grid designer should model the complete system. Generator integration Define: 1 Automatic or manual start. 1 Start threshold and battery reserve. 1 Generator continuous rating and efficient loading. 1 Battery charging power. 1 Fuel type, storage life and availability. 1 Exhaust, ventilation, noise and fire separation. 1 Exercise schedule, oil, filters and service intervals. 1 Failure alarm and manual bypass strategy. Running a large generator at very low load for long periods can be inefficient and harmful to some equipment.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Failure alarm and manual bypass strategy. Running a large generator at very low load for long periods can be inefficient and harmful to some equipment. Size and control it as part of the system. DC appliances and dedicated circuits Direct-DC loads may reduce conversion losses in specialised off-grid designs, but create compatibility, protection, spare-part and electrician-familiarity considerations. Standard AC appliances may be easier to replace. Use DC distribution only when it is deliberately engineered. Off-grid operating discipline

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 50 1 Track state of charge and forecast weather. 1 Run flexible loads during strong generation. 1 Delay non-essential high loads in poor weather. 1 Test generator and transfer systems. 1 Maintain fuel safely. 1 Keep filters, panels and battery area clear. 1 Record alarms, maintenance and replacements. 1 Teach all occupants the load priorities and shutdown process. Urban disconnection test Before leaving an available grid connection, compare: 1 Ongoing supply charge versus extra batteries, inverter capacity and generator. 1 Network reliability versus self-managed reliability. 1 Fuel, maintenance, replacement and monitoring. 1 Space, noise and planning constraints. 1 Ability to support multi-day extreme weather. 1 Property resale, insurance and future occupant needs.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Ability to support multi-day extreme weather. 1 Property resale, insurance and future occupant needs. 1 A grid-connected system with essential-load backup as an alternative. Full independence can be a lifestyle objective, but it should not be disguised as an automatic financial saving. Sources: [1] cer.gov.au/schemes/renewable-energy-target/small-scale-renewable-... [2] www.energy.gov.au/solar/get-know-solar-technology/batteries

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 51 Electric Vehicles and Home Charging The household energy decision is not only which vehicle to drive. It is whether the vehicle fits daily travel, parking, charging access, electrical capacity, tariff, solar availability, accessibility, insurance and long trips.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Vehicle types Type Propulsion and charging Strong fit Main tradeoff Battery electric vehicle Electric motor and rechargeable traction battery Reliable charging and trips within practical range Charging access, trip planning, battery size and purchase price Plug-in hybrid Electric drive for a limited range plus combustion engine Regular short trips with reliable charging and occasional long travel Two powertrains, fuel use if not charged, smaller electric range Non-plug-in hybrid Fuel engine with small battery charged by vehicle No external charging access Still depends on fuel and cannot use home solar directly Fuel-cell electric Electric drive supplied by hydrogen fuel cell Specialised use with available refuelling Very limited household refuelling relevance and infrastructure Start with a driving and parking diary For at least two typical weeks, record: 1 Distance driven each day.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Longest ordinary and exceptional trip. 1 Time parked at home, work and regular destinations. 1 Secure off-street parking and distance to electricity. 1 Public charging available on regular routes. 1 Towing, roof load, payload and rural-road needs. 1 Hot, cold, wet and high-speed conditions. 1 Accessibility, child-seat and cargo needs. 1 Expected vehicle use over the ownership period. The daily requirement matters more than a desire to refill from empty. Most drivers top up rather than fully charge every day. Compare total ownership cost Include: 1 Purchase price and finance. 1 Registration, tax and incentives current in the jurisdiction. 1 Insurance. 1 Home charger, switchboard, cable route and metering. 1 Electricity at home, work and public chargers. 1 Fuel for a plug-in hybrid or backup vehicle. 1 Scheduled servicing, tyres and repairs. 1 Battery and vehicle warranty.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Scheduled servicing, tyres and repairs. 1 Battery and vehicle warranty. 1 Depreciation and resale uncertainty. 1 Road-user charges if applicable at the time.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 52 1 Parking or charging subscriptions. Do not assume all public charging costs the same, or that home charging uses the flat headline electricity rate. Vehicle efficiency and range Compare energy use in kWh per 100 km under a recognised test, then allow for real conditions. Range falls with: 1 High speed and aggressive acceleration. 1 Cold battery or cabin heating. 1 Extreme heat and cabin cooling. 1 Towing, roof racks, heavy loads and hills. 1 Headwind, rain and soft surfaces. 1 Low tyre pressure. 1 Battery age and condition. Build a buffer for detours, charger faults and weather. The best vehicle is not necessarily the one with the largest battery; a smaller efficient vehicle with dependable charging may cost and weigh less.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Build a buffer for detours, charger faults and weather. The best vehicle is not necessarily the one with the largest battery; a smaller efficient vehicle with dependable charging may cost and weigh less. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/buying-electric-vehicle/prepa... [2] www.greenvehicleguide.gov.au/ Charging levels and equipment Standard household outlet Portable charging from a suitable outlet is commonly called Level 1 charging. It is slow but may cover normal daily travel. Check: 1 The outlet and circuit are suitable for long-duration load. 1 The charging cable is approved and undamaged. 1 The plug connects directly, without a power board or extension lead. 1 The outlet is protected from weather and cable strain. 1 The cable does not cross a public path or create a trip hazard. 1 Other loads on the circuit are understood.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 The cable does not cross a public path or create a trip hazard. 1 Other loads on the circuit are understood. 1 A licensed electrician assesses old, warm, damaged or uncertain wiring. Dedicated AC charger A permanently installed Level 2 charger can provide higher power, scheduling, solar following, access control and load management. It requires licensed electrical installation and may require switchboard or supply upgrades. Faster is not automatically better. Choose enough power to replace normal daily driving during the available parking window. DC fast charging Public DC charging bypasses the vehicle's onboard AC charger. Charge rate is limited by the charger, vehicle, battery temperature, state of charge and charging curve. The fastest advertised peak may occur only briefly.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Charge rate is limited by the charger, vehicle, battery temperature, state of charge and charging curve. The fastest advertised peak may occur only briefly. Estimate charging time and energy Energy needed from the wall = battery energy added divided by charging efficiency.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 53 Approximate charging time = wall energy needed divided by charging power. Allow for charging taper, thermal management, battery conditioning and other vehicle loads. A nominal 7 kW charger may not deliver 7 kW to every vehicle or installation. Daily travel method 1 Multiply daily kilometres by vehicle kWh per 100 km. 2 Add a reasonable charging-loss allowance. 3 Divide by hours parked and available charging power. 4 Check that the schedule fits the tariff and departure time. Plugs and compatibility Common Australian vehicle connections include Type 2 for AC and CCS2 for DC fast charging. Some older vehicles use other DC formats. Check the exact inlet, cable, adaptor rules, maximum AC phases and DC charge capability of the vehicle. Do not assume an adaptor makes every charger safe or fully functional.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Check the exact inlet, cable, adaptor rules, maximum AC phases and DC charge capability of the vehicle. Do not assume an adaptor makes every charger safe or fully functional. Follow vehicle and charging-equipment instructions. Electrical capacity and load management A dedicated charger can be one of the largest household loads. A site assessment should consider: 1 Single-phase or three-phase supply. 1 Main-switch and service capacity. 1 Switchboard condition and space. 1 Existing air conditioning, cooking, hot water, pool, battery and workshop loads. 1 Charger circuit protection and cable route. 1 Maximum demand and network requirements. 1 Static or dynamic load management. 1 Solar diversion and tariff scheduling. 1 Future second vehicle or shared charging. Dynamic load management reduces charging power when the home is heavily loaded.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Future second vehicle or shared charging. Dynamic load management reduces charging power when the home is heavily loaded. In an apartment, building-level management can allocate capacity across many vehicles and avoid expensive uncontrolled peaks. SAFETY A dedicated charger, new outlet, switchboard change or fixed cable is electrical work. Use a licensed electrician. Stop using any plug, outlet or cable that becomes unusually warm, discoloured, loose, cracked, wet or damaged. Charge from rooftop solar Options include: 1 Manual daytime charging. 1 Charger schedule matched to common solar hours. 1 Charger that adjusts power to measured solar surplus. 1 A lower charge rate that tracks variable generation. 1 Battery coordination where a home battery is already justified.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 54 Check the vehicle's minimum charging current. A charger may stop or draw from the grid when solar falls below that threshold. A large home battery is not automatically needed to charge a vehicle; direct daytime solar usually avoids extra battery conversion and wear. Solar sizing for travel Estimate annual vehicle energy from kilometres and efficiency, then model whether the vehicle is home during generation. Annual solar energy equal to annual vehicle energy does not guarantee direct solar charging. Tariffs for charging Compare: 1 Flat versus time-of-use rates. 1 Dedicated EV windows or controlled circuits. 1 Demand charges created by high-rate charging. 1 Midday solar or free-use windows. 1 Public charging cost for regular trips. 1 Solar feed-in credit forgone when charging from surplus.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Public charging cost for regular trips. 1 Solar feed-in credit forgone when charging from surplus. Schedule after checking the whole household. Starting an EV charger, water heater, oven and air conditioner together may create a peak. Renters and apartments Renter with a suitable existing outlet Obtain written permission if the agreement requires it. Ask a licensed electrician to assess safety if the outlet, circuit, parking location or sustained load is uncertain. Agree on electricity payment where the outlet is not on the tenant's meter. Personal charger in strata The process may involve: 1 Owner or landlord approval. 1 Owners-corporation approval for common property. 1 Building electrical-capacity assessment. 1 Cable route and fire-safety review. 1 Metering and cost recovery. 1 Load management and future expansion. 1 Insurance, maintenance and removal when the resident leaves.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Load management and future expansion. 1 Insurance, maintenance and removal when the resident leaves. Shared charging Specify booking, access, billing, idle fees, visitor use, accessibility, fault support, network connectivity, future charger count and fair allocation of upgrade costs. RENTER Do not run an extension lead from a dwelling, balcony or common outlet to a parking space. Use the written approval process and a compliant charging solution. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/owning-electric-vehicle/charg... [2] www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/owning-electric-vehicle/charg... Public and road-trip charging Plan with more than one charging location where possible. Check:

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 55 1 Connector and maximum power. 1 Current operating status. 1 Access hours, parking restrictions and towing risk. 1 Account, app, card or payment method. 1 Pricing by kWh, minute, session or idle time. 1 Nearby amenities and personal safety. 1 Alternative charger if occupied or out of service. 1 Arrival state-of-charge buffer. Charge rate often slows at high state of charge. On a long trip, several shorter stops can be faster than waiting for a full charge, depending on the vehicle and route. Buying a used electric vehicle Check: 1 Service and accident history. 1 Remaining vehicle and battery warranty. 1 Battery state-of-health report and how it was measured. 1 Usable range in the buyer's conditions. 1 AC and DC charging function. 1 Included charging cables and their condition.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 AC and DC charging function. 1 Included charging cables and their condition. 1 Software, account ownership and feature transfer. 1 Recalls and outstanding updates. 1 Underbody, charging-port and water damage. 1 Tyres, brakes, suspension and 12 V battery. 1 Insurance and repair access. A dashboard range estimate is not a battery-health certificate. Obtain qualified inspection appropriate to the vehicle. Vehicle-to-load, vehicle-to-home and vehicle-to-grid Vehicle-to-load The vehicle supplies plug-in appliances through approved outlets or an adaptor. Follow output, earthing, weather and load limits. Do not connect it to fixed wiring. Vehicle-to-home The vehicle supplies an isolated home system through approved bidirectional equipment. Compatibility depends on vehicle, charger, inverter, network, electrical standards and local approval.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Vehicle-to-home The vehicle supplies an isolated home system through approved bidirectional equipment. Compatibility depends on vehicle, charger, inverter, network, electrical standards and local approval. Vehicle-to-grid The vehicle can export to the grid or participate in energy services. Availability remains dependent on compatible vehicles, chargers, connection rules and programs. Do not buy solely on a promised future bidirectional feature unless it is approved, enabled and contractually supported in the location now. Flood, fire and collision safety 1 Do not charge a damaged or flood-affected vehicle until professionally assessed.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 56 1 Keep clear of exposed high-voltage components. 1 Follow emergency-service directions after collision or fire. 1 Do not park or charge where known flooding will submerge equipment. 1 Install chargers with appropriate impact and weather protection. 1 Keep the charging area free of combustible storage and damaged cables. EV charger quote checklist 1 [ ] Vehicle inlet and maximum AC charge rate confirmed. 1 [ ] Daily travel and parking window measured. 1 [ ] Existing outlet or dedicated charger decision justified. 1 [ ] Single-phase or three-phase supply confirmed. 1 [ ] Maximum demand and other large loads assessed. 1 [ ] Load management specified. 1 [ ] Circuit, protection, cable route and switchboard work included. 1 [ ] Charger location, weather and impact protection documented.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 [ ] Circuit, protection, cable route and switchboard work included. 1 [ ] Charger location, weather and impact protection documented. 1 [ ] Solar, tariff and schedule integration explained. 1 [ ] Access control and metering agreed. 1 [ ] Internet, app, subscription and data requirements disclosed. 1 [ ] Strata, landlord and common-property approvals obtained. 1 [ ] Commissioning test and owner demonstration included. 1 [ ] Future second charger or bidirectional plans treated as separate requirements. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/owning-electric-vehicle/how-c... [2] www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/owning-electric-vehicle/elect...

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 57 Heating, Cooling and Fans Heating and cooling can be the largest household energy load. Reduce heat gain and heat loss first, then choose efficient equipment sized to the rooms and climate. Reduce the required system size 1 Shade hot-season sun before it reaches glazing. 1 Seal uncontrolled gaps while keeping deliberate ventilation and combustion-air requirements. 1 Repair or complete ceiling, wall and floor insulation where appropriate and safe. 1 Use curtains or blinds with side, top and lower gap control. 1 Close doors to create sensible zones. 1 Use ceiling and portable fans for air movement. 1 Ventilate at cooler times when outdoor conditions help. 1 Reduce internal heat from lighting, cooking and appliances. 1 Maintain roof, duct and underfloor systems.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Reduce internal heat from lighting, cooking and appliances. 1 Maintain roof, duct and underfloor systems. Do not seal a home with unflued or open-flued combustion appliances without professional assessment. Moisture, indoor air quality and carbon monoxide safety take priority over energy saving. Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/energy/heating-and-cooling [2] www.energy.gov.au/households/heating-and-cooling Heating and cooling options Reverse-cycle split system One outdoor unit serves one indoor unit. It can efficiently heat and cool a room or connected zone. Strong fit: 1 Occupied rooms or open living areas. 1 Staged replacement of existing heaters. 1 Homes where zoning matters. Questions: 1 Indoor-unit airflow and noise. 1 Outdoor-unit noise, airflow, condensate and neighbours. 1 Low-temperature heating performance where relevant. 1 Minimum modulation for mild conditions.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Low-temperature heating performance where relevant. 1 Minimum modulation for mild conditions. 1 Defrost behaviour. 1 Circuit and switchboard capacity. Multi-split system One outdoor unit serves several indoor units. It can reduce outdoor-unit count but creates shared capacity, refrigerant complexity and a larger single failure point. Check simultaneous performance, pipe limits and whether room units can truly operate independently. Ducted reverse-cycle system One central system distributes conditioned air through ducts. Strong fit:

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 58 1 Whole-home operation where duct routes and insulation are suitable. 1 Homes needing concealed outlets and coordinated zones. Risks: 1 Duct losses through hot roof or cold underfloor spaces. 1 Poorly sealed, compressed or undersized ducts. 1 Large fan energy and excessive return-air leakage. 1 Zones too small for the system's minimum airflow. 1 One failure affecting the whole home. Window or through-wall unit A self-contained refrigerative unit can serve one room without a separate outdoor unit. Check sealing around the opening, drainage, security, noise and permission. Portable refrigerative air conditioner Exhausts heat through a hose. Single-hose units can draw hot outside air into the room through leakage.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Portable refrigerative air conditioner Exhausts heat through a hose. Single-hose units can draw hot outside air into the room through leakage. They may be a renter option where no fixed unit is possible, but usually have lower whole-room efficiency and higher noise than a well-installed fixed system. Seal the window insert securely and manage condensate as instructed. Evaporative cooling Uses water evaporation and airflow. It performs best in dry conditions and needs open relief paths for humid air. Effectiveness falls in humid weather. Consider water use, maintenance, roof duct losses, smoke events and local climate. Fans Fans cool people through air movement rather than materially lowering room temperature. They use far less energy than refrigerative cooling and can extend the comfortable thermostat range.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Fans Fans cool people through air movement rather than materially lowering room temperature. They use far less energy than refrigerative cooling and can extend the comfortable thermostat range. 1 Ceiling fans: choose correct diameter, mounting height, clearances and reversible direction where useful. 1 Pedestal or desk fans: portable and renter-friendly. 1 Whole-house fans: require careful climate, air-sealing, smoke, security and roof-space design. 1 Exhaust fans: remove moisture or pollutants; they are not general comfort fans. Turn comfort fans off when no one is benefiting, unless they serve a separate ventilation function. Resistance electric heating Portable fan heaters, radiant panels, bar heaters and electric resistance systems convert electricity directly to heat.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Turn comfort fans off when no one is benefiting, unless they serve a separate ventilation function. Resistance electric heating Portable fan heaters, radiant panels, bar heaters and electric resistance systems convert electricity directly to heat. They can be useful for short, local heating but typically use more electricity to deliver the same heat than a heat pump. Gas heating Gas ducted, wall, space and hydronic systems have combustion, ventilation, servicing and emissions considerations. Unflued gas heaters release combustion products and moisture indoors and may be restricted. Never use an outdoor gas appliance for indoor heating. Wood heating Can provide strong radiant heat but creates air-pollution, fuel-storage, chimney, fire, neighbour and maintenance issues. Local rules and health guidance apply. It is not a neutral default for dense urban areas.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Local rules and health guidance apply. It is not a neutral default for dense urban areas. Hydronic heating Moves heated water through radiators or floors. The heat source can be gas, resistance electric or heat pump. Comfort can be excellent, but slow response, slab losses, insulation, zoning and heat-source efficiency matter. A hydronic system is not automatically efficient because it uses water.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 59 Size equipment from a room load calculation Rules of thumb based only on floor area can be badly wrong. A load calculation should consider: 1 Climate design temperatures. 1 Floor area, ceiling height and room volume. 1 Glazing area, orientation, shading and glass performance. 1 Wall, ceiling and floor insulation. 1 Air leakage and ventilation. 1 Occupants, appliances and solar gains. 1 Adjacent conditioned or unconditioned spaces. 1 Zoning and door use. 1 Desired indoor temperature and humidity. Oversizing can cause short cycling, temperature swings, poor humidity control, noise and cost. Undersizing can lead to continuous operation without reaching comfort in design conditions. Efficiency labels and performance data Compare like capacity and climate rating.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Undersizing can lead to continuous operation without reaching comfort in design conditions. Efficiency labels and performance data Compare like capacity and climate rating. Look for: 1 Rated heating and cooling capacity in kW. 1 Input power. 1 Seasonal efficiency or zoned energy-rating information. 1 Heating output at relevant low outdoor temperature. 1 Minimum and maximum modulation. 1 Standby power. 1 Indoor and outdoor sound data. 1 Refrigerant and service requirements. Do not compare star ratings across different capacity classes without reading the underlying annual energy figures. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/energy-rating Thermostat and operating strategy 1 Use the narrowest comfortable temperature difference from outdoors. 1 Condition occupied zones and close unused zones where the system permits.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/energy-rating Thermostat and operating strategy 1 Use the narrowest comfortable temperature difference from outdoors. 1 Condition occupied zones and close unused zones where the system permits. 1 Start earlier at moderate output rather than demanding an extreme setting after the home overheats or overcools. 1 Use fans to improve perceived comfort. 1 Keep doors and windows appropriate to system type: closed for refrigerative operation, managed relief for evaporative cooling. 1 Use timers and occupancy schedules carefully. 1 Avoid simultaneous heating and cooling by different systems. 1 Pre-heat or pre-cool with solar only if the building can retain the benefit and the tariff supports it. Thermostat numbers do not make equipment heat or cool faster beyond its available capacity. An extreme setting often causes longer operation and overshoot.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 60 Installation details that affect performance Indoor unit 1 Air can circulate through the occupied zone. 1 Sensor is not misled by sun, kitchen heat or another air stream. 1 Filter is accessible. 1 Condensate drain has correct fall and safe discharge. 1 Noise and appearance are acceptable. Outdoor unit 1 Required airflow and service clearances. 1 Protection from recirculating hot discharge air. 1 Stable, vibration-controlled mounting. 1 Condensate and defrost water managed. 1 Noise assessed at bedrooms, neighbours and boundaries. 1 Protection from flooding, impact, corrosion and extreme sun where appropriate. Ducted system 1 Duct insulation and air sealing. 1 Return-air path and grille size. 1 Zone minimum airflow and pressure relief. 1 Access for filter, fan and coil service.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Zone minimum airflow and pressure relief. 1 Access for filter, fan and coil service. 1 Commissioned airflow at outlets. Air-conditioning quote checklist 1 [ ] Room-by-room heat-load calculation supplied. 1 [ ] Heating and cooling capacities stated. 1 [ ] Climate performance and minimum modulation checked. 1 [ ] Indoor and outdoor locations drawn. 1 [ ] Sound data and neighbour impact considered. 1 [ ] Electrical circuit and switchboard work included. 1 [ ] Refrigerant pipe, drain and duct routes documented. 1 [ ] Penetrations, sealing and weatherproofing included. 1 [ ] Duct insulation, leakage and zoning specified. 1 [ ] Controls, timers and smart features explained. 1 [ ] Removal and refrigerant recovery for old equipment included. 1 [ ] Commissioning temperatures, pressures and airflow recorded. 1 [ ] Filter and maintenance access demonstrated.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 [ ] Commissioning temperatures, pressures and airflow recorded. 1 [ ] Filter and maintenance access demonstrated. Maintenance 1 Clean user-serviceable filters as instructed.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 61 1 Keep outdoor airflow clear without obstructing required protection. 1 Watch for ice, unusual noise, smell, water leaks, poor airflow or rising energy. 1 Keep condensate drainage clear through qualified service where needed. 1 Have gas appliances and flues serviced as required. 1 Inspect ducts for damage, disconnection or crushed insulation. 1 Record settings and energy before and after service. SAFETY Burning smell, smoke, electrical arcing, gas smell, soot, persistent headache, carbon-monoxide alarm or unusual flame requires immediate safety action. Stop use if safe, ventilate where appropriate, leave danger areas and contact emergency or qualified services.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 62 A Room-by-Room Comfort Plan Living area 1 External shade to hot-season sun. 1 Ceiling fan or portable fan. 1 Efficient reverse-cycle system sized to the actual zone. 1 Doors or curtains that preserve zoning. 1 Thermometer and humidity measurement. 1 Afternoon solar alignment if west-facing loads dominate. Bedrooms 1 Quiet fan and low-noise heating or cooling. 1 External shade and secure night ventilation where climate allows. 1 Small dedicated zone rather than whole-home conditioning overnight. 1 Avoid direct airflow on occupants who are sensitive. 1 Maintain humidity and mould control. Home office 1 Account for computer and screen heat. 1 Shade glare without eliminating useful daylight. 1 Condition the occupied room, not the empty house. 1 Schedule equipment sleep and shutdown.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Condition the occupied room, not the empty house. 1 Schedule equipment sleep and shutdown. Nursery, older person or health-sensitive room 1 Prioritise stable temperature, air quality, quiet operation and backup plan. 1 Use simple controls and visible temperature monitoring. 1 Do not compromise medical needs to chase a generic energy target. 1 Seek health advice for individual vulnerability. Rental home 1 Portable fans and safe window sealing. 1 Curtains where permitted. 1 Written request for efficient fixed heating or cooling supported by temperature and bill evidence. 1 Ask for filter service, draught repair and maintenance before requesting a larger system. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/household-guides/renters [2] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/design-climate

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 63 Hot Water: Reduce the Load, Then Choose the System Water heating is a large, recurring load. Start with safe demand reduction, then compare systems by household pattern, climate, fuel, space, noise, electrical capacity, tariff, maintenance and replacement urgency. Reduce hot-water demand 1 Repair leaking hot taps, tempering valves and pressure problems. 1 Use water-efficient showerheads that still provide acceptable performance. 1 Shorten showers without compromising health or care needs. 1 Wash clothes in cold water where appropriate. 1 Use full dishwasher and washing-machine loads. 1 Insulate accessible hot-water pipework where safe and permitted. 1 Avoid unnecessarily high delivery temperature while preserving legally required storage, hygiene and tempering settings.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Insulate accessible hot-water pipework where safe and permitted. 1 Avoid unnecessarily high delivery temperature while preserving legally required storage, hygiene and tempering settings. 1 Turn off or schedule hot-water circulation where the design permits. 1 Maintain taps and mixing valves. SAFETY Do not lower storage temperatures, alter tempering valves or change plumbing controls without qualified advice. Legionella prevention, scald protection and jurisdictional plumbing rules apply. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/hot-water-systems [2] www.waterrating.gov.au/consumers/water-rating-label Hot-water options Heat-pump water heater Moves heat from air into a storage tank. Strengths: 1 Can deliver several units of heat per unit of electricity under suitable conditions. 1 Can run during solar or lower-tariff periods. 1 Supports all-electric homes.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Can run during solar or lower-tariff periods. 1 Supports all-electric homes. Questions: 1 Rated performance in local cold and hot conditions. 1 Tank size and recovery time. 1 Noise, airflow and condensate. 1 Resistance booster size and control. 1 Refrigerant and service access. 1 Location near bedrooms or neighbours. 1 Anode or tank maintenance. 1 Whether a controlled-load circuit remains suitable.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 64 Electric resistance storage Simple electric element heats a tank. Strengths: 1 Straightforward technology. 1 Can use controlled-load or solar-diversion timing. 1 Stored hot water can act as thermal storage. Tradeoff: 1 Uses more electricity per unit of heat than an efficient heat pump. Solar thermal water heater Roof collectors directly heat water, with electric or gas boosting. Strengths: 1 Direct use of solar heat. 1 Can perform well on a suitable unshaded roof. Questions: 1 Freeze and overheating protection. 1 Pump or thermosiphon design. 1 Roof load and plumbing route. 1 Booster energy. 1 Tank and collector maintenance. 1 Roof-space competition with solar PV. Continuous-flow electric Heats water as it flows. Whole-home units can require very high electrical power and may trigger supply upgrades.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Continuous-flow electric Heats water as it flows. Whole-home units can require very high electrical power and may trigger supply upgrades. Point-of-use units can reduce pipe delay in special applications but add circuits and maintenance points. Gas storage or continuous-flow May remain where gas is already used, but include supply charge, combustion safety, ventilation, servicing, emissions and future fuel-switching cost. A nominally efficient appliance does not remove the fixed gas connection cost. Size the tank and recovery Use: 1 Number of occupants and guests. 1 Shower duration and flow. 1 Bath use. 1 Dishwasher and washing-machine connection. 1 Morning versus evening demand. 1 Available heating window. 1 Climate and incoming water temperature. 1 Recovery rate and booster. 1 Space and structural support.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 65 Oversizing increases standing loss and cost. Undersizing can force frequent booster use or run out. A controlled daytime heating window needs enough stored water to last until the next cycle. Timing hot water with solar and tariffs Options: 1 Built-in timer. 1 Controlled-load circuit. 1 Smart relay installed and configured by a qualified electrician. 1 Solar-diversion controller. 1 Heat-pump schedule. Check minimum run time, legionella cycle, recovery after guests, cloudy-day behaviour and manual boost. A timer that repeatedly causes cold showers will be overridden and save nothing. Hot-water quote checklist 1 [ ] Household demand and existing system measured. 1 [ ] Technology alternatives compared. 1 [ ] Tank volume and recovery rate justified. 1 [ ] Climate performance supplied.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 [ ] Tank volume and recovery rate justified. 1 [ ] Climate performance supplied. 1 [ ] Booster type and control explained. 1 [ ] Tariff or solar schedule documented. 1 [ ] Noise, airflow, condensate and neighbours assessed. 1 [ ] Plumbing, tempering, drainage and pressure work included. 1 [ ] Electrical circuit and switchboard work included. 1 [ ] Removal and lawful disposal of old system included. 1 [ ] Warranty, anode, refrigerant and service requirements stated. 1 [ ] Current public rebate eligibility checked.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 66 Cooking and Household Electrification Electrification replaces fossil-fuel appliances with efficient electric alternatives and coordinates them with the home, supply, tariff and renewable electricity. Plan the transition before failure Create a replacement register: Appliance Fuel and age Condition Preferred replacement Electrical or building work Trigger date Space heating Cooling Hot water Cooktop and oven Vehicle charging Pool heating Plan switchboard, circuits and locations once rather than paying for repeated emergency upgrades. Induction cooking Induction heats compatible cookware using a magnetic field. Potential benefits: 1 Fast control and high cooking efficiency. 1 No combustion products in the kitchen.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Potential benefits: 1 Fast control and high cooking efficiency. 1 No combustion products in the kitchen. 1 Cooler surrounding surface than a conventional resistance element, though cookware and glass still become hot. 1 Easier integration with an all-electric home. Check: 1 Cookware compatibility with a magnet. 1 Bench cut-out and ventilation. 1 Circuit and power-management requirements. 1 Control accessibility and user preference. 1 Pacemaker or medical-device advice where relevant. 1 Portable single-zone induction as a low-cost trial for renters, used on a suitable circuit. Continue using a functioning appliance if replacement would be premature and no safety or policy reason requires immediate change. Electrification can be staged at normal end of life. Switchboard and supply planning A licensed electrician can prepare a load schedule covering: 1 Existing maximum demand.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Electrification can be staged at normal end of life. Switchboard and supply planning A licensed electrician can prepare a load schedule covering: 1 Existing maximum demand. 1 Reverse-cycle systems. 1 Heat-pump water heating. 1 Induction and oven circuits.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 67 1 EV charging. 1 Pool and workshop loads. 1 Solar and battery inverters. 1 Load management and controlled circuits. 1 Single-phase or three-phase options. 1 Surge protection, safety switches and main switch. Smart load management may avoid a supply upgrade by preventing large flexible loads from operating simultaneously. It must fail safely and preserve essential services. Gas disconnection If removing the last gas appliance, compare retailer closure, meter removal, pipe capping and abolishment requirements. Use licensed gas work. Check whether daily gas charges continue until the account and physical connection are handled correctly. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/electrification [2] www.energy.gov.au/households/appliances

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 68 Appliances, Lighting and Standby Power Compare appliances by annual energy Use the energy-rating label and calculator to compare similar size and function. A larger appliance may have more stars but still use more annual kWh than a smaller suitable appliance. Consider: 1 Annual kWh under the label test. 1 Capacity actually needed. 1 Standby and networked standby. 1 Water use for washers and dishwashers. 1 Noise and placement. 1 Repairability and spare parts. 1 Expected life and warranty support. 1 Heat released into the room. 1 Demand and circuit requirements. 1 User behaviour and default modes. Sources: [1] www.energyrating.gov.au/consumer-information/understand-energy-ra... [2] www.energyrating.gov.au/calculator Refrigeration 1 Consolidate little-used extra refrigerators or freezers.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 User behaviour and default modes. Sources: [1] www.energyrating.gov.au/consumer-information/understand-energy-ra... [2] www.energyrating.gov.au/calculator Refrigeration 1 Consolidate little-used extra refrigerators or freezers. 1 Set safe food-storage temperatures, not colder than necessary. 1 Keep seals clean and replace damaged seals. 1 Allow required ventilation around condenser surfaces. 1 Keep away from ovens, direct sun and hot enclosed spaces where practical. 1 Defrost manual-defrost units before ice becomes excessive. 1 Measure old units over several days before replacement. 1 Recycle refrigerant and appliance through an appropriate service. Laundry 1 Wash full loads at the lowest suitable temperature. 1 Use high spin speed before drying when fabrics permit. 1 Line-dry where practical. 1 If using a dryer, clean filters and maintain airflow.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Line-dry where practical. 1 If using a dryer, clean filters and maintain airflow. 1 Heat-pump dryers can use less energy but have different cycle time, maintenance and condensate needs. 1 Schedule safely into solar or lower-tariff periods. Dishwashing 1 Run full loads. 1 Use eco mode where time permits.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 69 1 Avoid unnecessary pre-rinsing with hot water. 1 Maintain filters and spray arms. 1 Air-dry if the machine provides a suitable option. Lighting 1 Use efficient LED lighting where compatible. 1 Choose lumens for light output, not watts. 1 Select colour temperature and colour rendering for the task. 1 Use task lighting rather than over-lighting the whole room. 1 Turn off unneeded lights. 1 Maintain safe clearances from insulation around fittings as required. 1 Address flicker, buzzing, heat or discolouration through qualified assessment. Do not replace a fixed light fitting or dimmer unless authorised and qualified under local electrical rules. Entertainment and home office 1 Enable automatic sleep and power management. 1 Shut down unused screens, speakers, printers and game equipment.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Entertainment and home office 1 Enable automatic sleep and power management. 1 Shut down unused screens, speakers, printers and game equipment. 1 Use a switched power board only within its rating and without daisy-chaining. 1 Keep routers and essential network equipment powered if needed for safety or communications. 1 Measure the complete setup, including external power supplies. Standby decision rule Standby reduction is worthwhile when the load is measurable and the action is convenient. Do not switch off: 1 Refrigeration. 1 Medical and accessibility equipment. 1 Smoke, security or safety systems. 1 Sump, wastewater or critical pumps. 1 Devices that require power for moisture protection or safe shutdown.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 70 Pools, Spas and Pumps Pool equipment can dominate electricity use in some homes. Filtration pump 1 Use the lowest speed that maintains required circulation and water quality. 1 Variable-speed pumps can reduce power sharply at lower speed, but runtime and hydraulic performance must be set correctly. 1 Keep baskets, filters and pipes clean. 1 Repair leaks and air ingress. 1 Schedule outside expensive tariff periods or into solar hours. 1 Do not reduce filtration below safe water-quality requirements. Pool heating Options include: 1 Solar thermal collectors. 1 Heat-pump pool heater. 1 Gas heater for rapid or occasional heating. 1 Resistance heating in limited applications. 1 No active heating, seasonal use or a smaller heated zone. A cover can reduce evaporation and heat loss.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 No active heating, seasonal use or a smaller heated zone. A cover can reduce evaporation and heat loss. Compare cover handling, child safety, water chemistry and durability. Other pumps 1 Hot-water circulation. 1 Irrigation and bore pumps. 1 Rainwater pressure pumps. 1 Pond and aquarium circulation. 1 Sump and wastewater pumps. Check whether each needs continuous operation. Use correct sizing, controls, leak repair and maintenance. Never switch off a pump required for sanitation, flood protection, livestock or life support without a safe plan. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/pool-pumps [2] www.energy.gov.au/households/household-guides/reduce-energy-bills

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 71 Smart Homes: Measure, Automate and Keep Control A smart device is useful only if it improves a defined outcome without creating excessive complexity, privacy risk or failure dependence. Start with measurement, then add the smallest reliable control. The control hierarchy 1 Manual clarity. Labels, accessible switches, simple timers and written routines. 2 Measurement. Bills, interval data, plug meters, built-in appliance data and whole-home monitoring. 3 Scheduling. Run flexible loads in safe, favourable windows. 4 Sensing. Respond to temperature, humidity, occupancy, solar surplus or electricity price. 5 Coordination. A home energy management system balances solar, battery, EV, hot water and major loads. 6 External dispatch. Demand response or a virtual power plant may control agreed equipment.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 6 External dispatch. Demand response or a virtual power plant may control agreed equipment. Do not automate a bad schedule or faulty appliance. Verify the manual process first. Measurement options Smart meter data Useful for whole-home patterns and tariff analysis. It usually does not identify individual appliances by itself. Plug-in energy meter Measures compatible plug-in appliances. Check current rating and instructions. It is not for fixed wiring or unsuitable high-power loads. Whole-home current sensors Measure circuits or supply conductors. Installation inside a switchboard is electrical work. Accuracy can depend on sensor direction, phase allocation, voltage assumptions and calibration. Solar and battery monitoring Can show generation, import, export, consumption, state of charge and power flow. Confirm which quantities are measured and which are estimated.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Solar and battery monitoring Can show generation, import, export, consumption, state of charge and power flow. Confirm which quantities are measured and which are estimated. Submetering Dedicated meters for an EV charger, tenancy, apartment charger, hot water or shared equipment can support cost allocation. Billing use may require approved metering and formal arrangements. Useful sensors 1 Indoor and outdoor temperature. 1 Relative humidity. 1 Carbon dioxide as a ventilation indicator, not a complete air-quality measure. 1 Occupancy or motion. 1 Door and window state. 1 Water leaks. 1 Smoke and carbon monoxide using approved life-safety devices. 1 Solar irradiance or local weather for advanced control.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 72 Consumer air-quality sensors can help identify patterns but are not medical or regulatory instruments. Place and interpret them carefully. Practical automations Hot water Heat during solar or lower-tariff windows while preserving hygiene and household supply. Include a manual boost and recovery plan. EV charging Schedule by departure time, tariff, solar surplus and household maximum demand. Preserve the ability to charge urgently. Pool pump Run during a suitable solar or low-price window, at the lowest effective speed and safe water-treatment duration. Heating and cooling Use occupancy, temperature and tariff schedules. Avoid extreme pre-conditioning and simultaneous heating and cooling. Battery Coordinate reserve, solar charging, tariff charging, demand limits, export and backup.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Avoid extreme pre-conditioning and simultaneous heating and cooling. Battery Coordinate reserve, solar charging, tariff charging, demand limits, export and backup. Review after every tariff change. Standby control Switch non-essential entertainment or office groups off on a schedule. Exclude safety, medical, refrigeration and equipment that needs a proper shutdown sequence. Demand response Demand response reduces or shifts electricity use when the grid is constrained or prices are high. Programs may control air conditioners, water heaters, pool pumps, batteries or EV chargers. Check: 1 Which device is controlled. 1 Event frequency and duration. 1 Temperature or service limits. 1 Payment or credit. 1 Manual override. 1 Data shared. 1 Contract and exit rights. 1 Behaviour during communications failure.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Contract and exit rights. 1 Behaviour during communications failure. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/smart-homes Interoperability and lock-in Ask: 1 Does the device work locally without cloud service? 1 Can it operate if the internet is down? 1 Can data be exported in a standard format?

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 73 1 Does it use an open or widely supported protocol? 1 Can another controller operate it later? 1 Is there a subscription? 1 What happens if support ends? 1 Can the account transfer to a buyer or tenant? 1 Are core functions available from physical controls? A single app for everything can be convenient but creates a larger failure and privacy domain. Simple independent controls can be more resilient. Cybersecurity checklist 1 Use a long, unique passphrase for every account. 1 Enable multi-factor authentication where available. 1 Replace default credentials. 1 Keep device, app, phone and router software updated. 1 Check the declared support end date before purchase. 1 Remove or isolate devices that no longer receive security updates. 1 Use a separate guest or device network if supported and understood.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Remove or isolate devices that no longer receive security updates. 1 Use a separate guest or device network if supported and understood. 1 Disable unnecessary remote access, microphones, cameras and data sharing. 1 Review household member and former-occupant access. 1 Secure the email account used for password recovery. 1 Export needed data before closing an account. 1 Factory-reset and remove ownership before disposal or sale. Consumer smart devices manufactured after the current national commencement date should provide a statement of compliance with mandatory smart-device security rules. Check the current public guidance. Sources: [1] www.cyber.gov.au/protect-yourself/securing-your-devices/how-secur... [2] www.energy.gov.au/households/smart-homes Privacy questions 1 What data is collected: energy, occupancy, location, video, voice or device identifiers?

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Check the current public guidance. Sources: [1] www.cyber.gov.au/protect-yourself/securing-your-devices/how-secur... [2] www.energy.gov.au/households/smart-homes Privacy questions 1 What data is collected: energy, occupancy, location, video, voice or device identifiers? 1 Is detailed data necessary for the feature? 1 Where is it stored and for how long? 1 Who receives it? 1 Can the user delete it? 1 Is data used for advertising, credit, insurance or profiling? 1 Does an installer retain administrator access? 1 What data remains when the property changes occupant? Smart-home failure plan For each critical automation, define: 1 Safe state when internet fails. 1 Safe state when the controller fails.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 74 1 Manual override. 1 Restart after a power outage. 1 Clock and schedule recovery. 1 Notification if a device remains off. 1 Account recovery without an old phone number. Test the plan. An automation that nobody can override is not resilient. A renter-friendly smart kit 1 Plug-in energy meter for suitable appliances. 1 Thermometer and humidity monitor. 1 Portable fan. 1 Approved plug timer or smart plug within load rating. 1 Leak sensor near a water heater or washing machine where safe. 1 Utility-provided interval data. 1 Reversible curtains or window treatments permitted by the lease. Keep receipts, instructions and account-transfer details. Restore the property at the end of the tenancy unless another arrangement is agreed in writing.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 75 Electrical Safety and Capacity Work a householder should not do 1 Fixed wiring or switchboard changes. 1 Solar DC cable or connector work. 1 Installing or modifying an EV charger circuit. 1 Replacing a hardwired appliance or light fitting where licensed work is required. 1 Creating a generator inlet or transfer switch. 1 Opening equipment covers to test live parts. 1 Bypassing a safety switch, breaker or isolation device. Warning signs 1 Repeated tripping. 1 Warm, loose, cracked or discoloured outlets. 1 Buzzing, arcing, burning smell or smoke. 1 Electric shock or tingling from taps or equipment. 1 Flickering across multiple circuits. 1 Water in electrical equipment. 1 Damaged solar isolators or cables. 1 Unlabelled or overcrowded switchboard. Stop use where safe and seek urgent qualified help.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Unlabelled or overcrowded switchboard. Stop use where safe and seek urgent qualified help. Electric shock, fire or fallen lines can be an emergency. Pre-purchase electrical assessment For a home purchase or major electrification plan, consider a qualified inspection covering: 1 Switchboard type, safety switches and spare capacity. 1 Earthing and visible defects. 1 Supply phase and main capacity. 1 Asbestos-suspect board material. 1 Existing solar, battery, generator and EV equipment. 1 Old or altered wiring indicators. 1 High-load circuits and future upgrade needs. 1 Compliance documentation available from previous work. This is distinct from a general building inspection. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/electrification

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 76 Renters: Control What You Can and Build the Case for More Renters can reduce energy use, improve comfort, choose a better plan where retail choice exists, and document property problems. Fixed solar, batteries, wiring, hot water, air conditioning and EV charging normally require written owner approval and licensed work. Start with the account 1 Confirm whose name the electricity and gas accounts are in. 1 Check whether the property is in an embedded network. 1 Compare plans using actual bill or interval data where choice exists. 1 Apply eligible concessions and hardship support. 1 Check actual versus estimated meter reads. 1 Record the meter identifier and take safe photos at move-in and move-out. 1 Ask how common-area or shared hot-water energy is allocated.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Record the meter identifier and take safe photos at move-in and move-out. 1 Ask how common-area or shared hot-water energy is allocated. No-alteration actions 1 Use fans and occupied-room conditioning. 1 Close doors to create zones. 1 Use curtains and blinds already fitted. 1 Add removable window coverings only if permitted and safe. 1 Shift laundry, dishwashing and EV charging to suitable tariff or solar windows. 1 Measure plug-in appliances. 1 Remove unused spare refrigeration. 1 Set efficient appliance modes. 1 Shorten showers and report leaks. 1 Clean user-serviceable filters. 1 Use safe portable induction as a trial where the circuit and tenancy rules allow. 1 Turn off non-essential standby loads. Maintenance issues to report 1 Hot-water leak, pressure fault or unreliable supply. 1 Broken window or door seals. 1 Damaged exhaust fan or persistent condensation.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Broken window or door seals. 1 Damaged exhaust fan or persistent condensation. 1 Heating or cooling fault. 1 Unsafe outlet, repeated tripping or burning smell. 1 Water near electrical equipment. 1 Gas smell, soot or appliance fault. 1 Solar inverter error where solar is part of the rental property.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 77 1 Pool pump or shared equipment running abnormally. Report hazards promptly through the prescribed channel. Keep photos, dates and a copy of the request. Use emergency repair procedures where local tenancy law applies. Build a landlord request Make the request easy to assess. Problem State the room, time, measured temperature or energy issue, how long it has occurred and the effect on reasonable use. Evidence Attach photos, interval-data pattern, relevant bills, maintenance history and safe measurements. Remove unnecessary personal information. Requested outcome Ask for the function, not a brand. Examples: 1 Repair the failed fixed heater. 1 Install an efficient fixed heater/cooler sized to the main occupied zone. 1 Replace end-of-life resistance hot water with an efficient electric option.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Install an efficient fixed heater/cooler sized to the main occupied zone. 1 Replace end-of-life resistance hot water with an efficient electric option. 1 Repair building gaps, exhaust or insulation defects. 1 Assess rooftop solar for the property. 1 Permit a compliant EV charger assessment. Owner benefit Mention preservation of the property, reduced moisture risk, improved tenant retention, future marketability, planned replacement before emergency failure, and available public assistance without assuming eligibility. Permissions and restoration Propose written approval, licensed installation, certificate handover, insurance notification, ownership of equipment and end-of-tenancy treatment. RENTER Keep the tone factual and do not organise fixed work before written approval. Tenancy rules differ by state and territory, and strata approval may also be needed.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: RENTER Keep the tone factual and do not organise fixed work before written approval. Tenancy rules differ by state and territory, and strata approval may also be needed. Ready-to-use renter request Subject: Request to assess an energy and comfort improvement at [address] > The issue is [plain description]. It occurs [times/conditions] and has been recorded by [temperatures, photos, bills, fault codes or dates]. I have already taken these safe steps: [actions]. >

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 78 I request that the owner arrange a qualified assessment of [functional outcome]. A suitable solution should address [comfort, safety, moisture, energy or reliability need], include any required approval and be installed by appropriately licensed people. > I am available for access on [options]. Please confirm the proposed next step and timeframe in writing. Solar options for renters Existing solar on the rental 1 Confirm it operates and monitoring access is transferred. 1 Check the electricity account is configured for exports. 1 Use flexible loads during generation where practical. 1 Report inverter faults rather than attempting resets beyond documented user steps. 1 Clarify responsibility for monitoring, maintenance and internet connection.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Report inverter faults rather than attempting resets beyond documented user steps. 1 Clarify responsibility for monitoring, maintenance and internet connection. Request owner-funded solar Provide annual use, daytime occupancy, suitable roof evidence and a simple owner benefit case. Avoid promising a payback. The owner must control procurement and permissions. Cost-sharing agreement If the renter contributes, obtain independent tenancy and legal advice. Define ownership, rent changes, relocation, early termination, maintenance, warranty and what happens when the renter leaves. A long-lived fixture is usually an owner asset. Portable solar Use only with compatible portable equipment and within tenancy, balcony, wind, fire and electrical rules. Never connect a portable panel or inverter into fixed household wiring or an outlet to energise the home.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Portable solar Use only with compatible portable equipment and within tenancy, balcony, wind, fire and electrical rules. Never connect a portable panel or inverter into fixed household wiring or an outlet to energise the home. Batteries for renters A fixed home battery requires owner approval, compliant location, electrical work and likely network involvement. Portable power can support selected plug-in devices, but it does not create a compliant home backup system. Before buying a portable unit, check storage, charging location, exit paths, capacity, power, warranty, repair, safe transport and whether it solves a real need. EV charging for renters 1 Record parking right and distance to the tenant's meter. 1 Ask whether a compliant outlet or charger already exists. 1 Do not assume a common-property outlet is free to use. 1 Obtain owner and strata approval.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Do not assume a common-property outlet is free to use. 1 Obtain owner and strata approval. 1 Include electrical assessment, metering, load management, cable route and restoration. 1 Define who pays electricity, maintenance and removal. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/household-guides/renters [2] www.energy.gov.au/electric-vehicles/owning-electric-vehicle/charg...

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 79 Strata and Apartment Energy Shared buildings require decisions about common property, private lots, metering, electrical capacity, fire safety, cost allocation and future residents. Start with building data 1 Common-area electricity bills and interval data. 1 Embedded-network contract and expiry. 1 Main switchboard, distribution boards and spare capacity. 1 Roof and common-property ownership. 1 Lot and common meters. 1 Existing solar, battery, hot-water, ventilation, lifts, pumps and carpark loads. 1 Planned capital works and building defects. 1 Fire-safety systems and essential services. 1 Parking allocation and expected EV uptake. Strata solar models Common-area solar Supplies lifts, lighting, ventilation, pumps, common hot water or other shared daytime loads.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Parking allocation and expected EV uptake. Strata solar models Common-area solar Supplies lifts, lighting, ventilation, pumps, common hot water or other shared daytime loads. It can be simpler than allocating energy to lots. Individual lot systems Separate arrays or entitlements supply specific lots. Roof allocation, inverter location, cable route, maintenance and future equity need rules. Shared solar allocation One array is allocated virtually or physically among participating meters. Confirm approved metering, settlement, retailer compatibility, fees and what happens when a lot changes occupant. Solar plus shared battery Can support common loads, peak control or resilience. Define ownership, control, reserve, benefits, replacement and emergency responsibility. Strata decision questions 1 Who owns the equipment? 1 Which property title carries it?

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: Strata decision questions 1 Who owns the equipment? 1 Which property title carries it? 1 Who receives savings, exports, certificates and program payments? 1 How are capital and operating costs allocated? 1 Who monitors and authorises service? 1 What roof rights remain for non-participants? 1 How are leaks, roof replacement and temporary removal handled? 1 What happens when a lot is sold or rented? 1 How are vulnerable residents protected in an outage?

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: POWER YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME ENERGY SYSTEMS GUIDE Snapshot: 25 August 2026 80 1 Is the building locked into one platform or energy seller? Embedded networks Residents may buy electricity through a private network rather than directly from a retail market provider. Check: 1 Right to choose an external retailer. 1 Meter compatibility and exit cost. 1 Tariff transparency and comparison benchmark. 1 Solar export and shared-generation treatment. 1 Concessions and hardship access. 1 Complaint and ombudsman jurisdiction. 1 Contract end date and renewal process. Building-wide EV readiness Plan for expected future charger count, not one cable at a time. 1 Assess incoming supply and main switchboard. 1 Install shared cable pathways and communications where economical. 1 Use dynamic load management. 1 Meter individual energy accurately. 1 Create fair access, booking and billing rules.

chunks.sourceTitle: Power You Control: Australian Home Energy Systems Guide
chunks.text: 1 Meter individual energy accurately. 1 Create fair access, booking and billing rules. 1 Preserve accessible parking and visitor options. 1 Define maintenance and fault response. 1 Avoid an exclusive long contract without exit and interoperability review. Owners-corporation proposal structure 1 Problem and forecast demand. 2 Existing electrical and metering evidence. 3 Options, including no-action consequences. 4 Concept design and approvals. 5 Capital, operating and replacement costs. 6 Benefit allocation. 7 Safety, fire, insurance and maintenance. 8 Procurement and conflict-of-interest controls. 9 Contract, data and exit terms. 10 Staged implementation and review point.
