chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 16 Hinged external doors Treat the door as four edges and a pressure system. Check first 1 Does the door hang square, or has it dropped? 1 Is the stop straight and continuous? 1 Does the latch pull the door evenly against the stop? 1 Is the threshold level, weatherproof and safely traversable? 1 Does water enter? Weatherproofing and drainage come before air sealing. 1 Is there a security screen door that limits the seal position? 1 Is the door a fire, smoke, acoustic or BAL-rated assembly? Sides and head Use a compression or purpose-made perimeter seal where the door closes against the stop. Clean the contact area. Choose a profile that compresses enough to seal but still permits latching. Continuous contact matters more than maximum thickness.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Choose a profile that compresses enough to seal but still permits latching. Continuous contact matters more than maximum thickness. Bottom Options include: 1 Fabric door snake: reversible, cheap, manually repositioned and not weatherproof. 1 Surface-mounted sweep: simple on a smooth, level threshold. 1 Brush seal: tolerates texture and small variations, but is not watertight. 1 Roller or fluffy seal: can move over carpet. 1 Automatic drop seal: retracts while the door moves and drops when closed; useful where drag is unacceptable. 1 Threshold plate plus bottom seal: creates a defined landing surface for an uneven or missing threshold. 1 Door repair or replacement: appropriate where warping, rot or very large gaps defeat a seal. After installation, check latch operation, egress, floor clearance, water shedding and that the seal does not create a trip or accessibility hazard.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Door repair or replacement: appropriate where warping, rot or very large gaps defeat a seal. After installation, check latch operation, egress, floor clearance, water shedding and that the seal does not create a trip or accessibility hazard. French and double doors There are three leakage zones: the outer perimeter, the centre meeting stile and the bottom thresholds. Identify the active leaf and passive leaf, bolts and opening sequence. 1 Seal head and outer jambs as for a hinged door. 1 Use a compatible meeting-stile or astragal seal at the centre. It must respect which leaf opens first. 1 Treat both bottoms and the junction where the centre seal meets the threshold. 1 Adjust bolts and latches before adding thick seals. 1 Do not compromise emergency egress. Internal doors and comfort zoning Internal seals can keep conditioned air in a bedroom, study or living zone.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Do not compromise emergency egress. Internal doors and comfort zoning Internal seals can keep conditioned air in a bedroom, study or living zone. They are most useful when the heating or cooling system can serve that smaller zone independently. Do not seal an internal door if the gap is required for air return, pressure relief, mechanical ventilation or a combustion appliance. A room supplied by ducted air may need a return-air path when the door is closed. If closing the door

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 17 makes it slam, whistle or become difficult to move while the system runs, ask an HVAC professional about return-air design. Aluminium sliding doors Sliding doors typically leak at interlocks, meeting stiles, jambs and worn brushes. Water drainage paths in the sill must remain open. 1 Clean tracks and drainage holes. 1 Check rollers and alignment; a panel that does not close square cannot seal well. 1 Replace failed original pile where possible. 1 Apply a slim seal only on a clean, stable face that will not enter the running track. 1 Test the full open-close cycle repeatedly. 1 Keep child-safety, security and drainage functions intact. Cavity sliding doors Cavity or pocket doors are difficult because the leaf must enter the wall. Air can travel through the pocket and wall cavity.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Cavity sliding doors Cavity or pocket doors are difficult because the leaf must enter the wall. Air can travel through the pocket and wall cavity. Options include side brushes, head seals, a bottom treatment compatible with the guide, and better sealing around the cavity structure during renovation. Avoid loose material that can be drawn into the pocket. If the cavity connects to a dusty or unlined space, a building professional may need to address the enclosure, not just the visible edge. Security and screen doors A brush or sweep can reduce air at the bottom of a screen or security door, but the primary weather line is usually the solid external door. Do not make a security door bind, obstruct its latch or reduce required egress. A seal on an open mesh door cannot make the entrance airtight. Door-seal installation checklist 1 [ ] Correct door type and direction of movement.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: A seal on an open mesh door cannot make the entrance airtight. Door-seal installation checklist 1 [ ] Correct door type and direction of movement. 1 [ ] Gap measured at several points with door closed. 1 [ ] Door aligned and hardware adjusted first. 1 [ ] Surface clean, dry and compatible with adhesive or fasteners. 1 [ ] Required permission obtained. 1 [ ] Seal cut cleanly without stretched adhesive backing. 1 [ ] Corners meet without bunching or gaps. 1 [ ] Door opens, closes and latches without excessive force. 1 [ ] Egress, drainage, accessibility and rated performance preserved. 1 [ ] Checked again after 24 hours and after a week of use. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/insulation-and-draught-proofing [2] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/ventilation-airtightness

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 18 Windows: Air, Glass and Sun Treat three different problems A window can be uncomfortable because: 1 Air leaks through the sash, tracks, frame junction or wall junction. 2 Heat conducts and radiates through the glass and frame. 3 Sun passes through the glass and becomes heat inside. A seal only solves the first problem. A curtain or secondary pane mainly helps the second. External shading is usually strongest for the third. Double-hung and sash windows Likely leakage points are the meeting rails, side channels, top rail and bottom rail. Old cords, weights and pockets complicate the path. Options: 1 Repair sash alignment, locks and cords so the meeting rails pull together. 1 Add purpose-shaped brush or compression seals at sliding interfaces.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Options: 1 Repair sash alignment, locks and cords so the meeting rails pull together. 1 Add purpose-shaped brush or compression seals at sliding interfaces. 1 Seal fixed frame-to-wall cracks with a compatible flexible sealant after checking moisture paths. 1 Use full-length curtains with side returns and a sealed pelmet. 1 Add a removable or fixed secondary glazing system where the frame is sound. 1 Restore or replace the window where decay or severe distortion prevents operation. Do not paint a sash shut or block drainage. Preserve escape requirements for bedroom windows. Awning, casement and wind-out windows These windows usually close against a compression surface. 1 Adjust or repair hinges, stays, winders and latches first. 1 Identify the exact face that meets the frame when closed. 1 Apply a compatible compression seal around the continuous contact line.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Identify the exact face that meets the frame when closed. 1 Apply a compatible compression seal around the continuous contact line. 1 Use a profile that compresses without overloading the winder or latch. 1 Check corners and hardware cut-outs. For outward-opening windows, secondary glazing can often be fitted on the room side, but handles and access for opening must be planned. Aluminium sliding windows 1 Clean tracks, weep holes and original pile channels. 1 Repair rollers and latches. 1 Replace original pile or add a fine slim seal without blocking water paths. 1 Do not place bulky foam where the sash slides. 1 Address the frame-to-wall junction separately.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 19 Frameless, sashless and lapped-glass windows These may rely on overlapping glass edges. Use a clear or purpose-made flexible seal designed for the overlap and movement. Confirm that the seal will not scratch glass, interfere with drainage or catch during operation. Fixed windows Fixed panes do not leak at an opening sash but can leak at glazing beads, frames and the wall junction. Repair failed weather seals and water entry professionally. Interior caulk must not conceal an exterior flashing or drainage problem. Window upgrade ladder 1. Operate and repair Clean, align, latch and maintain the window. Use existing shade and furnishings at the right time. 2. Seal air leaks Treat operating joints with compatible seals and fixed construction gaps with compatible sealant. Preserve drainage and operation. 3.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Preserve drainage and operation. 3. Improve furnishings Use closely fitted curtains or blinds. Aim for coverage above, below and at the sides. A pelmet reduces warm indoor air circulating behind a cold curtain and glass. Layering a blind and curtain can help, provided condensation remains visible and manageable. 4. Temporary seasonal layer Purpose-made shrink film, removable panels or even bubble-wrap demonstrations can add a still-air layer. These are temporary measures, can affect appearance and daylight, and may trap condensation. Check glass compatibility and lease requirements. Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/glazing 5. Secondary glazing An interior acrylic or glass pane creates a still-air gap over existing glass. Options include magnetic, clip-in, fixed, hinged or removable systems. Check: 1 Accurate measurement and squareness.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Options include magnetic, clip-in, fixed, hinged or removable systems. Check: 1 Accurate measurement and squareness. 1 Access to handles, locks and cleaning. 1 Fire egress and emergency opening. 1 Expansion allowance for acrylic. 1 Scratch protection and compatible cleaners. 1 Air seal around the secondary pane. 1 Condensation management between panes. 1 Whether the existing frame can carry the system. DIY secondary glazing generally uses a three-stage process: estimate, accurately measure and cut components, then fit the frame and clear panel with careful handling. The broader decision is whether DIY accuracy, window geometry and required access make a chosen system suitable. Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/glazing 6. High-performance replacement Full window replacement can address glass, frame, seals and installation junctions.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/glazing 6. High-performance replacement Full window replacement can address glass, frame, seals and installation junctions. Compare: 1 Whole-window U-value: lower generally means less heat flow.

chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 20 1 Solar heat gain coefficient: select for climate, orientation and shading rather than assuming one value is best everywhere. 1 Frame conductivity: thermally broken aluminium, timber and uPVC can reduce frame heat transfer compared with unbroken aluminium. 1 Air infiltration test performance. 1 Acoustic requirements. 1 Bushfire, cyclone, security and fall-prevention requirements. 1 Installation flashing, sill drainage and wall integration. Double glazing without good frames, seals and installation can disappoint. Conversely, repaired single glazing with effective external shade, seals and curtains may be the sensible first stage. Skylights and roof windows Skylights can add daylight but also heat gain, heat loss and air leakage.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Conversely, repaired single glazing with effective external shade, seals and curtains may be the sensible first stage. Skylights and roof windows Skylights can add daylight but also heat gain, heat loss and air leakage. Options include external shades, insulated shafts, high-performance glazing, fitted internal covers, diffuser design and replacement. Do not block required ventilation or safe operation. Check for water entry before interior sealing.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 21 Shade Before You Refrigerate Why external shade comes first in summer Sun stopped before it reaches glass does not become a large indoor cooling load. Internal blinds improve glare and comfort but allow solar energy through the glass first. External shade is generally more effective.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Internal blinds improve glare and comfort but allow solar energy through the glass first. External shade is generally more effective. Match shade to orientation Orientation Solar pattern Useful responses North Higher summer sun, lower winter sun Correctly sized eaves, horizontal awnings, adjustable pergolas, deciduous planting East Low morning sun External vertical screens, shutters, adjustable blinds, planting with airflow West Strong low afternoon sun Deep external shade, vertical screens, shutters, trees, reduced exposed glass South Little direct sun in much of southern Australia, but still diffuse heat and some seasonal sun Glazing performance, curtains, climate-specific shade where needed In tropical latitudes, solar paths and desired seasonal response differ. Use the YourHome climate guidance for the site.

chunks.text: Match shade to orientation Orientation Solar pattern Useful responses North Higher summer sun, lower winter sun Correctly sized eaves, horizontal awnings, adjustable pergolas, deciduous planting East Low morning sun External vertical screens, shutters, adjustable blinds, planting with airflow West Strong low afternoon sun Deep external shade, vertical screens, shutters, trees, reduced exposed glass South Little direct sun in much of southern Australia, but still diffuse heat and some seasonal sun Glazing performance, curtains, climate-specific shade where needed In tropical latitudes, solar paths and desired seasonal response differ. Use the YourHome climate guidance for the site. Shade options from reversible to permanent 1 Close existing external shutters or awnings before the sun hits. 1 Use a freestanding umbrella or screen where wind and access allow.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Shade options from reversible to permanent 1 Close existing external shutters or awnings before the sun hits. 1 Use a freestanding umbrella or screen where wind and access allow. 1 Apply a removable reflective screen designed for windows, checking thermal stress and glass compatibility. 1 Install exterior roller blinds, louvres or shutters. 1 Add a fixed or adjustable awning. 1 Add pergola shade cloth or operable roofing. 1 Use deciduous planting where winter sun is valuable; evergreen planting where year-round shade is wanted. 1 Reduce heat from exposed paving and dark surfaces with landscape and material changes. 1 Select lower-solar-gain glazing where appropriate during replacement. 1 Use a light-coloured, reflective roof or wall finish suited to the climate and construction when renewing finishes.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Select lower-solar-gain glazing where appropriate during replacement. 1 Use a light-coloured, reflective roof or wall finish suited to the climate and construction when renewing finishes. SAFETY External fabric and foil can become dangerous in wind, obstruct egress, damage glass or breach strata and bushfire requirements. Use a product designed for the location and obtain approvals. Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/shading [2] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/design-climate

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 22 Insulation: Complete the Thermal Layer What insulation does and does not do Insulation slows heat flow. It does not create heat or coolth, repair a leak, provide shade, guarantee airtightness or manage moisture by itself. It works best as a continuous layer combined with appropriate glazing, shading, air sealing and ventilation. R-value measures resistance to heat flow. Higher is more resistant, but the relevant value is the total installed system, not just the label on a batt. Compression, gaps, thermal bridges, moisture and poor fit reduce real performance. Existing-home inspection Before adding insulation, determine: 1 What material is already present? 1 Is it dry, clean, evenly distributed and at full thickness? 1 Are there gaps at edges, around ducts, above walls and around penetrations?

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Is it dry, clean, evenly distributed and at full thickness? 1 Are there gaps at edges, around ducts, above walls and around penetrations? 1 Is it compressed by storage or services? 1 Are there pest nests, droppings, water stains or contamination? 1 Are wiring and downlights safe for the proposed installation? 1 Is the material compatible with the new layer? 1 Is there a vapour-permeable membrane or other moisture-control layer in the correct location? 1 Can installers work and walk safely?

chunks.text: Material families Family Examples Strengths Questions and risks Fibrous bulk Glass wool, mineral wool, polyester, natural wool Batts and rolls fit common framing; acoustic benefit Fit, irritation or PPE, moisture, fire classification, compression Loose fill Cellulose and other fibres Can cover irregular ceiling areas Settlement, wind movement, downlight clearances, access, removal Rigid board Wood fibre, PIR, PUR, XPS and others Continuous layers and high resistance per thickness Fire, vapour behaviour, joints, compatibility, environmental impact Reflective Foil membranes and foil-faced products Reduces radiant heat when facing an air space Electrically conductive, needs maintained air gap, dust and orientation matter Spray foam Open or closed cell systems Can combine insulation and air sealing in complex areas Chemistry, fire, moisture trapping, roof inspection, removal, installer

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: quality Composite Foil-faced blankets, boards or batts Combines mechanisms Must be designed as a system; air gaps and vapour direction matter Do not choose by marketing claim alone. Ask for declared R-value, fire performance, moisture suitability, installation standard, safety data, expected life and end-of-life implications. Ceiling and roof For many existing homes with accessible pitched roofs and flat ceilings, insulation is placed at ceiling level. The highest-value work is often achieving continuous coverage without unsafe contact with fittings. Options: 1 Top up sound existing insulation with a compatible layer.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 23 1 Remove contaminated, wet or incompatible material and reinstall a designed system. 1 Install batts or rolls between joists, then a cross layer where structure and clearances allow. 1 Use loose fill installed to controlled depth by a competent installer. 1 Insulate and weather-seal the roof-space access hatch. 1 Replace open-vented or unsuitable downlights with properly selected fittings through an electrician to reduce insulation holes. 1 Repair duct insulation and supports if retained. 1 For cathedral, raked or skillion roofs, redesign at roof replacement or interior renovation to create enough insulation and drainage or ventilation space. 1 Consider a warm-roof approach during major reroofing where designed by a competent professional.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 For cathedral, raked or skillion roofs, redesign at roof replacement or interior renovation to create enough insulation and drainage or ventilation space. 1 Consider a warm-roof approach during major reroofing where designed by a competent professional. Never block eave, roof or mechanical ventilation required by the roof design. Do not guess the vapour-control layer in a cold or humid climate. Underfloor insulation: timber floors Exposed timber floors can feel cold because they conduct heat and because air moves through boards and subfloor gaps. Underfloor bulk insulation should contact the underside of the floor continuously without sagging. For polyester rolls and similar systems, allow compressed material to regain thickness, use suitable lighting and PPE, work with another person, support the insulation frequently, keep it flat against the floor and avoid voids that invite pests.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Underfloor bulk insulation should contact the underside of the floor continuously without sagging. For polyester rolls and similar systems, allow compressed material to regain thickness, use suitable lighting and PPE, work with another person, support the insulation frequently, keep it flat against the floor and avoid voids that invite pests. Fixing methods must match the selected material and structure. Plan the job 1 Confirm safe subfloor access, clearance, lighting and communication. 1 Check for damp ground, plumbing leaks, termites, rot, pests and exposed wiring. 1 Maintain required subfloor ventilation and termite inspection zones. 1 Measure joist spacing in many locations and map obstructions. 1 Select a product and fixing system certified for the application. 1 Fit snugly around services without compressing or leaving bypass gaps. 1 Keep the top face in contact with the floor.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Fit snugly around services without compressing or leaving bypass gaps. 1 Keep the top face in contact with the floor. 1 Support edges and joins so the material cannot slump. 1 Do not cover electrical equipment or create unsafe contact with foil. 1 Photograph the full installation before access closes. Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/insulation [2] www.energy.gov.au/households/insulation-and-draught-proofing Steel-framed floors Steel joists conduct heat and are difficult to staple. Options include proprietary clips or support systems, straps, rigid continuous layers or designed combinations. Thermal bridging through steel remains even when cavities are filled; a continuous thermal break may improve performance. Do not create galvanic corrosion, trap water or conceal termite inspection paths.

chunks.text: Thermal bridging through steel remains even when cavities are filled; a continuous thermal break may improve performance. Do not create galvanic corrosion, trap water or conceal termite inspection paths. Floors over enclosed or semi-enclosed spaces If the space below is a garage, carport, basement or another dwelling, fire and acoustic requirements may govern the lining and insulation system. Use a designed assembly rather than exposed DIY material.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 24 Concrete slabs Existing slabs are hard to retrofit from below. Options include: 1 Slab-edge insulation during accessible perimeter work, designed for termites, moisture and durability. 1 Insulated floating floor systems during interior renovation, checking floor height, doors and moisture. 1 Rugs and underlays for local comfort, without claiming equivalent building R-value. 1 Under-slab insulation for new work or major reconstruction. Walls Wall retrofits are most practical when linings or cladding are already being removed. Options include: 1 Fit batts accurately between timber studs during renovation. 1 Add a continuous internal service layer or insulated lining. 1 Add external continuous insulation when recladding.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Add a continuous internal service layer or insulated lining. 1 Add external continuous insulation when recladding. 1 Blow or inject a product into verified empty cavities using a competent system and installer. 1 Insulate internal walls for acoustic separation or room zoning, understanding that this does not improve the external envelope unless the boundary is appropriate. 1 Address thermal bridges at steel framing, corners, lintels and junctions. Blind injection is not automatically safe. The wall must be assessed for cavity condition, electrical services, fire stops, moisture, drainage and whether the proposed material can be installed uniformly. Roof, walls and floors as one system Do not stop at the large flat areas. Junctions often dominate discomfort: 1 Ceiling perimeter at eaves. 1 Wall-roof junction. 1 Wall-floor junction and bearer lines. 1 Rim or band joists.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Wall-floor junction and bearer lines. 1 Rim or band joists. 1 Window and door reveals and lintels. 1 Corners and party-wall junctions. 1 Attached garages and unconditioned rooms. 1 Behind baths, stairs and built-in cupboards on external walls. Insulation quality checklist 1 [ ] Design suits climate, construction and moisture direction. 1 [ ] Electrical safety assessment complete. 1 [ ] Asbestos and contamination risks resolved. 1 [ ] Roof, plumbing and ground-water leaks resolved. 1 [ ] Declared R-value and thickness documented. 1 [ ] Full coverage at edges, corners and around services. 1 [ ] No compression, folds or unsupported sagging. 1 [ ] Fitting and flue clearances correct.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 25 1 [ ] Roof, subfloor and cavity ventilation preserved as designed. 1 [ ] Vapour-permeable and vapour-control layers correctly located. 1 [ ] Fire, termite, bushfire and acoustic requirements preserved. 1 [ ] Photos, product data, installer details and warranties retained.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 26 Hidden Openings and Special Cases Chimneys and fireplaces An unused open chimney can be a large air leak. Options include a purpose-made removable chimney draught stopper, a damper repair or a professionally designed permanent closure when the fireplace is decommissioned. Before blocking: 1 Confirm no appliance uses the chimney or flue. 1 Check for damp, falling masonry, nests and contamination. 1 Choose a visible reminder so the blocker is removed before any fire is lit. 1 Maintain any required moisture ventilation and comply with fireplace and heritage requirements. 1 Obtain professional advice for permanent closure.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Maintain any required moisture ventilation and comply with fireplace and heritage requirements. 1 Obtain professional advice for permanent closure. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/heating-and-cooling [2] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/ventilation-airtightness Exhaust fans and rangehoods An open exhaust can leak air when off. Options include an exterior gravity damper, inline non-return damper, purpose-made ceiling-side cover that opens under fan pressure, or fan replacement with an integrated backdraft damper. The system must still: 1 Move the required airflow. 1 Discharge outdoors, not into the roof space. 1 Open reliably despite grease, dust or wind. 1 Avoid dangerous negative pressure near combustion appliances. 1 Be accessible for cleaning.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Avoid dangerous negative pressure near combustion appliances. 1 Be accessible for cleaning. Disused ducted-heating vents After a ducted system is permanently decommissioned, old registers and return-air paths can be sealed and, where appropriate, insulated. First confirm the system is genuinely disused and disconnected. A surface cover alone may leave a cold, dirty duct cavity below. A durable solution may involve removing or capping ductwork, air-sealing the opening, restoring the floor or ceiling and reinstating insulation. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/electrification [2] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/ventilation-airtightness Wall and floor vents Some vents are historic uncontrolled openings; others are required for gas combustion, room ventilation, subfloor moisture or code compliance. Identify function first. 1 Do not seal a required combustion-air vent.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Identify function first. 1 Do not seal a required combustion-air vent. 1 Do not close subfloor vents without a moisture and termite strategy. 1 If deliberate room ventilation is needed, replace uncontrolled holes with a designed controllable or mechanical system where permitted. 1 If a vent is redundant, seal both the air barrier and the insulation layer rather than taping only the grille. Floorboard and skirting gaps Options include flexible gap sealant for stable narrow gaps, timber slivers or repair for larger boards, compressible backing rod plus sealant, underfloor air sealing, and rugs for local comfort.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 27 Account for timber movement, finishes and moisture. Do not inject foam blindly into cavities containing wiring, damp or termite inspection zones. A clear flexible seal can be less visible at skirtings, but surface preparation and a neat bead matter. Service penetrations Pipes, cables and refrigerant lines often leave gaps. Use a sealant or collar compatible with the wall, service, movement, fire rating, pests, UV and weather exposure. Electrical enclosures and fire-rated penetrations require appropriate licensed or specialist work. Downlights and ceiling penetrations Do not tape over lights or cover fittings unless they are classified and installed for that condition. A licensed electrician can replace leaky recessed fittings with suitable IC-rated units or surface-mounted lights.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Downlights and ceiling penetrations Do not tape over lights or cover fittings unless they are classified and installed for that condition. A licensed electrician can replace leaky recessed fittings with suitable IC-rated units or surface-mounted lights. Seal the ceiling line around compatible fittings using tested systems. Roof-space hatches Add a compressible perimeter seal and rigid insulation to the hatch where compatible. Ensure latches hold the seal evenly and insulation cannot fall on the occupant. Maintain safe access. Evaporative coolers Evaporative cooling requires open relief paths during operation. Off-season ceiling outlets and the unit can be a major winter leak. Use the manufacturer's winter-shutoff method, dampers or purpose-made covers only when the system is off and safe to close. Add a seasonal reminder before startup.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Use the manufacturer's winter-shutoff method, dampers or purpose-made covers only when the system is off and safe to close. Add a seasonal reminder before startup. Pet doors and mail slots Use well-fitting flaps, magnetic closures, brushes or insulated multi-flap designs. Check animal safety, accessibility, security and weather exposure. A removable internal cover can help when not in use. Old through-wall air conditioners If retained, seal the chassis-to-wall junction without blocking drainage or service access. If removed, reconstruct the wall with weatherproofing, structure, insulation, air barrier and interior lining, not just a thin cover plate.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 28 Ventilation, Humidity and Mould Replace random leakage with reliable ventilation Healthy air requires outdoor air and pollutant removal. A better-sealed home needs more attention to: 1 Bathroom, laundry and kitchen exhaust. 1 Outdoor discharge and non-return dampers. 1 Window opening or mechanical ventilation strategy. 1 Combustion safety. 1 Moisture and pollutant sources. 1 Filter maintenance. 1 Occupancy, especially in bedrooms overnight. Moisture sources to control 1 Showers and baths. 1 Cooking, especially boiling and unflued gas cooking. 1 Clothes drying indoors. 1 Occupants breathing and sleeping. 1 Aquariums and many indoor plants. 1 Plumbing, roof and envelope leaks. 1 Ground moisture below floors. 1 Unflued combustion heaters.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Ground moisture below floors. 1 Unflued combustion heaters. Practical condensation response 1 Measure indoor temperature and relative humidity. 2 Run exhaust during showers and cooking and continue until moisture clears. 3 Confirm exhaust discharges outdoors. 4 Dry clothes outside or use an effective vented or heat-pump dryer as designed. 5 Keep furniture slightly clear of cold external walls and allow wardrobe air movement. 6 Improve surface temperature with insulation, window furnishings and better glazing. 7 Heat occupied rooms adequately in cold weather while managing ventilation. 8 Use a correctly sized dehumidifier where the climate or building requires it. 9 Repair water leaks and external moisture entry. 10 Seek professional investigation for large, hidden or recurring mould. Do not permanently hide condensation behind a sealed curtain or secondary panel.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 10 Seek professional investigation for large, hidden or recurring mould. Do not permanently hide condensation behind a sealed curtain or secondary panel. Inspect and dry the zone. Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation [2] www.health.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/2022/07/enhealth-... Natural ventilation Use cross-ventilation when outdoor air is more comfortable than indoor air. Open windows or doors on opposite sides, use high and low openings where safe, and purge heat in the evening after a hot day. Close the home and shade it when outdoor conditions become worse.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 29 Natural ventilation is weather-dependent, can introduce smoke, pollen, noise and humidity, and may conflict with security. It is an operating strategy, not a guaranteed ventilation rate. Mechanical ventilation options 1 Local exhaust fans for bathrooms, toilets and laundries. 1 Ducted rangehood exhausting outdoors. 1 Continuous low-flow exhaust with planned make-up air. 1 Supply ventilation with filtration. 1 Balanced ventilation. 1 Heat-recovery ventilation for climates and homes where retaining heat matters. 1 Energy-recovery ventilation where moisture transfer is part of the design. Balanced systems need design, commissioning, cleanable ducts and filter maintenance. They are not a substitute for fixing water leaks or unsafe combustion.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Balanced systems need design, commissioning, cleanable ducts and filter maintenance. They are not a substitute for fixing water leaks or unsafe combustion. Air cleaners and monitors Portable HEPA cleaners can reduce particles in a room but do not remove carbon dioxide and are not a substitute for ventilation. Activated-carbon performance varies and media saturates. Choose a clean-air delivery rate suitable for the room and account for noise at the speed you will actually use. CO2 monitors can indicate whether occupied-space ventilation may be inadequate, but readings require context. Carbon-monoxide alarms are a separate safety device and do not make an unsafe appliance safe. Smoke alarms must meet local rules and be maintained.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 30 Heat and Cool the People and Rooms That Need It Reduce the load first Heating and cooling is often the largest household energy use. Before replacing equipment: 1 Shade exposed glass and roofs where appropriate. 1 Seal safe air leaks. 1 Complete insulation. 1 Improve window furnishings and glazing. 1 Zone the area being conditioned. 1 Measure actual room temperatures and operating patterns. 1 Repair ducts, controls and airflow faults. Then size equipment for the improved load. Oversized equipment can cycle poorly, cost more and dehumidify less effectively. Undersized equipment may never reach comfort in extreme weather. Use an installer who performs a load assessment rather than selecting only by floor area.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Undersized equipment may never reach comfort in extreme weather. Use an installer who performs a load assessment rather than selecting only by floor area. Operating temperatures Australian Government household guidance suggests winter heating setpoints around 18 to 20 degrees C and summer cooling around 25 to 27 degrees C as an energy-saving starting point. Health, age, disability, medication and weather may require different settings. Treat these as adjustable starting points, not a rule that overrides wellbeing. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/household-guides/reduce-energy-bills [2] www.energy.gov.au/households/heating-and-cooling Fans Fans improve comfort by moving air across skin; they do not materially lower empty-room temperature. Options include ceiling, pedestal, desk and wall fans. 1 Turn off a fan in an empty room unless it serves another planned ventilation purpose.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Options include ceiling, pedestal, desk and wall fans. 1 Turn off a fan in an empty room unless it serves another planned ventilation purpose. 1 Use the lowest comfortable speed to reduce noise and energy. 1 Check ceiling-fan direction if the model has a seasonal reverse mode. 1 Keep blades clean and balanced. 1 Ensure safe clearances and licensed installation for fixed fans. 1 Combine with a higher cooling setpoint where comfortable. Reverse-cycle air conditioning Reverse-cycle systems are heat pumps: they move heat rather than creating all heat by resistance. Forms include: 1 Single split: one indoor unit and one outdoor unit, effective for a priority room or open zone. 1 Multi-split: several indoor heads on one outdoor unit, with diversity and part-load tradeoffs. 1 Ducted reverse cycle: whole-home distribution and zoning, with duct losses and fan energy to manage.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Multi-split: several indoor heads on one outdoor unit, with diversity and part-load tradeoffs. 1 Ducted reverse cycle: whole-home distribution and zoning, with duct losses and fan energy to manage. 1 Window or through-wall heat pump: simple form for a room where permitted. 1 Portable single-duct air conditioner: generally a last resort because it can draw hot outdoor air into the room; installation and condensate management matter.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 31 Selection checklist 1 Climate-appropriate heating and cooling performance, including at design extremes. 1 Zoned Energy Rating Label and annual energy consumption. 1 Low-load modulation and part-load efficiency. 1 Indoor and outdoor noise. 1 Defrost behaviour in cold climates. 1 Dehumidification performance in humid climates. 1 Filtration and cleanability. 1 Refrigerant, serviceability and installer support. 1 Outdoor-unit location with unobstructed intake and discharge. 1 Condensate drainage. 1 Electrical capacity and demand-management capability. Operating checklist 1 Condition only occupied zones. 1 Close windows and doors while refrigerative equipment runs, unless deliberate ventilation is required. 1 Use timer and scheduling functions deliberately. 1 Clean user-serviceable filters.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Use timer and scheduling functions deliberately. 1 Clean user-serviceable filters. 1 Keep outdoor coils and airflow clear. 1 Do not use rapid extreme setpoints expecting faster delivery; set the temperature you need. 1 Record unusual noise, ice, smells, water or loss of performance and arrange service. Evaporative cooling Evaporative cooling can be effective in dry climates. It adds moisture and requires relief openings so air can leave the home. It is less suitable when outdoor humidity is high. Do not close all windows while it operates unless the system is specifically designed otherwise. Maintain pads, water distribution, drainage and seasonal sealing. Off-season dampers or covers can reduce winter leakage. Resistance electric heaters Fan heaters, panel heaters, oil-filled column heaters and radiant heaters convert electricity to room heat at the point of use.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Off-season dampers or covers can reduce winter leakage. Resistance electric heaters Fan heaters, panel heaters, oil-filled column heaters and radiant heaters convert electricity to room heat at the point of use. They can be useful for short, local or occasional loads but usually use more electricity for the same delivered heat than an efficient reverse-cycle system. 1 Choose an appropriate heater for the room and supervision level. 1 Plug directly into a suitable wall outlet unless the manufacturer explicitly permits otherwise. 1 Keep clear of bedding, curtains, clothes and water. 1 Do not leave portable heaters unattended. 1 Use thermostats and timers safely.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 32 Gas heating Room-sealed flued gas equipment is safer than open-flued or unflued equipment, but all gas appliances require correct installation, ventilation where specified and servicing. Unflued heaters release water vapour and pollutants indoors. Open-flued heaters can be affected by negative pressure. When replacement is due, compare a suitable reverse-cycle heat pump and the cost of retiring gas. Coordinate electrical upgrades and do not block gas vents before appliances are safely decommissioned. Wood heating Wood heaters require correct flue design, dry fuel, clearances, maintenance and local approval. They emit particles and can affect neighbours and household health. Before choosing one, compare passive upgrades and efficient electric heating, particularly in urban areas.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: They emit particles and can affect neighbours and household health. Before choosing one, compare passive upgrades and efficient electric heating, particularly in urban areas. Never close a flue or ventilation path while the heater remains usable. Hydronic heating Hydronic systems distribute hot water through radiators or floors. Heat sources may include gas, electric resistance, heat pumps or solar-assisted systems. Upgrade options include controls, weather compensation, pipe insulation, hydraulic balancing, lower-temperature emitters and a heat-pump heat source. A heat-pump conversion must be designed for required water temperatures and emitter capacity, not treated as a simple appliance swap. Ducts and zoning Duct leakage and weak insulation can waste energy in roof or subfloor spaces.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: A heat-pump conversion must be designed for required water temperatures and emitter capacity, not treated as a simple appliance swap. Ducts and zoning Duct leakage and weak insulation can waste energy in roof or subfloor spaces. 1 Inspect accessible ducts for disconnection, crushed sections, failed outer jackets and unsupported runs. 1 Seal joints with systems designed for ducts, not generic cloth tape. 1 Insulate to the appropriate level. 1 Commission airflow and zone balance. 1 Ensure closed rooms have suitable return-air paths. 1 Remove and close abandoned systems carefully when electrifying. Resilience and a climate-safe room If whole-home upgrades are unaffordable, create one room that can remain safer during heat, cold or smoke events. 1 Select a room with manageable size, limited exposed west glass and good egress. 1 Seal safe leaks and improve curtains, pelmet and shade.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Select a room with manageable size, limited exposed west glass and good egress. 1 Seal safe leaks and improve curtains, pelmet and shade. 1 Add or repair insulation at its boundaries. 1 Use an efficient reverse-cycle unit and a fan. 1 Use a HEPA air cleaner for smoke particles where appropriate. 1 Provide reliable temperature, humidity and carbon-monoxide alarms as relevant. 1 Plan for medication, pets, mobility, power outage and community cooling or warming locations. Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/energy/heating-and-cooling [2] www.energy.gov.au/households/heating-and-cooling

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 33 Hot Water: Reduce the Load, Then Choose the System Start with delivered hot water 1 Repair leaks promptly. 1 Use a suitable WELS-rated showerhead. 1 Take shorter showers where comfortable and safe. 1 Wash clothes in cold water when appropriate. 1 Run dishwashers and washing machines with full loads and efficient cycles. 1 Insulate accessible hot-water pipes with a compatible product, especially near the heater. 1 Set controls and schedules to suit actual use, while maintaining safe storage and delivery temperatures through a plumber. 1 Avoid flicking a mixer tap into the hot zone when only cold water is needed. A small but useful habit is keeping a flick mixer fully in the cold position when hot water is not needed.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Avoid flicking a mixer tap into the hot zone when only cold water is needed. A small but useful habit is keeping a flick mixer fully in the cold position when hot water is not needed. This can avoid firing a hot-water system or drawing heated water for a task that did not need it. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/household-guides/reduce-energy-bills Heat-pump water heaters A heat-pump water heater extracts heat from surrounding air and transfers it to stored water. Check: 1 Climate operating range and cold-weather performance. 1 Tank size, recovery rate and household peak demand. 1 Noise and location near bedrooms or neighbours. 1 Airflow and whether the unit cools the space around it. 1 Condensate drainage. 1 Booster element operation. 1 Timer or demand-response capability to use solar or off-peak periods. 1 Warranty, anode and service network.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Timer or demand-response capability to use solar or off-peak periods. 1 Warranty, anode and service network. 1 Plumbing, electrical and structural requirements. Solar thermal hot water Solar thermal systems heat water using roof collectors, with electric or gas boost. They can be effective with appropriate solar access and demand. Check roof structure, orientation, shading, freeze or overheat protection, tempering, pump energy, tank location, maintenance and booster strategy. Compare whole-of-life cost with heat-pump hot water plus rooftop solar. Electric storage Electric-resistance storage is simple but can use substantial electricity. Improve performance through correct sizing, tank and pipe insulation, controlled tariffs or solar-diversion scheduling where appropriate. Do not lower stored-water temperature below safe levels without professional advice.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 34 Continuous-flow and storage gas Gas systems have standing, flue or cycling characteristics and keep the gas connection in use. When replacement is due, compare electrification including switchboard work and gas abolishment. If retained, service through a licensed gasfitter and keep flues and combustion air safe. Apartment and central systems Central hot water may involve embedded energy billing, recirculation losses and strata-owned equipment. Options include balancing recirculation, insulating central pipes, fixing meters and leaks, efficient central plant or staged electrification. Individual occupants should not alter common systems.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 35 Cooking, Lighting and Appliances Induction and electric cooking Induction heats compatible cookware directly and avoids indoor combustion emissions. Options range from a plug-in single hob used within its electrical rating to a fixed cooktop installed by an electrician. Plan for: 1 Cookware compatibility. 1 Circuit and switchboard capacity. 1 Bench cut-out and ventilation requirements. 1 Controls accessible to the household. 1 Rangehood exhausting outdoors. 1 Safe use of portable appliances and no overloaded power boards. 1 A staged transition if a rental provider is not ready for a fixed replacement. Gas cooking contributes moisture and pollutants. Use the rangehood and ventilation, keep burners maintained and plan an electric replacement.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Gas cooking contributes moisture and pollutants. Use the rangehood and ventilation, keep burners maintained and plan an electric replacement. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/electrification [2] www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation Lighting 1 Use daylight without adding unwanted glare or summer heat. 1 Replace failed incandescent and halogen lamps with compatible efficient LEDs. 1 Use task lighting rather than lighting an entire zone unnecessarily. 1 Select lumen output, colour temperature, colour rendering, dimmer compatibility and beam angle for the task. 1 Use occupancy or daylight controls where they will not create nuisance or safety issues. 1 Have fixed wiring and fittings installed by a licensed electrician. 1 Prefer surface-mounted or appropriately classified sealed downlights where ceiling continuity matters.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Have fixed wiring and fittings installed by a licensed electrician. 1 Prefer surface-mounted or appropriately classified sealed downlights where ceiling continuity matters. Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/energy/lighting Refrigerators and freezers 1 Choose the capacity you need before comparing stars and annual kWh. 1 Locate away from ovens and direct sun and maintain manufacturer clearances. 1 Keep door seals clean and test for poor contact. 1 Set suitable temperatures and avoid prolonged door opening. 1 Allow hot food to cool safely before storage according to food-safety guidance. 1 Defrost models that require it. 1 Clean accessible condenser areas if the manufacturer instructs. 1 Retire an unnecessary second fridge or freezer after checking actual use. Laundry 1 Wash full loads with cold water where suitable.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Retire an unnecessary second fridge or freezer after checking actual use. Laundry 1 Wash full loads with cold water where suitable. 1 Match cycle to soil level rather than defaulting to the longest hot cycle.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 36 1 Spin effectively before drying. 1 Use a clothesline when weather and household needs allow. 1 If buying a dryer, compare heat-pump, condenser and vented types, Energy Rating Label consumption, cycle time, moisture removal and room ventilation. 1 Maintain lint filters and ducts to reduce fire risk and preserve performance. Dishwashing 1 Scrape rather than pre-rinse under running hot water. 1 Run full loads without obstructing spray arms. 1 Use eco cycles when time permits. 1 Maintain filters, spray arms and seals. 1 Compare both Energy Rating and WELS information when replacing. Entertainment, office and standby 1 Measure before buying standby gadgets. A plug-in meter can reveal actual watts. 1 Use switched power boards for groups that can safely lose power.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: A plug-in meter can reveal actual watts. 1 Use switched power boards for groups that can safely lose power. 1 Preserve power to medical devices, networks, security, refrigeration and devices that require continuous operation. 1 Enable sleep settings on computers and displays. 1 Shut down high-performance computers when not needed. 1 Match screen size and brightness to the room. 1 Consolidate duplicate printers, old set-top boxes and idle equipment. Pools and spas 1 Use a correctly sized variable-speed pump and optimise run time. 1 Keep filters clean and hydraulic restrictions low. 1 Use a pool cover to reduce heat and water loss. 1 Compare heat-pump or solar heating with resistance or gas systems. 1 Shift flexible operation to suitable tariff or solar periods. 1 Maintain water chemistry so efficiency work does not damage equipment. Buying an appliance 1 Define required size and features.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Maintain water chemistry so efficiency work does not damage equipment. Buying an appliance 1 Define required size and features. 2 Compare models of similar size and function. 3 Use the Energy Rating Label annual kWh, not stars alone. 4 Multiply annual kWh by your relevant tariff for a simple running-cost estimate, adjusting for your use. 5 Check noise, standby, repairability, warranty and service. 6 Check WELS consumption for water-using appliances. 7 Consider total installed cost and expected life. The official Energy Rating Label is based on standardised testing. Actual use can differ. More stars means greater efficiency only when comparing similar products of similar size and features. Sources: [1] www.energyrating.gov.au/consumer-information/understand-energy-ra... [2] www.waterrating.gov.au/consumers/water-rating-label

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 37 Understand and Control Energy Use Read the bill Separate: 1 Daily supply charge. 1 Usage charge in kWh or MJ. 1 Time-of-use periods. 1 Demand charges if present. 1 Controlled-load hot water. 1 Solar export credit. 1 Concessions, discounts and expiry dates. 1 Estimated versus actual meter reads. Compare the same season year to year, then normalise mentally for weather, occupancy, new appliances and tariff changes. A lower bill does not always mean lower use; price changes matter. Government comparison services Use Energy Made Easy for participating National Electricity Market jurisdictions and the Victorian Government comparator in Victoria. Retail choice differs in Western Australia, the Northern Territory, Tasmania and regional Queensland.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Government comparison services Use Energy Made Easy for participating National Electricity Market jurisdictions and the Victorian Government comparator in Victoria. Retail choice differs in Western Australia, the Northern Territory, Tasmania and regional Queensland. Use actual interval data where available and check contract conditions, demand charges and solar export terms. Avoid assuming a commercial comparison site is independent; some earn commissions. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/household-guides/reduce-energy-bills [2] www.energymadeeasy.gov.au/ Smart meters and interval data Interval data can show: 1 Overnight baseload. 1 Heating or cooling peaks. 1 Hot-water cycles. 1 Solar self-consumption and export. 1 Whether flexible loads can move away from expensive periods. 1 Unexpected use while the home is empty. Download several seasons if the portal allows.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Unexpected use while the home is empty. Download several seasons if the portal allows. Match patterns to a diary before attributing a load to an appliance. Plug-in meter method For a compatible plug-in appliance: 1 Check the meter current and power rating. 2 Record standby watts. 3 Measure a normal cycle or at least 24 hours for cycling loads. 4 Convert to kWh over the relevant period. 5 Multiply by the applicable tariff.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 38 6 Repeat after a control change. Do not use a plug-in meter for fixed equipment, unsafe plugs, high loads beyond its rating or equipment that must not be interrupted. Flexible demand Possible flexible loads include hot water, EV charging, dishwasher, laundry, pool pump, battery charging and pre-heating or pre-cooling. The best timing depends on tariff, solar production, weather, noise and household needs. Automation options include timers, smart plugs within rating, appliance scheduling, home energy management, demand-response programs and retailer-controlled loads. Protect privacy and account security. Keep manual override and fail-safe behaviour. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/smart-homes

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 39 Solar, Batteries and Electrification Efficiency before generation, but do both strategically Solar panels do not stop draughts or make a hot bedroom comfortable. Envelope upgrades reduce the load; efficient electric systems improve the work done per kWh; solar can then supply some of that electricity. The sequence can overlap when roof, equipment or finance timing makes coordination sensible. Rooftop solar decision Assess: 1 Safe roof condition and remaining life. 1 Orientation, tilt, shading and usable area. 1 Current and future electricity profile. 1 Switchboard, inverter and network limits. 1 Export tariff and curtailment risk. 1 Quality and warranty of modules, inverter, mounting and monitoring. 1 Accredited designer and installer requirements. 1 Retailer credentials and complaint pathway.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Accredited designer and installer requirements. 1 Retailer credentials and complaint pathway. 1 Fire, emergency isolation, labelling and maintenance. 1 Strata, heritage, planning or landlord approval. Obtain multiple itemised quotes using the same assumptions. Do not accept a savings figure without the assumed tariff, degradation, export, self-consumption and finance terms. Batteries A battery can shift solar into the evening, provide selected backup if designed for it, respond to tariffs or join a virtual power plant. It is not automatically economic or capable of whole-home backup. Check: 1 Usable capacity, power and surge rating. 1 Which circuits operate in backup and for how long. 1 Black-start and solar operation during outage. 1 Chemistry, enclosure, location and temperature limits. 1 Fire and emergency requirements. 1 Cycle and throughput warranty.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Fire and emergency requirements. 1 Cycle and throughput warranty. 1 Control rights in a virtual power plant. 1 Tariff spread, exports and expected cycling. 1 Future EV and electrification loads. 1 Accredited installation and product eligibility for any incentive. Sources: [1] cer.gov.au/schemes/renewable-energy-target/small-scale-renewable-... Electrification plan List every gas or combustion load and its likely replacement year:

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 40 1 Space heating. 1 Hot water. 1 Cooking. 1 Pool or spa heating. 1 Fireplace or decorative gas. Then coordinate: 1 Envelope work that reduces required capacity. 1 Switchboard and service capacity. 1 Efficient heat-pump equipment. 1 Induction cooking. 1 Solar, battery and EV charging. 1 Removal, capping and abolishment of gas services. 1 Closure of genuinely disused ducts, vents and flues. Electrical and gas work must be done by appropriately licensed people. Renters need the property owner's decision and approval. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/electrification Electric vehicles Charging options include a standard outlet used only as permitted by the vehicle and electrical system, a dedicated circuit and wall charger, solar-aware charging and managed strata charging.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Renters need the property owner's decision and approval. Sources: [1] www.energy.gov.au/households/electrification Electric vehicles Charging options include a standard outlet used only as permitted by the vehicle and electrical system, a dedicated circuit and wall charger, solar-aware charging and managed strata charging. Plan cable route, outlet condition, circuit capacity, residual-current protection, weather exposure, load management, tariff and future vehicles. Never use improvised extension leads. In apartments, coordinate fire, metering, common property and equitable access.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 41 Water Efficiency and Home Utility Why water and energy are linked Every litre of hot water carries both water and energy cost. Start with showers and leaks, then appliances and hot-water generation. Showerheads and taps Use WELS registration, star rating and litres per minute. More stars means greater water efficiency, but the fixture must suit pressure and user needs. 1 Measure existing flow with a container and timer safely. 1 Repair dripping taps and leaking mixers. 1 Choose a showerhead with tested spray performance. 1 Check tenancy rules before replacing a fixture. 1 Keep the original rental fixture if an approved temporary swap must be reversed. 1 Have plumbing changes done by a licensed plumber where required. Toilets 1 Repair a leaking inlet or flush valve promptly.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Have plumbing changes done by a licensed plumber where required. Toilets 1 Repair a leaking inlet or flush valve promptly. 1 Use full and half flush appropriately. 1 Replace inefficient end-of-life toilets with a suitable WELS-rated dual-flush model. 1 Check pan, set-out, drainage and accessibility compatibility. 1 Do not use improvised cistern displacement that compromises flushing. Rainwater and garden Options include rainwater tanks, garden irrigation scheduling, drip systems, mulch, soil improvement, climate-suitable planting and leak detection. Tank water systems require appropriate screens, first-flush treatment, backflow prevention, pumps and maintenance. Check local rules and intended potable or non-potable use. Greywater Greywater reuse can reduce mains demand but involves health, salt, detergent, storage and plumbing risks.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: Check local rules and intended potable or non-potable use. Greywater Greywater reuse can reduce mains demand but involves health, salt, detergent, storage and plumbing risks. Use an approved system and comply with state, territory and council requirements. Do not store untreated greywater or apply it where people may contact it. Sources: [1] www.waterrating.gov.au/consumers/water-rating-label/what-wels-sta... [2] www.waterrating.gov.au/consumers/water-saving-tips

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 42 Room-by-Room Rescue Entry and hallway Diagnose 1 External-door perimeter and bottom gaps. 1 Letter slot, pet door and sidelights. 1 Stairwell stack effect pulling warm air upward. 1 Open plan to conditioned rooms. 1 Cold floor over a ventilated subfloor. Options 1 Adjust hinges, latch and strike. 1 Seal sides, head and bottom with compatible profiles. 1 Repair threshold and water entry. 1 Add a curtain or internal airlock arrangement where egress and access allow. 1 Seal letter slot and pet-door leakage with purpose-made components. 1 Zone the hallway from living rooms with a safe internal door. 1 Insulate exposed floor or ceiling above if applicable. Bedroom Diagnose 1 Cold glass and frames beside the bed. 1 West sun stored into the evening. 1 Air leaks at sash windows.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 West sun stored into the evening. 1 Air leaks at sash windows. 1 Poor ceiling or floor insulation. 1 High overnight humidity and closed-door ventilation. 1 Duct imbalance with the door shut. Options 1 Repair and seal the window. 1 Use external summer shade. 1 Fit full-length curtains, side returns and a pelmet. 1 Add secondary glazing or replace high-impact windows. 1 Complete ceiling and underfloor insulation. 1 Use an efficient quiet reverse-cycle unit or fan where appropriate. 1 Maintain a safe overnight ventilation strategy. 1 Move bed slightly from cold external surfaces. 1 Use a quiet HEPA cleaner during smoke events if needed. Do not trade quiet for unsafe air. A closed bedroom with multiple occupants can become stuffy even if temperature is controlled.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 43 Living room Diagnose 1 Large glazed area and solar orientation. 1 Open fireplace or unused chimney. 1 External doors and open-plan leakage. 1 Oversized zone heated for one seating area. 1 Duct or return-air losses. Options 1 External shade and high-performance window furnishings. 1 Safe chimney closure only when unused. 1 Perimeter and bottom door seals. 1 Secondary glazing or strategic window replacement. 1 Ceiling, wall and floor insulation. 1 Ceiling fan and efficient heat-pump heating or cooling. 1 Furniture arrangement away from cold downdraughts and direct summer sun. 1 Zoning doors or curtains where safe and suitable. Study and home office 1 Use task lighting and computer sleep settings. 1 Measure computer, display, printer and network loads. 1 Shade screen glare externally where possible.

chunks.text: 1 Measure computer, display, printer and network loads. 1 Shade screen glare externally where possible. 1 Seal the small room and condition it separately only if ventilation remains adequate. 1 Prefer a fan and personal comfort measures before overcooling the whole home. 1 Schedule high-compute tasks if tariffs or solar make that useful, without disrupting work. Kitchen 1 Exhaust cooking moisture and pollutants outdoors. 1 Maintain rangehood filters and non-return dampers. 1 Plan induction at appliance replacement or trial a safe portable unit. 1 Use lids, appropriately sized cookware and small appliances when they suit the task. 1 Keep fridge and freezer away from heat and maintain ventilation clearances. 1 Run a full efficient dishwasher and maintain filters. 1 Avoid blocking required make-up air or creating gas-appliance negative pressure.

Bathroom and laundry 1 Repair leaks and failed seals at the water source. 1 Use an effective exhaust discharging outdoors. 1 Provide make-up air so the fan can move its rated flow. 1 Use a backdraft damper that opens reliably.

chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 44 1 Choose a suitable WELS showerhead. 1 Shorten showers where possible. 1 Dry towels and clothes effectively; avoid releasing large moisture loads into cold rooms. 1 Insulate accessible hot-water pipes. 1 Use cold washes and full loads. 1 Investigate condensation, not just surface mould. Nursery, older person or health-sensitive room Prioritise stable temperature, low noise, safe equipment, cleanable filters and simple controls. Avoid portable combustion heaters. Secure blind cords, heaters and furniture. Consider professional advice for medical temperature needs, respiratory illness or life-support equipment. Register life-support needs with the retailer and distributor where applicable. Apartment The thermal boundary may include neighbours, corridors and common walls rather than outside air.

chunks.text: Register life-support needs with the retailer and distributor where applicable. Apartment The thermal boundary may include neighbours, corridors and common walls rather than outside air. High-impact areas often include exposed facade glass, balcony doors, top-floor roof, garage floors and central exhaust. Apartment options: 1 Repair and seal operable windows and balcony doors within ownership rules. 1 Add approved internal furnishings or secondary glazing. 1 Use external shade only with facade and wind approval. 1 Improve local heating, cooling and hot water. 1 Work through strata on central systems, roof insulation, facade glazing, solar and EV charging. 1 Check whether exhaust and make-up air are centralised before altering grilles.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 45 Climate and Season Playbooks Hot humid and tropical Priorities: 1 Deep external shade for walls and glass. 1 Light-coloured roof and appropriate radiant barrier design. 1 Cross-ventilation and fans when outdoor conditions allow. 1 Efficient air conditioning sized to dehumidify, not oversized. 1 Moisture-aware insulation and vapour design. 1 Seal conditioned rooms while providing deliberate ventilation. 1 Control rain entry, mould and cyclone requirements. Avoid importing a cool-climate vapour strategy. In air-conditioned humid climates, condensation can occur toward the exterior side of assemblies. Hot dry Priorities: 1 Strong solar control and thermal mass used with night purging. 1 Secure night ventilation when outdoor air cools. 1 Evaporative cooling where water use and humidity are suitable.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Secure night ventilation when outdoor air cools. 1 Evaporative cooling where water use and humidity are suitable. 1 High roof and ceiling protection. 1 Seal hot daytime air leaks. 1 Landscape shade without compromising bushfire or termite requirements. Warm temperate Use adjustable shade, ceiling fans, cross-ventilation, roof and ceiling insulation and selective winter solar gain. A reversible system is valuable because heating and cooling seasons both matter. Cool temperate and alpine Priorities: 1 High continuous insulation. 1 Strong airtightness with deliberate ventilation. 1 Low-U glazing and improved frames. 1 Curtains, pelmets and reduced thermal bridges. 1 Efficient heat-pump heating selected for low outdoor temperatures. 1 Condensation and roof-space moisture design. 1 Airlocks or well-sealed entries.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 46 Bushfire-prone areas Bushfire Attack Level requirements can govern gaps, vents, glazing, screens, seals and materials. Do not assume a brush or perimeter seal makes an opening BAL compliant. Preserve tested assemblies and use products and installers appropriate for the assessed BAL. Coordinate energy work with bushfire resilience and ember protection. Smoke and heatwave mode Before an event: 1 Shade early and pre-cool appropriately. 1 Check seals, filters and air-cleaner capacity. 1 Prepare a climate-safe room. 1 Charge essential batteries and plan outages. 1 Know when outdoor air is safe enough to ventilate. During smoke, close openings when official advice indicates, run suitable filtration and avoid activities that add particles. During cooler clean-air periods, ventilate as conditions allow.

chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 47 Budget Ladders No-cost actions 1 Compare current bills and interval data. 1 Use existing curtains, blinds, doors and windows at the right time. 1 Zone occupied rooms. 1 Adjust thermostat gradually. 1 Use fans for personal cooling. 1 Clean accessible filters and vents according to instructions. 1 Turn off avoidable standby loads. 1 Use cold laundry cycles and full loads. 1 Reduce hot-water waste. 1 Move furniture to reduce radiant discomfort and improve airflow. 1 Photograph defects and request repairs. Under about $50 per item Actual prices vary; this is an order-of-magnitude category, not a quotation. 1 Thermometer and humidity meter. 1 Fabric door snake. 1 Small quantities of removable or fixed seals. 1 Backing rod and compatible sealant for a bounded gap. 1 LED lamps compatible with existing fittings.

Under about $250 per project 1 A quality external-door sealing system. 1 Selected window sealing. 1 Curtains and a simple pelmet for one room. 1 Removable secondary panel for a small window. 1 Plug-in energy meter or higher-quality environmental sensors. 1 Exhaust backdraft solution installed appropriately. 1 Professional service or minor repair, depending on trade and location. Medium projects 1 Secondary glazing for priority windows. 1 External awnings or blinds.

Major projects 1 Wall insulation during relining or recladding. 1 High-performance window replacement. 1 Whole-home HVAC redesign. 1 Roof redesign, warm roof or major cathedral-ceiling work. 1 Whole-home electrification and switchboard upgrade. 1 Rooftop solar, battery and EV charging. 1 Deep energy retrofit with measured airtightness and balanced ventilation. A sequencing example Cold leaky weatherboard home 1 Gas and electrical safety checks. 2 Seal external doors, unused chimney and safe gaps. 3 Repair sash operation; add curtains and pelmets. 4 Complete ceiling insulation.

Hot west-facing apartment 1 Confirm strata rules and window ownership. 2 Use existing blinds early; add approved reflective or blackout layers. 3 Seek external vertical shade approval. 4 Repair balcony-door and sliding-window seals. 5 Use fans and zone the bedroom. 6 Install or optimise efficient split cooling. 7 Add approved internal secondary glazing if winter or noise also matters. 8 Work through strata on facade and central-system upgrades.

Windows 1 Operation and repair. 1 Sash, pile and compression seals. 1 Curtains, liners, side returns and pelmets. 1 Cellular blinds and tightly fitted shutters. 1 Temporary film or panels. 1 Interior or exterior secondary glazing. 1 Full double or triple glazing. 1 Thermally improved frames. 1 External shade by orientation.

chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 52 Working With Trades and Suppliers A useful quote request Give every bidder the same scope: 1 Address and building type. 1 Problem and measured evidence. 1 Relevant photos and plans. 1 Exact rooms and surfaces included. 1 Performance outcome sought. 1 Known hazards, access limits and occupancy needs. 1 Required licences, certifications, insurance and approvals. 1 Request for product data, installation method, exclusions, warranty and disposal. 1 Request for commissioning, photos and completion documents. Questions for an insulation installer 1 What existing material and hazards did you identify? 1 Who performs the electrical safety assessment? 1 What R-value and thickness will be installed? 1 How will gaps, eaves, hatches, ducts and penetrations be treated?
