chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 53 1 What happens in outage, frost, very hot weather or high humidity? 1 What rebates are assumed, and who carries eligibility risk? Red flags 1 Guaranteed bill savings without tariff, weather and usage assumptions. 1 A product chosen before inspection or measurement. 1 No discussion of gas ventilation, wiring, downlights, asbestos or moisture. 1 Insulation quoted only by bag count or area, with no installed R-value and coverage method. 1 Window performance quoted for glass only. 1 Oversized HVAC offered "to be safe" without a load calculation. 1 Pressure to sign before receiving product and installer details. 1 Rebates presented as cash certainty without current eligibility evidence. 1 Requests for unusual payment methods or full payment before reasonable milestones.

chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 54 Maintenance and Verification After each upgrade 1 Photograph completed work. 1 Record model, batch, R-value, installer, licence, invoice and warranty. 1 Check doors, windows, fans, drains and controls operate. 1 Recheck temperature, humidity and energy use under comparable conditions. 1 Look for new condensation or pressure effects. 1 Confirm smoke alarms and safety systems remain functional. 1 Keep instructions where future occupants and trades can find them. Seasonal routine Before winter 1 Inspect seals and adjust doors and windows. 1 Remove chimney blockers before any intended fireplace use; otherwise confirm the fireplace remains decommissioned. 1 Fit approved seasonal covers to evaporative-cooling outlets only as designed. 1 Clean heat-pump filters and arrange service if needed.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Fit approved seasonal covers to evaporative-cooling outlets only as designed. 1 Clean heat-pump filters and arrange service if needed. 1 Inspect accessible insulation after trade access or pest activity. 1 Test safety alarms as required. Before summer 1 Deploy and inspect external shade. 1 Remove winter-only covers from systems that need airflow. 1 Clean fans, filters and outdoor-unit surroundings. 1 Check window screens and safe night-ventilation options. 1 Review the heatwave and outage plan. Every bill cycle 1 Compare use with the same season last year. 1 Check tariff changes and discount expiry. 1 Investigate unexpected baseload or peaks. 1 Track solar generation and equipment alerts. Seal maintenance 1 Clean gently with compatible products. 1 Replace crushed, torn or hardened inserts. 1 Re-adhere only after resolving surface or alignment causes.

chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 55 Insulation maintenance Insulation generally needs little attention, but inspect after roof work, electrical work, pest treatment, leaks or storm damage. Trades often move batts and fail to restore them. Wet or contaminated insulation needs investigation, not a cosmetic top-up.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 56 Templates Seven-day comfort sprint Day 1: baseline 1 [ ] Record bills, tariffs and seven days of interval data if available. 1 [ ] Place temperature and humidity monitors in the main problem rooms. 1 [ ] Photograph windows, doors, vents, heaters and visible defects. Day 2: operate 1 [ ] Set a curtain and shading routine. 1 [ ] Zone occupied rooms. 1 [ ] Adjust thermostat one step and use fans or personal comfort. Day 3: find leaks 1 [ ] Test external doors and windows. 1 [ ] Check chimney, fans, old ducts, hatches, floorboards and skirtings. 1 [ ] Mark required vents separately from suspected waste leaks. Day 4: moisture 1 [ ] Confirm bathroom and kitchen exhaust operation and outdoor discharge. 1 [ ] Check leaks, indoor drying and furniture against cold walls. 1 [ ] Log humidity morning and night.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 [ ] Check leaks, indoor drying and furniture against cold walls. 1 [ ] Log humidity morning and night. Day 5: equipment 1 [ ] Clean permitted filters. 1 [ ] Measure selected plug loads. 1 [ ] Note fixed-equipment models and age. Day 6: permissions and quotes 1 [ ] Separate reversible, consent-required and licensed work. 1 [ ] Send one evidence-based repair or upgrade request. 1 [ ] Obtain comparable scopes for high-priority work. Day 7: plan 1 [ ] Choose the top three actions by evidence, impact, ease and risk. 1 [ ] Define what success will look like. 1 [ ] Set a date to verify. chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 58 Buying, Renting or Renovating Inspecting a home before commitment 1 Ask for several seasons of electricity and gas bills where available and lawful. 1 Note orientation and external shade at different times. 1 Inspect ceiling insulation through safe, permitted access or a professional. 1 Look for halogen downlights and insulation gaps. 1 Check window frame material, glass type, seals and coverings. 1 Operate every external door and window. 1 Smell for damp and inspect behind furniture and in wardrobes. 1 Identify heating, cooling, hot water and cooking fuels, models and ages. 1 Check roof condition before planning solar. 1 Identify switchboard condition and available capacity through an electrician. 1 Check strata records for major energy, window, waterproofing and EV issues.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Identify switchboard condition and available capacity through an electrician. 1 Check strata records for major energy, window, waterproofing and EV issues. 1 Consider an accredited Home Energy Rating for an existing home. Sources: [1] www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/buying-existing-house [2] www.homeenergyrating.gov.au/find-accredited-assessor Renovation trigger points Use unavoidable work to add energy performance: 1 Reroofing: roof blanket, membranes, ventilation and solar coordination. 1 Ceiling replacement: air barrier, lighting and insulation continuity. 1 Recladding: external continuous insulation and window integration. 1 Relining: wall batts, service cavity and airtightness. 1 Flooring replacement: slab or floor insulation where practical. 1 Window replacement: whole-window performance and external shade.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 Flooring replacement: slab or floor insulation where practical. 1 Window replacement: whole-window performance and external shade. 1 Kitchen: induction, efficient appliances and outdoor-exhaust rangehood. 1 Bathroom: WELS fixtures, exhaust, hot-water pipes and moisture detailing. 1 Equipment failure: efficient electric replacement rather than like-for-like gas by default. 1 Switchboard work: future heat pumps, solar, battery and EV capacity. New build or major addition Brief the designer for climate-responsive orientation, appropriate glazing area, exterior shade, continuous insulation, reduced thermal bridges, a documented air barrier, deliberate ventilation, efficient all-electric systems, solar-ready roof and measured commissioning. A minimum code solution is a floor, not necessarily the best lifetime comfort outcome.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 59 Final Decision Checklist Before buying or installing any comfort or efficiency product: 1 [ ] I can name the exact problem it is meant to solve. 1 [ ] I have evidence that the problem exists. 1 [ ] I know whether the opening or vent is required. 1 [ ] Gas, electrical, asbestos, moisture, fire and access risks are resolved. 1 [ ] Rental, strata, heritage and planning permissions are clear. 1 [ ] The product suits the exact door, window, structure, climate and movement. 1 [ ] I understand what the option will not solve. 1 [ ] Installation details are at least as strong as the product specification. 1 [ ] I have compared repair, reversible, retrofit and replacement options. 1 [ ] I have a way to measure the result. 1 [ ] I will retain records for the next occupant and tradesperson.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: 1 [ ] I have a way to measure the result. 1 [ ] I will retain records for the next occupant and tradesperson. Comfort is not a single purchase. It is a managed home: shade before heat arrives, keep useful heat where it is wanted, remove moisture and pollutants deliberately, choose efficient equipment, and verify that every layer still works together.

chunks.sourceTitle: Comfort You Control: Australian Renter and Homeowner Field Guide
chunks.text: COMFORT YOU CONTROL AUSTRALIAN HOME COMFORT FIELD GUIDE Snapshot: 24 August 2026 60 Independence, Scope and Limitations This handbook is independent and non-commercial. It contains no company endorsement, retailer recommendation, brand comparison, catalog listing, current price or affiliate relationship. Options are described by function so readers can compare any suitable solution on evidence, fit, safety, durability, installed performance and whole-of-life cost. The advice is general and Australia-wide. Climate, construction, health needs, rental rules, strata requirements, bushfire exposure and trade licensing can change the correct answer for a particular home. Programs, rebates and technical requirements also change. Check the linked public sources and obtain qualified advice before fixed, hazardous or regulated work. DECISION A product name is not evidence.

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: Data Analytics report Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide Practical response guidance derived from privacy-reduced home-energy community questions and replies. Aug 25, 2026, 2:37 AM UTC Executive Summary People ask about decisions, not isolated products. Questions combine household comfort, bills, equipment, tariffs, climate, neighbours, roof constraints, installers and timing. A useful AI response must treat the home as a connected system. The strongest responses turn anecdotes into a structured decision. They ask for location, measured energy use, equipment details and constraints; quantify likely demand; compare options; and explain what could change the answer. Community experience is valuable but not authoritative. The captured replies include practical examples, conflicting opinions, commercial interests and claims that may be outdated.

Those 11 threads contain retained, privacy-reduced responses; five appear complete for the observed count and six are partial. chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: What Real Households Actually Ask Users usually begin with an outcome and a constraint. They rarely supply every technical input needed for a confident answer. Their questions commonly take these forms: Diagnose an unexpected outcome. "Why is usage so high?" or "Why is the battery empty by evening?" Establish the billing period, interval data, major loads, battery state, inverter data, household count and recent changes. Choose between technologies. Heat-pump versus resistive hot water, or desiccant versus compressor dehumidifier. Establish climate, temperature, humidity, noise, available space, usage pattern, running hours and budget. Test whether a strategy will work. A typical example is charging a large battery during a free-electricity window. Establish the actual load profile, tariff caps, inverter and supply limits, losses, solar seasonality and plan-change risk.

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: A typical example is charging a large battery during a free-electricity window. Establish the actual load profile, tariff caps, inverter and supply limits, losses, solar seasonality and plan-change risk. Evaluate a brand, installer or quote. "Is this company or product any good?" Compare performance specifications, installer quality, warranty, support, identical scope and independent evidence. Solve an installation detail. Examples include blinds on high-performance windows or exhaust-fan ducting. Establish the building-envelope impact, moisture path, manufacturer instructions, applicable requirements and trade advice. Work around availability or compatibility. A product is out of stock or a retailer does not support an inverter. Confirm the exact model, current compatibility, temporary alternatives, control options and consequences of switching. Fill a missing-information gap.

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: Confirm the exact model, current compatibility, temporary alternatives, control options and consequences of switching. Fill a missing-information gap. If a photo, model number or monitoring record is absent, ask for the missing evidence instead of guessing. So what: the AI should not rush to a product recommendation. It should first identify which missing facts would materially change the decision. chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: What Strong Community Responses Do - and Where They Fail Useful response behaviours Give measured examples, such as heater power, daily energy, operating hours, humidity change or battery capacity. Connect several systems: solar surplus, hot-water timing, controlled load, gas supply charges, EV charging, insulation and household schedules. Ask location-specific questions because winter solar, humidity, heating demand and tariffs differ materially by region. Compare options instead of declaring a universal winner. Surface practical issues that specifications miss, including noise, condensate drainage, maintenance, installer workmanship and whether equipment is actually supported. Explain the reasoning behind a recommendation, allowing the household to test whether the example fits its own circumstances.

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: Surface practical issues that specifications miss, including noise, condensate drainage, maintenance, installer workmanship and whether equipment is actually supported. Explain the reasoning behind a recommendation, allowing the household to test whether the example fits its own circumstances. Common weaknesses the AI must correct Anecdotes are treated as proof that a product will perform the same elsewhere. Recommendations arrive before the question has been diagnosed. Current tariff, VPP, rebate and compatibility claims are repeated without verification. Brand loyalty and price reactions replace comparison of performance and total cost. Commercial contributors may recommend products they sell. Safety and building advice can be oversimplified or contradictory. Financial claims may ignore finance costs, battery losses, opportunity cost, warranty life or changing electricity plans.

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: Safety and building advice can be oversimplified or contradictory. Financial claims may ignore finance costs, battery losses, opportunity cost, warranty life or changing electricity plans. So what: the AI should synthesise the useful variables and reasoning, not reproduce the loudest or most confident comment. Source: MEEH privacy-reduced community extract File: outputs/meeh-ai-knowledge-pack/meeh-industry-knowledge.jsonl Case Pattern : High Bills, Battery Drain and Free-Power Plans Observed question: a multi-dwelling property reported about 120 kWh daily use, a large bill and a battery emptying early in the evening. Other battery discussions asked whether a large battery could be charged during a three- or fourhour free-power window.

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: Source: MEEH privacy-reduced community extract File: outputs/meeh-ai-knowledge-pack/meeh-industry-knowledge.jsonl Case Pattern : High Bills, Battery Drain and Free-Power Plans Observed question: a multi-dwelling property reported about 120 kWh daily use, a large bill and a battery emptying early in the evening. Other battery discussions asked whether a large battery could be charged during a three- or fourhour free-power window. How the community responded: replies discussed tariff windows, daily caps, inverter charging rates, simultaneous household load, seasonal solar output, shading, EV demand, insulation, battery size, finance cost and the risk of designing around a retail plan that may change. Some answers were numerical and conditional; others jumped directly to switching retailer or buying capacity. Direction for the AI: diagnose before optimising.

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: Some answers were numerical and conditional; others jumped directly to switching retailer or buying capacity. Direction for the AI: diagnose before optimising. A tariff cannot explain or fix an unidentified 120 kWh daily load. Request interval data, separate grid import from solar generation and battery discharge, confirm the billing period, list major loads and check whether metering covers several dwellings. Only then model battery and tariff scenarios. 1

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: Decision-changing inputs: -minute or finer interval data, ideally covering representative summer and winter periods Battery capacity, usable state-of-charge range, charge/discharge limits and round-trip efficiency Solar size, orientation, shading and seasonal production Heating, cooling, hot water, pumps, pool, workshop and EV loads Supply phase and current limits, inverter limits and export limits Full tariff terms, including free-window caps, peak rates, supply charges and plan-change risk Purchase price, finance source, warranty and expected cycling Safe response boundary: do not recommend electrical alterations or diagnose wiring faults remotely. Escalate unexplained extreme consumption, metering concerns or suspected faults to the retailer, distributor or a licensed electrician as appropriate.

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: Escalate unexplained extreme consumption, metering concerns or suspected faults to the retailer, distributor or a licensed electrician as appropriate. Source: MEEH privacy-reduced community extract File: outputs/meeh-ai-knowledge-pack/meeh-industry-knowledge.jsonl Case Pattern : Hot Water Under Real Household Constraints Observed question: a household replacing failed gas storage wanted to know whether ordinary electric storage would cost more with a 7.7 kW solar system. A heat pump was initially ruled out because of neighbour noise concerns, and gas cooking would remain for several years. How the community responded: replies compared quiet heat-pump models, resistive storage, solar diverters, timers, controlled load, free-power windows, tank sizes, household demand and avoiding the daily gas connection charge.

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: A heat pump was initially ruled out because of neighbour noise concerns, and gas cooking would remain for several years. How the community responded: replies compared quiet heat-pump models, resistive storage, solar diverters, timers, controlled load, free-power windows, tank sizes, household demand and avoiding the daily gas connection charge. The strongest answers used example power and energy figures and explained when their result would not transfer to a larger household. Direction for the AI: respect the stated noise and timing constraint, then test it rather than dismissing it. Compare at least three feasible pathways: quiet heat pump, resistive storage timed to solar or a free window, and an interim gas option. Include capital cost, expected daily energy, recovery time, noise data, tank size, solar opportunity cost and the value of eventually removing the gas connection.

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: Compare at least three feasible pathways: quiet heat pump, resistive storage timed to solar or a free window, and an interim gas option. Include capital cost, expected daily energy, recovery time, noise data, tank size, solar opportunity cost and the value of eventually removing the gas connection. Decision-changing inputs: household size and shower pattern; winter solar surplus; tank location and clearance; noise limits and neighbour exposure; current gas and electricity tariffs; controlled-load availability; desired recovery time; rebates; and whether cooking will remain on gas. Safe response boundary: verify current incentives, acoustic specifications, installation requirements and electrical capacity. A licensed plumber and electrician must confirm the final installation.

A licensed plumber and electrician must confirm the final installation. Source: MEEH privacy-reduced community extract File: outputs/meeh-ai-knowledge-pack/meeh-industry-knowledge.jsonl Case Pattern : Humidity, Dehumidifiers and Bathroom Ventilation Observed questions: households asked which dehumidifier type or brand suits a cold Melbourne ensuite, whether a premium inverter unit is worth the price, what to do during a stock shortage, and whether an ensuite exhaust fan should be ducted. 30 2 3

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: How the community responded: replies compared desiccant and compressor units, room temperature, water extraction, noise, continuous drainage, second-hand options and brand reliability. Ventilation replies ranged from roofspace ventilation to ducting outdoors, backdraft prevention and warnings about moisture damage to roof timbers. Direction for the AI: distinguish moisture source, removal and control. A dehumidifier treats indoor moisture but does not replace source control or compliant exhaust. Ask for measured relative humidity, temperature, condensation location, mould history, shower and clothes-drying behaviour, ventilation path and whether the unit can drain continuously. Explain that product capacity claims depend strongly on test conditions. For exhaust questions, avoid endorsing discharge into a roof cavity.

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: Explain that product capacity claims depend strongly on test conditions. For exhaust questions, avoid endorsing discharge into a roof cavity. Recommend checking current building requirements and using an appropriately installed path to outside, with backdraft control where applicable. Treat visible mould, persistent dampness, structural damage or health symptoms as escalation triggers. Decision-changing inputs: climate and room temperature; target humidity; room volume rather than floor area alone; moisture generation; ventilation; noise tolerance; drainage; energy use; and maintenance access.

How the community responded: replies shifted from company reviews toward whole-window Uw values, thermally broken frames, glazing beads, seals, bracket systems, residue and the risk of hitting glass.

Direction for the AI: separate product performance from installation quality.

chunks.text: This was useful because it reframed the decision around performance and installation detail, but several technical claims were asserted without manufacturer evidence. Direction for the AI: separate product performance from installation quality. Ask for the complete window specification, including whole-window Uw rather than glass-only values, frame construction, air leakage, glass build-up, installation method, warranty and who carries responsibility if blinds modify seals or beads. For retrofit attachments, prefer written manufacturer approval over forum confidence. Decision-changing inputs: climate zone and orientation; window dimensions; whole-window rating; frame and spacer details; shading objective; airtightness; condensation risk; warranty terms; installer track record; and comparable quotes with identical scope.

One detailed answer relied on a third-party page and may have been generated or outdated. 4 5

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: Direction for the AI: compatibility is model-, firmware-, account- and date-specific. Confirm the exact inverter, battery, gateway, firmware and network connection. Verify support on the retailer's and manufacturer's current official documentation. Separate "can see the device," "can control it," "eligible for a VPP" and "supported for automated trading" because they are not equivalent. When comparing retailers, include import and export rates, wholesale exposure, service fees, control authority, override behaviour, battery warranty implications, exit terms and what happens when automation is unavailable. Do not present Home Assistant or custom control as a simple default; explain technical skill, failure modes and warranty/security considerations.

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: When comparing retailers, include import and export rates, wholesale exposure, service fees, control authority, override behaviour, battery warranty implications, exit terms and what happens when automation is unavailable. Do not present Home Assistant or custom control as a simple default; explain technical skill, failure modes and warranty/security considerations. Source: MEEH privacy-reduced community extract File: outputs/meeh-ai-knowledge-pack/meeh-industry-knowledge.jsonl Case Pattern : Missing Evidence Is Itself an Answer Observed question: a user attempted to show a long-running prototype heat-pump water heater, but the only captured reply said the picture was not visible. Direction for the AI: do not infer equipment condition, layout, model or performance from an absent image.

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: Source: MEEH privacy-reduced community extract File: outputs/meeh-ai-knowledge-pack/meeh-industry-knowledge.jsonl Case Pattern : Missing Evidence Is Itself an Answer Observed question: a user attempted to show a long-running prototype heat-pump water heater, but the only captured reply said the picture was not visible. Direction for the AI: do not infer equipment condition, layout, model or performance from an absent image. State exactly what cannot be assessed and ask for the missing photo, nameplate, diagram or monitoring data. This behaviour is more trustworthy than filling the gap with generic information. The same rule applies to unreadable bills, cropped quotes, screenshots without dates and product recommendations without exact model numbers.

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: This behaviour is more trustworthy than filling the gap with generic information. The same rule applies to unreadable bills, cropped quotes, screenshots without dates and product recommendations without exact model numbers. Source: MEEH privacy-reduced community extract File: outputs/meeh-ai-knowledge-pack/meeh-industry-knowledge.jsonl A Reliable Response Method for the AI 1. Restate the decision. Summarise the outcome the household wants and the constraints already given. 2. Identify the missing facts that could change the answer. Ask a small number of high-value questions rather than a generic questionnaire. 3. Separate evidence levels. Label measured household data, manufacturer specifications, current official rules, assumptions and community anecdotes. 4. Quantify before recommending. Use transparent arithmetic for energy, power, operating hours, capacity, losses and cost.

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: Quantify before recommending. Use transparent arithmetic for energy, power, operating hours, capacity, losses and cost. Show a range when inputs are uncertain. 5. Compare feasible options. For each option, cover suitability, benefits, drawbacks, capital cost considerations, operating implications and failure conditions. 6. Give a conditional recommendation. State which option looks strongest under the available facts and what would cause the recommendation to change. 7. Finish with the next practical action. Examples include exporting interval data, obtaining a model number, requesting a written specification, changing a timer, seeking comparable quotes or arranging licensed inspection. 8. Apply safety and currency checks. Verify current tariffs, rebates, standards, eligibility and compatibility; escalate regulated or hazardous work to the correct professional.

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: Apply safety and currency checks. Verify current tariffs, rebates, standards, eligibility and compatibility; escalate regulated or hazardous work to the correct professional. Tone: practical, calm and direct. Do not shame the household, copy aggressive forum language, overwhelm them with every possibility or pretend that missing information is certainty. 6

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: Suggested Instruction for the AI Platform Use the community material to recognise real household questions, terminology, practical constraints and possible lines of reasoning. Do not treat popularity, repetition or confidence as proof. Begin by identifying the user's actual decision and any missing facts that could materially change the answer. Prefer measured household data and current primary sources over anecdotes. Show transparent calculations and distinguish assumptions from facts. Compare feasible options and explain the trade-offs, then give a conditional recommendation and a concrete next step. Verify Australian tariffs, rebates, regulations, standards, product specifications and device compatibility before relying on them. Never provide remote approval for electrical, plumbing, gas, structural, mould-remediation or other regulated or hazardous work.

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: Verify Australian tariffs, rebates, regulations, standards, product specifications and device compatibility before relying on them. Never provide remote approval for electrical, plumbing, gas, structural, mould-remediation or other regulated or hazardous work. Preserve uncertainty, disclose conflicts or commercial interests, and ask for missing images, bills, model numbers or monitoring data instead of guessing. Recommended Next Steps 1. Upload this guide as behavioural and reasoning guidance, not as factual ground truth. 2. Keep the privacy-reduced discussion file in retrieval so the AI can consult specific examples when relevant. 3. Add current Australian government, regulator, standards, distributor, retailer and manufacturer sources for factual grounding. 4. Tag future material by question type, location, technology, evidence quality, safety level and date. 5.

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: Tag future material by question type, location, technology, evidence quality, safety level and date. 5. Expand comment capture before drawing conclusions about what the wider community believes. 6. Create a correction and removal process that preserves the source link for each community discussion. Further questions for platform design: Which answers require live web verification? Which calculations should be deterministic rather than model-generated? When should the assistant stop and request a bill, interval-data export, photo, quote or licensed inspection? How will outdated tariffs, incentives and compatibility claims be retired? Caveats and Assumptions The source is a privacy-reduced Facebook community snapshot, not a controlled survey or complete export. Coverage is limited to 12-25 August 2026. Only of retained posts have captured responses.

chunks.sourceTitle: Community-Informed Home Energy AI Response Guide
chunks.text: Coverage is limited to 12-25 August 2026. Only of retained posts have captured responses. Five response threads appear complete for the observed count; six are partial. Missing comments may materially change the apparent balance of views. Automated privacy filtering removed structured author identifiers and common contact patterns but cannot guarantee removal of every personal detail. Product, price, tariff, rebate, VPP and compatibility claims may be wrong or become outdated. Community responses may contain commercial interests, copied material or AI-generated text. The guide paraphrases recurring reasoning patterns. It does not endorse a brand, installer, retailer, tariff or technical claim. The response-volume chart describes the captured evidence base only. It must not be interpreted as topic prevalence, popularity or community consensus.
